modules.title: 1. Setup and tooling
modules.description: Install Go, write and run programs, understand modules and packages, and use the go command like a professional.
modules.intro:
By the end of this module you will have a working Go setup, understand how Go code is organized into modules and packages, and know the tools you will use every day. You finish by building a small but properly structured command line tool.

**Time:** about 2 hours, plus exercises.

modules.title: 2. Language basics
modules.description: Variables, types, constants, strings, control flow, functions, defer, pointers and scope: the core of the language, including the gotchas.
modules.intro:
This module covers the core of the language. You already know what a variable or a loop is, so the focus is on **how Go does it differently**, and on the gotchas that bite developers coming from other languages.

**Time:** about 3 hours, plus exercises.

modules.title: 3. Composite types
modules.description: Arrays, slices, maps, structs, embedding and iterators: how Go groups data, and the memory behavior you need to understand to use them safely.
modules.intro:
Slices, maps and structs are the data structures you will use in almost every Go program. They look familiar, but their **memory behavior** is different from lists, dictionaries and classes in other languages. This module explains what happens underneath, so the surprising cases stop being surprising.

**Time:** about 3 to 4 hours, plus exercises and the project.

modules.title: 4. Methods, interfaces and generics
modules.description: Attach behavior to types with methods, write flexible code with implicit interfaces, and remove duplication with generics, including Go 1.27 generic methods.
modules.intro:
This module is where Go's design really shows. There are no classes and no inheritance; instead you have **methods** on any named type, **interfaces** that are satisfied implicitly, and **generics** for code that works across types. Together they replace most of what class hierarchies do in other languages, with less coupling.

**Time:** about 4 hours, plus exercises.

modules.title: 5. Errors
modules.description: Errors as values, wrapping with context, sentinel errors and error types, joining multiple errors, panic and recover, and error handling patterns from real codebases.
modules.intro:
Go has no exceptions. Functions return errors as ordinary values, and callers decide what to do with them. This module shows how to do that **well**: errors that carry useful context, that callers can inspect reliably, and that are handled in the right place.

**Time:** about 2 to 3 hours, plus exercises and the project milestone.

modules.title: 6. Concurrency fundamentals
modules.description: Goroutines, channels, select, the sync and atomic packages, the race detector and the Go memory model.
modules.intro:
Concurrency is where Go stands out, and also where the hardest bugs live. This module builds the foundations carefully: what goroutines cost, how channels synchronize, when a mutex is the better tool, how to find data races, and what the memory model actually guarantees.

**Time:** about 4 hours, plus exercises. Run every example and exercise in this module with `-race`.

modules.title: 7. Concurrency patterns and context
modules.description: context for cancellation and deadlines, worker pools, pipelines, errgroup, rate limiting, goroutine leaks and graceful shutdown, plus two projects.
modules.intro:
Module 6 gave you the primitives. This module turns them into the patterns that real Go services are made of, all built around `context.Context`, the standard way to carry cancellation and deadlines through a program.

**Time:** about 4 to 5 hours, plus exercises and two projects. Keep using `-race`.

modules.title: 8. Standard library deep dives
modules.description: io and bufio, encoding/json and json/v2, time, log/slog, files and embed, formatting, and a correct net/http client, then a mini Redis server built only on the standard library.
modules.intro:
Go's standard library is large, consistent and production quality. Many Go services use few third party packages because the standard library already covers so much. This module goes deep on the packages you will use every week.

**Time:** about 4 to 5 hours, plus exercises and the project.

modules.title: 9. Testing in depth
modules.description: Table-driven tests, helpers and golden files, testable examples, fakes, httptest, fuzzing, benchmarks with b.Loop, coverage, integration tests and testing/synctest.
modules.intro:
Testing is built into Go: `go test`, the `testing` package and a handful of conventions cover almost everything, with no framework to install. This module goes from the basics you have already used to fuzzing, benchmarks and deterministic concurrency tests.

**Time:** about 4 hours, plus exercises. One exercise turns things around: you write the tests, and the repository checks whether they catch deliberately planted bugs.

modules.title: 10. Profiling and performance
modules.description: Measure with benchmarks and benchstat, find hot spots with pprof, see scheduling with the execution tracer and flight recorder, cut allocations with escape analysis, apply PGO and sync.Pool.
modules.intro:
This module follows one rule: **measure first**. Every claim about speed in it comes from a benchmark or a profile that was actually run, on a 2-core cloud VM, and you can rerun every one of them yourself. The running example is a log analyzer that gets about 140 times faster over the course of the module, guided by data at every step.

**Time:** about 3 to 4 hours, plus the exercise.

modules.title: 11. Runtime internals
modules.description: How the Go runtime actually works: the scheduler, goroutine stacks, the garbage collector and its knobs, memory layout, interfaces, slices and maps, each shown with experiments you can run.
modules.intro:
Module 10 taught you to measure. This module explains **why** the measurements come out the way they do. You do not need any of this to write correct Go, but it is what lets you predict performance, read profiles with understanding, and configure services well, especially in containers.

Every claim in this module is backed by a small experiment in `examples/m11`. Run them: several give different answers on different Go versions, and those differences are part of the lesson.

**Time:** about 3 to 4 hours, plus the exercise.

modules.title: 12. Building HTTP services
modules.description: Production HTTP services with the standard library: ServeMux routing, middleware, JSON APIs with proper validation and errors, configuration, logs, metrics and traces, and the security settings every server needs.
modules.intro:
Part 4 is about running Go in production. It starts where most Go services start: an HTTP API. Go's standard library is enough to build one properly. Since Go 1.22 its router understands methods and path parameters, so many teams no longer need a web framework at all.

This module builds the pieces one at a time, each with tests, and then assembles them into **milestone 2 of the URL shortener**: a complete service with JSON endpoints, redirects, request IDs, access logs, Prometheus metrics, rate limiting, health checks and graceful shutdown. Module 15 deploys it to Kubernetes.

**Time:** about 5 to 6 hours, plus the exercise and project.

modules.title: 13. Working with data
modules.description: PostgreSQL from Go with database/sql and pgx, connection pools, migrations, transactions and locking, caching with Redis, and two projects: the shortener on Postgres and a job queue.
modules.intro:
Most services are, at their core, a careful layer over a database. This module covers the parts that decide whether that layer is correct under load: pools, parameters, transactions, locks, migrations and caches. It uses **PostgreSQL** and **Redis**, the most common pair in Go services, and every example runs against real servers.

The database examples live in the `examples/thirdparty` module (they need the pgx and go-redis libraries). They are skipped unless a database is available; the [setup takes two docker commands](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/examples/thirdparty#databases-module-13).

**Time:** about 5 to 6 hours, plus the exercise and projects.

modules.title: 14. CLIs and tooling
modules.description: Command-line tools in Go: subcommands with flag and Cobra, layered configuration, code generation with go generate and go tool, and reproducible, versioned releases with GoReleaser.
modules.intro:
Go is the language of command-line tools: `kubectl`, `docker`, `terraform`, `gh` and `hugo` are all Go programs. A single static binary that starts instantly, cross-compiles to every platform with one environment variable, and needs no runtime installed: that is hard to beat for tools.

This module covers what makes a CLI pleasant to use and easy to ship: a clear command structure, sensible configuration, generated code where it saves effort, and releases people can trust. It ends with **shortctl**, a client for the shortener API.

**Time:** about 3 to 4 hours, plus the exercise and project.

modules.title: 15. Go for cloud native
modules.description: Containers and Kubernetes from the Go side: small secure images, services that behave well under rolling updates, client-go, and a real operator built with controller-runtime, all run on a Kubernetes cluster.
modules.intro:
Kubernetes, Docker, containerd, Prometheus, etcd, Helm, Argo CD: the cloud native world is largely written in Go. This module covers both directions of that relationship: **running Go in Kubernetes** well, and **writing Go that drives Kubernetes**.

Everything here was run on a real cluster (k3s, Kubernetes 1.37) while the lessons were written: the images were built with the Dockerfiles shown, the manifests were applied, rolling updates were measured under load, and the operator created and deleted real short links. The output you see is from those runs.

**Time:** about 5 to 6 hours, plus the exercise and the project. You need Docker and a local cluster (kind, k3d, k3s or Docker Desktop) to follow along.

lessons.title: 1.1 Why Go, and when not to use it
lessons.description: What Go was designed for, where it shines, and the cases where another language is the better choice.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The problems Go was designed to solve
- The handful of design choices that make Go feel different from Java, Python or JavaScript
- Where Go is a strong choice, and where it honestly is not
- How Go releases and its compatibility promise work

## The idea

Go is a statically typed, compiled, garbage collected language with built-in concurrency. It was designed at Google, starting in 2007, by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson. It was open sourced in 2009 and reached version 1.0 in 2012.

The designers were frustrated by a specific set of problems in large codebases: very slow builds, complicated dependency management, languages that had grown too many features, and the difficulty of writing correct concurrent servers. Go is their answer to those problems, which is why it often feels like it is missing things on purpose.

A useful way to think about Go: **it optimizes for the team and the codebase over years, not for the individual writing clever code today.**

## What makes Go feel different

| Design choice | What it means in practice |
|---|---|
| Small language | The spec is short enough to read in an afternoon. There is usually one obvious way to write something. |
| Fast compilation | Large projects build in seconds, so the edit, build, test loop stays tight. |
| Single static binary | `go build` produces one executable with no runtime to install. Deploying is copying a file. |
| Cross-compiling built in | Build a Linux binary from a Mac with two environment variables. No extra toolchain. |
| Goroutines and channels | Concurrency is part of the language. Starting thousands of goroutines is normal. |
| Garbage collector tuned for low latency | You do not manage memory by hand, and GC pauses are typically very short. |
| Composition over inheritance | No classes, no inheritance. Structs, methods and small interfaces that are satisfied implicitly. |
| Errors are values | No exceptions. Functions return an `error`, and you handle it where it happens. |
| One formatting style | `gofmt` formats all Go code the same way. Nobody argues about braces. |
| Strong standard library | HTTP servers, JSON, crypto, testing and profiling are all in the box. |

If you come from **Java**, expect fewer abstractions and no framework that dominates everything. If you come from **Python or JavaScript**, expect a compiler that catches far more mistakes and code that runs much faster, at the cost of a bit more typing. If you come from **Rust or C++**, expect a much simpler language that gives up some control (a garbage collector, no manual memory layout tricks by default) in exchange for speed of development.

## Where Go is a strong choice

- **Cloud infrastructure and platform tooling.** Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Prometheus and etcd are all written in Go. If you work on infrastructure, you will read Go code whether you choose to or not.
- **Network services and APIs.** The standard library HTTP server is production ready, and goroutines make handling many concurrent connections straightforward.
- **Command line tools.** Single binaries that start instantly and cross-compile easily are ideal for CLIs.
- **Concurrent data processing.** Pipelines, workers and fan-out patterns are natural to express.
- **Large teams.** Simple, uniform code is easier to review and to hand over.

## Where another language may fit better

Being honest about this is part of learning a language well.

- **Hard real-time or ultra-low-latency systems.** Go's GC pauses are short, but they exist. If a few hundred microseconds of jitter is unacceptable, consider Rust, C or C++.
- **Data science and machine learning.** The Python ecosystem (NumPy, pandas, PyTorch) has no real equivalent in Go.
- **Desktop GUI applications.** Possible, but the ecosystem is thin compared to other platforms.
- **Very small embedded devices.** Standard Go binaries are several megabytes. TinyGo exists for microcontrollers, but it is a separate compiler with limitations.
- **Problems that want a rich type system.** Go has generics, but it deliberately lacks features like sum types or pattern matching. If you want to encode lots of rules in types, Rust, Scala or Haskell will feel more natural.

We will look at real examples of both sides, including a company that moved a service away from Go, in the [case studies](/case-studies/) (see [Discord](/case-studies/discord/)).

## Releases and the compatibility promise

Two facts shape how you work with Go over time:

1. **A new major release ships every six months**, in February and August. Each release is supported until two newer major releases exist, so you get about a year of security fixes per version.
2. **The Go 1 compatibility promise.** Code written for Go 1.0 should still compile and run with the latest Go 1.x release. New features are added carefully, and old code keeps working. This is why ten year old Go tutorials still mostly work, and why upgrading Go is usually uneventful.



```gopath-callout
callout-0
```



## Common mistakes

### Writing Go like your previous language

The most common problem for experienced developers is not syntax. It is importing patterns that fight the language: deep inheritance hierarchies rebuilt with embedding, getters and setters for every field, an interface for every struct "just in case", or exceptions simulated with `panic`. Each lesson in this course calls out these habits where they appear.

### Expecting a framework to decide everything

Many languages have one dominant framework. In Go, the standard library is the framework for a surprising amount of work. Reach for a third party library when it clearly earns its place, not by default.

## Key takeaways

- Go was designed for large codebases and teams: fast builds, simple code, easy deployment and built-in concurrency.
- It is a natural fit for infrastructure, network services and CLIs.
- It is a weaker fit for hard real-time systems, data science, GUIs and tiny embedded devices.
- New releases come every six months, and the compatibility promise means upgrades rarely break code.

## Further reading

- [Go at Google: Language Design in the Service of Software Engineering](https://go.dev/talks/2012/splash.article), Rob Pike's explanation of why Go looks the way it does
- [Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)](https://go.dev/doc/faq) on go.dev
- [Go 1 and the Future of Go Programs](https://go.dev/doc/go1compat), the compatibility promise
- [Go release history](https://go.dev/doc/devel/release)

lessons.title: 1.2 Installing Go and setting up your editor
lessons.description: Install the Go toolchain, understand GOPATH and GOROOT, set up gopls in your editor, and learn how Go manages toolchain versions.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to install Go on macOS, Linux and Windows
- What `GOROOT`, `GOPATH`, `GOBIN` and the module cache are
- How to set up your editor with `gopls`, the official language server
- How the `go` command can switch toolchain versions for you

## Install Go

Always download from the official page: [go.dev/dl](https://go.dev/dl/). It lists the current stable release for every platform.





### macOS


Download the `.pkg` installer from go.dev/dl and run it. It installs Go into `/usr/local/go` and adds `/usr/local/go/bin` to your `PATH`.

If you use Homebrew, this also works:

```bash
brew install go
```




### Linux


Download the `linux-amd64` (or `linux-arm64`) archive from go.dev/dl, then replace any existing install and extract it:

```bash
# Replace go1.27.x with the exact file name you downloaded.
sudo rm -rf /usr/local/go
sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.x.linux-amd64.tar.gz
```

Add Go to your `PATH` in `~/.profile`, `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`:

```bash
export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/go/bin:$HOME/go/bin
```

Open a new terminal so the change takes effect.



```gopath-callout
callout-1
```






### Windows


Download the `.msi` installer from go.dev/dl and run it. It installs Go and updates your `PATH`. Restart any open terminals afterwards.

With winget:

```powershell
winget install GoLang.Go
```





Check that it worked:

```bash
go version
```

```text
go version go1.27.x linux/amd64
```

The exact patch version and platform will match your machine.

## Where Go keeps things

Run `go env` to see every setting the `go` command uses. These are the ones worth knowing on day one:

```bash
go env GOROOT GOPATH GOBIN GOMODCACHE
```

| Variable | What it is | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| `GOROOT` | Where the Go toolchain itself is installed. You almost never set this. | `/usr/local/go` |
| `GOPATH` | Your Go workspace. Today it mainly holds downloaded modules and installed binaries. | `$HOME/go` |
| `GOBIN` | Where `go install` puts binaries. Empty means `$GOPATH/bin`. | empty |
| `GOMODCACHE` | Downloaded module source code, shared by all your projects. | `$HOME/go/pkg/mod` |

Add `$HOME/go/bin` to your `PATH` (the Linux snippet above already does). Otherwise tools you install with `go install` will not be found.



```gopath-callout
callout-2
```



You can change settings permanently with `go env -w`, which writes to a per-user config file instead of your shell profile:

```bash
go env -w GOBIN=$HOME/bin
go env -u GOBIN   # undo, back to the default
```

## Set up your editor

All good Go editor support is built on **gopls** (pronounced "go please"), the official language server. It provides completion, go to definition, find references, rename, inline errors and formatting on save.





### VS Code


Install the official **Go** extension (published by the Go team at Google). On first use it offers to install `gopls` and other tools. Accept.

Recommended settings:

```json
{
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "[go]": {
    "editor.codeActionsOnSave": {
      "source.organizeImports": "explicit"
    }
  }
}
```




### GoLand


JetBrains GoLand works out of the box with its own analysis engine. Enable **Settings → Tools → Actions on Save → Reformat code** and **Optimize imports**.




### Neovim / others


Install `gopls` yourself and point your LSP client at it:

```bash
go install golang.org/x/tools/gopls@latest
```

Any editor with LSP support (Neovim, Helix, Zed, Emacs, Sublime) can use it.





Whatever editor you choose, make sure **format on save** is on. In Go, formatting is not a matter of taste; lesson 1.7 explains why.

## Toolchains: let `go` manage versions

Since Go 1.21, the `go` command can download and run a different Go version for you. A project's `go.mod` file says which version of Go it needs:

```text
go 1.27
```

If your installed Go is older than that, the default setting (`GOTOOLCHAIN=auto`) makes the `go` command download the required toolchain into the module cache and use it automatically. This means:

- You rarely need a version manager like `gvm` or `asdf` for Go.
- A team can upgrade Go by editing one line in `go.mod`.

You can see which toolchain is actually being used:

```bash
go version          # inside a project, shows the toolchain selected for it
go env GOTOOLCHAIN  # usually "auto"
```

To try a specific release side by side without changing your main install:

```bash
go install golang.org/dl/go1.26.0@latest
go1.26.0 download
go1.26.0 version
```

## Verify your setup

Clone this course and run the examples. If this passes, your setup is ready for the rest of the module.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy.git
cd gopath-academy
go test ./examples/...
```

```text
ok  	github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/examples/m01/buildinfo	0.004s
ok  	github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/examples/m01/greeting	0.003s
...
```

## Common mistakes

### `go: command not found` after installing

The installer or archive put Go on disk, but your shell's `PATH` does not include it yet. Open a new terminal. On Linux, check that the `export PATH=...` line is in the file your shell actually reads.

### Installed tools are "not found"

You ran `go install some/tool@latest` successfully, but typing `tool` fails. The binary is in `$(go env GOPATH)/bin` (or `GOBIN`), which is not on your `PATH`.

### Two Go versions fighting

A Homebrew install and a manual `/usr/local/go` install on the same Mac, or an old distro package on Linux, can shadow each other. Run `which -a go` to see every `go` on your `PATH` and remove the one you do not want.

### Setting `GOROOT` by hand

Setting `GOROOT` manually is almost never necessary and often breaks things after an upgrade. If you set it in your shell profile, remove it.

## Key takeaways

- Install Go from go.dev/dl and add both the Go `bin` folder and `$HOME/go/bin` to your `PATH`.
- `GOPATH` now mostly holds the module cache and installed tools. Your projects can live anywhere.
- `gopls` powers editor support everywhere. Turn on format on save.
- The `go` line in `go.mod` plus `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto` lets the `go` command fetch the right toolchain for each project.

## Further reading

- [Download and install](https://go.dev/doc/install) on go.dev
- [Managing Go installations](https://go.dev/doc/manage-install)
- [Go toolchains](https://go.dev/doc/toolchain), how `GOTOOLCHAIN` works
- [gopls documentation](https://go.dev/gopls/)

add $home/go/bin to your path (the linux snippet above already does). otherwise tools you install with go install will not be found.







you can change settings permanently with go env -w, which writes to a per-user config file instead of your shell profile:

all good go editor support is built on gopls (pronounced "go please"), the official language server. it provides completion, go to definition, find references, rename, inline errors and formatting on save.





 vs code


install the official go extension (published by the go team at google). on first use it offers to install gopls and other tools. accept.

recommended settings:






 goland


jetbrains goland works out of the box with its own analysis engine. enable settings → tools → actions on save → reformat code and optimize imports.




 neovim / others


install gopls yourself and point your lsp client at it:



any editor with lsp support (neovim, helix, zed, emacs, sublime) can use it.

- a team can upgrade go by editing one line in go.mod.

you can see which toolchain is actually being used:



to try a specific release side by side without changing your main install:



 verify your setup

clone this course and run the examples. if this passes, your setup is ready for the rest of the module.

 go: command not found after installing

the installer or archive put go on disk, but your shell's path does not include it yet. open a new terminal. on linux, check that the export path=... line is in the file your shell actually reads.

- [download and install](https://go.dev/doc/install) on go.dev

- [go toolchains](https://go.dev/doc/toolchain), how gotoolchain works
- [gopls documentation](https://go.dev/gopls/)

lessons.title: 1.3 Your first program, line by line
lessons.description: Write, run and build a Go program, understand every line of it, and learn the compiler rules that surprise newcomers.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What every line of a minimal Go program does
- The difference between `go run` and `go build`
- The strict compiler rules that catch experienced developers off guard
- How this course uses testable examples to keep code correct

## The program



```gopath-example
example-0
```



```text
Hello, Gopher!
```

Only a few lines, and each one carries a rule worth knowing.

### `package main`

Every Go file starts by declaring which package it belongs to. A package is Go's unit of code organization: a directory of `.go` files that are compiled together.

The name `main` is special. It tells the compiler to build an **executable** instead of a library. Any other package name produces a library that other code imports.

### `import "fmt"`

`fmt` is the standard library package for formatted input and output. Imports are by path: `"fmt"` for the standard library, or something like `"github.com/google/uuid"` for a third party package.

Several imports are grouped in parentheses:

```go
import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
)
```

### `func main()`

In package `main`, the function `main` is the entry point. It takes no arguments and returns nothing. Command line arguments come from `os.Args`, and you set the exit code with `os.Exit`. We use both in the checkpoint project.

### `fmt.Println("Hello, Gopher!")`

You call a function from another package as `package.Function`. `Println` is capitalized, which is how Go marks a name as **exported** (public). Lowercase names are private to their package. That one rule replaces `public` and `private` keywords entirely, and lesson 1.5 covers it in depth.

## Run it, build it

Create a new folder anywhere and try it yourself:

```bash
mkdir hello && cd hello
go mod init example.com/hello
```

Save the program as `main.go`, then:

```bash
go run .
```

`go run` compiles the program to a temporary location and runs it immediately. It is for quick iteration.

```bash
go build -o hello .
./hello
```

`go build` produces a real executable in the current folder. There is nothing else to ship: no virtual machine, no interpreter, no `node_modules`. You can copy `hello` to another machine with the same operating system and architecture and run it.



```gopath-callout
callout-3
```



## The compiler is strict, on purpose

Go refuses to compile some things that other languages only warn about. This feels annoying for a week and helpful forever after.

### Unused imports and variables are errors

```go
import "os" // error: "os" imported and not used
```

```go
x := 42 // error: declared and not used: x
```

Unused code in a large codebase is noise and often a sign of a bug. Go makes it a hard error. Your editor's "organize imports" action (from lesson 1.2) adds and removes imports for you.

When you really want to ignore a value, assign it to the blank identifier `_`:

```go
_, err := fmt.Println("hi") // ignore the byte count, keep the error
```

### The opening brace must be on the same line

```go
func main()
{ // syntax error: unexpected semicolon or newline before {
```

Go's grammar uses semicolons, but you never type them. The lexer inserts one automatically at the end of a line that ends with an identifier, a literal, `)` or `}`. A line ending in `func main()` gets a semicolon, which breaks the declaration. Keeping `{` on the same line avoids that, and `gofmt` always formats code this way.

## How this course checks its own examples

The program above is a real file in the course repository, and it is tested. Next to it is this test file:



```gopath-example
example-1
```



A function named `Example` (or `ExampleSomething`) in a `_test.go` file is a **testable example**. `go test` runs it, captures what it prints, and compares that with the `// Output:` comment. If they differ, the test fails.

```bash
go test -v ./examples/m01/hello
```

```text
=== RUN   Example
--- PASS: Example (0.00s)
PASS
ok  	github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/examples/m01/hello	0.003s
```

Every example in this course works this way, so the output shown in a lesson is exactly what the code prints. You will write your own examples and tests in Module 9.

## Common mistakes

### Running a single file

`go run main.go` works until you split your program into two files, then fails with `undefined:` errors for everything in the other file. Use `go run .`.

### Fighting unused-variable errors with dummy assignments

Writing `_ = x` everywhere to silence the compiler hides real bugs. Delete the variable, or finish the code that was supposed to use it.

### Expecting a `main` package to be importable

You cannot import a `package main` from other code. Put reusable logic in a separate package and keep `main` thin. The checkpoint project shows this pattern.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m01/greeting
```



## Key takeaways

- `package main` plus `func main()` makes an executable; every other package is a library.
- Names starting with an uppercase letter are exported. That is Go's whole visibility system.
- `go run .` for quick iteration, `go build` for a real binary.
- Unused imports and variables are compile errors, and the opening brace must stay on the same line.
- Testable examples with `// Output:` keep documentation and code in sync.

## Further reading

- [Tutorial: Get started with Go](https://go.dev/doc/tutorial/getting-started)
- [A Tour of Go](https://go.dev/tour/), great for quick practice alongside this course
- [Semicolons](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Semicolons) in the language specification
- [Testable examples in Go](https://go.dev/blog/examples) on the Go blog

lessons.title: 1.4 Go modules: go.mod, go.sum and dependencies
lessons.description: How Go modules define a project, record dependencies, pick versions and verify downloads.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What a module is, and how it relates to packages
- How to read every line of a `go.mod` file
- What `go.sum` is for, and why you commit it
- The everyday commands: `go mod init`, `go get`, `go mod tidy`
- How Go picks dependency versions, and the `/v2` rule for major versions

## The idea

A **module** is a collection of packages that are released and versioned together. A module is defined by a `go.mod` file at its root. Everything in that directory tree (except folders that contain their own `go.mod`) belongs to the module.

- **Package**: a directory of `.go` files. The unit you import.
- **Module**: a tree of packages with one `go.mod`. The unit you version and download.

Most projects are a single module. This course repository, for example, has one module at the root for examples and projects, and a separate module in `exercises/`.

## Creating a module

```bash
mkdir weather && cd weather
go mod init github.com/yourname/weather
```

```text
go: creating new go.mod: module github.com/yourname/weather
```

The argument is the **module path**. It is the prefix of every import path in your module, so a package in `weather/forecast/` is imported as `github.com/yourname/weather/forecast`.

Use the repository URL as the module path if you will publish the code. For code that will never be imported by anyone else, any name works, but a domain-like path (`example.com/weather`) avoids clashing with standard library names.

## Reading `go.mod`

A real `go.mod` after adding a few dependencies:

```text
module github.com/yourname/weather

go 1.27

require (
	github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0
	golang.org/x/sync v0.10.0
)

require golang.org/x/text v0.21.0 // indirect

tool golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer
```

| Directive | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `module` | The module path. |
| `go` | The minimum Go version this module needs. Also enables language features of that version. |
| `toolchain` | (Optional) a preferred toolchain, for example `toolchain go1.27.1`. |
| `require` | Dependencies and the **minimum** version of each. |
| `// indirect` | A dependency you do not import directly; one of your dependencies needs it. |
| `tool` | (Go 1.24+) a command line tool the project uses, run with `go tool stringer`. |
| `replace` | Use a different version or a local copy of a module. Only applies in the main module. |
| `exclude` | Never use a specific version of a module. |
| `retract` | Mark versions of **your own** module as broken so users avoid them. |

The version numbers above are illustrative. Your file will show whatever versions `go get` resolves.

## Adding and updating dependencies

```bash
# Add a dependency, or change its version
go get github.com/google/uuid@v1.6.0
go get github.com/google/uuid@latest

# Update all direct and indirect dependencies to newer minor or patch versions
go get -u ./...

# Remove a dependency (or just delete the import and run tidy)
go get github.com/google/uuid@none
```

In practice, the most common workflow is simpler: add an `import` to your code, then run:

```bash
go mod tidy
```

`go mod tidy` adds missing requirements, removes unused ones, and updates `go.sum`. Run it before every commit that touches imports.

### Tools as dependencies

Go 1.24 added the `tool` directive, so developer tools are versioned in `go.mod` like any other dependency:

```bash
go get -tool golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer
go tool stringer -type=Color
```

Everyone on the team, and CI, runs exactly the same version of the tool.

## `go.sum`: verifying downloads

`go.sum` contains cryptographic hashes of every module version your build uses:

```text
github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0 h1:<hash of the module's files>
github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0/go.mod h1:<hash of its go.mod file>
```

Each module version usually has two lines: one hash for the full source tree, and one for just its `go.mod` (which is all Go needs when it only has to read the dependency's requirements).

When the `go` command downloads a module, it checks the hash against `go.sum`. If someone tampered with the code, or a tag was moved, the build fails.

- **Commit `go.sum`** alongside `go.mod`.
- **Never edit it by hand.** `go mod tidy` maintains it.
- Merge conflicts in `go.sum` are resolved by taking both sides and running `go mod tidy`.

## Where modules come from

By default the `go` command downloads modules through the public Go module proxy and verifies them against the public checksum database:

```bash
go env GOPROXY GOSUMDB
```

```text
https://proxy.golang.org,direct
sum.golang.org
```

For private code (your company's repositories), tell Go not to use the public proxy or checksum database for those paths:

```bash
go env -w GOPRIVATE=github.com/yourcompany/*
```

## How versions are chosen

Go modules use **semantic versioning**: `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. A minor or patch release must stay backwards compatible. A new major version may break things.

Go then picks versions with **minimal version selection (MVS)**. For each dependency, it uses the **highest of the minimum versions** that anything in your build asks for. It never silently picks a newer version just because one exists.

For example, if your module requires `lib v1.2.0` and one of your dependencies requires `lib v1.4.0`, the build uses `v1.4.0`. Even if `v1.9.0` is available, it is not used until someone asks for it.

This makes builds **reproducible** without a separate lock file: the `go.mod` files themselves determine the result.

To see what was selected:

```bash
go list -m all                      # every module in the build, with versions
go mod why golang.org/x/text        # why a module is needed
go mod graph                        # the full requirement graph
```

### The major version rule

Starting at v2, the major version is **part of the module path**:

```go
import "github.com/some/lib/v2"
```

`github.com/some/lib` (v0 and v1) and `github.com/some/lib/v2` are, as far as Go is concerned, different modules. You can even use both in the same build during a migration. If you publish a v2 of your own module, the `module` line in its `go.mod` must end with `/v2`.

## Working on two modules at once

Sometimes you need to change a library and the app that uses it at the same time.

**Option 1: workspaces** (recommended for local development):

```bash
go work init ./app ./lib
```

This creates a `go.work` file that makes the `go` command use your local `lib` when building `app`. It is usually not committed.

**Option 2: `replace`** in `go.mod`:

```text
replace github.com/yourname/lib => ../lib
```

`replace` is simple, but it is easy to commit by accident and breaks builds for everyone else. Prefer workspaces.

## Common mistakes

### Forgetting `go mod tidy`

Code compiles on your machine, but CI fails with `missing go.sum entry` or `no required module provides package`. Run `go mod tidy` and commit both files.

### Expecting `replace` to apply to users of your library

`replace` and `exclude` only take effect in the **main module**, the one you run `go build` in. If you publish a library with a `replace` in its `go.mod`, the people who import it will not get your replacement.

### Publishing v2 without changing the module path

Tagging `v2.0.0` while `go.mod` still says `module github.com/you/lib` does not work as expected. The module path must become `github.com/you/lib/v2`, and importers update their imports.

### Choosing a module path that cannot be fetched

If your module path is `github.com/you/project` but the repository lives somewhere else, others cannot `go get` it. Match the module path to where the code is actually hosted.

## Key takeaways

- A module is a versioned tree of packages, defined by `go.mod`.
- `go.mod` lists minimum versions; `go.sum` locks hashes. Commit both, never hand-edit `go.sum`.
- `go mod tidy` is the command you run most.
- Minimal version selection makes builds reproducible without a lock file.
- Major versions 2 and above are part of the import path.

## Further reading

- [Go Modules Reference](https://go.dev/ref/mod), the complete specification
- [Tutorial: Create a Go module](https://go.dev/doc/tutorial/create-module)
- [Minimal version selection](https://research.swtch.com/vgo-mvs) by Russ Cox
- [Go modules: v2 and beyond](https://go.dev/blog/v2-go-modules) on the Go blog
- [Get familiar with workspaces](https://go.dev/blog/get-familiar-with-workspaces)

lessons.title: 1.5 Packages, visibility and project layout
lessons.description: How Go packages work, how exported names replace public and private, how to name packages, and how to lay out a project without over-engineering it.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What a package is, and how import paths map to directories
- How Go decides what is visible outside a package
- The special `internal/` and `cmd/` folders
- How to name packages well
- A sensible project layout, and what not to copy from other languages

## The idea

A **package** is a directory of `.go` files that all start with the same `package` clause. The files are compiled together and can freely use each other's names, even unexported ones. One directory, one package.

A package's **import path** is the module path plus the directory:

| Module path | Directory | Import path |
|---|---|---|
| `github.com/you/shop` | `cart/` | `github.com/you/shop/cart` |
| `github.com/you/shop` | `internal/db/` | `github.com/you/shop/internal/db` |

## Visibility: the capital letter rule

Go has no `public`, `private` or `protected` keywords. Visibility is decided by the **first letter of the name**:

- Starts with an uppercase letter: **exported**, usable from other packages.
- Anything else: **unexported**, visible only inside the same package.

This applies to everything: functions, types, struct fields, methods, constants and variables.



```gopath-example
example-2
```



From another package, `greeting.Hello` and `greeting.DefaultName` are available, and `greeting.normalize` does not exist. The test below lives in the external test package `greeting_test`, so it sees the package exactly as a user would:



```gopath-example
example-3
```



A test file with the **same** package name sits "inside" the package and can test unexported helpers directly:



```gopath-example
example-4
```



Visibility is per **package**, not per file or per type. Two files in the same package see each other's unexported names, and there is no way to hide a field from other code in the same package. This pushes you toward small, focused packages.

## Package names

The package name is what callers type, so it shapes how your API reads: `greeting.Hello("Ana")`.

Good package names are:

- **Short, lowercase, one word**: `http`, `json`, `cart`, `auth`. No underscores, no `mixedCaps`.
- **The last element of the import path**: the package in `.../internal/ratelimit` should be `package ratelimit`.
- **About what it provides**, not what it contains: `user` instead of `models`, `httputil` instead of `helpers`.

Avoid **stutter**. Because callers always write the package name, repeating it in identifiers is redundant:

| Stutters | Reads well |
|---|---|
| `user.UserService` | `user.Service` |
| `cart.NewCart()` | `cart.New()` |
| `config.ConfigLoad()` | `config.Load()` |

Avoid grab-bag names like `util`, `common`, `misc` and `base`. They give no hint about their contents and tend to collect unrelated code until everything depends on them.

## Special folders

### `internal/`

A package under a directory named `internal` can only be imported by code rooted at the parent of that `internal` directory. The compiler enforces this.

```text
github.com/you/shop/internal/db      importable by anything under github.com/you/shop/
                                      NOT importable by any other module
```

Use `internal/` for everything you do not intend to support as public API. You can then change it freely without breaking anyone.

### `cmd/`

By convention, each executable lives in its own folder under `cmd/`, named after the binary:

```text
cmd/greet/main.go    ->  go build ./cmd/greet  produces "greet"
cmd/greetd/main.go   ->  go build ./cmd/greetd produces "greetd"
```

Keep `main` packages thin: parse flags, wire things together, call into `internal/` packages that hold the real logic.

### `testdata/`

The `go` tool ignores directories named `testdata`. Put fixture files for tests there.

## A sensible layout

This is the layout of the checkpoint project you will build at the end of this module:



  
- 📁 projects/greet

    
- 📁 cmd

      
- 📁 greet

        
- 📄 main.go

        
- 📄 main_test.go

      

    

    
- 📁 internal

      
- 📁 greeter

        
- 📄 greeter.go

        
- 📄 greeter_test.go

      

      
- 📁 version

        
- 📄 version.go

        
- 📄 version_test.go

      

    

    
- 📄 Makefile

    
- 📄 README.md

  




And the right amount of structure depends on size:

- **A small tool or library**: everything in the root package. One folder, a few files. That is fine and common.
- **An app with one binary**: `main.go` at the root or in `cmd/name/`, logic in a few packages under `internal/`.
- **Several binaries**: one folder per binary in `cmd/`, shared code in `internal/`.

Start flat and add packages when a clear boundary appears. Splitting too early creates import cycles and packages that only exist to hold one type.



```gopath-callout
callout-4
```



## Initialization order, briefly

When a program starts, Go initializes packages from the bottom of the import graph upward: a package is fully initialized before any package that imports it.

Within a package, package-level variables are initialized first (in dependency order), then any `init()` functions run in the order they appear. Only then does `main()` start.

```go
var startedAt = time.Now()

func init() {
	// runs once, before main, after startedAt is set
}
```

Use `init()` sparingly. Hidden work at import time makes code harder to test and reason about. Prefer explicit setup functions that `main` calls.

## Common mistakes

### Import cycles

Package `a` imports `b`, and `b` imports `a`. Go forbids this and fails with `import cycle not allowed`. The fix is almost always a better boundary: move the shared piece into a third package, or have one side depend on a small interface instead of the concrete package.

### One package per type, Java style

Creating `models/user`, `models/order`, `services/user`, `services/order` and so on spreads one concept across many packages and makes cycles likely. In Go, group by what code is **about** (`user`, `order`), and keep related types together.

### Exporting everything

Uppercase names are a promise to callers. Export only what users of the package need. You can always export something later; un-exporting breaks code.

### A package name that does not match its folder

Legal, but confusing: readers see `import ".../storage"` and then `db.Open()`. Keep them identical.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m01/tempconv
```



## Key takeaways

- One directory is one package; the import path is the module path plus the directory.
- Uppercase first letter means exported. Visibility is per package.
- Name packages with short, lowercase nouns and avoid stutter and grab-bag names.
- `internal/` hides packages from other modules; `cmd/` holds one folder per binary.
- Start with a flat layout and add packages only when a real boundary appears.

## Further reading

- [Organizing a Go module](https://go.dev/doc/modules/layout), the official layout guide
- [Package names](https://go.dev/blog/package-names) on the Go blog
- [Effective Go: Names](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#names)
- [Package initialization](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Package_initialization) in the spec

lessons.title: 1.6 The go command toolbox
lessons.description: The go subcommands you use every day, cross-compiling for other platforms, build constraints, and stamping version information into binaries.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The `go` subcommands you will use daily, and what each is for
- How to cross-compile for another OS and CPU with two environment variables
- How build constraints select files per platform
- How to stamp a version into a binary with `-ldflags`, and how to read build info back

## The idea

Go ships one tool, `go`, that builds, tests, formats, documents, downloads dependencies and more. There is no separate build system to learn for most projects. Run `go help` to see everything; this lesson covers what matters in practice.

## Everyday commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `go run .` | Compile and run the package in the current directory. |
| `go build ./...` | Compile every package in the module. Libraries are compiled and discarded; this is a quick "does it all build?" check. |
| `go build -o bin/app ./cmd/app` | Build one binary to a chosen path. |
| `go test ./...` | Run all tests. Covered fully in Module 9. |
| `go install ./cmd/app` | Build and copy the binary to `$GOBIN` (or `$GOPATH/bin`). |
| `go install example.com/tool@v1.4.0` | Install a tool at a specific version, outside of any project. |
| `go vet ./...` | Report suspicious code. See lesson 1.7. |
| `go fmt ./...` | Format code (runs `gofmt -l -w` on the packages). |
| `go doc strings.TrimSpace` | Show documentation in the terminal. |
| `go env` | Show or change Go settings. |
| `go list ./...` | List packages. With `-json` or `-f`, a powerful query tool for scripts. |
| `go mod tidy` | Sync `go.mod` and `go.sum` with your imports (lesson 1.4). |
| `go clean -cache -testcache` | Clear the build and test caches when something seems stale. |

The pattern `./...` means "this directory and everything below it". It shows up everywhere.

Go caches build results aggressively. A second `go build` or `go test` with no changes is almost instant, and `go test` prints `(cached)` when it reuses a previous result.

## Useful build flags

| Flag | Use |
|---|---|
| `-o path` | Output file or directory. |
| `-v` | Print package names as they are compiled. |
| `-race` | Enable the race detector (Module 6). |
| `-trimpath` | Remove local file system paths from the binary. Use it for release builds. |
| `-ldflags "..."` | Pass flags to the linker; used for version stamping below. |
| `-tags a,b` | Enable build tags (see build constraints). |

## Cross-compiling

To build for another platform, set `GOOS` (operating system) and `GOARCH` (CPU architecture):



```gopath-example
example-5
```



```bash
GOOS=linux   GOARCH=amd64 go build -o dist/platform-linux-amd64 ./examples/m01/platform
GOOS=linux   GOARCH=arm64 go build -o dist/platform-linux-arm64 ./examples/m01/platform
GOOS=darwin  GOARCH=arm64 go build -o dist/platform-darwin-arm64 ./examples/m01/platform
GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build -o dist/platform-windows-amd64.exe ./examples/m01/platform
```

No extra toolchains, no Docker. Run `go tool dist list` to see every supported combination.

### CGO and static binaries

Some packages can use C code through **cgo**. When cgo is involved, cross-compiling needs a C cross-compiler, and binaries may depend on the system C library. For most services and CLIs you want a pure Go, fully static binary:

```bash
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -o app ./cmd/app
```

A static binary like this runs in a minimal container image with nothing else inside. We use exactly this in Module 15 and for the server that hosts this site.

## Build constraints: per-platform files

Sometimes code must differ per platform. Go selects files at build time in two ways.

**File name suffixes**: `paths_windows.go` is only compiled for Windows, `paths_linux.go` only for Linux, `cpu_arm64.go` only for arm64. The pattern is `name_GOOS.go`, `name_GOARCH.go` or `name_GOOS_GOARCH.go`.

**`//go:build` lines** at the top of a file, before `package`:

```go
//go:build linux || darwin

package paths
```

Constraints support `&&`, `||`, `!` and parentheses, and can use custom tags enabled with `-tags`. This course uses that for exercises: solutions start with `//go:build solution`, so they are only compiled when you run `go test -tags solution`.

## Stamping a version into the binary

A binary should be able to tell you what it is. The linker flag `-X` sets the value of a **package-level string variable** at build time:



```gopath-example
example-6
```



```bash
go build -ldflags "-X main.version=1.2.0 -X main.commit=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" \
  -o buildinfo ./examples/m01/buildinfo
./buildinfo
```

```text
version=1.2.0 commit=3f9c2ab
module version: (devel)
```

The second line depends on how the binary was built: `(devel)` outside a git checkout, a version or pseudo-version derived from git inside one, or the exact tag after `go install module@version`.

Without `-ldflags`, the defaults from the source are used. The test proves it:



```gopath-example
example-7
```



For variables outside `package main`, use the full import path: `-X github.com/you/app/internal/version.Version=1.2.0`. The checkpoint project does this.

Two more linker flags you will often see in release builds: `-s -w` strip the symbol table and debug information to make the binary smaller (at the cost of less useful crash dumps and debugger support).

### Build info the toolchain records for free

Go also embeds module and build metadata in every binary. You can read it from inside the program:



```gopath-example
example-8
```



And from outside, for any Go binary on your system:

```bash
go version -m ./buildinfo
```

This prints the Go version used, the module path and version, every dependency with its version and hash, and build settings like `GOOS`, `GOARCH`, `CGO_ENABLED` and the VCS commit. It is a great way to audit what is inside a binary you did not build.

## Common mistakes

### Using `-X` on a constant

`-X` only changes string **variables**. `const version = "dev"` silently stays `"dev"`. Use `var`.

### A typo in the `-X` path

If the import path or variable name in `-X pkg.name=value` is wrong, the linker does not complain; the value just does not change. Check by running `./app -version` after every change to your build script.

### Forgetting `CGO_ENABLED=0` for containers

A binary built with cgo on a glibc system may fail to start in Alpine or distroless images with a confusing "not found" error. For containers, build with `CGO_ENABLED=0` unless you know you need cgo.

### Committing binaries

Add `bin/` and `dist/` to `.gitignore`. Binaries belong in releases, not in the repository.

## Key takeaways

- One `go` command covers building, testing, formatting, docs and dependencies.
- `./...` means "every package from here down".
- Cross-compiling is just `GOOS` and `GOARCH`. Add `CGO_ENABLED=0` for static binaries.
- Build constraints (`_linux.go` suffixes and `//go:build` lines) select files per platform or tag.
- `-ldflags "-X pkg.var=value"` stamps versions; `go version -m` reads build info from any Go binary.

## Further reading

- [Command go](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go), full reference
- [Build constraints](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Build_constraints)
- [Command link](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/link), including `-X`
- [runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/debug#ReadBuildInfo)

lessons.title: 1.7 Formatting, vetting and linting
lessons.description: gofmt, goimports, go vet, staticcheck and golangci-lint: what each catches, and how to wire them into your editor and CI.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why Go has exactly one code style, and how `gofmt` enforces it
- What `go vet` catches that the compiler does not
- When to add `staticcheck` or `golangci-lint`
- How to write doc comments that tools understand
- A minimal setup for your editor and CI

## The idea

Go treats code quality tooling as part of the language experience, not an afterthought. Three layers, from strictest to most opinionated:

1. **The compiler** rejects code that is wrong (unused variables, type errors).
2. **`gofmt` and `go vet`** ship with Go. Formatting is non-negotiable, and vet flags code that compiles but is probably a bug.
3. **Linters** like `staticcheck` and `golangci-lint` add deeper checks and style rules. You choose how many.

## `gofmt`: one style for everyone

`gofmt` rewrites Go source into the canonical format: tabs for indentation, aligned comments and struct fields, consistent spacing and brace placement. There are no options to argue about.

```bash
gofmt -l .        # list files that are not formatted
gofmt -d file.go  # show the diff it would apply
gofmt -w .        # rewrite files in place
go fmt ./...      # same as gofmt -l -w on every package
```

The result is that all Go code, in every company and every open source project, looks the same. Code review is about logic, not style, and reading unfamiliar code is easier.

### `goimports`

`goimports` does everything `gofmt` does, plus adds missing imports and removes unused ones. Most editors run it (or the equivalent `gopls` action) on save, which is why you rarely type import lines by hand.

```bash
go install golang.org/x/tools/cmd/goimports@latest
goimports -w .
```

## `go vet`: compiles, but probably wrong

`go vet` runs a set of analyzers that find suspicious code. A classic example is a `Printf` format that does not match its arguments:

```go
fmt.Printf("%d items\n", "three") // compiles fine
```

```bash
go vet ./...
```

```text
./main.go:8:2: fmt.Printf format %d has arg "three" of wrong type string
```

Other things vet catches include copying a `sync.Mutex` by value, malformed struct tags, unreachable code, invalid `errors.As` targets and suspicious shifts. The checks are chosen to have very few false positives, so treat every vet warning as a bug until proven otherwise.

`go test` runs a subset of the vet checks automatically before running tests, which is why you sometimes see vet errors from `go test`.

## `go fix`: modernizing code

Go 1.26 rewrote `go fix` as a home for **modernizers**: automated rewrites that update old patterns to newer, simpler forms (for example, replacing hand-written loops with functions from the `slices` package). It only applies changes that keep behavior the same.

```bash
go fix -diff ./...   # preview
go fix ./...         # apply
```

Run it after upgrading Go, review the diff, and commit it separately from other changes.

## Linters

### `staticcheck`

[staticcheck](https://staticcheck.dev) is the most widely used standalone linter. It finds bugs, performance problems, deprecated API usage and simplifications, with a strong focus on avoiding false positives.

```bash
go install honnef.co/go/tools/cmd/staticcheck@latest
staticcheck ./...
```

If you only add one linter, add this one.

### `golangci-lint`

[golangci-lint](https://golangci-lint.run) runs many linters (including staticcheck's checks) in one fast pass with a single config file. It is the common choice in CI for teams.

```bash
golangci-lint run ./...
```

A conservative starting config, `.golangci.yml`:

```yaml
version: "2"
linters:
  default: standard
  enable:
    - errorlint
    - misspell
    - revive
```

Start small. A config that enables every available linter produces hundreds of warnings, people learn to ignore them, and the tool stops being useful.



```gopath-callout
callout-5
```



## Doc comments

A comment directly above a declaration, with no blank line in between, is its **doc comment**. `go doc`, `gopls` hovers and [pkg.go.dev](https://pkg.go.dev) all display it.

Conventions:

- Start with the name of the thing being documented: `// Hello returns ...`.
- Write full sentences.
- Every exported name deserves a doc comment. Linters like `revive` can enforce it.
- The **package comment** goes above the `package` clause in one file, starting with `// Package name ...`.



```gopath-example
example-9
```



```bash
go doc ./examples/m01/greeting
```

```text
package greeting // import "github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/examples/m01/greeting"

Package greeting builds friendly greetings.

It exists to show how Go decides what is visible outside a package: names that
start with an uppercase letter are exported, everything else is private to the
package.

const DefaultName = "Gopher"
func Hello(name string) string
```

## A minimal quality setup

**In your editor**: format on save and organize imports on save (lesson 1.2). Most editors also show vet and staticcheck results inline through `gopls`.

**In CI**, fail the build if any of these fail:

```bash
test -z "$(gofmt -l .)"   # formatting
go vet ./...              # vet
go test ./...             # tests
staticcheck ./...         # or: golangci-lint run
```

This course's own CI does the same. You can see it in [`.github/workflows/ci.yml`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml).

## Common mistakes

### Configuring your editor to format differently

Some editors default to spaces or a different line width. Let `gofmt` (or `goimports`) be the formatter. Never fight it.

### Silencing vet instead of fixing the code

Vet warnings are rarely false positives. If vet complains about a copied mutex, the program really has two independent locks where you think there is one.

### Turning on every linter at once

Large rule sets on an existing codebase create noise that hides the warnings that matter. Begin with `staticcheck` or golangci-lint's default set, fix what it finds, and add linters one at a time.

### Doc comments that repeat the signature

`// GetUser gets the user` adds nothing. Say what callers need to know: what happens when the user does not exist, whether it is safe for concurrent use, what units a value is in.

## Key takeaways

- `gofmt` gives all Go code one style. Format on save and stop thinking about it.
- `go vet` catches real bugs that compile. Run it everywhere; `go test` runs part of it automatically.
- `go fix` applies safe modernizations after upgrades.
- Add `staticcheck` first, or `golangci-lint` with a small config, and grow from there.
- Doc comments start with the name they document and appear in `go doc`, editors and pkg.go.dev.

## Further reading

- [gofmt](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/gofmt) and [Effective Go: Formatting](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#formatting)
- [cmd/vet](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/vet), list of analyzers
- [Go Doc Comments](https://go.dev/doc/comment), the full guide to doc comment syntax
- [staticcheck documentation](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/)
- [golangci-lint configuration](https://golangci-lint.run/usage/configuration/)

lessons.title: 1.8 Checkpoint project: the greet CLI
lessons.description: Build a small, properly structured command line tool with flags, tests, version stamping and cross-compiled releases.
lessons.body:
## What you will build

A command line tool called `greet`:

```bash
greet -name Ana -times 2 -shout
```

```text
HELLO, ANA!
HELLO, ANA!
```

It is deliberately small, so you can focus on structure and tooling instead of logic. By the end you will have used everything from this module: a module, several packages, `internal/`, `cmd/`, flags, tests, `-ldflags` version stamping and cross-compiling.

The finished code is in [`projects/greet`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/projects/greet). Try building it yourself first, using the steps below, and compare afterwards.

## The plan




### Lay out the project

Use the layout from lesson 1.5: one binary in `cmd/greet`, the logic in `internal/greeter`, build metadata in `internal/version`.

### Write the logic as a plain function

The greeting logic has no idea it is part of a CLI. It takes options and returns a string, which makes it trivial to test.



```gopath-example
example-10
```



`max` is a built-in function since Go 1.21, so `max(opts.Times, 1)` clamps the value without an `if`.

### Test it with a table



```gopath-example
example-11
```



This is a **table-driven test**: a slice of cases and one loop. It is the most common testing style in Go, and Module 9 covers it in depth.

### Keep `main` thin, and testable

`main` should only connect the program to the real world. Everything else goes in a `run` function that takes its arguments and output streams as parameters and returns an exit code.



```gopath-example
example-12
```



A few details worth noticing:

- `flag.NewFlagSet(..., flag.ContinueOnError)` returns errors instead of calling `os.Exit` itself, so `run` stays in control.
- `fs.SetOutput(stderr)` sends usage and error messages to the stream we pass in, not straight to the terminal.
- Exit code `2` for bad usage and `0` for success follow Unix conventions (and match what the `flag` package does by default).

### Test the whole program

Because `run` takes plain values, testing the full CLI needs no subprocesses:



```gopath-example
example-13
```



### Stamp the version



```gopath-example
example-14
```



### Automate builds with a Makefile



```gopath-example
example-15
```



```bash
cd projects/greet
make build
./bin/greet -version
```

```text
greet v0.1.0-3-g3f9c2ab (commit 3f9c2ab, built 2026-10-16T09:27:51Z)
```

Your version, commit and date will differ. Then cross-compile for four platforms in one command:

```bash
make release
ls dist
```

```text
greet-darwin-arm64  greet-linux-amd64  greet-linux-arm64  greet-windows-amd64.exe
```




## Exercise

The project uses `internal/greeter` with a slightly different API from the one below. This exercise asks you to write the parsing half yourself, in a form that is easy to test.



```gopath-exercise
m01/cli
```



## Stretch goals

Once the tests pass, try these on your own copy of the project:

1. Add a `-lang` flag supporting `en`, `ta` and `hi` greetings. Return an error for unknown languages.
2. Read a default name from the `GREET_NAME` environment variable when `-name` is not given. Write a test for it using `t.Setenv`.
3. Install your build with `go install ./cmd/greet` and run `go version -m $(which greet)` to see the build info.

## Module 1 recap

You can now:

- Install Go, manage toolchains and set up your editor
- Create modules, add dependencies, and read `go.mod` and `go.sum`
- Organize code into packages with clear visibility and good names
- Build, cross-compile and stamp versions into binaries
- Keep code formatted, vetted and linted

Next up is **[Module 2: Language basics](/learn/02-language-basics/)**, where we go through Go's types, control flow, functions and pointers in detail.

## Further reading

- [Package flag](https://pkg.go.dev/flag)
- [Tutorial: Add a test](https://go.dev/doc/tutorial/add-a-test)
- [Organizing a Go module: commands](https://go.dev/doc/modules/layout#package-or-command-with-supporting-packages)

lessons.title: 2.1 Variables, zero values and short declarations
lessons.description: The ways to declare variables in Go, what zero values are, and the rules of the := short declaration.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The different ways to declare a variable, and when to use each
- What **zero values** are and why they matter so much in Go
- The exact rules of `:=`
- Go's naming conventions for variables

## The idea

Go is statically typed: every variable has a type fixed at compile time. But you rarely write the type yourself, because the compiler infers it from the value.

The most important idea in this lesson is the **zero value**. In Go, there is no such thing as an uninitialized variable. Every variable you declare without a value is set to the zero value of its type. No garbage memory, no `undefined`, no compiler warning about "possibly uninitialized". This one rule shapes a lot of idiomatic Go design.

## Declaring variables



```gopath-example
example-16
```



Four forms, each with a typical use:

| Form | Where | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `var x T = v` | anywhere | You want a type different from what the value would infer, e.g. `var ratio float64 = 1` |
| `var x = v` | anywhere | Package-level variables with an initial value |
| `var x T` | anywhere | You want the zero value and will fill it in later |
| `x := v` | inside functions only | The everyday choice inside functions |

Several variables can be declared together, which is common at package level:

```go
var (
	defaultPort = 8080
	verbose     bool
)
```

## Zero values



```gopath-example
example-17
```



| Type | Zero value |
|---|---|
| numbers (`int`, `float64`, ...) | `0` |
| `bool` | `false` |
| `string` | `""` (empty string) |
| pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, interfaces | `nil` |
| structs | every field set to its own zero value |
| arrays | every element set to its zero value |

### Why zero values matter

Good Go types are designed so that **the zero value is useful**. You will see this everywhere in the standard library:

- A zero `strings.Builder` or `bytes.Buffer` is an empty buffer, ready to use.
- A zero `sync.Mutex` is an unlocked mutex. No constructor needed.
- A `nil` slice behaves like an empty slice: `len` is 0, you can `range` over it and `append` to it.

When you design your own types (Module 3 and 4), aim for the same property. It removes a whole class of "forgot to initialize" bugs.



```gopath-callout
callout-6
```



## The rules of `:=`

`:=` declares **and** assigns, inferring the type. Its rules are short but strict:

1. **Only inside functions.** At package level you must use `var`.
2. **At least one new variable on the left.** Variables that already exist **in the same scope** are assigned, not redeclared.
3. **It always declares in the current scope.** Inside an `if` or `for` block that is a new, inner scope, which is the source of the shadowing bug in lesson 2.9.



```gopath-example
example-18
```



Rule 2 is what makes this common pattern work:

```go
user, err := loadUser(id)
orders, err := loadOrders(user) // orders is new, err is reused
```

## Naming

- Use **mixedCaps**: `maxRetries`, `httpClient`. Never underscores.
- Acronyms keep one case: `userID`, `parseURL`, `HTTPServer` (not `userId` or `HttpServer`).
- **Short names for short scopes.** `i` for a loop index, `r` for a reader, `err` for an error. Longer, descriptive names for package-level variables and anything used far from where it is declared.
- Remember that an uppercase first letter exports a package-level name (lesson 1.5).

## Common mistakes

### Using `:=` at package level

```go
port := 8080 // syntax error: non-declaration statement outside function body
```

Use `var port = 8080`.

### Declaring a variable and never using it

Unused local variables are compile errors (lesson 1.3). This often happens while debugging. Delete the variable instead of silencing it with `_ = x`.

### Expecting `:=` to always create new variables

`a, err := f()` followed by `b, err := g()` reuses `err`. That is fine. But the same line inside a nested block creates a **new** `err`, which is a real bug. See lesson 2.9.

### Initializing to the zero value explicitly

`var count int = 0` or `name := ""` work, but they are noise. Prefer `var count int` and `var name string`, which say "start empty" clearly.

## Key takeaways

- Use `:=` inside functions and `var` at package level or when you want a zero value.
- Every variable starts at its type's zero value. There are no uninitialized variables.
- Design types so their zero value is useful, as the standard library does.
- `:=` needs at least one new variable on the left and always declares in the current scope.
- Use mixedCaps, consistent acronyms, and name length proportional to scope.

## Further reading

- [Variable declarations](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Variable_declarations) and [Short variable declarations](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Short_variable_declarations) in the spec
- [The zero value](https://go.dev/ref/spec#The_zero_value) in the spec
- [Effective Go: Names](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#names)

lessons.title: 2.2 Basic types, numeric conversions and overflow
lessons.description: Go's built-in types, why every conversion is explicit, how integer overflow and division behave, and how to convert between strings and numbers.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The built-in types and which ones to use by default
- Why Go never converts between numeric types automatically
- How integer overflow, division and float comparison really behave
- How to convert between numbers and strings correctly

## The built-in types

| Kind | Types | Default choice |
|---|---|---|
| Boolean | `bool` | |
| Text | `string` | |
| Signed integers | `int`, `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, `int64` | `int` |
| Unsigned integers | `uint`, `uint8`, `uint16`, `uint32`, `uint64`, `uintptr` | rarely needed |
| Aliases | `byte` = `uint8`, `rune` = `int32` | `byte` for raw data, `rune` for characters |
| Floating point | `float32`, `float64` | `float64` |
| Complex | `complex64`, `complex128` | rarely needed |

A few things to know:

- **`int` and `uint` are 32 or 64 bits** depending on the platform. On every 64-bit system you are likely to deploy to, `int` is 64 bits.
- **Use `int` by default** for counts, indexes and sizes. `len()` returns an `int`, and mixing types costs you conversions everywhere.
- **Use sized types** when the size is part of a contract: file formats, network protocols, database columns, or large arrays where memory matters.
- **Avoid unsigned types for quantities** that you subtract. `uint` underflow wraps to a huge number instead of going negative (shown below).
- `byte` and `rune` are aliases, not new types. `byte` and `uint8` are completely interchangeable.

## Conversions are always explicit

Go has no implicit numeric conversion. Not even from `int32` to `int64`, and not from `int` to `float64`. You write the conversion as `T(value)`:



```gopath-example
example-19
```



This feels verbose at first. It exists because implicit conversions are a classic source of bugs in C and Java: silent precision loss, sign changes and surprising results in mixed expressions. In Go, every place a value changes type is visible in the code.

Even two types with the same underlying representation are different:

```go
var a int = 1
var b int64 = 2
fmt.Println(a + b) // invalid operation: a + b (mismatched types int and int64)
```

## Overflow wraps at run time

Integer arithmetic that exceeds the type's range **wraps around** silently at run time. There is no exception and no panic:



```gopath-example
example-20
```



Constants are different. The compiler checks constant expressions, so this fails to build:

```go
var x int8 = 128 // cannot use 128 (untyped int constant) as int8 value in variable declaration (overflows)
```

Use `math.MaxInt64`, `math.MinInt32` and friends from the `math` package when you need the limits. If overflow is a real risk (money, counters that run for years), use `int64` and check before adding, or use `math/big` for arbitrary precision.

## Division and remainder

- Integer division **truncates toward zero**: `7 / 2` is `3`, and `-7 / 2` is `-3`.
- `%` has the sign of the dividend: `-7 % 2` is `-1`.
- Dividing an integer by zero **panics** at run time (or is a compile error with constants). Dividing a float by zero gives `+Inf`, `-Inf` or `NaN`.

## Floating point

`float64` follows IEEE 754, like every mainstream language. That means the usual surprises:



```gopath-example
example-21
```



Never compare floats with `==` after arithmetic. And **never use floats for money**: store amounts as integer minor units (paise or cents) in an `int64`, or use a decimal library.

## Numbers and strings

The `strconv` package converts between numbers and their text form:



```gopath-example
example-22
```



| Task | Function |
|---|---|
| string to int | `strconv.Atoi(s)` |
| int to string | `strconv.Itoa(n)` |
| string to int64 with base and size | `strconv.ParseInt(s, 10, 64)` |
| string to float | `strconv.ParseFloat(s, 64)` |
| string to bool | `strconv.ParseBool(s)` |
| number to string with formatting | `strconv.FormatFloat`, or `fmt.Sprintf("%.2f", f)` |

Every parse function returns an error. Always check it: user input is never as clean as you hope.

## Common mistakes

### `string(n)` to convert a number to text

`string(65)` is `"A"`, not `"65"`, because converting an integer to a string interprets it as a Unicode code point. `go vet` warns about this for non-rune integer types. Use `strconv.Itoa`.

### Unsigned subtraction

```go
var stock uint = 3
stock -= 5 // 18446744073709551614, not -2
```

Use `int` for anything that can conceptually go below zero, even if you think it never will.

### Floats for money or exact comparisons

Rounding errors accumulate. Use integers of the smallest currency unit, and compare floats with a tolerance.

### Converting a large `int64` to `int32` without checking

The conversion silently keeps the low 32 bits. Check the range first when the value comes from outside your program.

## Key takeaways

- Default to `int`, `float64`, `string`, `bool`, `byte` and `rune`.
- Every numeric conversion is explicit, even between integer sizes.
- Integer overflow wraps silently at run time; constant overflow is a compile error.
- Integer division truncates toward zero; integer division by zero panics.
- Compare floats with a tolerance, keep money in integers, and use `strconv` (not `string(n)`) for text conversion.

## Further reading

- [Numeric types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Numeric_types) and [Conversions](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Conversions) in the spec
- [Arithmetic operators](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Arithmetic_operators), including integer overflow
- [Package strconv](https://pkg.go.dev/strconv)
- [Package math](https://pkg.go.dev/math) for limits and functions
