lessons.title: 2.3 Constants and iota
lessons.description: Typed and untyped constants, how iota builds enumerations and bit flags, and the traps of changing enum values.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What constants can and cannot be in Go
- The difference between **typed** and **untyped** constants, and why untyped ones are so convenient
- How `iota` creates enumerations, sizes and bit flags
- How to design enums that are safe to change

## The idea

A constant is a value fixed at compile time. In Go, constants can only be **booleans, numbers, strings or runes**. There are no constant slices, maps or structs; use a package-level `var` for those.

Go constants have a feature most languages lack: they can be **untyped**, which lets one constant work naturally with many types.

## Untyped constants

`const timeout = 5` has no fixed type. It is just "the number 5". It takes on a type only when it is used, which means it fits wherever a 5 would fit:



```gopath-example
example-23
```



Two things make untyped constants powerful:

1. **No conversions needed.** `timeout * time.Second` works even though `time.Second` is a `time.Duration`. If `timeout` were an `int` variable, you would have to write `time.Duration(timeout) * time.Second`.
2. **Arbitrary precision.** Constant arithmetic happens at compile time with at least 256 bits of precision, so `1 << 100` is fine as an intermediate value. It only has to fit when it is finally assigned to a typed variable.

A **typed** constant behaves like a value of that type everywhere:

```go
const maxUsers int = 100
var limit int64 = maxUsers // error: cannot use maxUsers (constant 100 of type int) as int64 value in variable declaration
```

Prefer untyped constants unless you specifically want to restrict how the constant is used, as with enums below.

## `iota`: enumerations

Inside a `const ( ... )` block, `iota` is a counter: `0` on the first line, `1` on the second, and so on. If a line has no expression, it **repeats the previous expression** with the new value of `iota`.



```gopath-example
example-24
```



Defining a named type (`type Weekday int`) and giving the constants that type means a function can require a `Weekday`, and the compiler stops you from passing an arbitrary unrelated value like a `Month`. Named types are covered properly in Module 3. In Module 4 you will add a `String()` method so `Wednesday` prints as `"Wednesday"` instead of `3`; the `stringer` tool from lesson 1.4 can generate it.

## `iota` in expressions

Because the expression repeats, `iota` can build sequences that are not just 0, 1, 2:



```gopath-example
example-25
```



- `_ = iota` throws away the first value, so `KB` starts at `iota == 1`.
- `1 << (10 * iota)` gives 2^10, 2^20, 2^30.
- `1 << iota` gives one bit per constant, so flags can be combined with `|` and tested with `&`.

`iota` restarts at `0` in every new `const` block.

## Designing safe enums

### Make the zero value mean "unknown"

A variable of type `Weekday` that was never set holds `0`, which is `Sunday` above. That is a silent, plausible wrong value. For most enums, reserve `0` for "not set":

```go
const (
	StatusUnknown Status = iota // the zero value
	StatusActive
	StatusSuspended
)
```

Now a missing value is visibly `StatusUnknown` instead of quietly being the first real option.

### Never reorder or insert in the middle

`iota` values depend on **position**. If the numbers are stored in a database, sent over the network or written to a file, inserting a new constant in the middle changes the meaning of every stored value after it. Always **append** new values at the end, or assign explicit numbers when values are persisted.

## Common mistakes

### Expecting constant arrays or maps

`const days = []string{"Mon", "Tue"}` does not compile. Use `var`, and if you want callers not to modify it, keep it unexported and expose a function that returns a copy.

### Inserting a new enum value in the middle

Covered above, and it is the most damaging enum mistake because nothing fails at compile time.

### Using the first enum value as a meaningful default

If the zero value is a real option, you cannot tell "chosen" from "never set". Start with an `Unknown` or `Invalid` member.

### Assuming `iota` continues across blocks

Every `const` block starts over at `0`.

## Key takeaways

- Constants are compile-time values of boolean, numeric or string kind only.
- Untyped constants adapt to the type of their context and are computed with high precision.
- `iota` counts lines in a `const` block, and an omitted expression repeats the previous one.
- Use a named type for enums, reserve the zero value for "unknown", and only append new values.

## Further reading

- [Constants](https://go.dev/blog/constants) on the Go blog, an excellent deep dive
- [Constant declarations](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Constant_declarations) and [Iota](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Iota) in the spec

lessons.title: 2.4 Strings, bytes, runes and UTF-8
lessons.description: How Go strings really work: immutable byte sequences holding UTF-8, the difference between bytes and runes, and how to build and process text efficiently.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What a Go string is under the hood
- Why `len("héllo")` is not 5
- The difference between a `byte` and a `rune`, and when each one matters
- How `range` decodes UTF-8 for you
- How to build strings efficiently and the most useful `strings` functions

## The idea

A Go string is an **immutable sequence of bytes**. By convention (and in all Go source code) those bytes are **UTF-8** encoded text, but the string type itself does not enforce that.

UTF-8 uses 1 byte for ASCII characters and 2 to 4 bytes for everything else. So there are two different ways to count a string:

- **Bytes**: what `len(s)` returns, and what `s[i]` indexes.
- **Runes**: Unicode code points, which is closer to what people mean by "characters". A `rune` is an `int32` holding one code point.

For plain English text the two counts are the same, which is why bugs here often go unnoticed until someone types `é`, `ü`, `த` or an emoji.

## Bytes vs runes



```gopath-example
example-26
```



`"héllo, 世界"` has 9 characters but takes 14 bytes: `é` is 2 bytes and each Chinese character is 3. `s[1]` returns the **first byte** of `é` (195), not the character.

Slicing (`s[i:j]`) also works on byte offsets. Cutting in the middle of a multi-byte character gives you invalid UTF-8.

## `range` decodes UTF-8

A `for ... range` loop over a string is special: it walks the string **one rune at a time**, giving you the byte offset and the decoded rune:



```gopath-example
example-27
```



Notice the offsets jump from 1 to 3, because `é` occupied bytes 1 and 2. If the string contains invalid UTF-8, `range` yields `U+FFFD` (the replacement character `�`) for each bad byte instead of failing.

Use `range` whenever you process text character by character. Use byte indexing only when you know the data is ASCII or you really want bytes (parsing a protocol, for example).

## Converting between strings, bytes and runes



```gopath-example
example-28
```



- `[]byte(s)` gives a **mutable copy** of the bytes. Use it for I/O and binary data.
- `[]rune(s)` decodes into one element per code point. Use it when you need random access by character, such as reversing text.
- `string(b)` and `string(r)` convert back, again copying.

Strings are immutable: you cannot do `s[0] = 'N'`. You build a new string instead.

## Building strings

`s += "x"` in a loop creates a new string on every iteration. For more than a handful of pieces, use `strings.Builder`, which grows one buffer:



```gopath-example
example-29
```



The zero value of `strings.Builder` is ready to use (the zero value rule from lesson 2.1 again), and `fmt.Fprintf` can write straight into it.

The functions you will reach for most often in the `strings` package:

| Need | Function |
|---|---|
| Contains, prefix, suffix | `strings.Contains`, `HasPrefix`, `HasSuffix` |
| Find position | `strings.Index`, `LastIndex` |
| Split and join | `strings.Split`, `Fields`, `Join` |
| Split once around a separator | `strings.Cut` |
| Trim | `strings.TrimSpace`, `Trim`, `TrimPrefix`, `TrimSuffix` |
| Case | `strings.ToLower`, `ToUpper`, `EqualFold` (case-insensitive compare) |
| Replace | `strings.ReplaceAll`, `strings.NewReplacer` |
| Repeat | `strings.Repeat` |

The `bytes` package has the same functions for `[]byte`, and `unicode` has rune classification such as `unicode.IsLetter` and `unicode.IsSpace`.

## Raw string literals

Backquotes create a **raw string**: no escape sequences, and it can span lines. Ideal for regular expressions, file paths on Windows, SQL and embedded templates.



```gopath-example
example-30
```



## Going deeper: runes are not always characters

A rune is a code point, and some things a person sees as one character are several code points. `é` can be written as one code point (U+00E9) or as `e` followed by a combining accent (U+0301). Many emoji, flags and family emoji are sequences of several code points. These user-perceived characters are called **grapheme clusters**.

For most programs, runes are the right level. If you are building something like a text editor or truncating user names for display, use a package that handles grapheme clusters (for example `golang.org/x/text` for normalization, or a third party segmentation library).

## Common mistakes

### Using `len` as a character count

`len` counts bytes. For characters, use `utf8.RuneCountInString(s)`. For a display width limit, think about grapheme clusters too.

### Indexing to get "the nth character"

`s[n]` is the nth **byte**. Convert to `[]rune` first, or loop with `range` and count.

### Concatenating in a loop

`result += piece` inside a loop is quadratic for large inputs. Use `strings.Builder` or `strings.Join`.

### Comparing case-insensitively with `ToLower`

`strings.ToLower(a) == strings.ToLower(b)` allocates two new strings and is not correct for every language. `strings.EqualFold(a, b)` is both faster and more correct.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m02/palindrome
```



## Key takeaways

- A string is an immutable sequence of bytes, normally UTF-8.
- `len` and indexing work in bytes; `range` and `[]rune` work in runes.
- `[]byte(s)` and `[]rune(s)` copy. Strings themselves can never be modified.
- Build strings with `strings.Builder` or `strings.Join`, not `+=` in a loop.
- Runes are code points, not always what a user sees as one character.

## Further reading

- [Strings, bytes, runes and characters in Go](https://go.dev/blog/strings) on the Go blog
- [Package strings](https://pkg.go.dev/strings), [unicode/utf8](https://pkg.go.dev/unicode/utf8) and [unicode](https://pkg.go.dev/unicode)
- [For statements with range clause](https://go.dev/ref/spec#For_range) in the spec

lessons.title: 2.5 Control flow: if, for, switch and labels
lessons.description: Go's small set of control structures: if with init statements, the one loop keyword, switch without fallthrough, and labeled break and continue.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How `if` works, including the init statement idiom
- The forms of Go's only loop, `for`, including range over integers
- How `switch` differs from C and Java
- How to break out of nested loops with labels
- The `break` inside `switch` trap

## The idea

Go has very few control structures: `if`, `for`, `switch` (plus `select` for channels in Module 6, and `goto`, which you will almost never use). There is no `while`, no `do while`, no ternary `?:` operator, and no `foreach` keyword. Each of the few that exist is flexible enough to cover those cases.

Two syntax rules apply to all of them:

- **No parentheses** around conditions: `if x > 0 {`, not `if (x > 0) {`.
- **Braces are mandatory**, even for one-line bodies. There is no `if x > 0 return`.

## `if`, with an init statement

`if` can start with a short statement, separated by a semicolon. Variables declared there are scoped to the `if` and all its `else` branches:



```gopath-example
example-31
```



You will see this pattern constantly with errors:

```go
if err := save(user); err != nil {
	return err
}
```

`err` exists only where it is needed, which keeps the surrounding function free of stale variables.

### No ternary operator

Go deliberately has no `cond ? a : b`. Write it out:

```go
label := "off"
if enabled {
	label = "on"
}
```

It is two extra lines, and nested ternaries are impossible.

## `for`: the only loop



```gopath-example
example-32
```



| Form | Equivalent in other languages |
|---|---|
| `for i := 0; i < n; i++ { }` | C-style `for` |
| `for cond { }` | `while (cond)` |
| `for { }` | `while (true)` |
| `for i := range n { }` | `for i in range(n)` (Go 1.22+) |
| `for i, v := range slice { }` | `foreach` / `enumerate` |
| `for k, v := range m { }` | iterate a map (lesson 3.5) |
| `for r := range ch { }` | read a channel until closed (Module 6) |

With `range`, drop what you do not need: `for i := range s` for indexes only, `for _, v := range s` for values only.

Two details about `range`:

- The value is a **copy** of the element. Assigning to `v` does not change the slice. Use the index (`s[i] = ...`) to modify elements.
- **Map iteration order is random** and changes between runs on purpose. Never rely on it.

Since Go 1.22, each loop iteration gets **fresh** loop variables. This fixed a famous bug with closures and goroutines capturing the loop variable, which you will see in lesson 2.6. Old blog posts that warn about it describe behavior before Go 1.22.

## `switch`



```gopath-example
example-33
```



Differences from C, Java and JavaScript:

- **No automatic fallthrough.** Each case ends on its own, so no `break` is needed.
- **A case can list several values**: `case 200, 201, 204:`.
- **Cases do not have to be constants.** They can be any expression, evaluated top to bottom.
- **A switch with no expression** is a clean replacement for long `if / else if` chains, as in `grade` above.
- Like `if`, a `switch` can have an init statement: `switch n := compute(); n { ... }`.

If you really want to continue into the next case, say so with `fallthrough`. It is rare:



```gopath-example
example-34
```



`fallthrough` runs the next case's body **without** checking its condition. There is also a **type switch** for checking the dynamic type of an interface value, covered in lesson 4.3.

## Labels: breaking out of nested loops

`break` and `continue` apply to the innermost loop. To affect an outer loop, put a **label** on it:



```gopath-example
example-35
```



`continue outer` works the same way, skipping to the next iteration of the labeled loop.

## The `break` inside `switch` trap

Inside a `switch` (or `select`), a plain `break` exits the **switch**, not the surrounding loop. This surprises almost everyone once:



```gopath-example
example-36
```



When you need to leave a loop from inside a `switch` or `select`, use a labeled `break`. You will need this often with `select` in concurrent code.

## Common mistakes

### Modifying the range value instead of the element

```go
for _, p := range players {
	p.Score = 0 // changes a copy; players is untouched
}
```

Use `for i := range players { players[i].Score = 0 }`.

### Relying on map iteration order

Tests that pass locally and fail in CI often do so because of map order. Sort the keys first (`slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))`, lesson 3.4) when order matters.

### Plain `break` inside `switch` or `select` in a loop

It only leaves the switch. Use a label.

### Adding `break` at the end of every case

Harmless but noisy, and a sign of C or Java habits. Go cases end on their own.

## Key takeaways

- No parentheses, mandatory braces, no ternary operator.
- `if` and `switch` can take an init statement that scopes variables tightly.
- `for` is the only loop and covers C-style, while, infinite and range loops, including `range n` since Go 1.22.
- `switch` cases do not fall through, can list several values, and a bare `switch` replaces `if / else if` chains.
- Use labels to `break` or `continue` an outer loop, especially from inside `switch` or `select`.

## Further reading

- [Effective Go: Control structures](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#control-structures)
- [For statements](https://go.dev/ref/spec#For_statements) and [Switch statements](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Switch_statements) in the spec
- [Fixing for loops in Go 1.22](https://go.dev/blog/loopvar-preview) on the Go blog
- [Range over integers](https://go.dev/doc/go1.22#language) in the Go 1.22 release notes

lessons.title: 2.6 Functions: multiple returns, variadics and closures
lessons.description: Declaring functions, returning several values, named results, variadic parameters, functions as values, and closures.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How Go functions are declared, and why there is no overloading or default arguments
- Multiple return values and the `(value, error)` convention
- Named results, and when bare `return` is a good or bad idea
- Variadic functions and spreading a slice into them
- Functions as values, and closures that capture variables

## Declaring functions

```go
func add(a int, b int) int { return a + b }
func add2(a, b int) int    { return a + b } // same type: group the names
```

The type comes **after** the name, for parameters and results alike. Go reads left to right: "add takes a and b, both int, and returns an int".

What Go deliberately leaves out:

- **No overloading.** Two functions cannot share a name with different parameters. Use different names: `strings.Split` and `strings.SplitN`.
- **No default parameter values.** Pass the value explicitly, or for many optional settings use an options struct (lesson 4.8 and Module 12).
- **No keyword arguments.** Struct literals with field names (`Config{Port: 8080}`) fill that role.

These omissions keep every call site unambiguous: you can read a call and know exactly which function runs with which values.

## Multiple return values

A function can return several values. The most common use is a result plus an error:



```gopath-example
example-37
```



The convention is strong and you should follow it:

- The `error` is always the **last** result.
- When `err != nil`, the other results are usually zero values and should not be used.
- Check the error immediately after the call.

Other common pairs are `(value, ok bool)` for "found or not" (you will see it with maps and type assertions) and `(value, error)` for anything that can fail. Error handling gets a whole module (Module 5).

## Named results

Results can have names. They are declared at the top of the function, start at their zero values, and a bare `return` returns their current values:



```gopath-example
example-38
```



Named results are useful for two things:

1. **Documentation.** `func split(full string) (first, last string)` tells the reader what each string means.
2. **Changing results from a `defer`**, covered in lesson 2.7.

Bare `return` in a **short** function is fine. In a long function it hides what is being returned. A good rule: name results when it helps documentation, but write `return first, last` explicitly unless the function fits on one screen.

## Variadic functions

A final parameter of type `...T` accepts any number of `T` arguments. Inside the function it is a slice `[]T`:



```gopath-example
example-39
```



To pass an existing slice, spread it with `values...`. You have already used a variadic function many times: `fmt.Println(a ...any)`.

## Functions are values

Functions are first-class values. You can assign them to variables, pass them as arguments, return them and store them in structs or maps. A function's type is written like its signature: `func(int) int`.



```gopath-example
example-40
```



The second call uses a **function literal** (an anonymous function) written inline. This style is common for small callbacks, sorting comparisons (`slices.SortFunc`), HTTP handlers and test helpers.

The zero value of a function type is `nil`. Calling a `nil` function panics.

## Closures

A function literal can use variables from the surrounding function. It **captures the variable itself**, not a copy of its current value, and keeps it alive as long as the closure exists:



```gopath-example
example-41
```



Each call to `counter()` creates a new `count` variable, so `next` and `other` are independent. Closures are how Go does a lot of things other languages use classes or decorators for: generators, middleware, retry wrappers and lazy initialization.

### Closures in loops (fixed in Go 1.22)

Before Go 1.22, a `for` loop had **one** loop variable shared by all iterations, so closures created in the loop all saw its final value. A classic bug. Since Go 1.22, each iteration has its own variable:



```gopath-example
example-42
```



This applies to modules whose `go.mod` says `go 1.22` or later. If you maintain older code with an earlier `go` line, the old behavior still applies there until you raise it.

## Common mistakes

### Ignoring a returned error

`result, _ := strconv.Atoi(input)` throws away the only signal that `result` is garbage. Handle the error, or at least make ignoring it a deliberate, commented decision.

### Long functions with bare returns

Readers have to scroll up to find out what is being returned and whether it was set on this path. Return values explicitly.

### Simulating overloading with `...any`

`func Do(args ...any)` that inspects its arguments at run time loses all compile-time checking. Write separate, clearly named functions.

### Calling a `nil` function value

An unset callback field panics when called. Check `if f != nil` or give it a no-op default.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m02/stats
```



## Key takeaways

- Types come after names; there is no overloading, no default arguments and no keyword arguments.
- Return `(value, error)` with the error last, and check it right away.
- Name results for documentation; use bare `return` only in short functions.
- `...T` collects arguments into a `[]T`; spread a slice with `s...`.
- Functions are values, and closures capture variables. Since Go 1.22 each loop iteration has its own loop variable.

## Further reading

- [Function declarations](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Function_declarations) and [Function literals](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Function_literals) in the spec
- [Effective Go: Functions](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#functions)
- [Fixing for loops in Go 1.22](https://go.dev/blog/loopvar-preview)
- [Codewalk: First-Class Functions in Go](https://go.dev/doc/codewalk/functions/)

lessons.title: 2.7 defer, and how it is evaluated
lessons.description: How defer schedules cleanup, the exact moment its arguments are evaluated, how it interacts with named results and panics, and the traps of defer in loops.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What `defer` does and the order deferred calls run in
- Exactly **when** the arguments of a deferred call are evaluated
- The standard acquire, check, defer release pattern
- How deferred functions can change named results
- The traps: `defer` in loops, ignored `Close` errors and `os.Exit`

## The idea

`defer` schedules a function call to run **when the surrounding function returns**, however it returns: a normal `return`, falling off the end, or a panic. It is Go's answer to `try / finally`, `using` blocks and destructors.

The big benefit is locality. You write the cleanup right next to the thing being cleaned up, instead of at every return statement.

## Order: last in, first out

Deferred calls are pushed onto a stack. They run in **reverse** order:



```gopath-example
example-43
```



Reverse order is exactly what you want for cleanup: resources acquired later are released first, like closing a file before releasing the lock that protected it.

## When arguments are evaluated

This is the rule that trips people up. A deferred call's **function value and arguments are evaluated immediately**, at the `defer` statement. Only the call itself is delayed:



```gopath-example
example-44
```



If you want the deferred code to see the **latest** value, defer a closure. The closure captures the variable and reads it when it runs:



```gopath-example
example-45
```



## The standard cleanup pattern

Acquire the resource, check the error, then defer the release **immediately**:



```gopath-example
example-46
```



The order matters. If you write `defer f.Close()` **before** checking `err`, then on failure `f` is `nil` and the deferred `Close` runs on a nil file.

You will use the same shape everywhere:

```go
mu.Lock()
defer mu.Unlock()

resp, err := http.Get(url)
if err != nil {
	return err
}
defer resp.Body.Close()
```

## Changing results from a defer

A deferred **closure** can read and modify the function's **named** results, because they are ordinary variables that are still in scope. The deferred code runs after the `return` statement has set them, but before the caller sees them:



```gopath-example
example-47
```



The example uses `recover` to turn a panic into an error. Panics and `recover` are covered properly in Module 5; the point here is the mechanism: **deferred functions run even when the function panics**, and they can adjust named results.

A gentler, very common use is adding context to any error a function returns:

```go
func process(path string) (err error) {
	defer func() {
		if err != nil {
			err = fmt.Errorf("process %s: %w", path, err)
		}
	}()
	// ... many return statements, all wrapped automatically
}
```

## Cost

`defer` used to have a noticeable overhead, which led to advice to avoid it in hot paths. Since Go 1.14, most defers are compiled inline ("open-coded defers") and cost close to nothing. Use `defer` for correctness by default, and only remove one if a profile (Module 10) shows it matters.

## Common mistakes

### `defer` inside a loop

```go
for _, path := range paths {
	f, err := os.Open(path)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer f.Close() // nothing closes until the WHOLE function returns
	// ...
}
```

With thousands of files, you run out of file descriptors. Move the loop body into its own function, so each `defer` runs at the end of each iteration:

```go
for _, path := range paths {
	if err := processFile(path); err != nil { // processFile defers its own Close
		return err
	}
}
```

### Ignoring the error from `Close` on a file you wrote

For files opened for **reading**, ignoring `Close` errors is fine. For files you **wrote**, `Close` (or `Sync`) can be the moment you learn the data did not reach the disk. Return that error, for example with the named result pattern above:

```go
defer func() {
	if cerr := f.Close(); cerr != nil && err == nil {
		err = cerr
	}
}()
```

### Expecting defers to run on `os.Exit`

`os.Exit` ends the program immediately. **Deferred calls do not run**, and neither does any other cleanup. The same applies to `log.Fatal`, which calls `os.Exit`. This is one reason the checkpoint project in Module 1 kept all logic in `run()` and called `os.Exit` only in `main`.

### Deferring before the error check

`defer f.Close()` before `if err != nil` defers a call on a nil value. Always check first.

## Key takeaways

- `defer` runs a call when the surrounding function returns, including on panic.
- Deferred calls run in last in, first out order.
- Arguments are evaluated at the `defer` statement; use a closure to see later values.
- Pattern: acquire, check the error, `defer` the release on the next line.
- Deferred closures can modify named results, which is useful for wrapping errors.
- Avoid `defer` in loops, handle `Close` errors for written files, and remember that `os.Exit` skips defers.

## Further reading

- [Defer, Panic, and Recover](https://go.dev/blog/defer-panic-and-recover) on the Go blog
- [Defer statements](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Defer_statements) in the spec
- [Effective Go: Defer](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#defer)

defer used to have a noticeable overhead, which led to advice to avoid it in hot paths. since go 1.14, most defers are compiled inline ("open-coded defers") and cost close to nothing. use defer for correctness by default, and only remove one if a profile (module 10) shows it matters.

 common mistakes

 defer inside a loop



with thousands of files, you run out of file descriptors. move the loop body into its own function, so each defer runs at the end of each iteration:



 ignoring the error from close on a file you wrote

for files opened for reading, ignoring close errors is fine. for files you wrote, close (or sync) can be the moment you learn the data did not reach the disk. return that error, for example with the named result pattern above:

os.exit ends the program immediately. deferred calls do not run, and neither does any other cleanup. the same applies to log.fatal, which calls os.exit. this is one reason the checkpoint project in module 1 kept all logic in run() and called os.exit only in main.

defer f.close() before if err != nil defers a call on a nil value. always check first.

- defer runs a call when the surrounding function returns, including on panic.
- deferred calls run in last in, first out order.
- arguments are evaluated at the defer statement; use a closure to see later values.
- pattern: acquire, check the error, defer the release on the next line.
- deferred closures can modify named results, which is useful for wrapping errors.

- [defer, panic, and recover](https://go.dev/blog/defer-panic-and-recover) on the go blog
- [defer statements](https://go.dev/ref/specdeferstatements) in the spec
- [effective go: defer](https://go.dev/doc/effectivegodefer)

lessons.title: 2.8 Pointers without fear
lessons.description: What pointers are in Go, how pass-by-value works, why returning a pointer to a local variable is safe, and when you should and should not use pointers.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The two pointer operators, `&` and `*`
- Why every Go function call copies its arguments, and how pointers change that
- How pointers to structs work, including automatic dereferencing
- Why returning a pointer to a local variable is safe in Go
- Clear rules for when to use a pointer and when not to

## The idea

A pointer holds the **memory address** of a value. If you come from Java, Python or JavaScript, you already use pointers all the time; those languages just hide them behind "references". Go makes them explicit, and in exchange gives you precise control over whether a function gets a copy or shares the original.

Go pointers are much safer than C pointers:

- **No pointer arithmetic.** You cannot add to an address or walk through memory (outside the `unsafe` package).
- **Garbage collected.** Memory stays alive as long as anything points to it. No dangling pointers, no manual `free`.
- **Nil is checked.** Dereferencing `nil` panics with a clear message instead of silently corrupting memory.

## `&` and `*`

- `&x` gives the address of `x`. If `x` is an `int`, `&x` has type `*int`, read as "pointer to int".
- `*p` gives the value that `p` points to. It works for reading and for writing.



```gopath-example
example-48
```



The `*` symbol means two related things: in a **type** (`*int`) it means "pointer to", and in an **expression** (`*p`) it means "the value at".

## Go always passes by value

Every function argument is **copied** into the function. An `int` copies the number. A struct copies every field. A pointer copies the **address**, so both copies point to the same value:



```gopath-example
example-49
```



There is no pass-by-reference in Go. When you want a function to change something you own, pass a pointer to it.

## Pointers to structs

Pointers are most common with structs. Go dereferences them for you when you access fields, so you write `p.Score` instead of `(*p).Score`:



```gopath-example
example-50
```



Structs are covered in Module 3, and methods with pointer receivers (where this really pays off) in Module 4.

## Returning a pointer to a local variable is safe

In C, returning the address of a local variable is a serious bug, because the stack frame disappears. In Go it is normal and safe:



```gopath-example
example-51
```



The compiler performs **escape analysis**: if a variable's address outlives the function, the variable is allocated on the heap instead of the stack, and the garbage collector frees it when nothing points to it anymore. You never decide stack versus heap yourself. You can see the compiler's decisions with `go build -gcflags=-m`, which we explore in Module 10.

`new(T)` allocates a zero `T` and returns `*T`. In practice, `&T{...}` with a struct literal is far more common, because it lets you set fields at the same time.

## Nil pointers

The zero value of any pointer type is `nil`. Reading through a nil pointer panics:



```gopath-example
example-52
```



Guard with `if p == nil` wherever a nil pointer is a legitimate possibility, and document it. Where nil is never valid, let the panic happen; it points straight at the bug.

## When to use a pointer

Use a pointer when:

- **The function must modify the caller's value.** The most common reason.
- **The value is large** and copying it on every call would be wasteful. "Large" means many fields or big arrays, not a struct of three ints.
- **You need to express "no value".** A `*int` can be `nil`, while an `int` is always some number. This is common for optional fields in JSON or database rows.
- **The value must not be copied.** Types like `sync.Mutex` must stay in one place; pass a pointer to the struct containing them.

Do **not** reach for a pointer when:

- **The value is small and read-only**: ints, small structs, `time.Time`. Copying is cheap and avoids nil checks.
- **It is a slice, map, channel, function or interface.** These already contain internal pointers, so passing them by value is cheap, and a map passed by value can already be modified by the callee. (Slices have a subtlety around `append`, covered in lesson 3.2.)
- **Only to "be faster".** Pointers can make code slower by pushing values to the heap and adding GC work. Measure first.

## Common mistakes

### Dereferencing without a nil check where nil is possible

Values from optional JSON fields, lookups that can fail, or zero-value structs often hold `nil` pointers. Check before dereferencing, or make the API return a value and an `ok` flag instead.

### Pointers to slices and maps

`func add(m *map[string]int)` and `func f(s *[]int)` are almost never needed. Pass the map or slice directly; when a function needs to grow a slice, return the new slice (`s = append(s, x)` style).

### Taking the address of a range variable to keep it

Since Go 1.22, each iteration has its own variable, so `&v` in a loop gives a different pointer each time. That is correct, but it points to a **copy** of the element, not the element in the slice. Use `&items[i]` when you want to point into the slice.

### Using pointers everywhere "for performance"

A small struct passed by value often stays on the stack and is faster than a pointer to a heap value. Keep values by default and switch to pointers for the reasons listed above.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m02/ptr
```



## Key takeaways

- `&x` takes an address, `*p` reads or writes through it, and `*T` is a pointer type.
- Go passes everything by value. Pass a pointer when the callee must modify your value.
- Field access through a struct pointer is automatic: `p.Field`.
- Returning a pointer to a local is safe thanks to escape analysis and the garbage collector.
- Use pointers to mutate, to avoid copying large values, to represent "absent", or for types that must not be copied. Otherwise, prefer values.

## Further reading

- [Pointer types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Pointer_types) and [Address operators](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Address_operators) in the spec
- [Go FAQ: Should I define methods on values or pointers?](https://go.dev/doc/faq#methods_on_values_or_pointers)
- [Go FAQ: How do I know whether a variable is allocated on the heap or the stack?](https://go.dev/doc/faq#stack_or_heap)

lessons.title: 2.9 Scope and shadowing gotchas
lessons.description: How Go's block scopes work, how := can silently shadow variables, and the tools that catch shadowing bugs.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The levels of scope in Go, from universe to block
- What shadowing is and why `:=` makes it easy to do by accident
- The shadowed `err` bug, step by step
- How shadowing package names and built-ins causes confusing errors
- Tools that detect shadowing

## The idea

A **scope** is the region of code where a name refers to a particular declaration. Go has lexical (block) scoping, like most languages you know. The levels, from outermost to innermost:

| Scope | Contains | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Universe | Built-in names | `int`, `len`, `true`, `nil`, `error`, `make` |
| Package | Package-level declarations, across all files in the package | `var defaultPort`, `func Hello` |
| File | Imported package names | `fmt`, `strings` |
| Function | Parameters, results, local variables | `name`, `err` |
| Block | Anything declared inside `{ }`, and in `if`, `for` and `switch` init statements | `i` in `for i := ...` |

**Shadowing** happens when an inner scope declares a name that already exists in an outer scope. Inside the inner scope, the new declaration hides the outer one. Both variables exist; they are simply different variables with the same name.

## Shadowing in action



```gopath-example
example-53
```



Shadowing itself is not an error, and sometimes it is perfectly reasonable. The problem is that `:=` makes it **very easy to shadow by accident**, and the compiler stays quiet as long as both variables are used.

## The shadowed `err` bug

Almost every Go developer writes this bug once. The outer `err` is never set, because `:=` inside the `if` block declares a new `err`:



```gopath-example
example-54
```



Walk through `buggy`:

1. `var err error` declares `err` in the function scope.
2. Inside the `if` block, `data, err := load(name)` needs a new variable (`data`), so `:=` declares **both** `data` and a **new** `err` in the block scope, as lesson 2.1's rules say. The "reuse existing variables" rule only applies to variables in the **same** scope.
3. The block ends and its `err` disappears.
4. `return err` returns the outer `err`, which is still `nil`.

The fix is to use `=` for variables that already exist, and declare the others separately if needed:

```go
var data string
data, err = load(name)
```

## Shadowing package names

Imported packages live in file scope, so a local variable can hide them:

```go
func fetch(url string) error {
	u, err := url.Parse(url) // url.Parse undefined (type string has no field or method Parse)
	...
}
```

The parameter `url` shadows the `net/url` package. The compiler also reports `"net/url" imported and not used`, because inside the function nothing can reach the package anymore. Rename the variable (`rawURL`, `target`) instead of fighting the error. Common collisions: `url`, `path`, `filepath`, `time`, `errors`, `json`, `log`, `user`.

## Shadowing built-ins

Built-in names are **not keywords**. They live in the universe scope and can be shadowed:



```gopath-example
example-55
```



Variables named `len`, `cap`, `copy`, `new`, `min`, `max`, `string` or `error` compile fine and then produce baffling errors a few lines later. Avoid these names entirely. (This is why the exercise in lesson 2.6 uses `lo` and `hi` rather than `min` and `max`.)

## Tools that catch it

- **Your editor.** `gopls` can highlight shadowed variables if you enable its `shadow` analyzer.
- **The `shadow` analyzer.** It is not part of the default `go vet` set because it reports some intentional shadowing, but you can run it directly:

```bash
go install golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/shadow/cmd/shadow@latest
go vet -vettool=$(which shadow) ./...
```

- **golangci-lint** includes it through `govet` settings, and the `predeclared` linter flags shadowed built-ins.

The best prevention is a habit: inside a nested block, ask whether each `:=` is meant to create something new. If a variable already exists outside, use `=`.

## Common mistakes

### `:=` inside `if`, `for` or `switch` blocks for an outer variable

The `err` bug above. It also happens with results you meant to collect, like `total := total + n` inside a loop (that creates a new `total` each iteration).

### Naming variables after imported packages

`url`, `json`, `time`, `errors`. Pick names that describe the value instead.

### Naming variables after built-ins

`len`, `max`, `string`, `copy`. They compile, then break code further down.

### Assuming shadowing is always wrong

The `if v, ok := m[k]; ok { }` idiom and `err` inside a short `if err := f(); err != nil` are scoped declarations that do not shadow anything important. The goal is to avoid **accidental** shadowing, not to forbid nested scopes.

## Key takeaways

- Go has universe, package, file, function and block scopes.
- An inner declaration with the same name **shadows** the outer one; both variables exist.
- `:=` in a nested block always declares new variables, which causes the classic shadowed `err` bug.
- Avoid naming variables after imported packages or built-ins.
- Use the `shadow` analyzer or linters to catch accidental shadowing.

## Further reading

- [Declarations and scope](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Declarations_and_scope) in the spec
- [Blocks](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Blocks) in the spec
- [shadow analyzer](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/shadow)

lessons.title: 3.1 Arrays and why you rarely use them directly
lessons.description: Go arrays have a fixed length that is part of their type and are copied by value. Learn where that is useful and why slices are the everyday choice.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How arrays are declared and why their length is part of the type
- Why assigning or passing an array copies all of it
- The few places arrays are the right tool
- How arrays relate to slices, which you will use instead most of the time

## The idea

A Go array is a **fixed-size sequence of elements of one type**. The size is part of the type: `[3]int` and `[4]int` are different, incompatible types.

Arrays are **values**, not references. Assigning an array to another variable, or passing it to a function, copies every element. This is the opposite of arrays in Java, Python or JavaScript, where the variable is a reference to shared data.



```gopath-example
example-56
```



## Value semantics



```gopath-example
example-57
```



Copying is predictable and safe (no one else can change your copy), but for large arrays it is expensive. A function that takes a `[1_000_000]byte` copies a megabyte on every call.

Arrays whose element type is comparable can be compared with `==`, element by element.

## Where arrays are the right tool

You will rarely declare arrays in application code, but they do show up:

- **Fixed-size values with meaning**: a SHA-256 hash is `[32]byte` (`sha256.Sum256` returns exactly that), an IPv4 address fits in `[4]byte`, an RGB color in `[3]uint8`.
- **Map keys**: because arrays are comparable values, they work as keys where a slice cannot.
- **The backing store of a slice**: every slice points to an array underneath. That is the topic of the next lesson.



```gopath-example
example-58
```



## Arrays vs slices at a glance

| | Array `[N]T` | Slice `[]T` |
|---|---|---|
| Length | Fixed, part of the type | Can grow with `append` |
| Assignment and passing | Copies all elements | Copies a small header; elements are shared |
| Comparable with `==` | Yes (if elements are) | No (only to `nil`) |
| Usable as a map key | Yes | No |
| Typical use | Hashes, fixed-size buffers, keys | Almost everything else |

## Common mistakes

### Expecting a function to modify an array argument

```go
func reset(a [3]int) { a[0] = 0 } // modifies a copy
```

Pass a pointer (`*[3]int`) or, much more commonly, use a slice.

### Confusing `[]int{1, 2}` and `[2]int{1, 2}`

The first is a slice literal, the second an array literal. A missing number or `...` between the brackets is the only difference, and they behave very differently.

### Ranging over a large array by value

`for i, v := range bigArray` evaluates `bigArray` once, which copies it. Range over a slice of it instead (`bigArray[:]`) or over a pointer to it.

## Key takeaways

- An array's length is part of its type, and it never changes.
- Arrays are values: assignment and function calls copy every element.
- Use arrays for fixed-size values like hashes and for comparable map keys.
- For general lists of data, use slices.

## Further reading

- [Array types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Array_types) in the spec
- [Go Slices: usage and internals](https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro), which starts with arrays

- for general lists of data, use slices.

lessons.title: 3.2 Slices: length, capacity and the backing array
lessons.description: What a slice really is (a pointer, a length and a capacity), how slicing shares memory, how append grows, and the difference between nil and empty slices.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What a slice is under the hood: pointer, length and capacity
- How slicing an array or slice creates a **window** onto shared memory
- How `append` decides whether to reuse memory or allocate
- The difference between a `nil` slice and an empty slice
- How to use `make`, `copy` and multi-dimensional slices

## The idea

A slice is a small descriptor with three fields:

```text
slice header
+---------+-----+-----+
| pointer | len | cap |
+----|----+-----+-----+
     |
     v
backing array:  [ a | b | c | d | e | f ]
```

- **pointer**: where the slice's first element lives in an underlying array.
- **len**: how many elements the slice currently contains.
- **cap**: how many elements fit before the end of the underlying array.

When you pass a slice to a function or assign it, you copy this header (24 bytes on 64-bit systems). The elements are **not** copied. Both headers point at the same array.

## Creating slices



```gopath-example
example-59
```



- A **literal** `[]int{10, 20, 30}` creates an array and a slice over all of it.
- `make([]T, len)` creates a slice of `len` zero values.
- `make([]T, len, cap)` also reserves room to grow without reallocating. Use it when you know roughly how many elements you will add.

## Slicing shares memory

`s[low:high]` creates a new header that points into the same array. The new slice contains elements `low` up to (but not including) `high`:



```gopath-example
example-60
```



Two things to notice:

- `cap(s)` is 4, not 3. Capacity counts from the slice's start to the **end of the underlying array**, because the slice is allowed to grow into that space.
- Writing `s[0]` changed `arr[1]`. A slice is a window, not a copy.

Shortcuts: `s[:n]` is the first `n` elements, `s[n:]` drops the first `n`, and `s[:]` covers everything.

## How `append` works

`append(s, values...)` always returns a slice, and you must use the result:

1. If `len(s) + len(values) <= cap(s)`, it writes the new values into the existing backing array, right after the last element, and returns a header with a bigger length. **No allocation.**
2. Otherwise it allocates a **new, larger** array, copies the old elements over, adds the new ones and returns a header pointing to the new array.



```gopath-example
example-61
```



When it grows, Go roughly doubles the capacity for small slices and grows by a smaller factor for large ones. The exact amounts are an implementation detail, so never write code that depends on them (the example checks `cap(s) >= 3` rather than an exact number for that reason).

Because growth may or may not allocate, **after an `append` you cannot know whether the result shares memory with the original**. This is the root of the gotchas in the next lesson.



```gopath-callout
callout-7
```



## `nil` vs empty slices



```gopath-example
example-62
```



A `nil` slice has no backing array, and it behaves exactly like an empty slice for `len`, `cap`, `range` and `append`. Prefer `var s []T` when starting an empty list.

The difference only shows when something looks at `nil` specifically. The most common case is JSON: a `nil` slice encodes as `null` and an empty slice as `[]`. If an API must return `[]`, initialize with `[]T{}` or `make([]T, 0)`.

## `copy`

`copy(dst, src)` copies elements between slices and returns how many it copied, which is the smaller of the two lengths:



```gopath-example
example-63
```



`copy` never allocates and never grows `dst`. To duplicate a slice, use `slices.Clone(s)` (lesson 3.4).

## Two-dimensional slices

Go has no built-in matrix type. A `[][]T` is a slice of slices, and each inner slice must be created separately:



```gopath-example
example-64
```



## Common mistakes

### Indexing past the length

`s := make([]int, 0, 10); s[0] = 1` panics with `index out of range [0] with length 0`. Capacity is room to grow, not elements you can index. Use `append`, or `make([]int, 10)` if you want ten indexable zeros.

### `make([]T, n)` followed by `append`

```go
ids := make([]int, len(users)) // already has len(users) zeros
for _, u := range users {
	ids = append(ids, u.ID) // appends AFTER the zeros
}
```

Use `make([]int, 0, len(users))` with `append`, or `make([]int, len(users))` with `ids[i] = ...`.

### Comparing slices with `==`

Slices are only comparable to `nil`. Use `slices.Equal(a, b)`.

### Assuming a sub-slice is a copy

Writing through a sub-slice changes the original. Clone it when you need independence.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m03/ints
```



## Key takeaways

- A slice is a header of pointer, length and capacity over a backing array.
- Assigning, passing and slicing copy the header, not the elements.
- `append` reuses spare capacity when it can and reallocates when it cannot. Always use its result.
- `nil` and empty slices behave the same, except where code checks for `nil` (such as JSON encoding).
- Use `make` with a capacity hint when you know the size, and `copy` or `slices.Clone` to duplicate.

## Further reading

- [Go Slices: usage and internals](https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro) on the Go blog
- [Arrays, slices (and strings): The mechanics of 'append'](https://go.dev/blog/slices)
- [Slice types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Slice_types) and [Appending to and copying slices](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Appending_and_copying_slices) in the spec

lessons.title: 3.3 Slice gotchas: aliasing, append surprises, memory retention
lessons.description: The slice bugs that bite experienced developers: two appends overwriting each other, appends lost in functions, and small slices keeping huge arrays alive.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How two slices that share a backing array can overwrite each other through `append`
- How to prevent aliasing with `slices.Clone` and the full slice expression
- Why an `append` inside a function can be invisible to the caller
- How a tiny sub-slice can keep a huge array in memory
- Safe ways to filter and delete elements

## The idea

Every gotcha in this lesson comes from one fact from lesson 3.2: **slices share their backing array, and `append` writes into spare capacity when there is any.** Once you can picture the backing array, all of these bugs become easy to predict.

## Gotcha 1: two appends, one array



```gopath-example
example-65
```



`base` has length 3 and capacity 10. Both `append` calls fit into that spare capacity, so **both write into index 3 of the same array**. `a` and `b` end up as two headers looking at the same memory, and the second write wins.

This bug is nasty because it depends on capacity. If `base` had been created with `make([]int, 3)` (no spare capacity), each `append` would allocate a new array and the code would appear to work. A refactor that adds a capacity hint can silently break it.

### The fix: make the copy explicit



```gopath-example
example-66
```



- `slices.Clone(s)` returns an independent copy.
- The **full slice expression** `s[low:high:max]` sets the capacity to `max - low`. With `base[:3:3]` the capacity equals the length, so the next `append` must allocate. This is the idiom to use when you hand out a slice and do not want the receiver's appends to scribble over your data.

## Gotcha 2: `append` inside a function



```gopath-example
example-67
```



The function gets a **copy of the header**. `append` updates the copy's length (and maybe its pointer), and that copy disappears when the function returns. The caller's header still says length 0.

The idiomatic fix is to **return the new slice**, exactly like `append` itself does. Passing `*[]string` also works, but it is rarely the clearest choice.

Note that **changing existing elements** inside a function does work, because the elements live in the shared array:



```gopath-example
example-68
```



So a function that takes a slice can modify its elements but not its length. Document which one your function does.

## Gotcha 3: small slice, huge memory

A sub-slice keeps the **entire** backing array alive, because the garbage collector cannot free part of an array.

```go
data, _ := os.ReadFile("huge.log")   // 500 MB
header := data[:64]                  // still references all 500 MB
cache[name] = header                 // the 500 MB can never be freed
```

Clone the part you want to keep:



```gopath-example
example-69
```



The same applies to strings: `s[:10]` of a huge string shares its memory. Use `strings.Clone` when you keep a small piece of a large string for a long time.

A related effect: if a slice holds **pointers**, removing elements by reslicing (`s = s[:len(s)-1]`) leaves the removed pointer in the backing array, so the object it points to stays reachable. `slices.Delete` and `slices.Compact` clear the vacated elements for you since Go 1.22.

## Filtering and deleting safely

Removing elements while iterating with indexes is error-prone. Two clean patterns:



```gopath-example
example-70
```



- **Filter in place** with `keep := s[:0]`: it reuses the same array, which is fast and allocation free. It overwrites the original contents, so only do it when you own the slice.
- **`slices.DeleteFunc`** does the same thing with a predicate and clears the leftover tail.

## A mental checklist

When you see a slice crossing a boundary (a function call, a struct field, a channel, a cache), ask:

1. **Will anyone append to it?** If both sides might, give each side its own copy, or cap the capacity with `s[:len(s):len(s)]`.
2. **Will anyone modify elements?** If the caller expects its data to stay unchanged, clone before modifying.
3. **Is it a small piece of something big that will be kept for a long time?** Clone it.

## Common mistakes

### Returning internal slices from a type

A method that returns `t.items` lets callers modify your internal state and append into your spare capacity. Return `slices.Clone(t.items)`, or an iterator (lesson 3.8).

### Storing a sub-slice of a reused buffer

`bufio.Scanner.Bytes()` returns a slice that is **overwritten** on the next call to `Scan`. If you store it, you will later see different data. Copy it, or use `Text()`, which returns a new string.

### Forgetting to use the result of `slices.Compact` or `slices.Delete`

These functions work in place and return the shorter slice. The original variable still has the old length (and zeroed tail elements). Always assign the result: `s = slices.Delete(s, i, i+1)`.

## Key takeaways

- Slices that share a backing array can overwrite each other through `append` when there is spare capacity.
- Use `slices.Clone` or the full slice expression `s[a:b:b]` to stop aliasing.
- A function can modify a slice's elements but not its length; return the new slice instead.
- Sub-slices keep the whole backing array alive. Clone small pieces of big data you keep.
- Filter with `s[:0]` or `slices.DeleteFunc`, and always use the returned slice.

## Further reading

- [Arrays, slices (and strings): The mechanics of 'append'](https://go.dev/blog/slices)
- [Full slice expressions](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Slice_expressions) in the spec
- [Robust generic functions on slices](https://go.dev/blog/generic-slice-functions) on the Go blog, about zeroing in `slices.Delete` and friends

lessons.title: 3.4 The slices and maps packages
lessons.description: The generic helper packages for searching, sorting, editing and cloning slices and maps, and the built-in min, max and clear functions.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The most useful functions in `slices` and `maps`
- How to sort with a custom comparison using `slices.SortFunc` and `cmp`
- Which functions modify their input and which return copies
- The built-ins `min`, `max` and `clear`

## The idea

For years, Go developers wrote the same small loops again and again: "does this slice contain x?", "sort these structs by name", "copy this map". Since Go 1.21 the standard library has generic packages for these jobs:

- **`slices`**: searching, sorting, comparing, inserting, deleting and cloning slices.
- **`maps`**: cloning, comparing, copying and iterating maps.
- **`cmp`**: comparison helpers used for sorting.

They work with any element type (they are generic, Module 4). Use them instead of hand-written loops: they are tested, fast, and make intent obvious.

## Searching, sorting and comparing



```gopath-example
example-71
```



Look closely at the `Compact` line. `Compact` works **in place**: it moves the unique elements to the front and returns a shorter slice. The original variable still has length 5, and since Go 1.22 its leftover tail is zeroed, so `sorted` now prints `[2 5 8 9 0]`. Always use the returned slice.

| Need | Function | Modifies input? |
|---|---|---|
| Find an element | `slices.Contains`, `Index`, `IndexFunc` | no |
| Smallest, largest | `slices.Min`, `Max` (panic on empty) | no |
| Sort | `slices.Sort`, `SortFunc`, `SortStableFunc` | **yes** |
| Binary search on sorted data | `slices.BinarySearch`, `BinarySearchFunc` | no |
| Compare | `slices.Equal`, `Compare` | no |
| Remove consecutive duplicates | `slices.Compact`, `CompactFunc` | **yes**, use the result |
| Copy | `slices.Clone` | no |
| Reverse | `slices.Reverse` | **yes** |

## Sorting by your own rules

`slices.SortFunc` takes a comparison function that returns a negative number, zero or a positive number. `cmp.Compare` produces exactly that, and `cmp.Or` returns its first non-zero argument, which makes multi-key sorts read naturally:



```gopath-example
example-72
```



Swap `a` and `b` in a `cmp.Compare` call to reverse the order for that key. Use `slices.SortStableFunc` when elements that compare equal must keep their original order.



```gopath-callout
callout-8
```



## Inserting and deleting



```gopath-example
example-73
```



`Insert` and `Delete` return the updated slice. Like `append`, they may reuse the backing array, so the old variable should not be used afterwards. Assign the result back.

## The `maps` package



```gopath-example
example-74
```



- `maps.Keys(m)` and `maps.Values(m)` return **iterators** (lesson 3.8), not slices. `slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))` collects the keys into a sorted slice in one step, which is the standard way to iterate a map in a stable order.
- `maps.Clone` makes a shallow copy. The values are copied as values, so if they are pointers or slices, both maps still point at the same underlying data.
- `maps.Equal` compares two maps key by key.

## Built-ins: `min`, `max`, `clear`

Since Go 1.21 these are built into the language, no import needed:

- `min(a, b, ...)` and `max(a, b, ...)` work on numbers and strings.
- `clear(m)` deletes every key from a map. `clear(s)` sets every element of a slice to its zero value (it does **not** change the length).

## Common mistakes

### Sorting a slice you do not own

`slices.Sort(userSlice)` reorders the caller's data. Clone first if the caller does not expect that.

### Ignoring results of in-place functions

`slices.Compact(s)` without `s = ...` leaves you with a slice that has stale length and zeroed elements at the end.

### Calling `slices.Min` or `slices.Max` on an empty slice

They panic. Check `len(s) > 0` first.

### Assuming `maps.Clone` is a deep copy

A `map[string][]int` clone shares every inner slice with the original.

## Key takeaways

- Reach for `slices`, `maps` and `cmp` before writing loops by hand.
- Sort with `slices.Sort` or `slices.SortFunc` plus `cmp.Compare` and `cmp.Or`.
- `Sort`, `Reverse`, `Compact`, `Insert` and `Delete` modify in place; always use the returned slice.
- `slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))` gives you map keys in a stable order.
- `min`, `max` and `clear` are built-ins.

## Further reading

- [Package slices](https://pkg.go.dev/slices), [maps](https://pkg.go.dev/maps) and [cmp](https://pkg.go.dev/cmp)
- [Robust generic functions on slices](https://go.dev/blog/generic-slice-functions) on the Go blog
- [Built-in functions min, max and clear](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Min_and_max) in the spec

- clear(m) deletes every key from a map. clear(s) sets every element of a slice to its zero value (it does not change the length).

 common mistakes

 sorting a slice you do not own

slices.sort(userslice) reorders the caller's data. clone first if the caller does not expect that.

 ignoring results of in-place functions

slices.compact(s) without s = ... leaves you with a slice that has stale length and zeroed elements at the end.

 calling slices.min or slices.max on an empty slice

they panic. check len(s) > 0 first.

 assuming maps.clone is a deep copy

a map[string][]int clone shares every inner slice with the original.

 key takeaways

- reach for slices, maps and cmp before writing loops by hand.
- sort with slices.sort or slices.sortfunc plus cmp.compare and cmp.or.
- sort, reverse, compact, insert and delete modify in place; always use the returned slice.
- slices.sorted(maps.keys(m)) gives you map keys in a stable order.
- min, max and clear are built-ins.

 further reading

- [package slices](https://pkg.go.dev/slices), [maps](https://pkg.go.dev/maps) and [cmp](https://pkg.go.dev/cmp)
- [robust generic functions on slices](https://go.dev/blog/generic-slice-functions) on the go blog
- [built-in functions min, max and clear](https://go.dev/ref/specminandmax) in the spec

lessons.title: 3.5 Maps: usage, iteration order, concurrency warning
lessons.description: Creating and using maps, the comma-ok idiom, sets and grouping, nil maps, struct values, random iteration order and why maps are not safe for concurrent writes.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to create, read, update and delete map entries
- The **comma-ok** idiom to tell "missing" from "zero"
- Idiomatic sets, counters and group-by with maps
- Why writing to a `nil` map panics
- Why you cannot assign to a struct field inside a map
- Iteration order and the concurrency rule

## The idea

A map is Go's built-in hash table: `map[K]V` maps keys of type `K` to values of type `V`. Keys must be **comparable** (usable with `==`): numbers, strings, booleans, pointers, channels, arrays and structs of comparable fields. Slices, maps and functions cannot be keys.

Like slices, a map variable holds a small reference to the real data, so passing a map to a function lets the function modify it.

## The basics



```gopath-example
example-75
```



Reading a missing key returns the **zero value** for `V`, with no error and no panic. That is convenient, but it means `ages["nobody"]` and a real age of `0` look the same. Use the **comma-ok** form `v, ok := m[k]` whenever the difference matters.

`delete(m, k)` on a missing key is a no-op, so you never need to check first.

## `nil` maps



```gopath-example
example-76
```



A `nil` map behaves like an empty map for **reading**, `len`, `range` and `delete`. **Writing** panics. This is the one place where Go's zero value is not ready to use, so always create maps before adding entries:

```go
m := make(map[string]int)          // empty map
m := make(map[string]int, 1000)    // with a size hint, avoids rehashing while it grows
m := map[string]int{"a": 1}        // literal
```

A struct with a map field needs that field initialized too, usually in a constructor function (Module 4).

## Idioms you will use constantly

### Counting



```gopath-example
example-77
```



`counts[w]++` works on a missing key because the read returns `0` first. The zero value doing useful work again.

### Sets

Go has no set type. A map with empty-struct values is the idiom:



```gopath-example
example-78
```



`struct{}` takes zero bytes. `map[string]bool` also works and reads a little more simply (`if seen[x]`), at the cost of one byte per entry. Both are common.

### Grouping



```gopath-example
example-79
```



Appending to a missing key works because the zero value of a slice is `nil`, and `append` to `nil` is fine.

## Struct values cannot be modified in place



```gopath-example
example-80
```



`m[k].field = v` does not compile: `cannot assign to struct field accounts["ana"].balance in map`. Map elements are not addressable, because the map may move them in memory as it grows. Either read, modify and write back the whole value, or store pointers (`map[string]*account`) when you update fields often.

## Iteration order is random

`for k, v := range m` visits every entry, but **in an unspecified order that changes from run to run**. The Go runtime randomizes it deliberately, so that nobody can accidentally depend on it.

When you need a stable order (output, tests, hashing), sort the keys:

```go
for _, k := range slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) {
	fmt.Println(k, m[k])
}
```

It is safe to `delete` entries from a map while ranging over it. Entries added during iteration may or may not be visited.

## Maps and concurrency

**Maps are not safe for concurrent use.** If one goroutine writes to a map while another reads or writes it, the program can crash with:

```text
fatal error: concurrent map writes
```

This is a fatal error, not a panic: it cannot be recovered. Protect shared maps with a `sync.Mutex` or `sync.RWMutex`, or in some specific cases use `sync.Map`. Module 6 covers both. Concurrent **reads** with no writer are fine.

## Common mistakes

### Writing to a map that was never created

The most common map panic. Look for struct fields of map type that a constructor forgot to `make`.

### Using the zero value to mean "missing"

`if m[k] == 0` cannot tell "absent" from "present with value 0". Use comma-ok.

### Depending on iteration order

Tests that compare printed map output are flaky. Sort keys or compare with `maps.Equal`.

### Sharing a map between goroutines without a lock

Works in testing, crashes under load. Run your tests with `-race` (Module 6) to catch it early.

### Expecting a deep copy from assignment

`b := a` for maps makes both variables refer to the **same** map. Use `maps.Clone(a)` for a shallow copy.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m03/inventory
```



## Key takeaways

- `map[K]V` needs comparable keys; reading a missing key returns the zero value.
- Use `v, ok := m[k]` to distinguish missing from zero.
- A `nil` map is readable but panics on write; create maps with `make` or a literal.
- `map[T]struct{}` is a set; `m[k]++` counts; `m[k] = append(m[k], v)` groups.
- Map elements are not addressable: write back whole struct values or store pointers.
- Iteration order is random, and concurrent writes are a fatal error.

## Further reading

- [Go maps in action](https://go.dev/blog/maps) on the Go blog
- [Map types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Map_types) and [Index expressions](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Index_expressions) in the spec
- [Faster Go maps with Swiss Tables](https://go.dev/blog/swisstable), about the map implementation introduced in Go 1.24

lessons.title: 3.6 Named types, structs, tags and anonymous structs
lessons.description: Defining your own types, building structs with literals, struct comparison and copying, struct tags, and anonymous structs for one-off data.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How `type` creates a new, distinct type, and why that prevents bugs
- How to declare structs and build them with literals
- How copying and comparison work for structs
- What struct tags are and who reads them
- When anonymous structs are handy

## Named types

`type Name Underlying` creates a **new type**. It has the same representation as its underlying type, but the compiler treats it as different:



```gopath-example
example-81
```



`Celsius` and `Fahrenheit` are both `float64` underneath, but you cannot pass one where the other is expected without an explicit conversion. Named types let the compiler catch unit mix-ups, IDs of the wrong kind (`UserID` vs `OrderID`), and enums like `Weekday` from lesson 2.3. And, as you will see in Module 4, **you can define methods on named types**.

There is also a type **alias**, written with `=`: `type Temp = Celsius`. An alias is just another name for the **same** type, with no conversion needed. Aliases exist mainly for moving types between packages during refactors. When you want a new type, leave out the `=`.

## Structs

A struct groups named fields. It is Go's main way to model data, playing the role that classes play elsewhere, minus inheritance.



```gopath-example
example-82
```



Points worth knowing:

- **Use field names in literals** (`User{ID: 1, Name: "Ana"}`). Positional literals (`User{1, "Ana", "", ...}`) break as soon as someone adds a field, and `go vet` warns about them for structs from other packages.
- **Omitted fields get their zero values.** That is why it pays to design structs so the zero value of every field is a sensible default.
- **`%+v`** in `fmt` prints field names, which is the quickest way to inspect a struct while debugging. `%#v` prints it as Go syntax.
- Exported field names (uppercase) are visible from other packages, and they are the only fields that packages like `encoding/json` can see.

### Pointers to structs

You will often create structs through a pointer: `u := &User{Name: "Ana"}`. Field access is the same (`u.Name`), as lesson 2.8 showed. Functions that build structs usually return a pointer when the struct is large or will be modified, and a value when it is small and immutable.

## Copying and comparing



```gopath-example
example-83
```



- Assignment copies every field. But a **shallow** copy only: if a field is a slice, map or pointer, both copies share what it points to.
- Structs are comparable with `==` when all their fields are comparable. A struct containing a slice or map is not comparable, and cannot be a map key.

## Struct tags

A **tag** is a string literal after a field's type. The compiler ignores it; libraries read it at run time with reflection:



```gopath-example
example-84
```



The convention is space-separated `key:"value"` pairs. You will meet tags constantly:

| Tag key | Read by |
|---|---|
| `json` | `encoding/json` (field name, `omitempty`, `-` to skip) |
| `xml`, `yaml`, `toml` | the matching encoders |
| `db` | SQL helper libraries such as sqlx |
| `validate` | validation libraries |
| `env` | config loaders |

`go vet` checks that tags are well formed. A typo like `json:name` (missing quotes) is silently useless otherwise. The JSON details are covered in lesson 8.2.

## Anonymous structs

A struct type does not need a name. Anonymous structs are perfect for data that is used in exactly one place:



```gopath-example
example-85
```



Their most common use is **table-driven tests**, which you have already seen in the exercise tests. They are also handy for decoding one-off JSON responses and for template data.

## The empty struct

`struct{}` has no fields and takes **zero bytes**. You saw it as a set value in lesson 3.5. It is also used as a signal on channels (`chan struct{}`) in Module 6, where only the event matters, not any data.

## Common mistakes

### Positional struct literals

`Point{1, 2}` is fine for tiny, stable types. For anything else, name the fields.

### Expecting deep copies

Copying a struct with a slice field gives you two structs sharing one slice. Clone the slice when you need independence.

### Unexported fields and encoders

`encoding/json` skips unexported fields silently. If a field is missing from your JSON output, check its first letter.

### Malformed tags

`json: "name"` (with a space) or `json:name` are ignored. Let `go vet` check them.

## Key takeaways

- `type T U` creates a distinct type; use named types to prevent unit and ID mix-ups. `type T = U` is only an alias.
- Build structs with field-named literals; omitted fields are zero.
- Struct assignment is a shallow copy; `==` works if every field is comparable.
- Tags are metadata for libraries such as `encoding/json`, and `go vet` checks their format.
- Anonymous structs are ideal for test tables and one-off data.

## Further reading

- [Type declarations](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Type_declarations) and [Struct types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Struct_types) in the spec
- [Effective Go: Composite literals](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#composite_literals)
- [Package reflect: StructTag](https://pkg.go.dev/reflect#StructTag)

lessons.title: 3.7 Embedding and composition
lessons.description: How struct embedding promotes fields and methods, how name conflicts are resolved, and why embedding is composition rather than inheritance.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to embed one struct in another, and what **promotion** means
- That embedding promotes methods too, with `sync.Mutex` as the classic example
- How Go resolves name conflicts between embedded fields
- Why embedding is **not** inheritance, and what that means for your designs

## The idea

Go has no classes and no inheritance. To build bigger types from smaller ones, you **compose** them: put one struct inside another. Embedding is a shortcut for composition. When you include a type as a field **without a field name**, its fields and methods are **promoted**: you can use them as if they were declared on the outer type.

## Promoted fields



```gopath-example
example-86
```



An embedded field still exists as a normal field. Its name is the **type name** (`Person`), so `e.Person.Name` always works. `e.Name` is a shorthand the compiler expands to `e.Person.Name`.

In a literal you set the embedded value through its type name: `Employee{Person: Person{...}}`.

## Promoted methods

Methods of the embedded type are promoted too. Methods are the topic of Module 4, but you can already use one of the most common cases, embedding `sync.Mutex` to make a type lockable:



```gopath-example
example-87
```



The zero value of `Counter` is ready to use: an unlocked mutex and a zero count.

Be aware that embedding **exports** what it promotes. Here `Lock` and `Unlock` become part of `Counter`'s public API, so any caller can lock it. For types in a public API it is often better to use a named, unexported field (`mu sync.Mutex`) and keep locking internal.

## Name conflicts

If several embedded types have a field with the same name, the rule is about **depth**:

- A field declared directly on the outer struct (depth 0) wins over promoted ones.
- If two promoted fields with the same name are at the same depth, using the short name is a **compile error** (ambiguous selector). You must spell out the path.



```gopath-example
example-88
```



Ambiguity is only an error when you actually use the ambiguous name, so a conflict can sit unnoticed until someone writes `a.Name`.

## Embedding is not inheritance

This is the most important part of the lesson. An `Employee` **contains** a `Person`; it **is not** a `Person`:



```gopath-example
example-89
```



Differences from inheritance in Java, C# or Python:

- **No subtype relationship.** You cannot pass an `Employee` where a `Person` is required. Go gets polymorphism from **interfaces** instead (Module 4), and an `Employee` can satisfy an interface through its promoted methods.
- **No virtual dispatch.** If a promoted method of `Person` calls another `Person` method, it always calls `Person`'s version, even if `Employee` declares a method with the same name. The embedded value does not know it is embedded.
- **No `super`.** You call the inner implementation explicitly: `e.Person.Describe()`.

## When to embed

Embed when you want the outer type to **genuinely offer the inner type's behavior** as part of its own API:

- Adding locking to a type (`sync.Mutex`, with the caveat above).
- Wrapping a type to override one or two methods while keeping the rest, a common trick with interfaces like `http.ResponseWriter` (lesson 12.2).
- Sharing common fields across many structs, such as timestamps on database models.

Use a **named field** when the inner type is an implementation detail. A `Service` that uses a database should have `db *sql.DB`, not an embedded `*sql.DB`, otherwise every database method becomes a method of your service.

## Common mistakes

### Building class hierarchies with embedding

`Animal` embedded in `Dog` embedded in `Puppy` imports inheritance thinking and gets none of its benefits. Use small interfaces and plain composition.

### Accidentally exporting methods

Embedding a type puts all of its exported methods into your type's API. Readers of your documentation see them, and callers can use them.

### Embedding a pointer that is never set

You can embed a pointer type (`*Logger`). If it is nil, calling a promoted method or reading a promoted field panics. Initialize it in a constructor.

### Expecting overridden methods to be called from the inner type

There is no virtual dispatch. If you need the inner logic to call back into the outer type, pass an interface or a function to it explicitly.

## Key takeaways

- An embedded field is a field named after its type, whose fields and methods are promoted.
- Fields at shallower depth win; same-depth conflicts are an error when used.
- Embedding is composition: no subtyping, no virtual dispatch, no `super`.
- Embed to expose behavior on purpose; use a named field for implementation details.

## Further reading

- [Effective Go: Embedding](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#embedding)
- [Struct types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Struct_types) and [Selectors](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Selectors) in the spec, which define promotion and depth
- [Go FAQ: Why is there no type inheritance?](https://go.dev/doc/faq#inheritance)

 building class hierarchies with embedding

animal embedded in dog embedded in puppy imports inheritance thinking and gets none of its benefits. use small interfaces and plain composition.

embedding a type puts all of its exported methods into your type's api. readers of your documentation see them, and callers can use them.

you can embed a pointer type (logger). if it is nil, calling a promoted method or reading a promoted field panics. initialize it in a constructor.

there is no virtual dispatch. if you need the inner logic to call back into the outer type, pass an interface or a function to it explicitly.

- fields at shallower depth win; same-depth conflicts are an error when used.
- embedding is composition: no subtyping, no virtual dispatch, no super.
- embed to expose behavior on purpose; use a named field for implementation details.
