lessons.title: 3.8 Iterators and range-over-func
lessons.description: Write your own iterators with iter.Seq and iter.Seq2, range over them like slices, compose lazy pipelines, and use the iterator functions in the standard library.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What a Go iterator is: a function that pushes values to a `yield` callback
- How `for range` works over functions (Go 1.23+)
- How early `break` is communicated back to the iterator
- How to compose lazy pipelines like filter and map
- The iterators in `slices`, `maps` and `strings`, and pull iterators with `iter.Pull`

## The idea

Since Go 1.23, `for range` works not only over slices, maps, strings, channels and integers, but also over **functions** of a specific shape. A function that takes a `yield` callback and calls it once per value is an **iterator**:

```go
type Seq[V any]     func(yield func(V) bool)
type Seq2[K, V any] func(yield func(K, V) bool)
```

Those two types live in the `iter` package. (`[V any]` means they are generic, which Module 4 explains; for now read `iter.Seq[int]` as "an iterator of ints".)

Iterators let you expose sequences of values **without building a slice first**: walking a tree, reading database rows, generating numbers, paging through an API. Values are produced on demand.

## Writing and using an iterator



```gopath-example
example-90
```



How it works:

1. `for n := range Countdown(3)` calls the iterator function, passing a `yield` function that the compiler builds from the loop body.
2. Each `yield(i)` runs the loop body once with `n = i`.
3. `yield` returns `true` to ask for more, or `false` when the loop body executed `break` (or `return`).
4. The iterator **must stop** when `yield` returns `false`. Calling `yield` again after that panics.

The second loop shows the early stop: `Countdown(100)` only produces 100, 99, 98 and then returns, because the loop broke. It never counts all the way down.

## Pairs: `iter.Seq2`

`Seq2` yields two values per step, like ranging over a slice (index, value) or a map (key, value):



```gopath-example
example-91
```



## Composing lazy pipelines

Because iterators are just functions, you can wrap one in another. Nothing runs until someone ranges over the outermost iterator:



```gopath-example
example-92
```



Note the line `if keep(v) && !yield(v) { return }`. Forwarding the stop signal from the inner `yield` is what makes the whole pipeline stop early when the consumer breaks.

`slices.Collect` drains an iterator into a slice. It is the bridge back to ordinary slices.

## Iterators in the standard library



```gopath-example
example-93
```



| Function | Yields |
|---|---|
| `slices.All(s)` | index, value |
| `slices.Values(s)` | values |
| `slices.Backward(s)` | index, value from the end |
| `maps.Keys(m)`, `maps.Values(m)`, `maps.All(m)` | keys, values, pairs |
| `slices.Collect(seq)`, `slices.Sorted(seq)` | (consume an iterator into a slice) |
| `maps.Collect(seq2)` | (consume pairs into a map) |
| `strings.Lines(s)` | each line, including its newline (Go 1.24+) |
| `strings.SplitSeq(s, sep)`, `strings.FieldsSeq(s)` | split pieces without allocating a slice (Go 1.24+) |

## Pull iterators

The iterators so far are **push** iterators: the iterator drives the loop. Sometimes you need to **pull** values one at a time, for example to merge two sorted sequences. `iter.Pull` converts a push iterator into a `next` function and a `stop` function:



```gopath-example
example-94
```



Always call `stop` when you are done (a `defer` is the easy way), or the iterator's resources may never be released. Pull iterators are more expensive than ranging, so use them only when you need them.

## When to return an iterator

Return an iterator instead of a slice when:

- The sequence is **large or infinite**, and the caller might stop early.
- Producing each value is **expensive** (I/O, computation) and you want laziness.
- You want callers to **read but not modify** your internal data (an iterator over a slice field hides the slice).

Return a slice when the data is small, already in memory, and callers will want `len`, indexing or sorting.

## Common mistakes

### Ignoring the result of `yield`

An iterator that keeps calling `yield` after it returns `false` panics at run time. Always write `if !yield(v) { return }`.

### Doing work before the first `yield` that cannot be cancelled

If your iterator opens a file or a network connection, close it with `defer` inside the iterator function, so it is released when the loop ends early.

### Ranging over the same iterator twice and expecting the same results

Some iterators are single use (reading from a stream, for example). Document whether yours can be reused.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m03/seq
```



## Key takeaways

- An iterator is a function that calls `yield` per value; `for range` can loop over it (Go 1.23+).
- `yield` returns `false` when the loop stops early, and the iterator must then return.
- Iterators compose into lazy pipelines; `slices.Collect` turns them back into slices.
- `slices`, `maps` and `strings` provide iterator functions; `iter.Pull` gives you `next` and `stop`.
- Return iterators for large, lazy or read-only sequences; return slices for small in-memory data.

## Further reading

- [Range over function types](https://go.dev/blog/range-functions) on the Go blog
- [Package iter](https://pkg.go.dev/iter)
- [For statements with range clause](https://go.dev/ref/spec#For_range) in the spec

lessons.title: 3.9 Checkpoint project: wordfreq
lessons.description: Build a command line tool that counts word frequencies across files or standard input, using maps, slices, sorting and bufio.
lessons.body:
## What you will build

`wordfreq` reads text from files or standard input and prints the most frequent words:

```bash
go run ./projects/wordfreq/cmd/wordfreq -n 4 projects/wordfreq/internal/count/testdata/sample.txt
```

```text
      4  go
      3  is
      1  an
      1  and
```

It uses everything from this module: a map to count, slices and `slices.SortStableFunc` to rank, a struct for results, plus `bufio.Scanner` to read line by line (a preview of Module 8).

The code is in [`projects/wordfreq`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/projects/wordfreq).

## The design




### Split the problem

Two pure functions do the real work, so they are easy to test:

- `count.Words(r io.Reader) (map[string]int, error)` turns text into counts.
- `count.Top(counts, n) []Entry` turns counts into a ranked list.

`main` only handles flags, files and printing.

### Count words



```gopath-example
example-95
```



Things to notice:

- `bufio.Scanner` reads one line at a time, so even huge files use little memory. Its default limit is 64 KiB per line; `sc.Buffer` raises it.
- `strings.FieldsFunc` splits on every rune that is not part of a word.
- `words := fields[:0]` filters **in place**, the pattern from lesson 3.3.
- `Top` first sorts keys alphabetically, then does a **stable** sort by count. Stability keeps the alphabetical order among equal counts, which makes the output deterministic despite random map order.

### A bug the tests found

The first version only treated letters and digits as part of a word. A test with Tamil text failed: `வணக்கம்` was counted as two words.

In scripts such as Tamil, Hindi or Bengali, vowel signs and the virama are **combining marks** (`unicode.IsMark`), not letters. Treating them as separators breaks words apart. This is the grapheme lesson from 2.4 showing up in real code, and it is why the test file includes non-English input.

### Test it



```gopath-example
example-96
```



### Wire up the command



```gopath-example
example-97
```



`addFile` is a separate function so that each file's `defer f.Close()` runs right after that file is processed, avoiding the `defer` in a loop trap from lesson 2.7.




## Try it

```bash
cd projects/wordfreq
go test ./...
cat ../../site/content/learn/*/*.md | go run ./cmd/wordfreq -n 15
```

## Stretch goals

1. Add a `-min` flag to ignore words shorter than N runes (use `utf8.RuneCountInString`, not `len`).
2. Add a `-stop` flag with a file of stop words to ignore (a set from lesson 3.5).
3. Return an iterator from a new `count.WordsSeq(r io.Reader) iter.Seq[string]` and rebuild `Words` on top of it.
4. Print the output as JSON with a `-json` flag (a preview of lesson 8.2).

## Module 3 recap

You can now:

- Explain the difference between arrays and slices, and predict when slices share memory
- Avoid the common `append` and memory retention traps
- Use maps idiomatically for lookups, sets, counters and grouping
- Model data with named types, structs and tags
- Compose types with embedding, without mistaking it for inheritance
- Write and consume iterators

Next is **[Module 4: Methods, interfaces and generics](/learn/04-methods-interfaces-generics/)**, where these types get behavior.

lessons.title: 4.1 Methods: value vs pointer receivers
lessons.description: Declaring methods on any named type, choosing between value and pointer receivers, handling nil receivers, and using method values and expressions.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to declare a method, and that any named type can have methods
- The difference between **value** and **pointer** receivers, and how to choose
- How Go automatically takes addresses and dereferences for method calls
- Why a method on a nil pointer can be valid
- Method values and method expressions

## The idea

A method is a function with a **receiver**: a special parameter written before the function name. `func (r Rect) Area() float64` is a function called `Area` that is attached to `Rect` and called as `r.Area()`.

Go has no classes. Instead, **any named type declared in your package** can have methods: structs, but also slices, maps, numbers, strings or functions. The method and the type must be in the same package, so you cannot add methods to `int` or to a type from another package (define your own named type instead).

## Value and pointer receivers



```gopath-example
example-98
```



- **Value receiver** `(r Rect)`: the method gets a **copy**. It can read fields, and any changes affect only the copy.
- **Pointer receiver** `(r *Rect)`: the method gets the address. It can modify the original, and nothing is copied.

Go handles the `&` and `*` for you on calls: `r.Scale(2)` on an addressable `Rect` variable becomes `(&r).Scale(2)`, and calling a value method through a pointer dereferences automatically.

### The classic bug



```gopath-example
example-99
```



`IncBroken` compiles, runs and does nothing visible. If a method needs to change its receiver, it must take a pointer.

### How to choose

Use a **pointer receiver** when:

- the method modifies the receiver;
- the struct is large, so copying it on every call would be wasteful;
- the struct contains something that must not be copied, such as a `sync.Mutex`;
- **any other method on the type already uses a pointer receiver**. Consistency matters: mixing receiver kinds on one type confuses readers and complicates which interfaces the type satisfies (lesson 4.2).

Use a **value receiver** when the type is small and naturally immutable: `time.Time`, a `Point`, a `Celsius`, a small `Money` struct. Values are cheap to copy and safe to share.

When in doubt, use a pointer receiver for structs.

## Methods on non-struct types



```gopath-example
example-100
```



This is common in the standard library: `time.Duration` is an `int64` with methods, `http.HandlerFunc` is a function type with a `ServeHTTP` method, and `sort.StringSlice` is a `[]string` with methods.

## Nil receivers

A pointer receiver can be `nil`, and calling the method is **not** an automatic panic. The method runs and can check for `nil` itself:



```gopath-example
example-101
```



This makes recursive data structures elegant: the empty list or empty tree is just `nil`, and methods handle it. The panic only happens if the method **dereferences** the nil pointer (reading `n.Val` without a check).

## Method values and method expressions

Methods can be used as function values in two ways:



```gopath-example
example-102
```



- A **method value** `r.Area` binds the method to a specific receiver. For a value receiver, the receiver is **copied at that moment**, which is why changing `r.W` afterwards did not change the result.
- A **method expression** `(*Rect).Scale` turns the method into a plain function whose first parameter is the receiver.

Method values are handy for callbacks: `http.HandleFunc("/", srv.handleIndex)`, `defer mu.Unlock()`, or passing `strings.ToUpper` to a mapping function.

## Common mistakes

### Value receivers on methods that mutate

The `IncBroken` bug. If you see a method assigning to a field of a value receiver, it is almost always wrong.

### Mixing receiver kinds on one type

Pick one. If any method needs a pointer receiver, make all of them pointer receivers.

### Copying a struct that has pointer-receiver methods and a mutex

Passing such a struct by value copies the mutex, and `go vet` reports `passes lock by value`. Pass pointers.

### Calling pointer methods on non-addressable values

`Rect{1, 2}.Scale(2)` does not compile, because a composite literal used directly is not addressable. The same goes for map elements: `m["k"].Scale(2)`. Assign to a variable first, or store pointers.

## Key takeaways

- A method is a function with a receiver, and any named type in your package can have methods.
- Value receivers get a copy; pointer receivers can modify the original.
- Use pointer receivers to mutate, for large or non-copyable structs, and for consistency.
- A nil pointer receiver is valid until the method dereferences it.
- Method values bind a receiver; method expressions make the receiver an explicit parameter.

## Further reading

- [Method declarations](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Method_declarations) and [Method values](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Method_values) in the spec
- [Go FAQ: Should I define methods on values or pointers?](https://go.dev/doc/faq#methods_on_values_or_pointers)
- [Effective Go: Pointers vs. Values](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#pointers_vs_values)

lessons.title: 4.2 Interfaces: implicit satisfaction and small interfaces
lessons.description: How Go interfaces are satisfied without declarations, why small interfaces are better, how method sets decide what satisfies what, and how interfaces compose.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How an interface is defined and satisfied, with no `implements` keyword
- Why small interfaces lead to better designs, and how they make testing easy
- What an interface value contains
- How **method sets** decide whether `T` or only `*T` satisfies an interface
- How to compose interfaces and check satisfaction at compile time

## The idea

An interface is a **set of method signatures**. Any type that has all of those methods satisfies the interface, automatically. There is no declaration like `class Rect implements Shape`.



```gopath-example
example-103
```



This has a big consequence: **the code that uses an interface can define it, without the implementations knowing about it.** You can write an interface that a type from the standard library, or from a third party package, already satisfies. Producers and consumers stay decoupled.

## Small interfaces

The most useful interfaces in Go have one or two methods: `io.Reader`, `io.Writer`, `fmt.Stringer`, `error`, `http.Handler`. The Go proverb says it directly: *the bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction.*



```gopath-example
example-104
```



Because `alertOnHighLoad` only asks for something that can `Notify`, a test can pass a tiny in-memory recorder instead of a real email sender. No mocking framework needed. This is the main way Go code is made testable.

By convention, one-method interfaces are named after the method plus `-er`: `Reader`, `Writer`, `Notifier`, `Closer`, `Stringer`.

## Interface values

An interface value holds two things: the **dynamic type** of the value stored in it, and the **value** itself.



```gopath-example
example-105
```



When you call a method on an interface value, Go looks up the method for the dynamic type and calls it. An interface with no type and no value is `nil`, and calling a method on it panics. Lesson 4.4 looks at the tricky case where the type is set but the value is a nil pointer.

## Method sets: `T` vs `*T`

Which methods does a type have, for the purpose of satisfying an interface?

| Type | Method set |
|---|---|
| `T` (a value) | methods with **value** receivers |
| `*T` (a pointer) | methods with value receivers **and** pointer receivers |

So if any method in an interface is implemented with a pointer receiver, only a **pointer** satisfies that interface:



```gopath-example
example-106
```



Why the asymmetry? A value stored in an interface is a copy that is not addressable, so Go could not take its address to call a pointer method. Methods that modify state need a pointer, and that requirement carries over to interfaces.

The line `var _ Resetter = (*Buffer)(nil)` is a **compile-time assertion**. It costs nothing at run time, and the build fails if `*Buffer` ever stops satisfying `Resetter`. Use it when a type is meant to implement an interface but nothing in the package would otherwise prove it.

## Composing interfaces

Interfaces can embed other interfaces, combining their method sets:



```gopath-example
example-107
```



The standard library does this throughout `io`: `io.ReadWriter`, `io.ReadCloser`, `io.ReadWriteCloser`. Build big interfaces from small ones, and let functions ask for only the small piece they need.

## Where to define interfaces

Define an interface **in the package that uses it**, not next to the implementation. A storage package should export a concrete `*PostgresStore`. The service that needs storage declares the two or three methods it actually calls. Lesson 4.8 develops this into the rule "accept interfaces, return structs".

Do not create an interface until you have a reason: a second implementation, a test double, or a function that should accept several types. An interface with exactly one implementation and no tests using it is usually just indirection.

## Common mistakes

### Large "god" interfaces

A `UserRepository` interface with 20 methods is hard to implement, hard to fake and couples every caller to all 20. Split it, or let each consumer declare what it uses.

### Defining interfaces on the producer side

Exporting `type Store interface` next to `type store struct` (and returning the interface) prevents callers from using any method you did not put in the interface. Return the concrete type.

### Forgetting the pointer when satisfying an interface

`cannot use b (variable of struct type Buffer) as Resetter value in variable declaration: Buffer does not implement Resetter (method Reset has pointer receiver)`. Pass `&b`.

### Pointers to interfaces

`*io.Reader` is almost never what you want. An interface value already holds a pointer when the dynamic type is a pointer. Pass interfaces by value.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m04/kv
```



## Key takeaways

- A type satisfies an interface by having its methods; there is no `implements`.
- Keep interfaces small, often a single method, named with `-er`.
- An interface value holds a dynamic type and a value.
- `*T` has both value and pointer methods; `T` only value methods. Pointer-receiver methods mean only `*T` satisfies.
- Define interfaces where they are used, and check satisfaction with `var _ I = (*T)(nil)`.

## Further reading

- [Interface types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Interface_types) and [Method sets](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Method_sets) in the spec
- [Effective Go: Interfaces](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#interfaces)
- [Go Proverbs](https://go-proverbs.github.io/), including "The bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction"
- [Go FAQ: Why doesn't Go have "implements" declarations?](https://go.dev/doc/faq#implements_interface)

lessons.title: 4.3 The empty interface, any, type assertions and type switches
lessons.description: What any is, how to get a concrete value back out with a type assertion, how type switches work, and how to check for optional capabilities.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What `any` (the empty interface) is and when it is appropriate
- How a **type assertion** extracts a concrete value, and its two forms
- How a **type switch** branches on the dynamic type
- How to assert to an **interface** to check for optional behavior

## The idea

`interface{}` has no methods, so **every type satisfies it**. Since Go 1.18 it has a shorter name: `any`. They are exactly the same type.

`any` is the escape hatch for values whose type is genuinely not known until run time: `fmt.Println(a ...any)`, JSON decoded into `map[string]any`, or a container that holds anything. The price is that the compiler can no longer check what you do with the value. You have to ask at run time, with type assertions and type switches.

Before Go had generics, `any` (as `interface{}`) was also used for generic containers. Today, prefer generics (lesson 4.6) when the type is the same throughout and only varies between uses.

## Type assertions



```gopath-example
example-108
```



- `v.(string)` returns the string, or **panics** if `v` does not hold a string.
- `n, ok := v.(int)` never panics. If the assertion fails, `ok` is `false` and `n` is the zero value.

Use the single-value form only when a wrong type is a programming error you want to crash on. Otherwise, use comma-ok.

## Type switches

To branch on several possible types, use a type switch:



```gopath-example
example-109
```



Details that matter:

- In a case with **one type**, `x` has that type (`len(x)` works in the `string` case).
- In a case with **several types** (`case int, int64:`) or in `default`, `x` keeps the interface type, because the compiler cannot know which one it is.
- `case nil` matches a nil interface.
- Cases can be **interfaces**, like `error` and `fmt.Stringer`. The first matching case wins, so order matters: put specific cases before general ones.

## Asserting to an interface: optional capabilities

A type assertion can target an interface, which asks "does this value **also** have these methods?". The standard library uses this to unlock faster paths:



```gopath-example
example-110
```



Real examples of the pattern:

- `io.Copy` checks whether the source implements `io.WriterTo` or the destination implements `io.ReaderFrom`, and lets them copy directly.
- `http.ResponseWriter` values may also implement `http.Flusher` for streaming responses.
- `fmt` checks for `fmt.Stringer`, `error` and `fmt.Formatter` before printing.

This keeps the required interface small (just `io.Reader`) while still letting capable types do better.

## When `any` is the wrong tool

Signs that `any` is hiding a design problem:

- A function takes `any` and immediately type-switches over three known types. Consider three functions, or an interface with a method each type implements.
- A struct field is `any` but always holds the same type. Use that type, or make the struct generic.
- `map[string]any` is passed deep into your program after JSON decoding. Decode into a struct with the fields you expect instead (lesson 8.2).

## Common mistakes

### Single-value assertions on untrusted data

`data["age"].(float64)` panics the moment the JSON has a string there. Use comma-ok and handle the failure.

### Expecting JSON numbers to be `int`

Decoding into `any` produces `float64` for every number. A type switch with only `case int:` never matches.

### Wrong case order in type switches

`case fmt.Stringer:` before `case MyType:` makes the second case unreachable if `MyType` has a `String` method.

### Asserting to the wrong pointer-ness

If an interface holds a `*User`, then `v.(User)` fails. The dynamic type must match exactly.

## Key takeaways

- `any` is `interface{}`: every type satisfies it, so the compiler cannot help you.
- `v.(T)` panics on mismatch; `v, ok := v.(T)` does not.
- A type switch branches on the dynamic type; single-type cases give you a typed variable.
- Asserting to an interface checks for optional capabilities, a pattern used throughout the standard library.
- Prefer concrete types, interfaces with methods, or generics over passing `any` around.

## Further reading

- [Type assertions](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Type_assertions) and [Type switches](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Type_switches) in the spec
- [Effective Go: Interface conversions and type assertions](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#interface_conversions)
- [The Laws of Reflection](https://go.dev/blog/laws-of-reflection), which explains interface values in depth

lessons.title: 4.4 Nil interfaces vs interfaces holding nil
lessons.description: Why an interface that holds a nil pointer is not equal to nil, how this breaks error checks, and the simple rule that avoids it.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why `err != nil` can be true even though "nothing went wrong"
- The (type, value) pair inside every interface value
- The rule that prevents the bug
- How to check for a typed nil when you really need to

## The bug

This is one of the most famous Go gotchas, and it almost always involves `error`:



```gopath-example
example-111
```



`validateBroken(true)` returns a value that **is not equal to `nil`**, even though the pointer inside it is nil. Every caller that writes `if err != nil` thinks validation failed.

## Why it happens

Recall from lesson 4.2 that an interface value is a pair: **(dynamic type, value)**. An interface is `nil` only when **both** are unset.



```gopath-example
example-112
```



| Interface value | Dynamic type | Value | `== nil` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `var e1 error` | none | none | **true** |
| `var e2 error = (*MyError)(nil)` | `*MyError` | nil pointer | **false** |
| `var e3 error = &MyError{"x"}` | `*MyError` | pointer | false |

In `validateBroken`, `err` is a variable of type `*MyError`. Returning it as an `error` converts it to an interface value whose type is `*MyError`. The type is set, so the interface is not nil, regardless of the pointer.

## The rule

**Never return a concrete pointer type through an interface when you mean "nothing".** Return a literal `nil`:

```go
func validate(ok bool) error {
	if !ok {
		return &MyError{Msg: "invalid"}
	}
	return nil
}
```

Related habits that keep you safe:

- Declare functions to return `error`, not `*MyError`. Functions returning concrete error types invite this bug at every call site that stores the result in an `error` variable.
- Do not keep a typed error variable around and return it at the end. Return `nil` explicitly on the success path.
- The same applies to any interface, not only `error`: returning a nil `*Logger` as a `Logger` interface produces a non-nil interface whose method calls panic.

## Detecting a typed nil

You rarely need to, but sometimes you must handle values from code you do not control. `errors.As` finds the typed nil (the second line of the pair example), after which you can compare the pointer to `nil`. For arbitrary interfaces, the `reflect` package can check `reflect.ValueOf(v).IsNil()` for pointer kinds. If you find yourself doing this often, fix the code that produces typed nils instead.

## Common mistakes

### Returning `*MyError` from a function

The function signature itself is the bug waiting to happen. Return `error`.

### A shared `var err *MyError` in a long function

Assigning only in failure branches and returning `err` at the end produces a typed nil on success.

### Assuming `fmt.Println(err)` reveals the problem

It prints `<nil>` for a typed nil, exactly like a real nil error, which makes the bug confusing to debug. Print with `%T` to see the dynamic type.

## Key takeaways

- An interface value is `nil` only if both its dynamic type and its value are unset.
- Storing a nil pointer in an interface gives a non-nil interface.
- Return a literal `nil` for "no error", and declare results as `error`, not concrete error types.
- `%T` in `fmt` shows the dynamic type when debugging.

## Further reading

- [Go FAQ: Why is my nil error value not equal to nil?](https://go.dev/doc/faq#nil_error)
- [The Laws of Reflection](https://go.dev/blog/laws-of-reflection)

lessons.title: 4.5 Common standard interfaces
lessons.description: fmt.Stringer, io.Reader, io.Writer and sort.Interface: the small interfaces that make Go's standard library composable, and how to implement them yourself.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How `fmt.Stringer` controls how your types print
- The `io.Writer` and `io.Reader` contracts, and how to implement them correctly
- Why these two tiny interfaces make streams composable
- How `sort.Interface` works, and why `slices.SortFunc` usually replaces it
- Other interfaces you will meet soon

## The idea

A handful of one-method interfaces in the standard library are implemented by hundreds of types. Learn them, and your own types instantly work with `fmt`, `io.Copy`, compression, hashing, HTTP bodies, files and more.

## `fmt.Stringer`

```go
type Stringer interface {
	String() string
}
```

When `fmt` prints a value with `%v`, `%s` or `Println`, it checks whether the value is a `Stringer` and calls `String()`:



```gopath-example
example-113
```



This finishes the `Weekday` enum from lesson 2.3. For long enums, generate `String()` with the `stringer` tool (lesson 1.4) instead of writing the switch by hand.



```gopath-callout
callout-9
```



## `io.Writer`

```go
type Writer interface {
	Write(p []byte) (n int, err error)
}
```

The contract: write `len(p)` bytes from `p` and return how many were written. If `n < len(p)`, `err` must be non-nil. `Write` must not modify `p` or keep it after returning.

Files, network connections, `bytes.Buffer`, `strings.Builder`, HTTP response writers, hashers and gzip compressors are all writers. A **wrapper** that adds behavior to any writer is a few lines:



```gopath-example
example-114
```



`fmt.Fprintf` and `io.WriteString` accept any `io.Writer`, so they work with `CountingWriter` without knowing it exists.

## `io.Reader`

```go
type Reader interface {
	Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)
}
```

The contract is subtle, and worth reading twice:

- `Read` fills **up to** `len(p)` bytes and returns how many it read. Fewer bytes than requested is normal.
- At the end of the data it returns `io.EOF`. It may return `n > 0` **together with** `io.EOF` on the last call.
- So callers must **process the `n` bytes first, then look at the error.**



```gopath-example
example-115
```



`upperReader` processes `p[:n]` and passes the error through, which keeps it correct for both cases. In practice you rarely call `Read` yourself; you hand readers to `io.Copy`, `io.ReadAll`, `bufio.Scanner` or `json.NewDecoder`, which handle the loop. Module 8 goes much deeper.

### Why this matters

Because readers and writers are so small, they **stack**. A typical pipeline in real code:

```go
f, _ := os.Open("access.log.gz")        // io.Reader: file
gz, _ := gzip.NewReader(f)              // io.Reader: decompressing
sc := bufio.NewScanner(gz)              // reads lines from it
```

Each layer only knows that the layer below is an `io.Reader`. Swap the file for an HTTP response body and nothing else changes.

## `sort.Interface`

```go
type Interface interface {
	Len() int
	Less(i, j int) bool
	Swap(i, j int)
}
```



```gopath-example
example-116
```



This is the pre-generics way to sort, and you will see it in older code and in data structures like `container/heap` (which builds on it). For sorting a slice today, `slices.SortFunc` (lesson 3.4) is shorter, faster and type safe.

## Interfaces you will meet next

| Interface | Package | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| `error` | built in | Module 5 |
| `io.Closer`, `io.ReadCloser`, `io.WriterTo`, `io.ReaderFrom` | `io` | 8.1 |
| `json.Marshaler`, `json.Unmarshaler` | `encoding/json` | 8.2 |
| `encoding.TextMarshaler` | `encoding` | 8.2 |
| `http.Handler` | `net/http` | 12.1 |
| `context.Context` | `context` | 7.1 |
| `heap.Interface` | `container/heap` | (builds on `sort.Interface`) |

## Common mistakes

### Recursion in `String()`

Using `%v` or `%s` on the receiver inside its own `String` method. Convert to the underlying type.

### Ignoring `n` when `Read` returns an error

Dropping the last chunk of data because `err == io.EOF` arrived with it. Handle `p[:n]` first.

### Treating `io.EOF` as a failure

`io.EOF` means "done", not "broken". Helpers like `io.ReadAll` and `bufio.Scanner` hide it from you; code that loops over `Read` itself must check `errors.Is(err, io.EOF)`.

### Defining a `String()` with a pointer receiver on a value type

`fmt` receives a copy, which does not have pointer methods, so your `String` is ignored. Use a value receiver for `String()` on small types.

## Key takeaways

- `fmt.Stringer` controls printing; avoid recursion inside `String()`.
- `io.Writer` and `io.Reader` are the backbone of streaming in Go, and wrappers compose freely.
- `Read` may return data and `io.EOF` together: process `n` bytes before checking the error.
- `sort.Interface` still exists, but `slices.SortFunc` is the modern way to sort slices.

## Further reading

- [Package io](https://pkg.go.dev/io), especially the Reader and Writer docs
- [Package fmt: Stringer](https://pkg.go.dev/fmt#Stringer)
- [Package sort](https://pkg.go.dev/sort)

- why these two tiny interfaces make streams composable
- how sort.interface works, and why slices.sortfunc usually replaces it
- other interfaces you will meet soon

 the idea

a handful of one-method interfaces in the standard library are implemented by hundreds of types. learn them, and your own types instantly work with fmt, io.copy, compression, hashing, http bodies, files and more.

 fmt.stringer



when fmt prints a value with %v, %s or println, it checks whether the value is a stringer and calls string():







this finishes the weekday enum from lesson 2.3. for long enums, generate string() with the stringer tool (lesson 1.4) instead of writing the switch by hand.







 io.writer



the contract: write len(p) bytes from p and return how many were written. if n < len(p), err must be non-nil. write must not modify p or keep it after returning.

files, network connections, bytes.buffer, strings.builder, http response writers, hashers and gzip compressors are all writers. a wrapper that adds behavior to any writer is a few lines:







fmt.fprintf and io.writestring accept any io.writer, so they work with countingwriter without knowing it exists.

 io.reader



the contract is subtle, and worth reading twice:

- read fills up to len(p) bytes and returns how many it read. fewer bytes than requested is normal.
- at the end of the data it returns io.eof. it may return n > 0 together with io.eof on the last call.
- so callers must process the n bytes first, then look at the error.







upperreader processes p[:n] and passes the error through, which keeps it correct for both cases. in practice you rarely call read yourself; you hand readers to io.copy, io.readall, bufio.scanner or json.newdecoder, which handle the loop. module 8 goes much deeper.

 why this matters

because readers and writers are so small, they stack. a typical pipeline in real code:



each layer only knows that the layer below is an io.reader. swap the file for an http response body and nothing else changes.

 sort.interface









this is the pre-generics way to sort, and you will see it in older code and in data structures like container/heap (which builds on it). for sorting a slice today, slices.sortfunc (lesson 3.4) is shorter, faster and type safe.

 interfaces you will meet next

| interface | package | lesson |
|---|---|---|
| error | built in | module 5 |
| io.closer, io.readcloser, io.writerto, io.readerfrom | io | 8.1 |
| json.marshaler, json.unmarshaler | encoding/json | 8.2 |
| encoding.textmarshaler | encoding | 8.2 |
| http.handler | net/http | 12.1 |
| context.context | context | 7.1 |
| heap.interface | container/heap | (builds on sort.interface) |

- [package io](https://pkg.go.dev/io), especially the reader and writer docs

- [package sort](https://pkg.go.dev/sort)

lessons.title: 4.6 Generics: type parameters and constraints
lessons.description: Write functions and types that work across many types with type parameters, constrain them with any, comparable, cmp.Ordered and type unions, and rely on type inference.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to declare generic functions and generic types
- What a **constraint** is: `any`, `comparable`, `cmp.Ordered`, method constraints and type unions
- What `~` means in a constraint
- How type inference saves you from writing type arguments
- How to get the zero value of a type parameter

## The idea

Generics (added in Go 1.18) let you write code once for many types, **without** losing compile-time type checking. Before generics you had two options: copy the code for every type, or use `any` and type assertions. Generics remove that trade-off for code like containers, algorithms over slices and maps, and helpers like `Map` or `Filter`.

A generic function declares **type parameters** in square brackets before its normal parameters. Each type parameter has a **constraint** that says which types are allowed and what you can do with them.

## Generic functions



```gopath-example
example-117
```



`Map[T, U any]` has two type parameters. You almost never write type arguments yourself: the compiler **infers** `T` and `U` from the arguments. Explicit type arguments (`Map[int, int]`) are needed only when inference has nothing to work from, for example when a type parameter appears only in the result.

## Constraints

A constraint is an interface. It limits which types can be used **and** decides which operations are allowed inside the function.



```gopath-example
example-118
```



| Constraint | Allows | Operations you can use |
|---|---|---|
| `any` | every type | assign, pass, return; no operators |
| `comparable` | types usable with `==` | `==`, `!=`, map keys |
| `cmp.Ordered` | integers, floats, strings | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, plus `==` |
| an interface with methods | types having those methods | call those methods |
| a type union | the listed types | operators all of them support |

Choose the **loosest** constraint that lets the function do its job. `IndexOf` only needs `==`, so it uses `comparable`, and callers can use it with structs. `MaxOf` needs `>`, so it requires `cmp.Ordered`.

### Type unions and `~`



```gopath-example
example-119
```



- `int | int64 | float64` is a **type union**: T must be one of those types, and you can use operators they all support (here `+`).
- `~float64` means "**any type whose underlying type is** `float64`". Without the tilde, `Celsius` would not be allowed, even though it is a `float64` underneath.
- Interfaces containing unions can only be used as constraints, not as ordinary variable types.

The `cmp.Ordered` constraint in the standard library is built exactly this way, as a union of `~int`, `~int8`, ..., `~float64` and `~string`.

### Method constraints



```gopath-example
example-120
```



Notice how `JoinNames` calls `Map` with a function on `T`: generic functions compose.

## Generic types

Types can have type parameters too. Methods on a generic type use the type's parameters (written in the receiver as `Stack[T]`):



```gopath-example
example-121
```



`var zero T` is how you get the zero value of a type parameter. It is needed whenever a generic function must return "nothing", as in `Pop` on an empty stack.

You must instantiate a generic type with concrete type arguments before using it: `Stack[string]`, `Stack[int]`. A `Stack[string]` and a `Stack[int]` are different, unrelated types.

## How generics compile

Go compiles generic code using a mix of specialization and runtime dictionaries (called "GC shape stenciling"). You do not need the details, but two consequences are worth knowing:

- Generic code is fully type checked at compile time. There are no runtime type errors from generics.
- Generic code is usually as fast as hand-written code, but not always. In hot paths, measure (Module 10) before assuming.

## Common mistakes

### Constraints that are too strict

`func Contains[T cmp.Ordered]` when you only use `==`. Callers cannot use it with structs or pointers. Use `comparable`.

### Forgetting `~` for named types

`Sum[T int | float64]` rejects `Celsius` and `time.Duration`. Add `~` unless you deliberately want only the exact types.

### Making everything generic

A function used with exactly one type does not need type parameters. Lesson 4.7 covers when generics hurt more than they help.

### Expecting methods to add new type parameters (before Go 1.27)

Until Go 1.27, methods could only use the type parameters of their receiver type. Lesson 4.7 covers the new generic methods.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m04/set
```



## Key takeaways

- Type parameters go in square brackets; the compiler usually infers type arguments.
- Constraints are interfaces that restrict types and enable operations: `any`, `comparable`, `cmp.Ordered`, method sets and type unions.
- `~T` includes all types whose underlying type is `T`.
- Generic types like `Stack[T]` must be instantiated, and `var zero T` gives a zero value.
- Pick the loosest constraint that works.

## Further reading

- [Tutorial: Getting started with generics](https://go.dev/doc/tutorial/generics)
- [An Introduction To Generics](https://go.dev/blog/intro-generics) on the Go blog
- [Type parameter declarations](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Type_parameter_declarations) in the spec
- [Package cmp](https://pkg.go.dev/cmp)

lessons.title: 4.7 Generic methods (Go 1.27) and when generics are the wrong tool
lessons.description: Methods with their own type parameters arrived in Go 1.27. Learn the syntax, the limits around interfaces, and the cases where generics make code worse.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to declare a method with its **own** type parameters (Go 1.27+)
- Why generic methods cannot implement interface methods
- When generics are the right tool, and when interfaces or plain code are better



```gopath-callout
callout-10
```



## Generic methods

Before Go 1.27, a method could only use the type parameters of its receiver. You could write `func (s *Stack[T]) Push(v T)`, but not a `Map` method that converts a `List[T]` into a `List[U]`, because `U` would be a new type parameter. The workaround was a top-level function, `Map(list, f)`.

Go 1.27 allows a method to declare its own type parameters:



```gopath-example
example-122
```



As with generic functions, the type arguments are usually inferred: `nums.Map(strconv.Itoa)` infers `U = string`. You can also supply them explicitly: `nums.Map[int](...)`.

Generic methods also work on types that are not generic at all:



```gopath-example
example-123
```



The standard library uses them too. The Go 1.27 release notes mention `math/rand/v2`'s `(*Rand).N`, which is generic over the integer type.

## The interface limitation

Interface methods still **cannot** have type parameters, and a generic method **cannot satisfy** a non-generic interface method, even if one instantiation would match:

```go
type Converter interface {
	Convert(func(int) string) string
}

type Box struct{ n int }

func (b Box) Convert[T any](f func(int) T) T { return f(b.n) }

var _ Converter = Box{}
```

```text
cannot use Box{} (value of struct type Box) as Converter value in variable declaration:
Box does not implement Converter (wrong type for method Convert)
	have Convert[T any](func(int) T) T
	want Convert(func(int) string) string
```

The reason is that interface method calls are resolved at run time, while generic code is instantiated at compile time. The compiler cannot know which instantiations a dynamic call might need. So:

- Use generic methods for **convenience APIs** on concrete types (fluent transformations, typed accessors).
- Use **interfaces** when you need run-time polymorphism.

## When generics are the wrong tool

Generics are a power tool. Signs you are reaching for them too early:

**You only have one type.** A function only ever called with `[]User` should take `[]User`. Make it generic when the second type actually appears.

**An interface describes the behavior better.** If the function calls methods on its argument and nothing else, a plain interface parameter is simpler:

```go
// Generic, but no benefit:
func Describe[T fmt.Stringer](v T) string { return v.String() }

// Simpler, works the same for callers:
func Describe(v fmt.Stringer) string { return v.String() }
```

Generics win over interfaces when you need to **keep the concrete type** in the result (a `Max` that returns the same type it was given, a container that hands back `T` without type assertions), or when you need **operators** like `<` or `+`.

**The type parameter list is getting long.** Three or four type parameters with interdependent constraints make APIs hard to read and errors hard to understand. Often the design wants to be split up.

**You are simulating inheritance.** Generic "base" types with hooks are usually a sign that small interfaces and composition (lessons 3.7 and 4.2) would be cleaner.

A good rule from the Go team: **write the code without generics first. If you find yourself writing the same code a second time for a different type, then consider type parameters.**

## Common mistakes

### Using generic methods where callers need an interface

If several types must be handled through one interface variable, generic methods cannot help. Use interface methods with concrete types.

### Requiring Go 1.27 without saying so

A library with generic methods forces every user onto Go 1.27 or newer. Set the `go` line in `go.mod` accordingly, and mention it in your README.

### Generic code with constraints that leak implementation details

A constraint listing six specific types because the current implementation uses `+` is fragile. Prefer standard constraints like `cmp.Ordered` or small method sets.

## Key takeaways

- Since Go 1.27, methods can declare their own type parameters, on generic and non-generic types.
- Generic methods cannot implement interface methods; interfaces still cannot have type parameters.
- Use generics to preserve concrete types or use operators across types; use interfaces for behavior and run-time polymorphism.
- Write it concretely first, and generalize when the duplication is real.

## Further reading

- [Go 1.27 release notes: generic methods](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)
- [When To Use Generics](https://go.dev/blog/when-generics) on the Go blog
- [Generic interfaces](https://go.dev/blog/generic-interfaces) on the Go blog

lessons.title: 4.8 Designing APIs: accept interfaces, return structs
lessons.description: Put methods, interfaces and generics together into clean package APIs: consumer-defined interfaces, constructors, useful zero values, config structs and functional options.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The rule "accept interfaces, return structs", and why it keeps packages decoupled
- When to write a constructor, and how to name it
- How to make zero values useful
- Two ways to handle optional settings: config structs and functional options
- A short checklist for reviewing a package API

## Accept interfaces, return structs



```gopath-example
example-124
```



Two halves, each with a reason:

- **Accept interfaces.** `greeting` asks only for something with `GetUser`. It works with the in-memory store, a Postgres store, a cache, or a test fake, and its signature documents exactly what it depends on.
- **Return structs.** `NewMemoryStore` returns `*MemoryStore`, not an interface. Callers get every method (including `AddUser`), can see the real type in their editor, and can define their own narrow interfaces as needed. Returning an interface would hide methods and force callers to type-assert.

The interface `userGetter` is **unexported and lives with the consumer**. That is normal in Go. Interfaces describe what a piece of code needs, so they belong to that code.

There are sensible exceptions: return an interface when the concrete type is genuinely private and may vary (`errors.New` returns `error`; `io.MultiReader` returns `io.Reader`), or when the standard API of your domain is an interface (`hash.Hash`).

## Constructors

Go has no constructors in the language. By convention, a function named `New` or `NewThing` builds a ready-to-use value:

- `NewMemoryStore() *MemoryStore` in a package with several types.
- `New() *Client` when the package has one main type, so callers write `redis.New()` rather than `redis.NewRedis()` (no stutter, lesson 1.5).

Write a constructor when the zero value is not usable (a map must be created, a required dependency must be passed) or when invariants must be checked. If the constructor can fail, return `(*T, error)`.

## Make the zero value useful

When you can, design types so that `var x T` already works: `sync.Mutex`, `bytes.Buffer`, `strings.Builder` and `http.Client` all do. Techniques:

- Treat zero fields as "use the default" (see the config example below).
- Create maps lazily on first write instead of in a constructor.
- Avoid required fields that cannot have a sensible zero value.

A useful zero value means fewer constructors, fewer nil panics, and types that can be embedded or declared in structs without ceremony.

## Optional settings

Go has no default arguments or keyword arguments. Two patterns fill the gap.

### Config structs



```gopath-example
example-125
```



Simple, explicit and easy to document. Every setting is a visible field, and zero means default. This is a good default choice, especially for internal packages and for settings loaded from config files.

### Functional options



```gopath-example
example-126
```



Each option is a function that modifies the value being built. This pattern shines when:

- the zero value of a setting is meaningful and cannot double as "default" (a timeout of 0 meaning "no timeout");
- options need validation or side effects;
- you want to add options over time without changing the constructor signature, as many public libraries (gRPC, Zap, OpenTelemetry) do.

The cost is more code and slightly less discoverable documentation. Do not use functional options for two or three settings in an internal package; a struct is clearer.

## An API review checklist

Before publishing a package, check:

1. Does each exported name need to be exported?
2. Do functions accept the **smallest** interface they need?
3. Do constructors return concrete types?
4. Is the zero value of each exported type either useful or clearly documented as not usable?
5. Are there names that stutter (`user.UserService`)?
6. Are errors returned as `error`, never as concrete pointer types (lesson 4.4)?
7. Is it documented whether types are safe for concurrent use?
8. Would a caller need `any` or type assertions to use it? If so, consider generics or a better interface.

## Common mistakes

### Exporting an interface plus a single implementation

`type Service interface {...}` with `type service struct` and `func New() Service`. Callers lose access to the concrete type, and adding a method to the interface breaks every other implementation. Export the struct.

### Constructors that do work

Opening network connections or starting goroutines inside `New` makes types hard to test and use. Prefer a separate `Start` or `Connect` method, or accept already connected dependencies.

### Too many functional options for a small type

A `NewPoint(WithX(1), WithY(2))` API is ceremony. Use a struct literal.

## Key takeaways

- Accept small interfaces defined by the consumer; return concrete types from constructors.
- Name constructors `New` or `NewThing`, and return `(T, error)` when construction can fail.
- Design for a useful zero value.
- Use config structs by default; reach for functional options in public APIs with many evolving settings.

## Further reading

- [Go Code Review Comments: Interfaces](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments#interfaces)
- [Effective Go: Constructors and composite literals](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#composite_literals)
- [Self-referential functions and the design of options](https://commandcenter.blogspot.com/2014/01/self-referential-functions-and-design.html) by Rob Pike
- [Dave Cheney: Functional options for friendly APIs](https://dave.cheney.net/2014/10/17/functional-options-for-friendly-apis)

a useful zero value means fewer constructors, fewer nil panics, and types that can be embedded or declared in structs without ceremony.

 optional settings

go has no default arguments or keyword arguments. two patterns fill the gap.

 config structs







simple, explicit and easy to document. every setting is a visible field, and zero means default. this is a good default choice, especially for internal packages and for settings loaded from config files.

 functional options







each option is a function that modifies the value being built. this pattern shines when:

- the zero value of a setting is meaningful and cannot double as "default" (a timeout of 0 meaning "no timeout");
- options need validation or side effects;
- you want to add options over time without changing the constructor signature, as many public libraries (grpc, zap, opentelemetry) do.

the cost is more code and slightly less discoverable documentation. do not use functional options for two or three settings in an internal package; a struct is clearer.

 an api review checklist

before publishing a package, check:

1. does each exported name need to be exported?
2. do functions accept the smallest interface they need?
3. do constructors return concrete types?
4. is the zero value of each exported type either useful or clearly documented as not usable?
5. are there names that stutter (user.userservice)?
6. are errors returned as error, never as concrete pointer types (lesson 4.4)?
7. is it documented whether types are safe for concurrent use?
8. would a caller need any or type assertions to use it? if so, consider generics or a better interface.

 exporting an interface plus a single implementation

type service interface {...} with type service struct and func new() service. callers lose access to the concrete type, and adding a method to the interface breaks every other implementation. export the struct.

opening network connections or starting goroutines inside new makes types hard to test and use. prefer a separate start or connect method, or accept already connected dependencies.

 too many functional options for a small type

a newpoint(withx(1), withy(2)) api is ceremony. use a struct literal.

- accept small interfaces defined by the consumer; return concrete types from constructors.
- name constructors new or newthing, and return (t, error) when construction can fail.
- design for a useful zero value.
- use config structs by default; reach for functional options in public apis with many evolving settings.

- [go code review comments: interfaces](https://go.dev/wiki/codereviewcommentsinterfaces)
- [effective go: constructors and composite literals](https://go.dev/doc/effectivegocompositeliterals)
- [self-referential functions and the design of options](https://commandcenter.blogspot.com/2014/01/self-referential-functions-and-design.html) by rob pike
- [dave cheney: functional options for friendly apis](https://dave.cheney.net/2014/10/17/functional-options-for-friendly-apis)

lessons.title: 5.1 Errors are values
lessons.description: The error interface, creating errors with errors.New and fmt.Errorf, the if err != nil pattern, custom error types, and how to write good error messages.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What the `error` type actually is
- How to create errors with `errors.New` and `fmt.Errorf`
- The `if err != nil` pattern, and why Go chose it over exceptions
- How to define your own error types with structured data
- How to write error messages that are useful in logs

## The idea

In Go, an error is just a value of the built-in interface type `error`:

```go
type error interface {
	Error() string
}
```

Anything with an `Error() string` method is an error. Functions that can fail return an `error` as their **last** result, and `nil` means success.

This is a deliberate choice. Exceptions make the failure path invisible: any line might throw, and the code that handles it can be far away. Go makes failure **explicit at every call site**. It costs some typing, and in exchange you can read a function and see exactly where it can fail and what happens when it does.

## Creating errors



```gopath-example
example-127
```



- `errors.New("text")` creates a fixed error.
- `fmt.Errorf(format, args...)` creates an error with a formatted message. With the `%w` verb it also **wraps** another error, which lesson 5.2 covers.

## Handling errors



```gopath-example
example-128
```



The shape is always the same:

```go
v, err := doSomething()
if err != nil {
	// handle it: return it (usually with context), retry, fall back, or report it
}
// use v
```

Rules of thumb:

- **Check the error before using the other results.** When `err != nil`, the other results are usually zero values or garbage.
- **Handle it or return it, once.** Do not log an error and then also return it; the caller will log it again and you get duplicates (lesson 5.6).
- **Add context when you return it.** `parsePort` says *which* input failed. The low-level `strconv` error alone would not tell you that.
- **Keep the happy path unindented.** Return early on errors, so the main logic reads top to bottom on the left margin.

## Custom error types

When callers need more than a message, define a type:



```gopath-example
example-129
```



`errors.As` checks whether an error (or anything it wraps) is a `*ValidationError` and, if so, gives you the typed value. This lets an HTTP handler, for example, return the offending field name to the client. Lesson 5.3 discusses when a type is better than a plain error value.

Use a **pointer receiver** for `Error()` on struct error types, and return them as `error` (never as `*ValidationError`), to avoid the nil interface trap from lesson 4.4.

## Writing good error messages

Go error messages are often **chained**: `load profile: find user 42: not found`. A few conventions keep the chain readable:

- **Start lowercase, no trailing punctuation.** Messages get embedded in other messages.
- **Describe what was being done**, not that "an error occurred": `open config: ...` rather than `error opening config: ...`.
- **Include the identifying values**: the file name, the ID, the input. Quote strings with `%q` so empty values and spaces are visible.
- **Do not include secrets**: passwords, tokens, full credit card numbers.

## Common mistakes

### Ignoring errors with `_`

`data, _ := os.ReadFile(path)` turns a missing file into silently empty data. If ignoring an error is truly correct, leave a comment saying why.

### Comparing error strings

`if err.Error() == "not found"` breaks when someone rewords the message or wraps it. Use `errors.Is` with a sentinel error or `errors.As` with a type (lesson 5.2).

### Capitalized messages with punctuation

`errors.New("Could not connect.")` produces `fetch: Could not connect.: timeout` once wrapped. Write `could not connect`.

### Returning a typed nil

Covered in lesson 4.4: declare results as `error` and return a literal `nil`.

## Key takeaways

- `error` is an interface with one method, `Error() string`; `nil` means success.
- Errors are returned as the last result and checked with `if err != nil`.
- Return errors with context, and handle each error once.
- Define error types when callers need structured information, and inspect them with `errors.As`.
- Messages are lowercase, without trailing punctuation, and say what was being attempted.

## Further reading

- [Error handling and Go](https://go.dev/blog/error-handling-and-go) on the Go blog
- [Errors are values](https://go.dev/blog/errors-are-values) by Rob Pike
- [Go Code Review Comments: Error strings](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments#error-strings)

lessons.title: 5.2 Wrapping with %w, errors.Is and errors.As
lessons.description: Add context to errors without losing the original, inspect wrapped errors with errors.Is, errors.As and errors.AsType, and make your own types unwrappable.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How `%w` wraps an error and builds an error chain
- The difference between `%w` and `%v` in `fmt.Errorf`
- How `errors.Is` and `errors.As` search the chain
- The generic `errors.AsType` (Go 1.26+)
- How to make your own error types participate with `Unwrap`

## The idea

Each layer of a program should add context to an error ("load profile", "find user 42") so the final message explains what happened. But callers also need to recognize the **original** cause ("not found") to decide what to do.

Wrapping gives you both. `fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err)` produces a new error whose message includes the context **and** which remembers `err` underneath. The result is a chain you can search.

## Wrapping and `errors.Is`



```gopath-example
example-130
```



After two layers of wrapping, `err == ErrNotFound` is false: `err` is a wrapper, not the sentinel itself. `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` walks down the chain, comparing each error, and finds it.

**Always use `errors.Is` instead of `==` for errors**, even if you think nothing wraps them today. Someone will add context later.

## `%w` vs `%v`



```gopath-example
example-131
```



The messages are identical, but only `%w` keeps the original error inspectable. When to use which:

- **`%w`** when callers may reasonably want to check the cause. This is the common case.
- **`%v`** when you deliberately want to **hide** the underlying error, so it does not become part of your API. For example, a storage package might not want callers to depend on the specific database driver errors it happens to use today.

## `errors.As`: finding a type in the chain



```gopath-example
example-132
```



`errors.As(err, &target)` looks for the first error in the chain that can be assigned to `target`'s type, and if found, stores it in `target` and returns true. You pass a **pointer to a variable** of the type you are looking for, here a `*fs.PathError`, so the argument is a `**fs.PathError`. `go vet` checks that you get this right.

Notice also that `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)` works on the wrapped `os.Open` error. The standard library's file errors are designed to be checked this way, on every operating system.

### `errors.AsType` (Go 1.26+)

Go 1.26 added a generic version that needs no target variable:



```gopath-example
example-133
```



It is type safe at compile time (you cannot pass the wrong kind of pointer) and faster than `errors.As`. Prefer it in modules whose `go` line is 1.26 or later.

## Your own wrapping types

A custom error type can wrap another error by implementing `Unwrap() error`:



```gopath-example
example-134
```



With `Unwrap`, both `errors.Is(err, ErrTimeout)` and `errors.As(err, &qe)` see through the type. Without it, the chain stops at `QueryError`.

`errors.Unwrap(err)` returns one level down, or `nil` if `err` does not wrap anything. You rarely call it directly; `Is` and `As` do the walking.

## How the chain is searched

For each error in the chain, starting with `err` itself:

- `errors.Is` reports true if the error `==` target, **or** the error has a method `Is(error) bool` that returns true for target.
- `errors.As` succeeds if the error is assignable to the target type, **or** has a method `As(any) bool` that returns true.
- Then it moves on to `Unwrap()`. If an error has `Unwrap() []error` (lesson 5.4), the search goes depth-first through each wrapped error.

Custom `Is` methods let one error match a category; lesson 5.3 shows an example.

## Common mistakes

### Wrapping with `%v` and then calling `errors.Is`

`%v` flattens to a string. If callers must check the cause, use `%w`.

### Passing a non-pointer to `errors.As`

`errors.As(err, pathErr)` instead of `errors.As(err, &pathErr)` panics. `go vet` catches it.

### Wrapping the same context at every layer

`read config: read config: open config.yaml: ...` happens when both caller and callee add the same words. Each layer should add only what **it** knows: the function name, the ID it was working on.

### Wrapping errors from your dependencies into your public API without thinking

Everything you wrap with `%w` becomes something callers might check. Be intentional about it, especially in libraries.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m05/config
```



## Key takeaways

- `fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err)` adds context and keeps the original error in a chain.
- Compare errors with `errors.Is`, never `==`.
- Extract typed errors with `errors.As(err, &target)`, or `errors.AsType[T](err)` in Go 1.26+.
- Use `%v` to hide an underlying error on purpose.
- Implement `Unwrap() error` on wrapping error types.

## Further reading

- [Working with Errors in Go 1.13](https://go.dev/blog/go1.13-errors) on the Go blog
- [Package errors](https://pkg.go.dev/errors)
- [Go 1.26 release notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.26) for `errors.AsType`

lessons.title: 5.3 Sentinel errors vs custom error types
lessons.description: Three ways to let callers recognize errors: sentinel values, error types and behavior interfaces. When to use each, and what each commits you to.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What **sentinel errors** are and when they fit
- When an **error type** is better than a sentinel
- How **behavior checks** keep errors opaque but still useful
- How a custom `Is` method makes one error match a category
- How each choice affects your package's API

## The idea

Once callers need to react differently to different failures, your package has to offer them a way to tell errors apart. There are three common designs, and each one becomes part of your public API, so choose deliberately.

## Sentinel errors

A sentinel is an exported variable holding a specific error value. Callers check for it with `errors.Is`:



```gopath-example
example-135
```



Sentinels are named `ErrSomething`. The standard library is full of them: `io.EOF`, `fs.ErrNotExist`, `sql.ErrNoRows`, `context.Canceled`, `http.ErrServerClosed`.

**Use a sentinel when** the caller only needs to know **which** condition occurred, and there is no extra data to convey: not found, unauthorized, already exists, end of input.

## Error types

When callers need **data** about the failure, use a type:



```gopath-example
example-136
```



Examples from the standard library: `*fs.PathError` (operation and path), `*strconv.NumError` (function and input), `*net.OpError`, `*json.SyntaxError` (byte offset).

**Use an error type when** callers need fields: how long to wait, which field was invalid, which line failed, which HTTP status the upstream returned.

## Behavior checks: opaque errors

Sometimes you do not want callers to depend on either a specific value or a specific type. Instead, they ask **"can this error do X?"** through a small interface:



```gopath-example
example-137
```



The concrete error type can stay unexported and change freely. `net.Error` uses this idea with its `Timeout() bool` method, so callers can retry timeouts without knowing which of many network error types they got.

**Use a behavior check when** many different errors share a property callers care about (retryable, timeout, permanent), especially across package boundaries.

## Matching a category with `Is`

An error type can define `Is(target error) bool` to say "I count as that error too":



```gopath-example
example-138
```



This combines the two styles: callers who only care about the category check `errors.Is(err, ErrServer)`, while callers who need the status code use `errors.As` to get the `*HTTPError`.

## Choosing

| Caller needs to know | Use | Commits you to |
|---|---|---|
| Which condition happened | Sentinel `ErrX` | Keeping that variable and returning it (wrapped) in those cases |
| Details about the failure | Error type | Keeping the type and its fields |
| Whether a property holds | Behavior interface | Keeping the method |
| Nothing, just that it failed | Plain `fmt.Errorf` | Nothing |

Start with the last row. Many errors only need a good message. Add a sentinel or type when a real caller needs to branch on it.

## Common mistakes

### Too many sentinels

A package with thirty `ErrX` variables usually has callers that check only two. Every sentinel is API you must keep. Export only what callers need.

### Returning an error type by value in some places and by pointer in others

`errors.As` with `*MyError` will not find a `MyError` value. Be consistent; pointer receivers and pointer returns are the usual choice.

### Making sentinels mutable

`var ErrNotFound = errors.New(...)` is a variable, and someone could reassign it. That is a theoretical risk that the community accepts; the convention is simply never to assign to them.

### Leaking internal error types

Returning a database driver's error type straight to your callers makes them depend on your choice of driver. Translate it to your own sentinel or type at the package boundary.

## Key takeaways

- Sentinel errors (`ErrX`) identify a condition; check them with `errors.Is`.
- Error types carry data; extract them with `errors.As`.
- Behavior interfaces keep errors opaque but let callers test a property like "temporary".
- A custom `Is` method lets an error match a category.
- Everything you export becomes API. Start with plain errors and add structure when callers need it.

## Further reading

- [Don't just check errors, handle them gracefully](https://dave.cheney.net/2016/04/27/dont-just-check-errors-handle-them-gracefully) by Dave Cheney
- [Working with Errors in Go 1.13](https://go.dev/blog/go1.13-errors)
- [Package net: Error interface](https://pkg.go.dev/net#Error)

lessons.title: 5.4 errors.Join and multi-errors
lessons.description: Return several errors at once with errors.Join and multiple %w verbs, and inspect them with errors.Is, errors.As and Unwrap() []error.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- When reporting several errors at once is better than stopping at the first
- How `errors.Join` combines errors, and how it formats them
- How to wrap several errors with multiple `%w` verbs
- How `errors.Is` and `errors.As` search joined errors
- How to iterate over the individual errors

## The idea

Most functions stop at the first error. Some should not:

- **Validation**: tell the user about every invalid field in one response, not one per submission.
- **Cleanup**: when closing five resources, try all five and report every failure.
- **Fan-out work**: several independent operations ran; some failed.

Since Go 1.20 the standard library supports errors that wrap **more than one** error.

## `errors.Join`



```gopath-example
example-139
```



- `errors.Join(errs...)` returns an error wrapping all non-nil arguments.
- It returns **`nil`** if every argument is `nil` (or there are none), so you can always `return errors.Join(errs...)`.
- Its message is the messages of the joined errors, separated by newlines.
- `errors.Is` and `errors.As` find any of the joined errors.

## Multiple `%w` verbs

`fmt.Errorf` can wrap several errors at once:



```gopath-example
example-140
```



Use this when you want a custom one-line message rather than the newline-separated format of `Join`.

## Getting the individual errors

An error that wraps several errors implements `Unwrap() []error` (plural). `errors.Unwrap` only understands the single-error form, which is why it returned `nil` above. To list the errors, assert to the interface:

```go
if multi, ok := err.(interface{ Unwrap() []error }); ok {
	for _, e := range multi.Unwrap() {
		fmt.Println("-", e)
	}
}
```

You will do exactly this in the exercise to collect the names of failed form fields.

## Joining errors from cleanup

A pattern for functions that must release several resources:

```go
func (s *Server) Close() error {
	return errors.Join(
		s.listener.Close(),
		s.db.Close(),
		s.cache.Close(),
	)
}
```

Every `Close` runs (Go evaluates all arguments), nil results are dropped, and the caller learns about every failure.

## Common mistakes

### Returning a slice of errors

`func Validate() []error` forces every caller to check `len(errs) > 0` and does not compose with `error`-returning code. Return `errors.Join(errs...)`.

### Expecting one-line messages from `Join`

The newline-separated output can look odd in a single-line log. Format it yourself with multiple `%w`, or log the joined error as a structured field.

### Calling `errors.Unwrap` on a joined error

It returns `nil`. Use `errors.Is`, `errors.As`, or the `Unwrap() []error` interface.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m05/form
```



## Key takeaways

- Report several errors at once for validation, cleanup and fan-out work.
- `errors.Join` returns nil for no errors, joins messages with newlines, and works with `errors.Is` and `errors.As`.
- `fmt.Errorf` accepts several `%w` verbs.
- Errors wrapping several errors implement `Unwrap() []error`, which `errors.Unwrap` does not follow.

## Further reading

- [Go 1.20 release notes: wrapping multiple errors](https://go.dev/doc/go1.20#errors)
- [Package errors: Join](https://pkg.go.dev/errors#Join)

lessons.title: 5.5 panic and recover: when, and mostly when not
lessons.description: What a panic is, what causes them, how recover works, the narrow cases where panicking is right, and why a panic in any goroutine crashes the whole program.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What happens when a program panics
- The common causes of run-time panics
- How `recover` works, and why it only works inside a deferred function
- The few situations where calling `panic` yourself is correct
- How to recover at boundaries, and why goroutines need special care

## The idea

A **panic** stops normal execution of the current goroutine. Deferred functions run as the stack unwinds, and if nothing recovers, the program **crashes** and prints the panic value and a stack trace for every goroutine.

Panics are for **bugs and impossible situations**, not for expected failures. A missing file, bad user input or a network timeout are expected; they return `error`. An index out of range, a nil pointer dereference or a broken invariant are bugs; they panic.

## Run-time panics



```gopath-example
example-141
```



The runtime panics on: out-of-range indexes and slices, nil pointer dereferences, writes to nil maps, failed single-value type assertions, integer division by zero, closing a closed channel, sending on a closed channel, and calling `yield` after an iterator was told to stop.

## When it is right to panic

1. **Programmer errors that cannot be handled sensibly.** A function documented as "panics if n < 0" called with -1. The standard library does this, for example `strings.Repeat` with a negative count.
2. **Initialization of values fixed in the code.** `regexp.MustCompile`, `template.Must`: if the pattern written in the source is invalid, the program is broken and should fail immediately at startup.
3. **Truly impossible states.** A `default` branch of a switch over an enum that should never be reached, as an assertion.



```gopath-example
example-142
```



The convention: functions that panic instead of returning an error are named `MustXxx`, and have an error-returning sibling `Xxx` for input that is not under your control.

## `recover`

`recover()` stops a panic and returns the value passed to `panic`. It only has an effect when called **directly inside a deferred function** during a panic. Anywhere else it returns `nil`.



```gopath-example
example-143
```



The deferred closure converts the panic into an error by setting the **named result** `err`, the technique from lesson 2.7.

### Recover at boundaries only

Recovering everywhere hides bugs. Recover at the **boundary** of an independent unit of work, where crashing everything would be worse than failing one unit:

- an HTTP request handler (the standard `net/http` server already recovers panics per request and logs them);
- a job in a worker pool;
- a call into a plugin or user-supplied callback.

After recovering, **log the panic with its stack trace** (`runtime/debug.Stack()`), fail that unit of work, and keep the service running.

### Recover selectively



```gopath-example
example-144
```



If you recover a panic you do not understand, **re-panic** it. Swallowing unknown panics leaves the program running in a state you cannot reason about.

## Panics and goroutines

`recover` only catches panics in the **same goroutine**. A panic in a goroutine you started, with no recover in that goroutine, **crashes the entire program**, no matter how many recovers exist in `main` or the HTTP handler that started it:

```go
func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	go func() {
		var m map[string]int
		m["x"] = 1 // crashes the whole server, not just this request
	}()
}
```

If a goroutine runs code that might panic (third party callbacks, complex parsing), put a deferred recover at the top of that goroutine. Module 7 shows how worker pools and `errgroup` handle this.

## Common mistakes

### Using panic for ordinary errors

`panic(err)` on a failed database query turns a recoverable situation into a crash. Return the error.

### Using recover as try/catch

Wrapping ordinary code in recover to "handle" errors produces code that is slow, surprising and hard to follow. Go's error handling is `if err != nil`.

### Forgetting that `os.Exit` and `log.Fatal` skip defers and recovers

`log.Fatal` is not a panic. Deferred functions do not run. Use it only in `main`, if at all.

### Panicking across a package boundary

A library that panics on bad input forces every caller to add recovers. Libraries should return errors, and panic only on programmer errors that are documented.

## Key takeaways

- Panics are for bugs and impossible states; expected failures return `error`.
- `MustXxx` helpers panic on invalid constants at startup; use their error-returning siblings for runtime input.
- `recover` works only in a deferred function, in the same goroutine.
- Recover at boundaries (requests, jobs), log the stack, and re-panic what you do not understand.
- An unrecovered panic in any goroutine crashes the whole program.

## Further reading

- [Defer, Panic, and Recover](https://go.dev/blog/defer-panic-and-recover) on the Go blog
- [Handling panics](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Handling_panics) and [Run-time panics](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Run_time_panics) in the spec
- [Effective Go: Panic](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#panic) and [Recover](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#recover)
