lessons.title: 5.6 Error handling patterns in real codebases
lessons.description: Where errors should be handled, logged, translated and retried in a real service, plus patterns that reduce repetitive error checks.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Where in a program each error should be handled
- The "handle once" rule: log **or** return, not both
- How to translate domain errors into HTTP status codes at the edge
- How to retry only the errors that retrying can fix
- Patterns that keep repetitive error checks readable

## The idea

Errors flow **up** the call stack. Each layer has a different job:

| Layer | Job with errors |
|---|---|
| Low level (database, file, HTTP client) | Return errors with context, using sentinels or types where callers need them |
| Domain (business logic) | Translate low level errors into domain errors (`ErrNotFound`, `ErrConflict`), add context |
| Edge (HTTP handler, CLI `main`, worker loop) | **Decide**: map to a status code or exit code, log once, show a safe message to the user |

Most code is in the first two layers and simply returns. Only the edge handles.

## Handle each error once

```go
// Wrong: the error is logged here AND by the caller.
if err != nil {
	log.Printf("could not load user: %v", err)
	return err
}
```

Logging and returning produces duplicate log lines, often with less context than the final one. The rule:

- If you **return** the error, add context and do not log.
- If you **handle** it (log it, fall back, show it to the user), do not return it.

The edge of the program logs, because that is where you know the full context (request ID, user, route).

## Translate at the edge



```gopath-example
example-145
```



One function maps domain errors to HTTP status codes. Handlers call it, the domain layer never imports `net/http`, and the mapping lives in exactly one place. Anything unrecognized is a 500, and the details stay in your logs rather than in the response. The URL shortener's HTTP layer in Module 12 uses exactly this.

## Retry only what can succeed



```gopath-example
example-146
```



Retrying a validation error wastes time and load: it will fail the same way every time. Classify errors (sentinel, type or behavior check from lesson 5.3) and retry only transient ones, with **exponential backoff**. Real retry loops also add jitter and respect `context` cancellation, which Module 7 adds.

## Reducing repetition

Go code has many `if err != nil` checks, and that is fine: they are explicit and easy to scan. When the same check repeats many times in a row, two patterns help.

### Remember the first error



```gopath-example
example-147
```



This is the idea behind `bufio.Writer` and `bufio.Scanner`: operations become no-ops after the first failure, and you check once at the end (`w.Flush()`, `sc.Err()`).

### Wrap once with a deferred helper

```go
func (s *Service) Sync(id string) (err error) {
	defer func() {
		if err != nil {
			err = fmt.Errorf("sync %s: %w", id, err)
		}
	}()
	// many return statements, each returning a bare err
}
```

Every error that leaves `Sync` gets the same context, added in one place (lesson 2.7).

## A checklist for reviewing error handling

1. Is every returned error checked?
2. Does each returned error add context the caller does not have?
3. Is each error logged at most once?
4. Are callers checking causes with `errors.Is` or `errors.As`, never by string?
5. Are internal details (SQL, stack traces, secrets) kept out of user-facing messages?
6. Are only transient errors retried, with backoff and a limit?
7. Do goroutines report errors back instead of dropping them? (Module 7)

## Common mistakes

### Logging deep in the stack

Library code that logs errors forces its logging style on every user and duplicates messages. Return errors; let the application log.

### Exposing internal errors to users

A 500 response body containing `pq: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "users_email_key"` leaks your schema. Map it to a domain error and a safe message.

### Retrying forever

A retry loop without a limit or a deadline turns an outage into a pile-up of stuck requests.

## Key takeaways

- Low layers return errors with context; domain layers translate them; the edge decides and logs.
- Handle each error once: log it or return it, never both.
- Map domain errors to status codes in one place at the edge.
- Retry only transient errors, with backoff and limits.
- Sticky-error writers and deferred wrapping reduce repetition without hiding errors.

## Further reading

- [Errors are values](https://go.dev/blog/errors-are-values) by Rob Pike
- [Error handling and Go](https://go.dev/blog/error-handling-and-go)
- [Google Go Style Guide: Errors](https://google.github.io/styleguide/go/best-practices#error-handling)

lessons.title: 5.7 Project milestone: URL shortener core
lessons.description: Milestone 1 of the URL shortener: a domain package with sentinel errors, validation, a Store interface, an in-memory store and a fully tested Service.
lessons.body:
## The project

Over the rest of the course you will build a URL shortener in milestones, each one using the module you just finished:

| Milestone | After module | Adds |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Core** (this lesson) | 5. Errors | Domain types, errors, validation, `Service`, in-memory store |
| 2. HTTP API | 12. HTTP services | JSON API, redirects, middleware |
| 3. Postgres | 13. Working with data | A database-backed `Store`, migrations |
| 4. Deploy | 15. Cloud native | Container image and Kubernetes manifests |

The code lives in [`projects/shortener`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/projects/shortener).

## The design

The core is a package called `link` with **no** knowledge of HTTP or databases:

- A `Link` struct.
- **Sentinel errors** callers can check: `ErrNotFound`, `ErrCodeTaken`, `ErrInvalidURL`, `ErrInvalidCode`.
- A small `Store` interface (two methods in this milestone; milestone 4 adds a third, `Delete`), defined in the package that uses it (lesson 4.8).
- A `Service` holding the rules: validate input, generate codes, retry on collisions.



```gopath-example
example-148
```



### Things to notice

- **Wrapping with context, keeping causes inspectable.** Errors look like `create "my-link": code already in use`, and `errors.Is(err, ErrCodeTaken)` still works through the wrapper.
- **Validation errors carry detail.** `ErrInvalidURL` is wrapped with `%w` alongside the specific reason, so the HTTP layer can return a helpful message and a 400 status.
- **Retry only the retryable error.** A random code collision (`ErrCodeTaken`) is retried; any other store error is returned immediately. After five collisions, the final error says so and still wraps `ErrCodeTaken`.
- **Dependencies are fields.** `now` and `rand` are function fields, set to real implementations by `NewService`. Tests replace them to get fixed timestamps and to force collisions, without any mocking library.
- **Unbiased random codes.** `randomCode` uses `crypto/rand` (unguessable) and rejects bytes that would cause modulo bias. The alphabet leaves out characters that look alike.
- **The context parameter** is part of the `Store` interface from the start, because the database store in milestone 3 will need it. Module 7 explains it.

## The in-memory store



```gopath-example
example-149
```



The `sync.RWMutex` makes the store safe for concurrent use, which matters once the HTTP server handles requests in parallel. Module 6 explains mutexes; for now, note that every method locks before touching the map.

## The tests



```gopath-example
example-150
```



Every error path is tested with `errors.Is`, including the collision retry logic, which would be very hard to trigger with real randomness.

```bash
go test -race ./projects/shortener/...
```

## Stretch goals

1. Add an `ErrReservedCode` for codes like `api`, `admin` and `health`, which the HTTP layer will need for its own routes. Return it from `validateCode`.
2. Add an optional expiry time to `Link`, and make `Resolve` return a new `ErrExpired` for expired links.
3. Write a `CountingStore` decorator (like the `kv` exercise in lesson 4.2) that counts resolves per code.

## Module 5 recap

You can now:

- Create, return and handle errors idiomatically
- Wrap errors with context and inspect them with `errors.Is`, `errors.As` and `errors.AsType`
- Choose between sentinels, error types and behavior checks
- Report several errors at once with `errors.Join`
- Use `panic` and `recover` only where they belong
- Structure error handling across the layers of a real service

That completes **Part 1: Fundamentals**. Next is **[Module 6: Concurrency fundamentals](/learn/06-concurrency-fundamentals/)**.

the code lives in [projects/shortener](https://github.com/priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/projects/shortener).

 the design

the core is a package called link with no knowledge of http or databases:

- a link struct.
- sentinel errors callers can check: errnotfound, errcodetaken, errinvalidurl, errinvalidcode.
- a small store interface (two methods in this milestone; milestone 4 adds a third, delete), defined in the package that uses it (lesson 4.8).
- a service holding the rules: validate input, generate codes, retry on collisions.







 things to notice

- wrapping with context, keeping causes inspectable. errors look like create "my-link": code already in use, and errors.is(err, errcodetaken) still works through the wrapper.
- validation errors carry detail. errinvalidurl is wrapped with %w alongside the specific reason, so the http layer can return a helpful message and a 400 status.
- retry only the retryable error. a random code collision (errcodetaken) is retried; any other store error is returned immediately. after five collisions, the final error says so and still wraps errcodetaken.
- dependencies are fields. now and rand are function fields, set to real implementations by newservice. tests replace them to get fixed timestamps and to force collisions, without any mocking library.
- unbiased random codes. randomcode uses crypto/rand (unguessable) and rejects bytes that would cause modulo bias. the alphabet leaves out characters that look alike.
- the context parameter is part of the store interface from the start, because the database store in milestone 3 will need it. module 7 explains it.

 the in-memory store







the sync.rwmutex makes the store safe for concurrent use, which matters once the http server handles requests in parallel. module 6 explains mutexes; for now, note that every method locks before touching the map.

 the tests







every error path is tested with errors.is, including the collision retry logic, which would be very hard to trigger with real randomness.



 stretch goals

1. add an errreservedcode for codes like api, admin and health, which the http layer will need for its own routes. return it from validatecode.
2. add an optional expiry time to link, and make resolve return a new errexpired for expired links.
3. write a countingstore decorator (like the kv exercise in lesson 4.2) that counts resolves per code.

 module 5 recap

you can now:

- create, return and handle errors idiomatically
- wrap errors with context and inspect them with errors.is, errors.as and errors.astype
- choose between sentinels, error types and behavior checks
- report several errors at once with errors.join
- use panic and recover only where they belong
- structure error handling across the layers of a real service

that completes part 1: fundamentals. next is [module 6: concurrency fundamentals](/learn/06-concurrency-fundamentals/).

lessons.title: 6.1 Goroutines and the cost model
lessons.description: Start concurrent work with the go statement, wait for it correctly, understand why goroutines are cheap, and how GOMAXPROCS controls parallelism.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to start a goroutine, and why you must always plan how it ends
- How to wait for goroutines with `sync.WaitGroup`
- Why goroutines are cheap compared to OS threads
- The difference between concurrency and parallelism, and what `GOMAXPROCS` does
- What happens to running goroutines when `main` returns

## The idea

A **goroutine** is a function running concurrently with the rest of the program. You start one by putting `go` in front of a function call:

```go
go sendEmail(user) // returns immediately; sendEmail runs concurrently
```

That is the whole syntax. The hard part is everything around it: knowing when the goroutine finishes, getting its results back, and making sure it does not outlive what it was working for. A good rule to adopt from day one: **never start a goroutine without knowing how it will stop.**

## Starting and waiting



```gopath-example
example-151
```



- `wg.Add(1)` before each `go` statement, `defer wg.Done()` inside the goroutine, `wg.Wait()` to block until all are done.
- Each goroutine writes to **its own index** of `results`, so they never touch the same memory. That is why no lock is needed here. (Since Go 1.22, `i` is a fresh variable per iteration, so each closure sees its own value.)
- Goroutines run in **no particular order**. Collecting results by index is one way to get a deterministic result.

## Goroutines are cheap



```gopath-example
example-152
```



Ten thousand goroutines start in milliseconds. Why so cheap?

| | OS thread | Goroutine |
|---|---|---|
| Initial stack | typically 1 to 8 MB, fixed | a few KB, grows and shrinks as needed |
| Created and scheduled by | the operating system kernel | the Go runtime, in user space |
| Switching cost | a kernel context switch | a much cheaper switch inside the runtime |
| Practical count | thousands | hundreds of thousands, even millions |

The Go runtime multiplexes many goroutines onto a small number of OS threads (the **M:N scheduler**, covered in lesson 11.1). When a goroutine blocks on a channel, a lock, a sleep or network I/O, the runtime parks it and runs another one on the same thread.

Cheap does not mean free. Every goroutine holds its stack and whatever it references, and a goroutine that never ends is a **memory leak** (lesson 7.6).

## Concurrency vs parallelism

- **Concurrency** is structuring a program as independently executing tasks.
- **Parallelism** is actually running several of them at the same instant, on several CPU cores.

Go gives you concurrency through goroutines; the runtime provides parallelism by running goroutines on up to **`GOMAXPROCS`** threads at once. By default `GOMAXPROCS` is the number of CPUs available.

Since Go 1.25, on Linux the default also respects the **container CPU limit** (the cgroup CPU quota). A Go service in a Kubernetes pod limited to 2 CPUs uses `GOMAXPROCS=2` even on a 64-core node, and the runtime updates it if the limit changes. Before 1.25, people used a library such as `automaxprocs` for this; with current Go you usually do not need it.

## When `main` returns

When `main` returns (or `os.Exit` is called), the program ends **immediately**. Running goroutines are not waited for, and their deferred functions do not run.



```gopath-example
example-153
```



The work in the goroutine is simply lost. In a real program, any goroutine doing something important (writing a file, sending a request, flushing logs) must be waited for before `main` returns. Lesson 7.7 covers graceful shutdown.

## Common mistakes

### Calling `wg.Add` inside the goroutine

```go
go func() {
	wg.Add(1) // too late: Wait may already have returned
	defer wg.Done()
}()
```

Always `Add` before the `go` statement. `go vet` has a `waitgroup` analyzer (Go 1.25+) that reports this.

### Fire and forget

`go doSomething()` with no way to know when it ends, whether it failed, or how to stop it. Every goroutine needs an owner who waits for it and a way to signal it to stop (`context`, lesson 7.1).

### Using `time.Sleep` to "wait for goroutines"

Sleeping makes tests slow and flaky. Use a `WaitGroup`, a channel, or `testing/synctest` (lesson 6.3).

### Unbounded goroutines per request

Starting one goroutine per item for a million items works on your laptop and falls over in production. Bound concurrency with a worker pool (lesson 7.2).

## Key takeaways

- `go f()` starts `f` concurrently and returns at once.
- Wait for goroutines with `sync.WaitGroup`: `Add` before `go`, `Done` in a `defer`, then `Wait`.
- Goroutines start small and are scheduled by the runtime, so you can run very many of them.
- `GOMAXPROCS` limits parallelism; since Go 1.25 it respects container CPU limits on Linux.
- When `main` returns, everything stops. Plan how every goroutine ends.

## Further reading

- [Effective Go: Goroutines](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#goroutines)
- [Concurrency is not parallelism](https://go.dev/blog/waza-talk), Rob Pike's talk
- [Container-aware GOMAXPROCS](https://go.dev/blog/container-aware-gomaxprocs) on the Go blog
- [Go 1.25 release notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.25)

lessons.title: 6.2 Channels: unbuffered, buffered, direction
lessons.description: Send and receive values between goroutines, the difference between unbuffered and buffered channels, closing and ranging, direction types and ownership rules.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How channels pass values **and** synchronize goroutines
- The difference between unbuffered and buffered channels
- How closing works, and how `range` and comma-ok receives detect it
- How direction types (`chan<-`, `<-chan`) enforce who sends and who receives
- The ownership rules that keep channel code correct

## The idea

A **channel** is a typed pipe between goroutines. One goroutine sends a value with `ch <- v`; another receives it with `v := <-ch`.

Channels do two jobs at once: they **move data**, and they **synchronize**, because sends and receives block until the other side is ready (or the buffer has room). Go's motto captures the design: *Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating.*

## Unbuffered channels



```gopath-example
example-154
```



`make(chan string)` creates an **unbuffered** channel. A send blocks until a receiver takes the value, and a receive blocks until a sender provides one. The two goroutines meet at that moment, like a hand-off. This makes unbuffered channels a strong synchronization tool: when the send completes, you **know** the receiver has the value.

## Buffered channels



```gopath-example
example-155
```



`make(chan int, n)` creates a channel with a buffer of `n` values. Sends block only when the buffer is full; receives block only when it is empty. `len(ch)` and `cap(ch)` report the current number of buffered values and the capacity.

Use a buffer when you know how many values will be sent and want the sender not to wait (for example, a result channel with one slot per worker), or to absorb short bursts. Do **not** add a buffer to "fix" a deadlock; that usually just moves it.

## Closing and ranging



```gopath-example
example-156
```



- `close(ch)` signals "no more values will be sent".
- `for v := range ch` receives until the channel is closed **and** drained.
- After close, buffered values are still delivered. Then every receive returns the zero value immediately, and the comma-ok form `v, ok := <-ch` reports `ok == false`.
- Closing is optional. You only need to close when receivers need to know that the stream ended (for example, to stop a `range`).

The generator pattern in `produce` is idiomatic: a function creates a channel, starts a goroutine that sends and then closes it, and returns the channel as **receive-only**.

## Direction types



```gopath-example
example-157
```



- `chan<- T` can only send.
- `<-chan T` can only receive.
- A normal `chan T` converts to either automatically.

Use direction types in function signatures. They document intent and turn mistakes (receiving on an output channel, closing an input channel) into compile errors.

## Closing as a broadcast



```gopath-example
example-158
```



A receive on a closed channel succeeds immediately, so **closing a channel wakes every goroutine waiting on it**. `chan struct{}` is the conventional type for pure signals, because the values carry no data. `context.Context`'s `Done()` channel (lesson 7.1) works exactly this way.

## The rules of channel ownership

| Operation | nil channel | closed channel |
|---|---|---|
| send `ch <- v` | blocks forever | **panics** |
| receive `<-ch` | blocks forever | returns zero value, `ok == false` |
| `close(ch)` | **panics** | **panics** |

From that table follow the rules:

1. **Only the sender closes**, and only when it is the last sender. A receiver closing a channel can make the sender panic.
2. **Close at most once.** With several senders, use a `sync.WaitGroup` and close from a separate goroutine after all senders finish (exactly what `Merge` in the exercise does).
3. **The function that creates a channel usually owns it**: it sends, closes, and hands out the receive-only end.

## Common mistakes

### Deadlock: nobody on the other side

```go
ch := make(chan int)
ch <- 1 // fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!
```

The runtime detects when every goroutine is blocked and crashes with this message. In a larger program, a missing receiver usually shows up as a goroutine that never ends instead.

### Closing from the receiving side

Leads to `panic: send on closed channel` in a sender. Signal the sender to stop (with a separate done channel or a context) instead.

### Forgetting to close, so `range` never ends

A `for v := range ch` loop waits forever if the sender returns without closing. Use `defer close(out)` at the top of the sending goroutine.

### Using channels where a mutex is simpler

Protecting a counter or a map with a channel-based "server goroutine" is valid but often more complex than a `sync.Mutex`. Use channels to pass ownership of data or signal events; use mutexes to guard shared state (lesson 6.4).

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m06/pipeline
```



## Key takeaways

- Channels move values and synchronize goroutines.
- Unbuffered channels hand off directly; buffered channels decouple sender and receiver up to the buffer size.
- `close` signals the end of a stream; `range` and comma-ok receives detect it; closing wakes all receivers.
- Use direction types in signatures.
- The sender closes, exactly once; sending on or closing a closed channel panics.

## Further reading

- [Effective Go: Channels](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#channels)
- [Share Memory By Communicating](https://go.dev/blog/codelab-share) on the Go blog
- [Channel types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Channel_types) and [Close](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Close) in the spec

lessons.title: 6.3 select, timeouts and time.After pitfalls
lessons.description: Wait on several channel operations with select, implement timeouts and non-blocking sends, use timers and tickers correctly, and test time-dependent code with testing/synctest.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How `select` waits on several channel operations at once
- How to add a timeout to any blocking operation
- Non-blocking sends and receives with `default`
- How a nil channel disables a `select` case
- Timers and tickers, and what changed about them in Go 1.23
- Testing time-based code deterministically with `testing/synctest` (Go 1.25+)

## The idea

`select` is like a `switch` for channel operations. It blocks until **one** of its cases can proceed, then runs that case. If several are ready at the same time, it picks one **at random**, so no case can starve the others.



```gopath-example
example-159
```



## Timeouts

Combining a real operation with a timer channel gives you a timeout:



```gopath-example
example-160
```



`time.After(d)` returns a channel that receives a value after `d`. Notice that `slowLookup` uses a **buffered** channel of size one. When the timeout wins, nobody ever reads the result; with an unbuffered channel the goroutine would block on its send **forever**, leaking it. A buffer of one lets it deliver and exit. This small detail is one of the most common sources of goroutine leaks (lesson 7.6).

In real code, timeouts are usually expressed with `context.WithTimeout` instead, which composes across function calls and goroutines (lesson 7.1). The `select` mechanics are the same: you wait on `ctx.Done()`.

## Non-blocking operations

A `default` case runs immediately if no other case is ready:



```gopath-example
example-161
```



This is useful for dropping work when a queue is full (load shedding), for polling, and for "try" operations. Do not put a `default` in a `select` inside a busy loop: it turns blocking into spinning at 100% CPU.

## Disabling a case with a nil channel

Operations on a nil channel block forever, so a nil channel's case in a `select` can never be chosen. Setting a channel variable to `nil` is the idiomatic way to stop listening to it:



```gopath-example
example-162
```



When one input closes, its variable is set to `nil`, and the loop keeps receiving from the other until both are done.

## Timers and tickers



```gopath-example
example-163
```



- `time.NewTimer(d)` fires once; `time.NewTicker(d)` fires repeatedly. Both deliver on their channel `C`.
- Call `Stop` when you are done, typically with `defer`.
- `time.Tick` is a convenience for long-lived tickers you never stop.

### What changed in Go 1.23

Older articles warn that `time.After` inside a loop leaks memory until each timer fires, and describe complicated rules for `Reset` and `Stop`. Go 1.23 changed timers so that:

- timers and tickers that are no longer referenced are garbage collected **even if not stopped**;
- timer channels are **synchronous** (unbuffered), so after `Stop` or `Reset` returns, no stale value will be received.

Go 1.27 removed the `asynctimerchan` setting that could bring back the old behavior. Calling `Stop` is still good practice (it frees resources sooner and documents intent), and `time.After` in a hot loop still allocates a timer per iteration, so prefer one `time.NewTimer` or a `context` deadline in loops.

## Testing time with `testing/synctest`

Code with timeouts is hard to test: real sleeps make tests slow, and short sleeps make them flaky. Go 1.25 added `testing/synctest`, which runs a test inside a **bubble** with a fake clock:



```gopath-example
example-164
```



Inside `synctest.Test`, time only advances when every goroutine in the bubble is blocked, and then jumps straight to the next timer. The 20 ms timeout fires after exactly 20 ms of virtual time, and the test finishes in microseconds of real time. `synctest.Wait()` waits until all goroutines in the bubble are blocked, which is useful to check state after background work settles. Module 9 uses it more.

## Common mistakes

### Leaking the goroutine that lost the race

A worker sending its result on an unbuffered channel blocks forever when the caller timed out and left. Give result channels a buffer of one, or make the worker also select on a done signal.

### `default` in a loop

Turns a waiting loop into a CPU-burning spin. Remove the `default` or block on something.

### Assuming `select` checks cases in order

When several cases are ready, the choice is random. If one case must take priority, check it first in a separate non-blocking `select`, or restructure the logic.

### Sleeping in tests

`time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond)` to "let the goroutine run" is slow and flaky. Use channels, `WaitGroup`s, or `synctest`.

## Key takeaways

- `select` blocks until one case can proceed, choosing randomly among ready cases.
- Combine an operation with `time.After` or a `context` to add a timeout, and make sure the losing goroutine can still exit.
- `default` makes a `select` non-blocking; a nil channel disables a case.
- Since Go 1.23, unreferenced timers are collected and timer channels are synchronous; still `Stop` timers and avoid `time.After` in hot loops.
- `testing/synctest` (Go 1.25+) gives tests a fake clock for deterministic timeout testing.

## Further reading

- [Select statements](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Select_statements) in the spec
- [Go 1.23 release notes: timer changes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.23#timer-changes)
- [Testing concurrent code with testing/synctest](https://go.dev/blog/synctest) on the Go blog
- [Package testing/synctest](https://pkg.go.dev/testing/synctest)

time.after(d) returns a channel that receives a value after d. notice that slowlookup uses a buffered channel of size one. when the timeout wins, nobody ever reads the result; with an unbuffered channel the goroutine would block on its send forever, leaking it. a buffer of one lets it deliver and exit. this small detail is one of the most common sources of goroutine leaks (lesson 7.6).

in real code, timeouts are usually expressed with context.withtimeout instead, which composes across function calls and goroutines (lesson 7.1). the select mechanics are the same: you wait on ctx.done().

 non-blocking operations

a default case runs immediately if no other case is ready:







this is useful for dropping work when a queue is full (load shedding), for polling, and for "try" operations. do not put a default in a select inside a busy loop: it turns blocking into spinning at 100% cpu.

 disabling a case with a nil channel

operations on a nil channel block forever, so a nil channel's case in a select can never be chosen. setting a channel variable to nil is the idiomatic way to stop listening to it:







when one input closes, its variable is set to nil, and the loop keeps receiving from the other until both are done.

 timers and tickers







- time.newtimer(d) fires once; time.newticker(d) fires repeatedly. both deliver on their channel c.
- call stop when you are done, typically with defer.
- time.tick is a convenience for long-lived tickers you never stop.

 what changed in go 1.23

older articles warn that time.after inside a loop leaks memory until each timer fires, and describe complicated rules for reset and stop. go 1.23 changed timers so that:

- timers and tickers that are no longer referenced are garbage collected even if not stopped;
- timer channels are synchronous (unbuffered), so after stop or reset returns, no stale value will be received.

go 1.27 removed the asynctimerchan setting that could bring back the old behavior. calling stop is still good practice (it frees resources sooner and documents intent), and time.after in a hot loop still allocates a timer per iteration, so prefer one time.newtimer or a context deadline in loops.

 testing time with testing/synctest

code with timeouts is hard to test: real sleeps make tests slow, and short sleeps make them flaky. go 1.25 added testing/synctest, which runs a test inside a bubble with a fake clock:







inside synctest.test, time only advances when every goroutine in the bubble is blocked, and then jumps straight to the next timer. the 20 ms timeout fires after exactly 20 ms of virtual time, and the test finishes in microseconds of real time. synctest.wait() waits until all goroutines in the bubble are blocked, which is useful to check state after background work settles. module 9 uses it more.

 common mistakes

 leaking the goroutine that lost the race

a worker sending its result on an unbuffered channel blocks forever when the caller timed out and left. give result channels a buffer of one, or make the worker also select on a done signal.

 default in a loop

turns a waiting loop into a cpu-burning spin. remove the default or block on something.

 assuming select checks cases in order

when several cases are ready, the choice is random. if one case must take priority, check it first in a separate non-blocking select, or restructure the logic.

 sleeping in tests

time.sleep(100  time.millisecond) to "let the goroutine run" is slow and flaky. use channels, waitgroups, or synctest.

 key takeaways

- select blocks until one case can proceed, choosing randomly among ready cases.
- combine an operation with time.after or a context to add a timeout, and make sure the losing goroutine can still exit.
- default makes a select non-blocking; a nil channel disables a case.
- since go 1.23, unreferenced timers are collected and timer channels are synchronous; still stop timers and avoid time.after in hot loops.
- testing/synctest (go 1.25+) gives tests a fake clock for deterministic timeout testing.

- [select statements](https://go.dev/ref/specselectstatements) in the spec
- [go 1.23 release notes: timer changes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.23timer-changes)
- [testing concurrent code with testing/synctest](https://go.dev/blog/synctest) on the go blog
- [package testing/synctest](https://pkg.go.dev/testing/synctest)

lessons.title: 6.4 sync.WaitGroup, WaitGroup.Go, Mutex, RWMutex and Once
lessons.description: Guard shared state with Mutex and RWMutex, wait for goroutines with WaitGroup and WaitGroup.Go, and initialize lazily with Once, OnceValue and OnceFunc.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to protect shared state with `sync.Mutex`
- When `sync.RWMutex` helps, and when it does not
- `sync.WaitGroup`, and the shorter `WaitGroup.Go` (Go 1.25+)
- Lazy, thread-safe initialization with `sync.Once`, `OnceValue` and `OnceFunc`
- When to choose a mutex over a channel

## The idea

Channels are great for passing data between goroutines. But many programs simply have **shared state** (a cache, a counter, a connection pool) that several goroutines read and modify. For that, the `sync` package's mutual exclusion locks are simpler and faster.

The rule is short: **if more than one goroutine accesses a variable and at least one of them writes, every access must be synchronized.**

## `sync.Mutex`



```gopath-example
example-165
```



- `Lock` blocks until the mutex is free; `Unlock` releases it.
- `defer mu.Unlock()` right after `Lock` guarantees the unlock even on early returns or panics.
- Put the mutex **next to the data it protects**, in the same struct, and make the fields unexported so the only way to reach them is through methods that lock.
- The zero value of a `Mutex` is an unlocked mutex. Never copy a mutex after first use; `go vet` reports copies (lesson 4.1).

Keep critical sections short: lock, touch the data, unlock. Do not hold a lock while doing I/O or calling unknown code, or every other goroutine waits behind you.

## `sync.RWMutex`



```gopath-example
example-166
```



An `RWMutex` allows **many readers at once** (`RLock`), or **one writer** (`Lock`). It helps when reads vastly outnumber writes **and** the read sections do noticeable work. For tiny critical sections it can be slower than a plain `Mutex`, because the bookkeeping costs more. Start with `Mutex`; switch to `RWMutex` when a benchmark (Module 10) shows lock contention on reads.

## `sync.WaitGroup`

You have used it since lesson 6.1. The full pattern for collecting results:



```gopath-example
example-167
```



`Add` must happen **before** the goroutine starts, so that `Wait` cannot return early.

### `WaitGroup.Go` (Go 1.25+)

Go 1.25 added a method that does the `Add`, `go` and `Done` for you:



```gopath-example
example-168
```



It removes the two most common `WaitGroup` mistakes (forgetting `Done`, calling `Add` inside the goroutine). Prefer it in modules targeting Go 1.25 or later.

## `sync.Once`, `OnceValue`, `OnceFunc`

`sync.Once` runs a function exactly once, even if many goroutines call it at the same time, and makes everyone wait until it has finished. Go 1.21 added helpers that are more convenient:



```gopath-example
example-169
```



- `sync.OnceFunc(f)` returns a function that calls `f` only the first time.
- `sync.OnceValue(f)` also caches `f`'s result.
- `sync.OnceValues(f)` caches a `(value, error)` pair.

Use them for lazy initialization of expensive, shared things: parsed templates, compiled regular expressions, a client created on first use.

## Mutex or channel?

| Situation | Prefer |
|---|---|
| Several goroutines read and update shared state (cache, counter, registry) | Mutex |
| Passing ownership of data from one goroutine to another | Channel |
| Distributing work to workers, collecting results | Channel |
| Signaling an event to many goroutines (shutdown) | Close a channel, or `context` |
| A simple counter or flag | `sync/atomic` (lesson 6.5) |

The Go wiki puts it well: use whichever is most expressive and simple for the problem. Mixing both in one design is common and fine.

## Other tools in `sync`

- `sync.Map`: a concurrent map optimized for two specific cases (keys written once and read many times, or goroutines working on disjoint keys). For everything else, a `map` plus a `Mutex` is simpler and often faster.
- `sync.Pool`: reuses temporary objects to reduce garbage collection pressure (lesson 10.6).
- `sync.Cond`: waits for a condition; rarely needed, as channels usually express the same thing more clearly.

## Common mistakes

### Forgetting to unlock on an early return

Without `defer`, any `return` or panic between `Lock` and `Unlock` leaves the mutex locked forever. Use `defer mu.Unlock()`.

### Copying a struct that contains a mutex

Passing it by value creates a second, independent lock, so the "protected" data is no longer protected. Use pointer receivers and `go vet`.

### Locking in the wrong order

Goroutine A locks `x` then `y`; goroutine B locks `y` then `x`. Each waits for the other forever. Always acquire multiple locks in the same order, or redesign to need only one.

### Returning internal maps or slices from locked methods

The caller then uses them **without** the lock. Return copies (as `Snapshot` does in the exercise).

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m06/parallel
```



## Key takeaways

- Synchronize every access to a variable that is shared and written.
- `Mutex` with `defer Unlock`, kept next to the data it guards, is the default tool for shared state.
- `RWMutex` pays off only when reads dominate and are not trivial.
- `WaitGroup` waits for goroutines; `WaitGroup.Go` (Go 1.25+) removes common mistakes.
- `OnceValue` and friends give thread-safe lazy initialization.

## Further reading

- [Package sync](https://pkg.go.dev/sync)
- [Go wiki: Use a sync.Mutex or a channel?](https://go.dev/wiki/MutexOrChannel)
- [Go 1.25 release notes: WaitGroup.Go](https://go.dev/doc/go1.25)

lessons.title: 6.5 sync/atomic and atomic types
lessons.description: Lock-free counters, flags, compare-and-swap and atomically swapped snapshots with the typed atomics in sync/atomic.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What atomic operations are, and when they beat a mutex
- The typed atomics: `atomic.Int64`, `atomic.Bool`, `atomic.Pointer[T]` and friends
- Compare-and-swap for "exactly one winner" logic
- Publishing immutable snapshots with `atomic.Pointer`
- Why atomics are easy to misuse for anything bigger than one value

## The idea

An **atomic operation** reads or modifies a single value in one indivisible step. No other goroutine can see it half done, and no lock is needed. The CPU provides these operations directly, so they are very fast.

Atomics are perfect for **one independent value**: a request counter, a "shutting down" flag, a pointer to the current configuration. As soon as two values must change together consistently, use a mutex.

## Typed atomics

Since Go 1.19, `sync/atomic` has types whose methods are always atomic and whose zero values are ready to use:



```gopath-example
example-170
```



| Type | Methods |
|---|---|
| `atomic.Int32`, `Int64`, `Uint32`, `Uint64`, `Uintptr` | `Load`, `Store`, `Add`, `Swap`, `CompareAndSwap` (plus `And`, `Or` since Go 1.23) |
| `atomic.Bool` | `Load`, `Store`, `Swap`, `CompareAndSwap` |
| `atomic.Pointer[T]` | `Load`, `Store`, `Swap`, `CompareAndSwap` |
| `atomic.Value` | `Load`, `Store` for any type (older; prefer `Pointer[T]`) |

Prefer these types over the older functions like `atomic.AddInt64(&n, 1)`. With the functions, it is easy to forget to use them on **every** access; with the types, there is no other way to touch the value. `int64` atomics also need 64-bit alignment on 32-bit platforms, which the types guarantee for you.

## Compare-and-swap

`CompareAndSwap(old, new)` sets the value to `new` **only if** it currently equals `old`, and reports whether it did. It is the building block of lock-free algorithms:



```gopath-example
example-171
```



Exactly one goroutine wins the race to claim ownership, with no lock.

## Atomic snapshots with `atomic.Pointer`

A powerful pattern for read-heavy shared data: keep it **immutable**, and atomically swap a pointer to a new version when it changes.



```gopath-example
example-172
```



Readers call `Load` and get a consistent snapshot with no locking at all. A writer builds a **new** `Settings` and stores the pointer. Old readers keep using the old snapshot until they finish. This is how many services implement hot-reloadable configuration and routing tables.

The rule that makes it work: **never modify a value after publishing it.** Build a new one.

## When not to use atomics

- **Several related values.** Updating `count` and `total` with two atomic operations lets a reader see the new `count` with the old `total`. Use a mutex.
- **Check then act.** `if n.Load() < limit { n.Add(1) }` is not atomic as a whole; two goroutines can both pass the check. Use `CompareAndSwap` in a loop, or a mutex.
- **Clarity.** A mutex is easier to reason about. Reach for atomics when profiling shows lock contention, or for the clear single-value cases above.

## Common mistakes

### Mixing atomic and plain access

Using `atomic.AddInt64(&n, 1)` in one place and `n++` in another is a data race. The typed atomics prevent this.

### Assuming atomics make compound operations safe

Two atomic operations in a row are not one atomic operation.

### Mutating a published snapshot

Changing a field on a struct reachable through `atomic.Pointer` is a data race with every reader. Copy, modify the copy, store the new pointer.

## Key takeaways

- Atomics update a single value indivisibly and without locks.
- Use the typed atomics (`atomic.Int64`, `atomic.Bool`, `atomic.Pointer[T]`); their zero values are ready.
- `CompareAndSwap` enables "exactly one winner" logic.
- Publish immutable snapshots with `atomic.Pointer` for lock-free reads.
- For anything involving more than one value, use a mutex.

## Further reading

- [Package sync/atomic](https://pkg.go.dev/sync/atomic)
- [The Go Memory Model: Atomic values](https://go.dev/ref/mem#atomic)

lessons.title: 6.6 The race detector
lessons.description: What a data race is, how to find races with go test -race, how to read a race report, and the standard ways to fix them.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What exactly a data race is, and why it is worse than "a wrong number sometimes"
- How to run the race detector, and where to run it
- How to read a race report
- The three standard fixes
- The race detector's limits

## The idea

A **data race** happens when two goroutines access the same memory location concurrently, at least one access is a write, and nothing synchronizes them.

Races are not just "occasionally wrong results". The Go memory model (lesson 6.7) gives **no guarantees** for racy programs: you can see torn values, stale values that never update, and corrupted data structures. Some races on maps crash the program. Races are also notoriously hard to reproduce, because they depend on timing.

Go ships a **race detector** built on Google's ThreadSanitizer. It instruments memory accesses at compile time and reports races as they happen at run time.

## Running it

Add `-race` to `go test`, `go run` or `go build`:

```bash
go test -race ./...
go run -race ./cmd/server
go build -race -o server-race ./cmd/server
```

Here is a deliberate race. It lives behind a build tag, so it never runs in normal builds:



```gopath-example
example-173
```



## Reading a race report

```text
==================
WARNING: DATA RACE
Read at 0x00c000012118 by goroutine 9:
  .../demo.TestRacyCounter.func1()
      .../racy_test.go:23 +0x84

Previous write at 0x00c000012118 by goroutine 8:
  .../demo.TestRacyCounter.func1()
      .../racy_test.go:23 +0x96

Goroutine 9 (running) created at:
  .../demo.TestRacyCounter()
      .../racy_test.go:20 +0x...
==================
--- FAIL: TestRacyCounter
    testing.go: race detected during execution of test
```

Three parts to look at:

1. **The two conflicting accesses**: what kind (read or write), which goroutine, and the stack trace down to the file and line. Here, both are line 23, `n++`.
2. **Where each goroutine was created**: tells you which `go` statements started the conflicting goroutines.
3. **The test fails.** With `-race`, a detected race fails the test even if every assertion passed.

## The three standard fixes



```gopath-example
example-174
```



1. **Lock it**: guard every access with a `sync.Mutex`.
2. **Make it atomic**: for a single value, use `sync/atomic`.
3. **Do not share it**: give the data to one goroutine and send it messages over a channel.

A fourth fix, often the best: **restructure so goroutines do not share the variable at all.** Give each goroutine its own slot (as `Sum` did in the lesson 6.4 exercise) and combine results after `Wait`.

## Where to run it

- **Always in CI**: `go test -race ./...`. This course's CI does so.
- **Locally** while developing concurrent code.
- **In a canary or staging environment** with a `-race` build, if you can afford the overhead, to catch races that tests do not exercise.

The race detector typically slows programs down 2 to 20 times and uses 5 to 10 times more memory, so it is not meant for normal production builds.

## Limits

- It only finds races in code that **actually runs** during the test. A race in an untested branch stays hidden. Good concurrent tests exercise the concurrent paths.
- It finds data races, **not** logical race conditions (two correctly locked operations in the wrong order) and not deadlocks.
- It requires cgo on most platforms and is supported on common 64-bit systems (see the docs for the full list).

## Common mistakes

### Running tests without `-race`

Concurrent code that "passes" without `-race` may simply not have lost a race yet. Make `-race` the default for `go test` on concurrent packages.

### "Benign" races

"It is only a stats counter, a wrong value is fine." The memory model gives no such guarantee, and the compiler may optimize racy code in surprising ways. Fix it; atomics are cheap.

### Silencing the detector

There is no supported way to mark a race as acceptable. If it reports something, there is a real unsynchronized access.

## Key takeaways

- A data race is a concurrent unsynchronized access where at least one side writes; racy programs have no guarantees.
- Run `go test -race ./...` in CI and while developing.
- Race reports show both conflicting accesses and where their goroutines started.
- Fix with a mutex, an atomic, a channel, or by not sharing the data.
- The detector only sees code paths that run.

## Further reading

- [Data Race Detector](https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector) on go.dev
- [Introducing the Go Race Detector](https://go.dev/blog/race-detector) on the Go blog

- in a canary or staging environment with a -race build, if you can afford the overhead, to catch races that tests do not exercise.

the race detector typically slows programs down 2 to 20 times and uses 5 to 10 times more memory, so it is not meant for normal production builds.

 limits

- it only finds races in code that actually runs during the test. a race in an untested branch stays hidden. good concurrent tests exercise the concurrent paths.
- it finds data races, not logical race conditions (two correctly locked operations in the wrong order) and not deadlocks.
- it requires cgo on most platforms and is supported on common 64-bit systems (see the docs for the full list).

 common mistakes

 running tests without -race

concurrent code that "passes" without -race may simply not have lost a race yet. make -race the default for go test on concurrent packages.

"it is only a stats counter, a wrong value is fine." the memory model gives no such guarantee, and the compiler may optimize racy code in surprising ways. fix it; atomics are cheap.

there is no supported way to mark a race as acceptable. if it reports something, there is a real unsynchronized access.

 key takeaways

- a data race is a concurrent unsynchronized access where at least one side writes; racy programs have no guarantees.
- run go test -race ./... in ci and while developing.
- race reports show both conflicting accesses and where their goroutines started.
- fix with a mutex, an atomic, a channel, or by not sharing the data.

- [introducing the go race detector](https://go.dev/blog/race-detector) on the go blog

lessons.title: 6.7 The Go memory model, in plain words
lessons.description: What the Go memory model guarantees, what happens-before means, which operations create it, and why unsynchronized flags and double-checked locking fail.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why a write in one goroutine is not automatically visible in another
- What **happens before** means
- Which operations create happens-before relationships
- Why "spin until a flag is set" is broken
- The one-sentence rule that keeps you safe

## The idea

Modern CPUs and compilers reorder and cache memory operations to run faster. Within a single goroutine, this is invisible: your code behaves as if it ran in order. **Across goroutines, it is not.** Without synchronization, one goroutine may see another's writes late, out of order, or never.

The Go memory model is the contract that tells you when a write is **guaranteed** to be visible to a read in another goroutine. The guarantee is called **happens before**.

## Happens before

If event A **happens before** event B, then B sees the effects of A (and of everything that happened before A).

Within one goroutine, statements happen before each other in program order. **Between goroutines**, happens-before only exists when it is created by a synchronizing operation. The ones you will use:

| Operation | Guarantee |
|---|---|
| `go f()` | The `go` statement happens before `f` starts running |
| Channel send | A send happens before the corresponding receive completes |
| Channel close | A close happens before a receive that returns because the channel is closed |
| Unbuffered receive | The receive happens before the corresponding send completes |
| `Mutex.Unlock` | Unlocking happens before any later `Lock` returns |
| `WaitGroup.Done` | Each `Done` happens before the `Wait` it unblocks returns |
| `Once.Do(f)` | `f` returning happens before any `Do` call returns |
| Atomic operations | An atomic write is visible to atomic reads that observe it, like a sequentially consistent memory |

## A correct hand-off



```gopath-example
example-175
```



Everything the goroutine wrote to `r` before sending is visible to the receiver, because the send happens before the receive completes. After the send, the goroutine must not touch `r` again: ownership has moved to the receiver.

## A broken flag, and the fix



```gopath-example
example-176
```



In the broken version (shown in the comment), nothing synchronizes `ready`. The compiler is allowed to hoist the read of `ready` out of the loop, so it may spin forever; and even if it sees `ready == true`, it is not guaranteed to see `msg`. Real programs have hung exactly like this. The fix is any synchronizing operation from the table; a `WaitGroup` is the simplest here.

The same reasoning breaks "double-checked locking" (checking a plain variable before taking a lock to skip the lock). In Go, use `sync.Once` or `sync.OnceValue` instead.

## The rule

The memory model document itself says that if you need its details to understand your program, you are being too clever, and ends that advice with: "Don't be clever."

In practice: **every variable shared between goroutines and written by any of them must be accessed only through a channel, a mutex, an atomic, or another `sync` primitive.** Run `-race` to check yourself.

## What Go guarantees even with races

Go is more forgiving than C or C++ in one respect: a racy program cannot corrupt memory in arbitrary ways for **single-word** values; a read sees some value that was actually written. But multiword values like strings, slices and interfaces can be **torn** (you see the pointer from one write and the length from another), which can crash the program or read out of bounds. Do not rely on any of this. Synchronize.

## Common mistakes

### Unsynchronized "done" flags

`for !done {}` or `if !initialized { ... }` with plain booleans. Use a channel, `atomic.Bool`, or `sync.Once`.

### Publishing a pointer before the data is complete

Storing a pointer in a shared variable and then filling in its fields. Readers may see the pointer before the fields. Build completely, then publish through a synchronizing operation.

### Assuming `time.Sleep` synchronizes

Sleeping makes a race less likely to show up; it creates no happens-before relationship.

## Key takeaways

- Without synchronization, writes in one goroutine may never be seen by another.
- Happens-before is created by `go`, channel operations, mutexes, `WaitGroup`, `Once` and atomics.
- Hand off data through channels and stop touching it after sending.
- Never spin on plain flags; never use double-checked locking; use `sync.Once`.
- Do not be clever: synchronize every shared, written variable, and run `-race`.

## Further reading

- [The Go Memory Model](https://go.dev/ref/mem)
- [Updating the Go Memory Model](https://research.swtch.com/gomm) by Russ Cox

lessons.title: 7.1 context.Context: cancellation, deadlines, values
lessons.description: How context carries cancellation and deadlines across function calls and goroutines, the rules for using it, cancellation causes, AfterFunc, WithoutCancel and request-scoped values.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What problem `context.Context` solves
- `WithCancel`, `WithTimeout` and `WithDeadline`, and why you must always call `cancel`
- How cancellation flows from parent to child contexts
- Cancellation causes with `WithCancelCause` and `context.Cause`
- `AfterFunc` and `WithoutCancel`
- When to use context values, and when not to
- The conventions every Go API follows

## The idea

A request arrives at your server. To answer it, you query a database, call two other services and start a few goroutines. Then the client disconnects, or a deadline passes. All of that work should **stop**, now, everywhere.

`context.Context` is how Go propagates that "stop" signal (and deadlines, and a little request-scoped data) through every function and goroutine involved. It is an interface with four methods:

```go
type Context interface {
	Deadline() (deadline time.Time, ok bool)
	Done() <-chan struct{} // closed when the work should stop
	Err() error            // why: Canceled or DeadlineExceeded
	Value(key any) any
}
```

`Done()` is a channel that is **closed** on cancellation, the broadcast pattern from lesson 6.2. Any goroutine can `select` on it.

## Cancellation



```gopath-example
example-177
```



- `context.Background()` is the root: never cancelled, no deadline, no values. Use it in `main`, in tests and at the top of background jobs.
- `context.WithCancel(parent)` returns a child context and a `cancel` function.
- Long-running work checks `ctx.Done()` in a `select`, and returns `ctx.Err()` when it is closed.

## Timeouts and deadlines



```gopath-example
example-178
```



- `WithTimeout(parent, d)` cancels automatically after `d`; `WithDeadline(parent, t)` at time `t`.
- `ctx.Err()` is `context.DeadlineExceeded` for timeouts and `context.Canceled` for explicit cancels. Check with `errors.Is`.

**Always call `cancel`**, usually with `defer cancel()` right after creating the context, even when a timeout will fire anyway. It releases the context's resources as soon as the work is done instead of when the timer expires. `go vet` reports contexts whose `cancel` is never called.

## Cancellation flows down the tree

Contexts form a tree. Cancelling a parent cancels every descendant, but cancelling a child never affects its parent:



```gopath-example
example-179
```



A child can only **shorten** its parent's deadline, never extend it. A function that adds `WithTimeout(ctx, time.Hour)` to a context that expires in one second still stops after one second.

## Why was it cancelled?

`ctx.Err()` only says "canceled" or "deadline exceeded". `WithCancelCause` (Go 1.20) lets you record the reason:



```gopath-example
example-180
```



`WithTimeoutCause` and `WithDeadlineCause` (Go 1.21) do the same for timeouts. Since Go 1.26, `signal.NotifyContext` also sets a cause identifying the signal that arrived. Causes make logs far more useful: "context canceled" becomes "server shutting down".

## `AfterFunc` and `WithoutCancel`



```gopath-example
example-181
```



- `context.AfterFunc(ctx, f)` runs `f` in a new goroutine once `ctx` is done. Use it to tie cleanup to cancellation without writing a goroutine that waits on `Done()` yourself. It returns a `stop` function to unregister `f`.
- `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` keeps the parent's values but is never cancelled. Use it sparingly, for work that must complete even if the request was abandoned, such as recording an audit event.

## Context values

`WithValue` attaches a key-value pair. Use it **only for request-scoped data that crosses API boundaries**: a request ID, a trace span, the authenticated user. Never for optional function parameters or dependencies like a database handle.



```gopath-example
example-182
```



- Use an **unexported key type** so no other package can collide with your keys.
- Provide typed accessor functions (`WithRequestID`, `RequestID`) instead of making callers use `Value` and type assertions.
- Looking up a value walks up the tree, so deep chains of `WithValue` are slow. Store one struct rather than many separate values.

## The conventions

Every Go API that blocks or does I/O follows these rules. Follow them in yours:

1. **`ctx` is the first parameter**, named `ctx`: `func Fetch(ctx context.Context, url string) error`.
2. **Do not store a context in a struct.** Pass it to each call. (Exceptions are rare and documented.)
3. **Never pass a `nil` context.** Use `context.TODO()` when you have not wired one through yet; it is a searchable marker for "fix this later".
4. **The function that creates a context with `cancel` is responsible for calling it.**
5. **Respect it.** A function that takes a `ctx` and ignores it is lying to its callers.

The standard library honors context everywhere: `http.NewRequestWithContext`, `db.QueryContext`, `net.Dialer.DialContext`, `exec.CommandContext`. In an HTTP handler, `r.Context()` is cancelled when the client disconnects.

## Common mistakes

### Forgetting `defer cancel()`

Leaks a timer and a goroutine reference until the parent is cancelled, which for `Background` is never. `go vet`'s `lostcancel` check catches it.

### Checking `ctx` only at the start

A loop that checks `ctx.Err()` once and then runs for a minute cannot be cancelled. Check in every iteration, and pass `ctx` to every blocking call.

### Using `context.Background()` deep in the call stack

It cuts the cancellation chain: the work below it can no longer be stopped by the caller. Accept a `ctx` parameter and pass it down.

### Context values as a bag of parameters

Hidden dependencies that the compiler cannot check. If a function needs it, make it a parameter.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m07/poll
```



## Key takeaways

- `context.Context` carries cancellation, deadlines and request-scoped values through calls and goroutines.
- `Done()` is closed on cancellation; select on it and return `ctx.Err()`.
- Create children with `WithCancel`, `WithTimeout` or `WithDeadline`, and always `defer cancel()`.
- Cancellation flows from parent to children; record reasons with `WithCancelCause` and read them with `context.Cause`.
- Pass `ctx` as the first parameter, never store it, never pass `nil`, and use values only for request-scoped data.

## Further reading

- [Package context](https://pkg.go.dev/context)
- [Go Concurrency Patterns: Context](https://go.dev/blog/context) on the Go blog
- [Contexts and structs](https://go.dev/blog/context-and-structs) on the Go blog

lessons.title: 7.2 Worker pools
lessons.description: Process a stream of jobs with a fixed number of goroutines: the four parts of a worker pool, collecting results in order, cancellation, and sizing the pool.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why bounding concurrency matters
- The four parts of a worker pool: workers, feeder, closer and collector
- How to keep results in input order
- How to make every part of the pool cancellable
- How to choose the number of workers

## The idea

"One goroutine per item" is fine for ten items. For a million it is not: you open a million connections, allocate a million stacks, and overwhelm whatever you are calling. A **worker pool** runs a **fixed number** of goroutines that pull jobs from a channel, so concurrency stays bounded no matter how much work arrives.

## The pattern



```gopath-example
example-183
```



Four pieces, each with one job:

1. **Workers** (`workers` goroutines) loop over `jobs` until it is closed. They are the only goroutines doing real work.
2. **The feeder** sends every job, then **closes** `jobs`, which ends the workers' `range` loops.
3. **The closer** waits for all workers (`wg.Wait()`), then closes `results`. This must be a separate goroutine: if the collector called `Wait` itself, it would deadlock, because workers block on sending results that nobody is receiving yet.
4. **The collector** (here, the calling function) ranges over `results` until it is closed.

Every send selects on `ctx.Done()` too, so cancelling the context unblocks every goroutine and nothing leaks.

## Keeping results in order

Workers finish in any order. Carry the input's **index** with each job and result, and write results into a pre-sized slice by index, as `counts[r.id] = r.words` does. This is cheaper and simpler than sorting afterwards.

## Handling errors

The example has no errors. With real work you choose a policy:

- **Fail fast**: stop everything on the first error. Cancel a shared context and return the error. `errgroup` (lesson 7.4) packages exactly this.
- **Collect all**: keep going, put each error in its result, and report them together (for example with `errors.Join`, lesson 5.4).

The `pmap` exercise below implements fail fast.

## How many workers?

| Work type | Starting point |
|---|---|
| CPU-bound (hashing, parsing, compression) | `runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0)`, the number of usable CPUs |
| I/O-bound (HTTP calls, database queries) | Higher, limited by what the **other side** can handle: connection pool size, API rate limits |
| Mixed | Measure. Start small and increase while throughput improves |

More workers than useful only adds contention. For I/O, the downstream service's limits usually decide the number, which is why worker pools pair naturally with rate limiting (lesson 7.5).

## Common mistakes

### Calling `wg.Wait()` before reading results

Workers block sending results, `Wait` never returns: deadlock. Close `results` from a separate goroutine.

### Forgetting to close the jobs channel

Workers wait forever for the next job. The feeder must `close(jobs)` when done.

### A worker that returns early without draining

If one worker exits on error while the feeder keeps sending, the remaining workers handle the load, but if **all** exit, the feeder blocks forever. Make the feeder select on `ctx.Done()` and cancel the context when workers give up.

### Unbounded result buffering

Making `results` a channel with a huge buffer to "avoid blocking" hides backpressure and can use lots of memory. Let the collector set the pace.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m07/pmap
```



## Key takeaways

- A worker pool bounds concurrency with a fixed number of goroutines reading from a jobs channel.
- Four roles: workers, a feeder that closes jobs, a closer that waits and closes results, and a collector.
- Carry indexes to keep results in order.
- Make every send cancellable with `select` on `ctx.Done()`.
- Size CPU-bound pools by CPUs, I/O-bound pools by downstream capacity.

## Further reading

- [Go Concurrency Patterns: Pipelines and cancellation](https://go.dev/blog/pipelines) on the Go blog
- [Package golang.org/x/sync/errgroup](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/errgroup), the fail-fast pool in a box (lesson 7.4)

- carry indexes to keep results in order.
- make every send cancellable with select on ctx.done().
- size cpu-bound pools by cpus, i/o-bound pools by downstream capacity.

 further reading

- [go concurrency patterns: pipelines and cancellation](https://go.dev/blog/pipelines) on the go blog
- [package golang.org/x/sync/errgroup](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/errgroup), the fail-fast pool in a box (lesson 7.4)

lessons.title: 7.3 Pipelines and fan-out / fan-in
lessons.description: Compose concurrent stages connected by channels, spread work across stages with fan-out, merge results with fan-in, and stop the whole pipeline early with context.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to structure work as a pipeline of stages connected by channels
- Fan-out: several goroutines reading from one channel
- Fan-in: merging several channels into one
- How to stop every stage when the consumer is done early
- When a pipeline is the wrong shape for a problem

## The idea

A **pipeline** is a series of **stages** connected by channels. Each stage is a function that receives values from an inbound channel, does something, and sends values on an outbound channel. Stages run concurrently, so while stage 3 processes item 1, stage 2 can work on item 2 and stage 1 on item 3.

You built a pipeline without cancellation in the lesson 6.2 exercise. Here every stage also takes a `ctx`.

## Cancellable stages



```gopath-example
example-184
```



Every stage follows the same template:

1. Create the outbound channel.
2. Start a goroutine that `defer close(out)` and loops over the input.
3. Every send is a `select` with `case <-ctx.Done(): return`.
4. Return the outbound channel as receive-only.

With that template, any stage can be combined with any other.

## Fan-out and fan-in



```gopath-example
example-185
```



- **Fan-out**: several `square` stages read from the **same** source channel. Each value is received by exactly one of them, so the work is shared. Use it when one stage is slower than the others.
- **Fan-in**: `merge` combines several channels into one, closing the output when all inputs are closed.

Fan-out loses ordering. If order matters, carry an index and reorder at the end, as in the worker pool lesson.

## Stopping early

The consumer might not want every value. Without cancellation, upstream stages would block forever trying to send values nobody reads:



```gopath-example
example-186
```



`defer cancel()` in the consumer closes `ctx.Done()` when it returns, every stage's send `select` picks the `Done` case, the stages return, and their deferred `close` calls cascade down the pipeline. No goroutine is left behind.

## Pipelines vs iterators vs plain loops

Not every sequence of steps needs goroutines:

| Use | When |
|---|---|
| A plain loop | Each step is cheap; there is nothing to overlap |
| Iterators (lesson 3.8) | You want lazy, composable stages but no concurrency |
| A channel pipeline | Stages do slow work (I/O) that can overlap, or a stage benefits from fan-out |

Channel operations cost far more than function calls. A pipeline of trivial CPU stages is usually **slower** than a single loop. Measure (Module 10).

## Common mistakes

### Stages without cancellation

The consumer stops reading, upstream goroutines block on send forever. Every send needs `case <-ctx.Done()`.

### Closing a channel from the wrong place

Only the stage that owns the outbound channel closes it, and `merge` closes only after all its inputs are done.

### Pipelines for CPU-trivial work

Splitting `x * x` into its own goroutine costs more than it saves.

## Key takeaways

- A pipeline is a chain of stages connected by channels, each running concurrently.
- Each stage owns and closes its outbound channel and selects on `ctx.Done()` for every send.
- Fan-out shares work among several goroutines; fan-in merges their results.
- `defer cancel()` in the consumer tears the whole pipeline down cleanly.
- Use pipelines for overlapping slow work; use loops or iterators otherwise.

## Further reading

- [Go Concurrency Patterns: Pipelines and cancellation](https://go.dev/blog/pipelines) on the Go blog
- [Go Concurrency Patterns](https://go.dev/talks/2012/concurrency.slide), Rob Pike's talk
headings: Pipelines vs iterators vs plain loops

lessons.title: 7.4 errgroup and bounded concurrency
lessons.description: Run a group of goroutines where the first error cancels the rest, limit how many run at once, and see how golang.org/x/sync/errgroup works by building a small version of it.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The "first error cancels everything" pattern
- How `golang.org/x/sync/errgroup` implements it, by building a version yourself
- How `SetLimit` bounds concurrency with a semaphore
- How to use the real `errgroup` package
- Its limits, and when to choose something else

## The idea

A very common shape of concurrent work: start N tasks, wait for all of them, and if **any** fails, stop the others and report the error. Writing it by hand each time means a `WaitGroup`, a `sync.Once` for the first error, a cancellable context and a semaphore. The `errgroup` package, maintained by the Go team in `golang.org/x/sync`, wraps all of that.

## Building it from the standard library

Here is a compact version with the same API, so you can see exactly what happens inside:



```gopath-example
example-187
```



- `WithContext` derives a cancellable context. The group cancels it, with the first error as the cause, as soon as any function fails.
- `sync.Once` keeps only the **first** error.
- `SetLimit` creates a buffered channel used as a **semaphore**: `Go` must put a token in before starting a goroutine, so when `n` are running, the next `Go` call blocks.
- `Wait` waits for everything, then cancels the context to release resources.

Using it:



```gopath-example
example-188
```



One task fails, the other four see `ctx.Done()` and return early, and `Wait` returns the original failure.



```gopath-example
example-189
```



## Using the real package

In real code, use `golang.org/x/sync/errgroup` rather than your own copy. It lives in this course's separate [`examples/thirdparty`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/examples/thirdparty) module, so the main course module stays dependency-free:



```gopath-example
example-190
```



The `x/sync/errgroup` API also has `TryGo`, which starts a goroutine only if the limit has room and reports whether it did, and the zero `errgroup.Group` (without `WithContext`) when you want first-error collection without cancellation.

## Limits of errgroup

- **Only the first error.** If you need every error, collect them yourself and join them (lesson 5.4).
- **Results are up to you.** `Go` takes `func() error`. Write results into an indexed slice or guard a shared structure with a mutex, as `fetchAll` does.
- **Panics are not converted to errors.** A panic in a group goroutine crashes the program like any other goroutine panic (lesson 5.5). Recover inside the function if the code might panic.
- **Cancellation is cooperative.** The context is cancelled, but each function must actually check it.

## Common mistakes

### Ignoring the derived context

Using the outer `ctx` instead of the one returned by `WithContext` means failures cannot cancel the other tasks.

### Shared results without synchronization

Appending to a shared slice from several `g.Go` functions without a mutex is a data race. Use indexes or a lock.

### No limit on huge inputs

`g.Go` for a million items without `SetLimit` starts a million goroutines. Set a limit.

## Key takeaways

- `errgroup` runs functions concurrently, waits for all, returns the first error and cancels the rest.
- It is built from a `WaitGroup`, a `sync.Once`, a cancellable context and an optional semaphore.
- `SetLimit` bounds concurrency; `TryGo` starts work only if there is room.
- Collect results with indexes or a mutex, recover panics yourself, and pass the derived context to every task.

## Further reading

- [Package golang.org/x/sync/errgroup](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/errgroup)
- [Package golang.org/x/sync/semaphore](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/semaphore) for weighted semaphores
headings: Building it from the standard library

lessons.title: 7.5 Rate limiting and backpressure
lessons.description: Limit how much work happens at once and how fast: channel semaphores, ticker spacing, the token bucket algorithm, golang.org/x/time/rate, and bounded queues that push back on producers.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The difference between limiting **concurrency** and limiting **rate**
- A buffered channel as a counting semaphore
- Spacing work out with a ticker
- How the **token bucket** algorithm works, and the `x/time/rate` package
- Backpressure: making producers slow down or fail fast instead of piling up work

## The idea

Two different limits protect systems:

- **Concurrency limit**: at most N things **at the same time** (database connections, open files, in-flight requests).
- **Rate limit**: at most N things **per unit of time** (an API that allows 100 requests per second).

And when work arrives faster than you can handle it, you need **backpressure**: a way for the slow part to push back on the fast part, instead of queuing without limit until memory runs out.

## Limiting concurrency: a channel semaphore



```gopath-example
example-191
```



Sending into a buffered channel of capacity N "acquires" a slot, receiving "releases" it. When all N slots are taken, the next send blocks. It is the same mechanism inside `errgroup.SetLimit`. For weighted limits (some tasks take several slots), use `golang.org/x/sync/semaphore`.

## Limiting rate: a ticker



```gopath-example
example-192
```



Waiting for a tick before each request gives a steady rate. It is simple, but it allows **no bursts**: even after an idle minute, the next request still waits for a tick.

## The token bucket

Most real rate limiters use a **token bucket**:

- The bucket holds up to `burst` tokens and starts full.
- Tokens are added at `rate` per second, never beyond `burst`.
- Each event takes one token. With no token available, the event is rejected or waits.

This allows short bursts (up to `burst` events at once after an idle period) while keeping the long-term average at `rate`. The standard implementation is `golang.org/x/time/rate`:



```gopath-example
example-193
```



- `Allow()` answers "may I, right now?" without blocking. Good for rejecting requests with HTTP 429.
- `Wait(ctx)` blocks until a token is available, or returns an error if `ctx` ends first. Good for outbound calls you want to slow down rather than drop.
- `Reserve()` tells you how long you would have to wait, for schedulers.

In lesson 7.8 you will look at a token bucket written from scratch with only the standard library, including a per-key limiter for "N requests per second **per client**".

## Backpressure



```gopath-example
example-194
```



A bounded queue gives three choices when it is full:

| Strategy | Code | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Block** the producer | plain send | Batch jobs where waiting is fine |
| **Fail fast** | `select` with `default` | Request handling: return 429 or 503 and let the client retry |
| **Wait with a deadline** | `select` with `ctx.Done()` | Callers that can wait a little but not forever |

What you should **not** do is accept unlimited work. An unbounded queue turns a short overload into an outage: memory grows, latency grows, and by the time work is processed, the clients have long given up.

## Common mistakes

### Confusing concurrency limits with rate limits

A semaphore of 10 can still make thousands of requests per second if each is fast. If the other side limits rate, limit rate.

### One limiter per request

Creating a new `rate.Limiter` inside each handler call means every request gets a full bucket. The limiter must be shared (per service, or per key).

### Per-key limiters that never forget keys

A map of limiters per IP address grows forever. Prune idle keys (the `Keyed` limiter in lesson 7.8 does this).

### Using `time.Sleep` for rate limiting

`time.Sleep(10 * time.Millisecond)` between calls ignores cancellation and drifts. Use a ticker or a token bucket with `Wait(ctx)`.

## Key takeaways

- Limit concurrency with a semaphore; limit rate with a ticker or token bucket.
- A buffered channel of capacity N is a counting semaphore.
- Token buckets allow bursts up to `burst` while averaging `rate`; `x/time/rate` is the standard implementation.
- Bound every queue, and decide whether producers block, fail fast or wait with a deadline.

## Further reading

- [Package golang.org/x/time/rate](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/time/rate)
- [Token bucket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Token_bucket) on Wikipedia
