lessons.title: 7.6 Goroutine leaks: finding and preventing them
lessons.description: Why goroutines leak, the patterns that cause most leaks, how to detect them in tests and production, and the goroutineleak profile in Go 1.27.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What a goroutine leak is and why it matters
- The handful of patterns that cause almost every leak
- How to test for leaks
- How to find leaks in a running service with `pprof`
- The `goroutineleak` profile, new in Go 1.27

## The idea

A goroutine **leaks** when it can never finish: it is blocked forever on a channel, a lock or I/O that will never complete. The garbage collector does not free goroutines that are blocked, nor anything they reference. Each leak is small, but leaks usually happen **per request**, so memory and goroutine counts grow steadily until the service is restarted or killed.

## The usual causes

Almost every leak is one of these:

1. **A send nobody receives.** The receiver returned early (timeout, error, first result won).
2. **A receive nobody sends to, or a `range` over a channel nobody closes.**
3. **A goroutine waiting on a context nobody cancels**, or not watching any context at all.
4. **A lock that is never unlocked.**
5. **Blocking I/O without a timeout**, such as an HTTP request with no deadline.

Here is cause 1 in its most common form, "ask several, take the fastest":



```gopath-example
example-195
```



After the first value is received, every other replica blocks on its send forever. The fix gives the channel enough buffer for every send, so all goroutines can finish. The other standard fix is to make the sender `select` on `ctx.Done()`.

## Prevent leaks by design



```gopath-example
example-196
```



Rules that make leaks rare:

- **Every goroutine has an owner** who knows how it stops.
- **Every blocking operation has a way out**: a `ctx.Done()` case, a closed channel, a timeout.
- **Result channels that may be abandoned have a buffer** big enough for all senders.
- **`defer cancel()`** right after creating a context.

## Detecting leaks in tests

The simplest check counts goroutines before and after:



```gopath-example
example-197
```



Because goroutines take a moment to exit, poll for a short time rather than checking once. The exercises in Modules 6 and 7 use exactly this technique. For larger projects, `go.uber.org/goleak` does it more thoroughly: it lists the leaked goroutines' stacks and ignores known background goroutines.

## Finding leaks in production

Import `net/http/pprof` in your service (on an internal port only), and you get:

```bash
# How many goroutines, grouped by stack:
curl -s http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=1 | head -40

# Or explore interactively:
go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine
```

A leak shows up as a stack with an ever-growing count, all blocked at the same line (`chan send`, `chan receive`, `select`). The `runtime/metrics` value `/sched/goroutines` (Go 1.26+) is a good thing to graph and alert on.

## The `goroutineleak` profile (Go 1.27)

The goroutine profile shows **every** blocked goroutine, and many of them are blocked legitimately (waiting for the next request, say). Go 1.26 introduced, as an experiment, and Go 1.27 made generally available, a profile that reports only goroutines the runtime can **prove** are leaked: goroutines blocked on a channel, mutex or condition that no running goroutine can reach anymore. The garbage collector finds them during its reachability analysis.



```gopath-example
example-198
```



In a service it is served at `/debug/pprof/goroutineleak` by `net/http/pprof`. It cannot find every leak (a goroutine blocked on a channel that is still referenced somewhere is not provably leaked), but what it reports is almost certainly a bug.

## Common mistakes

### Assuming the garbage collector will clean up

It does not free blocked goroutines. A leaked goroutine lives until the process exits.

### Timeouts on the caller side only

`select` with `time.After` protects the caller, but if the worker's send is unbuffered, the worker leaks. Fix both sides.

### HTTP clients without timeouts

`http.Get` with the default client has **no** timeout. A hung server leaks the goroutine (and the connection) forever. Use a client with `Timeout`, or a request context with a deadline (lesson 8.7).

## Key takeaways

- A leaked goroutine is blocked forever and is never freed, along with everything it references.
- Most leaks are unreceived sends, unclosed channels, uncancelled contexts or I/O without timeouts.
- Give every goroutine an owner and every blocking operation an exit.
- Test for leaks by comparing goroutine counts, or with `goleak`.
- In production, watch the goroutine profile and metrics; on Go 1.27, check `/debug/pprof/goroutineleak`.

## Further reading

- [Go 1.27 release notes: goroutineleak profile](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)
- [Package runtime/pprof](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/pprof) and [net/http/pprof](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http/pprof)
- [go.uber.org/goleak](https://pkg.go.dev/go.uber.org/goleak)

3. a goroutine waiting on a context nobody cancels, or not watching any context at all.
4. a lock that is never unlocked.
5. blocking i/o without a timeout, such as an http request with no deadline.

here is cause 1 in its most common form, "ask several, take the fastest":







after the first value is received, every other replica blocks on its send forever. the fix gives the channel enough buffer for every send, so all goroutines can finish. the other standard fix is to make the sender select on ctx.done().

 prevent leaks by design







rules that make leaks rare:

- every goroutine has an owner who knows how it stops.
- every blocking operation has a way out: a ctx.done() case, a closed channel, a timeout.
- result channels that may be abandoned have a buffer big enough for all senders.
- defer cancel() right after creating a context.

 detecting leaks in tests

the simplest check counts goroutines before and after:







because goroutines take a moment to exit, poll for a short time rather than checking once. the exercises in modules 6 and 7 use exactly this technique. for larger projects, go.uber.org/goleak does it more thoroughly: it lists the leaked goroutines' stacks and ignores known background goroutines.

 finding leaks in production

import net/http/pprof in your service (on an internal port only), and you get:



a leak shows up as a stack with an ever-growing count, all blocked at the same line (chan send, chan receive, select). the runtime/metrics value /sched/goroutines (go 1.26+) is a good thing to graph and alert on.

 the goroutineleak profile (go 1.27)

the goroutine profile shows every blocked goroutine, and many of them are blocked legitimately (waiting for the next request, say). go 1.26 introduced, as an experiment, and go 1.27 made generally available, a profile that reports only goroutines the runtime can prove are leaked: goroutines blocked on a channel, mutex or condition that no running goroutine can reach anymore. the garbage collector finds them during its reachability analysis.







in a service it is served at /debug/pprof/goroutineleak by net/http/pprof. it cannot find every leak (a goroutine blocked on a channel that is still referenced somewhere is not provably leaked), but what it reports is almost certainly a bug.

 common mistakes

 assuming the garbage collector will clean up

it does not free blocked goroutines. a leaked goroutine lives until the process exits.

 timeouts on the caller side only

select with time.after protects the caller, but if the worker's send is unbuffered, the worker leaks. fix both sides.

 http clients without timeouts

http.get with the default client has no timeout. a hung server leaks the goroutine (and the connection) forever. use a client with timeout, or a request context with a deadline (lesson 8.7).

 key takeaways

- a leaked goroutine is blocked forever and is never freed, along with everything it references.
- most leaks are unreceived sends, unclosed channels, uncancelled contexts or i/o without timeouts.
- give every goroutine an owner and every blocking operation an exit.
- test for leaks by comparing goroutine counts, or with goleak.
- in production, watch the goroutine profile and metrics; on go 1.27, check /debug/pprof/goroutineleak.

 further reading

- [go 1.27 release notes: goroutineleak profile](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)
- [package runtime/pprof](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/pprof) and [net/http/pprof](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http/pprof)
- [go.uber.org/goleak](https://pkg.go.dev/go.uber.org/goleak)

lessons.title: 7.7 Graceful shutdown
lessons.description: Stop a Go service cleanly: catch SIGINT and SIGTERM with signal.NotifyContext, stop accepting work, let in-flight work finish, and respect a deadline that fits inside Kubernetes' grace period.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why services must shut down gracefully, especially on Kubernetes
- Turning OS signals into a context with `signal.NotifyContext`
- Shutting down an HTTP server with `Shutdown`
- Draining background workers
- Choosing shutdown deadlines

## The idea

Services are stopped all the time: every deploy, every autoscaling event, every node drain. If a process simply dies, in-flight requests fail, half-written data is lost and clients see errors. A **graceful shutdown**:

1. stops accepting new work,
2. lets work already in progress finish,
3. releases resources (flushes logs, closes database connections),
4. and gives up after a deadline, so a stuck request cannot block the shutdown forever.

## Signals to context

Kubernetes, systemd and Docker stop a process by sending **SIGTERM**; pressing Ctrl+C sends **SIGINT**. `signal.NotifyContext` turns them into a cancelled context, which composes with everything from lesson 7.1:



```gopath-example
example-199
```



After the first signal, `stop()` restores the default behavior, so a second Ctrl+C kills the process immediately. That is a good escape hatch when shutdown hangs during development.

## Shutting down an HTTP server



```gopath-example
example-200
```



- `srv.Serve` runs in a goroutine, and its error goes to a buffered channel.
- `srv.Shutdown(ctx)` closes the listeners (no new connections), closes idle connections, and **waits for active requests to finish**, or until `ctx` expires.
- After `Shutdown`, `Serve` returns `http.ErrServerClosed`, which means "stopped on purpose", not a failure.

The demo starts a slow request, triggers shutdown while it is still running, and shows that the request completes:



```gopath-example
example-201
```



Note: `Shutdown` does not wait for hijacked connections such as WebSockets. Use `srv.RegisterOnShutdown` to notify them.

## Draining workers

The same idea applies to background workers:

1. Cancel the context the workers watch, or close their jobs channel, so they stop taking new work.
2. `Wait` on their `WaitGroup` (or `errgroup`) with a deadline.
3. Then close shared resources such as database pools, **after** everything using them has stopped.

The order matters: close resources last, in the reverse order of creating them.

## Deadlines and Kubernetes

When Kubernetes deletes a pod, it:

1. removes the pod from Service endpoints (new traffic stops arriving, eventually),
2. runs any `preStop` hook,
3. sends SIGTERM,
4. waits up to `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (30 seconds by default),
5. sends SIGKILL.

Two consequences:

- Your shutdown deadline must be **shorter** than the grace period, or the process is killed mid-shutdown.
- Endpoint removal is not instant. Load balancers may still send requests for a few seconds after SIGTERM. A common practice is a short `preStop` sleep (a few seconds) or a delay in your handler before calling `Shutdown`, and failing readiness checks as soon as shutdown begins. Lesson 15.2 covers probes and these settings in detail.

## Common mistakes

### Calling `os.Exit` or `log.Fatal` during shutdown

They skip deferred cleanup. Return from `main` instead.

### No deadline on `Shutdown`

A single hung request (or a client that never closes its connection) blocks shutdown until SIGKILL arrives.

### Treating `http.ErrServerClosed` as an error

It is the normal result of `Shutdown`. Check for it with `errors.Is`.

### Closing the database before workers finish

Workers then fail with "database is closed" errors during every deploy. Stop the users of a resource before the resource.

## Key takeaways

- Graceful shutdown means: stop accepting, finish in-flight work, release resources, give up at a deadline.
- `signal.NotifyContext` turns SIGINT and SIGTERM into context cancellation.
- `http.Server.Shutdown(ctx)` waits for active requests; `Serve` then returns `http.ErrServerClosed`.
- Drain workers before closing the resources they use.
- Keep the shutdown deadline below Kubernetes' termination grace period.

## Further reading

- [Package os/signal: NotifyContext](https://pkg.go.dev/os/signal#NotifyContext)
- [net/http: Server.Shutdown](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Server.Shutdown)
- [Kubernetes: Termination of Pods](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination)

lessons.title: 7.8 Projects: token bucket rate limiter and concurrent crawler
lessons.description: Two complete concurrent programs: a token bucket rate limiter written from scratch, and a polite web crawler with a coordinator goroutine, a worker pool and cancellation.
lessons.body:
These two projects put Modules 6 and 7 together. The crawler uses the rate limiter, so read them in order.

## Project 1: a token bucket rate limiter

Code: [`projects/ratelimit`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/projects/ratelimit)

Lesson 7.5 introduced the token bucket and used `golang.org/x/time/rate`. This project implements the same algorithm with only the standard library, so you can see every detail.



```gopath-example
example-202
```



Design points:

- **Lazy refill.** There is no background goroutine adding tokens. Each call computes how many tokens accumulated since the last call (`elapsed * rate`, capped at `burst`). An idle bucket costs nothing.
- **One mutex** guards all fields. Every method locks, refills, and acts.
- **`WaitN` reserves before sleeping.** It subtracts the tokens immediately (the balance may go negative) and sleeps until they would be earned. That makes concurrent waiters fair: each is scheduled after the ones before it. If the context ends first, the reservation is returned.
- **Fail fast on impossible deadlines.** If the required wait is longer than the time left on the context, `WaitN` returns immediately instead of sleeping and failing later.
- **Injected clock.** The `now` field lets tests advance time manually and check exact token counts.

### Per-key limiting



```gopath-example
example-203
```



`Keyed` gives every key (a client IP, an API key) its own bucket, created on first use. `Prune` deletes buckets that have been idle, so memory does not grow with every client ever seen. In Module 12 this becomes HTTP middleware that returns 429 Too Many Requests.

### Tests



```gopath-example
example-204
```



With a fake clock, refill math can be checked exactly, and 500 concurrent goroutines get **exactly** 100 tokens. On Go 1.25 and later, [`synctest_test.go`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/blob/main/projects/ratelimit/synctest_test.go) also checks `Wait`'s real timer behavior on a virtual clock. The benchmarks are used again in Module 10.

## Project 2: a concurrent web crawler

Code: [`projects/crawler`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/projects/crawler)

The crawler starts at a URL, follows links on the same host up to a depth limit, and reports every page's status.

### Architecture

```text
              tasks (unbuffered)
coordinator  ───────────────────▶  worker 1 ─┐
  owns:      ───────────────────▶  worker 2 ─┤  fetch (rate limited)
  - queue    ───────────────────▶  worker N ─┘
  - seen set ◀───────────────────  outcomes (unbuffered)
  - results
```

- **One coordinator goroutine owns all state**: the queue, the set of seen URLs and the results. Nothing is shared, so there are no mutexes at all; channels are the only synchronization.
- **A fixed pool of workers** only fetches pages and reports outcomes.
- **The coordinator's loop** selects between "send the next task" and "receive an outcome". The send case uses the **nil channel trick** from lesson 6.3: when the queue is empty, the send channel is `nil`, which disables that case.
- **Termination**: the crawl is done when the queue is empty **and** nothing is in flight. This is the classic subtle part of crawlers: an empty queue alone is not enough, because a running fetch may discover new links.



```gopath-example
example-205
```



### Fetching



```gopath-example
example-206
```



- The `Fetcher` interface keeps the crawler testable.
- Every request carries the context, so cancelling the crawl aborts in-flight HTTP requests too.
- The body is read through `io.LimitReader`, so a huge page cannot exhaust memory.
- Links are found with a regular expression. That is **not** a correct HTML parser, and the code says so; a production crawler should use `golang.org/x/net/html`. It keeps the project dependency-free.

### Testing without the internet



```gopath-example
example-207
```



`httptest.NewServer` serves a small fake site on localhost with a cycle (`/a` links back to `/`), a fragment link to an already seen page, a broken link, an external link and a slow page. The tests check that every page is fetched **exactly once** (the server counts hits), that depth and page limits work, that a timeout cancels the crawl, and that no goroutines leak.

### Running it

```bash
make serve                                                  # in one terminal: the course site
go run ./projects/crawler/cmd/crawler -url http://localhost:1313/ -depth 2 -rate 20
```

Only crawl sites you own or have permission to crawl, and keep the rate low. Being polite is part of the design.

## Stretch goals

1. Respect `robots.txt` before crawling a site.
2. Add per-host rate limiting with `ratelimit.Keyed` so a crawler following several hosts is polite to each.
3. Replace the regular expression with `golang.org/x/net/html` in the `examples/thirdparty` module style (a separate module with the dependency).
4. Stream results to the caller through an `iter.Seq[Result]` instead of returning a slice at the end.

## Part 2, first half: recap

You can now:

- Start, wait for and stop goroutines without leaking them
- Use channels, `select`, mutexes and atomics, and know when to pick each
- Find data races with `-race` and explain the memory model's guarantees
- Propagate cancellation with `context`
- Build worker pools, pipelines and error groups
- Rate limit and apply backpressure
- Shut a service down gracefully

Next is **[Module 8: Standard library deep dives](/learn/08-standard-library/)**.

lessons.title: 8.1 io: composing readers and writers
lessons.description: io.Copy, TeeReader, MultiWriter, LimitReader, Pipe, bufio.Scanner and bufio.Writer: how to build streaming programs from small, composable pieces.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to move data with `io.Copy` instead of reading everything into memory
- The composition helpers: `TeeReader`, `MultiWriter`, `MultiReader`, `LimitReader`
- Reading lines and words with `bufio.Scanner`, and its limits
- Why `bufio.Writer` needs `Flush`
- Connecting a writer to a reader with `io.Pipe`

## The idea

Lesson 4.5 introduced `io.Reader` and `io.Writer`. Their power comes from **composition**: small wrappers that each do one thing, stacked into a pipeline. Data flows through in chunks, so a 10 GB file uses a few kilobytes of memory.

## Copying



```gopath-example
example-208
```



`io.Copy(dst, src)` moves everything from any reader to any writer, in chunks, and returns the number of bytes copied. It is how you stream a file to an HTTP response, a response to a file, or stdin to a compressor.

`io.ReadAll` reads **everything** into one slice. That is fine for small, bounded inputs (a config file, a small API response) and dangerous for anything controlled by someone else. Wrap untrusted input in `io.LimitReader` first.

## Splitting and joining streams



```gopath-example
example-209
```



- `io.TeeReader(r, w)` returns a reader that also writes everything it reads to `w`. Here it hashes a stream while it is copied, in one pass. Any `hash.Hash` is an `io.Writer`.
- `io.MultiWriter(w1, w2, ...)` duplicates every write. Useful for writing a log to a file and stdout at once.



```gopath-example
example-210
```



- `io.LimitReader(r, n)` stops after `n` bytes: protection against huge inputs.
- `io.MultiReader(r1, r2, ...)` reads its inputs one after the other, as one stream.

## `bufio.Scanner`: lines, words and custom tokens



```gopath-example
example-211
```



- `Scan()` advances to the next token and returns `false` at the end **or on error**. Always check `sc.Err()` after the loop, or read errors vanish silently.
- The default split function returns lines without the newline. `bufio.ScanWords`, `ScanRunes` and `ScanBytes` are built in, and you can write your own `SplitFunc`.
- A token is limited to **64 KiB** by default. Longer lines make `Scan` fail with `bufio.ErrTooLong`. Raise the limit with `sc.Buffer(buf, max)`, as the wordfreq project does.
- `sc.Bytes()` returns a slice that is **overwritten** by the next `Scan`. Copy it, or use `sc.Text()`, if you keep it (lesson 3.3).

## `bufio.Writer`: batching small writes



```gopath-example
example-212
```



Every `Write` on a file or socket is a system call. `bufio.Writer` collects small writes in memory and sends them in large chunks. The catch: data sits in the buffer until it fills up or you call **`Flush`**. Forgetting the final `Flush` is a classic way to lose the end of a file. `Flush` also returns any write error, so check it.

`bufio.Reader` does the same for reads, and adds helpers such as `ReadString('\n')` and `Peek`.

## `io.Pipe`: connecting a writer to a reader



```gopath-example
example-213
```



Sometimes one API wants to **write** (an encoder, a compressor) and another wants to **read** (an HTTP request body, an upload). `io.Pipe` connects them: what one goroutine writes to `pw`, another reads from `pr`. It is synchronous and unbuffered, so the writer must run in its own goroutine, and closing `pw` signals EOF to the reader. `pw.CloseWithError(err)` passes a failure through instead.

## Optional faster paths

`io.Copy` checks whether the source implements `io.WriterTo` or the destination implements `io.ReaderFrom`, and lets them do the copy directly (lesson 4.3). Files and network connections use this to copy with fewer allocations, and on Linux even without copying through user space. You get that for free by using `io.Copy` instead of a manual read loop.

## Common mistakes

### Reading everything into memory

`io.ReadAll` on an upload or a large file. Stream with `io.Copy`, or bound it with `io.LimitReader`.

### Ignoring `sc.Err()`

`for sc.Scan() {}` stops on errors as well as on EOF. Check the error after the loop.

### Forgetting `Flush`

The last chunk never reaches the file. `defer w.Flush()` is not enough on its own either, because the error is lost; flush explicitly and return its error.

### Writing your own read loop

Hand-written `for { n, err := r.Read(buf) ... }` loops often get the `n > 0` with `io.EOF` case wrong (lesson 4.5). Use `io.Copy`, `io.ReadFull` or `bufio`.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m08/grep
```



## Key takeaways

- Stream with `io.Copy`; use `io.ReadAll` only for small, bounded data.
- Compose behavior with `TeeReader`, `MultiWriter`, `MultiReader` and `LimitReader`.
- `bufio.Scanner` reads lines or words; check `Err()`, and raise the 64 KiB limit for long lines.
- `bufio.Writer` batches writes; always `Flush` and check its error.
- `io.Pipe` connects a writer-style API to a reader-style API across goroutines.

## Further reading

- [Package io](https://pkg.go.dev/io) and [Package bufio](https://pkg.go.dev/bufio)
- [Package testing/iotest](https://pkg.go.dev/testing/iotest)

- scan() advances to the next token and returns false at the end or on error. always check sc.err() after the loop, or read errors vanish silently.
- the default split function returns lines without the newline. bufio.scanwords, scanrunes and scanbytes are built in, and you can write your own splitfunc.
- a token is limited to 64 kib by default. longer lines make scan fail with bufio.errtoolong. raise the limit with sc.buffer(buf, max), as the wordfreq project does.
- sc.bytes() returns a slice that is overwritten by the next scan. copy it, or use sc.text(), if you keep it (lesson 3.3).

 bufio.writer: batching small writes







every write on a file or socket is a system call. bufio.writer collects small writes in memory and sends them in large chunks. the catch: data sits in the buffer until it fills up or you call flush. forgetting the final flush is a classic way to lose the end of a file. flush also returns any write error, so check it.

bufio.reader does the same for reads, and adds helpers such as readstring('\n') and peek.

 io.pipe: connecting a writer to a reader







sometimes one api wants to write (an encoder, a compressor) and another wants to read (an http request body, an upload). io.pipe connects them: what one goroutine writes to pw, another reads from pr. it is synchronous and unbuffered, so the writer must run in its own goroutine, and closing pw signals eof to the reader. pw.closewitherror(err) passes a failure through instead.

 optional faster paths

io.copy checks whether the source implements io.writerto or the destination implements io.readerfrom, and lets them do the copy directly (lesson 4.3). files and network connections use this to copy with fewer allocations, and on linux even without copying through user space. you get that for free by using io.copy instead of a manual read loop.

 common mistakes

 reading everything into memory

io.readall on an upload or a large file. stream with io.copy, or bound it with io.limitreader.

 ignoring sc.err()

for sc.scan() {} stops on errors as well as on eof. check the error after the loop.

 forgetting flush

the last chunk never reaches the file. defer w.flush() is not enough on its own either, because the error is lost; flush explicitly and return its error.

 writing your own read loop

hand-written for { n, err := r.read(buf) ... } loops often get the n > 0 with io.eof case wrong (lesson 4.5). use io.copy, io.readfull or bufio.

 exercise







 key takeaways

- stream with io.copy; use io.readall only for small, bounded data.
- compose behavior with teereader, multiwriter, multireader and limitreader.
- bufio.scanner reads lines or words; check err(), and raise the 64 kib limit for long lines.
- bufio.writer batches writes; always flush and check its error.
- io.pipe connects a writer-style api to a reader-style api across goroutines.

 further reading

- [package io](https://pkg.go.dev/io) and [package bufio](https://pkg.go.dev/bufio)
- [package testing/iotest](https://pkg.go.dev/testing/iotest)

lessons.title: 8.2 encoding/json and encoding/json/v2
lessons.description: Encode and decode JSON with struct tags, stream with Encoder and Decoder, customize types, handle unknown and polymorphic data, and use the encoding/json/v2 API that became generally available in Go 1.27.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How struct fields and tags map to JSON
- Decoding into structs, and what happens with missing, extra or mistyped fields
- Strict decoding and streaming with `Decoder` and `Encoder`
- Custom encoding with `MarshalText` and `MarshalJSON`
- Delaying decoding with `json.RawMessage`, and the trouble with numbers in `any`
- `omitzero` (Go 1.24) versus `omitempty`
- The `encoding/json/v2` and `jsontext` packages (Go 1.27)

## The idea

`encoding/json` uses **reflection** to map Go values to JSON and back. Exported struct fields become JSON object members; **tags** control the names and options. There is no code generation and no schema: the struct is the schema.



```gopath-callout
callout-11
```



## Encoding



```gopath-example
example-214
```



| Tag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `json:"name"` | Use `name` as the member name |
| `json:"name,omitempty"` | Leave out if the value is empty: `0`, `""`, `false`, `nil`, empty slice or map |
| `json:"name,omitzero"` | (Go 1.24+) Leave out if the value is the zero value, or its `IsZero()` method returns true |
| `json:"-"` | Never encode or decode this field |
| `json:"name,string"` | Encode a number or bool as a JSON string |

Unexported fields (`internal`) are invisible to the encoder. Pointer fields (`Address *Address`) encode as `null` or are omitted with `omitempty` when nil, which is the usual way to make a nested object optional. `time.Time` encodes as RFC 3339.

## Decoding



```gopath-example
example-215
```



- Pass a **pointer**; `Unmarshal` fills the value it points to.
- Member names match field names **case-insensitively** in `encoding/json`.
- Members with no matching field (`extra`) are **ignored**.
- Fields missing from the JSON keep whatever value they had (usually the zero value). If you need to know whether a field was present, use a pointer field.
- A type mismatch returns a `*json.UnmarshalTypeError` with the field name. Inspect it with `errors.As`.

## Strict decoding



```gopath-example
example-216
```



For APIs and config files, silently ignoring unknown fields hides typos (`nmae`). `Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields()` turns them into errors.

## Streaming



```gopath-example
example-217
```



`json.NewDecoder(r)` reads values from any `io.Reader` one at a time, so it handles large inputs and streams of concatenated values (newline-delimited JSON). `json.NewEncoder(w)` writes values to any `io.Writer`. Use them directly on HTTP request and response bodies instead of reading the body into a byte slice first.

## Custom encoding



```gopath-example
example-218
```



Implement `encoding.TextMarshaler` and `TextUnmarshaler` when a type has a natural text form (enums, IDs, IP addresses). JSON then encodes it as a string, it works as a **map key**, and other encoders (YAML, XML, flags) understand it too. Implement `json.Marshaler` / `json.Unmarshaler` (`MarshalJSON`, `UnmarshalJSON`) only when you need full control over the JSON structure.

Note the receivers: `MarshalText` on the value, `UnmarshalText` on the pointer, because unmarshaling must modify the value.

## Polymorphic data with `RawMessage`



```gopath-example
example-219
```



`json.RawMessage` keeps a member's raw bytes undecoded. Decode the envelope first, look at the discriminator (`type`), then decode the payload into the right struct. This is the standard way to handle event streams and webhooks with several payload shapes.

## Numbers in `any`



```gopath-example
example-220
```



Decoding into `any` turns **every** number into `float64`, which silently loses precision for integers above 2^53 (IDs from other systems are a common victim). Decode into typed struct fields, or call `Decoder.UseNumber()` to get `json.Number` values that keep the original text.

## `omitzero` vs `omitempty`



```gopath-example
example-221
```



`omitempty` never omits a struct value, so an unset `time.Time` appears as `"0001-01-01T00:00:00Z"`. `omitzero` (Go 1.24+) omits zero values, and respects an `IsZero()` method, which is what you usually want for times and other structs.

## `encoding/json/v2` (Go 1.27)



```gopath-callout
callout-12
```



The v2 API takes **options** as extra arguments instead of requiring a `Decoder` for every setting, and has stricter, more predictable defaults:



```gopath-example
example-222
```





```gopath-example
example-223
```



Differences from v1 worth knowing:

| | v1 (`encoding/json`) | v2 (`encoding/json/v2`) |
|---|---|---|
| nil slice or map | `null` | `[]` or `{}` |
| Member name matching | case-insensitive | case-sensitive (option `MatchCaseInsensitiveNames`) |
| Duplicate member names | last one wins | error |
| Invalid UTF-8 in strings | replaced silently | error |
| Unknown members | ignored (`DisallowUnknownFields` on a `Decoder`) | ignored (option `RejectUnknownMembers`) |
| Streaming | `NewEncoder`, `NewDecoder` | `MarshalWrite`, `UnmarshalRead`, or `jsontext` |

The low-level `jsontext` package reads and writes JSON tokens, always producing valid JSON:



```gopath-example
example-224
```



**Which should you use?** For existing code, keep `encoding/json`: it is supported, and on Go 1.27 it already runs on the faster v2 engine (unmarshaling in particular is significantly faster). For new code on Go 1.27+, v2's stricter defaults and option-based API are a good choice. Check the duplicate-name and case-sensitivity differences before switching an existing API, since clients may depend on the old behavior.

## Common mistakes

### Unexported fields

`name string` is never encoded or decoded. Capitalize it and add a tag.

### Unmarshaling into a non-pointer

`json.Unmarshal(data, u)` instead of `&u` returns an `InvalidUnmarshalError` and changes nothing.

### Relying on case-insensitive matching

It works in v1 and fails in v2. Use exact names in tags and in JSON.

### Matching error strings

The text of JSON errors changed in Go 1.27. Use `errors.As` with `*json.UnmarshalTypeError`, `*json.SyntaxError` and friends.

### Large integers through `any`

Precision loss above 2^53. Use typed fields or `UseNumber`.

## Key takeaways

- Exported fields plus tags define the JSON shape; `-`, `omitempty`, `omitzero` and `string` are the main options.
- Decoding ignores unknown members unless you ask for strictness; type mismatches return typed errors.
- Use `Decoder` and `Encoder` to stream from and to readers and writers.
- Implement `MarshalText`/`UnmarshalText` for types with a text form; use `RawMessage` for polymorphic payloads.
- Go 1.27: `encoding/json/v2` and `jsontext` are available, and `encoding/json` runs on the v2 engine with the same behavior.

## Further reading

- [Package encoding/json](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json)
- [Package encoding/json/v2](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json/v2) and [encoding/json/jsontext](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json/jsontext)
- [Go 1.27 release notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)
- [JSON and Go](https://go.dev/blog/json) on the Go blog

lessons.title: 8.3 time: durations, monotonic clock, time zones
lessons.description: Work with time.Duration, format and parse with Go's reference layout, handle time zones correctly, measure elapsed time with the monotonic clock, and avoid the classic date arithmetic surprises.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How `time.Duration` works and how to convert to and from it
- Go's unusual formatting layouts, based on a reference time
- Time zones: `In`, `FixedZone`, `LoadLocation`, `ParseInLocation`
- Why you compare instants with `Equal`, not `==`
- The monotonic clock and measuring elapsed time
- Date arithmetic surprises with `AddDate`

## Durations



```gopath-example
example-225
```



A `time.Duration` is an `int64` count of **nanoseconds** with methods. Constants like `time.Second` make durations readable: `90 * time.Minute`. Two rules:

- Multiplying a constant by a duration works (`3 * time.Second`), but an `int` **variable** needs a conversion: `time.Duration(n) * time.Second`.
- Never pass plain numbers as durations (`time.Sleep(5)` sleeps 5 **nanoseconds**). Always multiply by a unit.

Durations print in a readable form (`1h30m0s`) and parse with `time.ParseDuration`, which is what the `flag` package uses for duration flags.

## Formatting and parsing layouts

Go does not use `YYYY-MM-DD` style patterns. A layout is the **reference time** written the way you want your output to look:

```text
Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006
```

It reads as 1 2 3 4 5 6 7: month 1, day 2, hour 3 (15 in 24-hour), minute 4, second 5, year 2006, time zone -07.



```gopath-example
example-226
```



| Want | Layout |
|---|---|
| Year | `2006` (or `06`) |
| Month | `01`, `1`, `Jan`, `January` |
| Day | `02`, `2`, `_2` |
| Hour | `15` (24h), `03` or `3` (12h) with `PM` |
| Minute, second | `04`, `05` |
| Fractional seconds | `.000`, `.000000`, `.999` (trailing zeros trimmed) |
| Time zone | `MST`, `-0700`, `-07:00`, `Z07:00` |

Use the predefined constants (`time.RFC3339`, `time.RFC3339Nano`, `time.DateOnly`, `time.DateTime`, `time.Kitchen`) whenever they fit. For APIs and logs, **RFC 3339 in UTC** is the safe default.

## Time zones

A `time.Time` is an **instant** plus a **location** used for display. Changing the location with `In` does not change the instant:



```gopath-example
example-227
```



- `t.Equal(u)` compares instants. `==` compares the whole struct, including the location and the monotonic reading, so two equal instants in different zones are `!=`. Use `Equal` (and `Before`, `After`, `Compare`).
- `time.Parse` without an offset in the input assumes **UTC**. Use `time.ParseInLocation` to interpret a local wall-clock time in a specific zone.
- `time.FixedZone` creates a zone with a constant offset. For real zones with daylight saving rules, use `time.LoadLocation("Asia/Kolkata")` or `"America/New_York"`. It reads the system's time zone database; in minimal containers that database may be missing, so add `import _ "time/tzdata"` to embed it in your binary (about 450 KB).

A good rule for services: **store and compute in UTC, convert to a user's zone only for display.**

## Measuring elapsed time



```gopath-example
example-228
```



The wall clock can jump: NTP corrections, daylight saving changes, an admin setting the clock. `time.Now()` also records a **monotonic** clock reading that only moves forward, and `time.Since`, `time.Until` and `t.Sub` use it automatically when both times have one. So measuring durations with `time.Now()` and `time.Since()` is safe. The monotonic reading is stripped by `t.Round(0)` and by serialization, so a time read back from JSON or a database has none.

## Date arithmetic



```gopath-example
example-229
```



- `Add` adds an exact duration.
- `AddDate(years, months, days)` works on the calendar, and **normalizes overflow**: January 31 plus one month is "February 31", which becomes March 3. If you need "the last day of next month", compute it explicitly.
- Around daylight saving transitions, a calendar day is not always 24 hours. `AddDate(0, 0, 1)` keeps the wall-clock time; `Add(24 * time.Hour)` does not.
- `t.Unix()` and `time.Unix(sec, nsec)` convert to and from Unix timestamps.

## Testing code that uses time

Code that calls `time.Now()` directly is hard to test. Two approaches from earlier lessons:

- **Inject a clock**: a `now func() time.Time` field, replaced in tests (the URL shortener and rate limiter projects do this).
- **`testing/synctest`** (Go 1.25+): run the test in a bubble with a fake clock that advances only when all goroutines are blocked (lesson 6.3). Go 1.27 adds `synctest.Sleep`, which sleeps and then waits for the bubble to settle.

## Common mistakes

### `time.Sleep(5)`

Five nanoseconds. Write `5 * time.Second`.

### Comparing times with `==`

Fails for equal instants in different zones, and when one time has a monotonic reading and the other does not. Use `Equal`.

### Parsing local times as UTC

`time.Parse("2006-01-02 15:04", "...")` assumes UTC. Use `ParseInLocation` when the input is local time.

### Assuming the time zone database exists

`LoadLocation` fails in `scratch` or distroless images without `tzdata`. Embed it with `import _ "time/tzdata"`.

### Using wall-clock differences for timeouts

Computing timeouts from two wall-clock readings breaks when the clock jumps. Use `time.Since`, timers, or context deadlines.

## Key takeaways

- `Duration` is nanoseconds; always multiply by a unit, and convert int variables explicitly.
- Layouts are the reference time `Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006`; prefer the predefined constants, especially RFC 3339.
- A `Time` is an instant plus a display location; compare with `Equal`, store in UTC.
- `time.Now` carries a monotonic reading, so `time.Since` is safe for measuring.
- `AddDate` normalizes overflowing dates; check edge cases.

## Further reading

- [Package time](https://pkg.go.dev/time)
- [Package time/tzdata](https://pkg.go.dev/time/tzdata)
- [Monotonic clocks](https://pkg.go.dev/time#hdr-Monotonic_Clocks) in the time package documentation

lessons.title: 8.4 log/slog structured logging
lessons.description: Structured logging with log/slog: key-value attributes, text and JSON handlers, levels, With and groups, context-aware handlers, redaction with LogValuer, and MultiHandler in Go 1.26.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why structured logs beat formatted strings
- Logging with `slog.Info`, attributes and levels
- Text and JSON handlers, and `HandlerOptions`
- Adding common attributes with `With` and grouping them
- Changing the level at run time
- Redacting secrets with `LogValuer`
- Writing a handler that adds request IDs from the context
- Sending logs to several destinations with `NewMultiHandler` (Go 1.26+)

## The idea

`log.Printf("user %d bought %s for %d", id, item, price)` produces a string a human can read and a machine has to parse with regular expressions. **Structured logging** records each value as a separate key-value pair:

```text
level=INFO msg="purchase" user_id=7 item=book price=499
{"level":"INFO","msg":"purchase","user_id":7,"item":"book","price":499}
```

Log platforms (Loki, Elasticsearch, CloudWatch, Datadog) can then filter and aggregate on fields directly: every purchase over 400, every error for user 7. `log/slog` (Go 1.21) is the standard library's structured logger, and most new Go code uses it.

## Basics



```gopath-example
example-230
```



- Messages are short, constant descriptions of the event ("server started"). The variable parts go in **attributes**.
- Attributes are passed as alternating keys and values, or as typed `slog.Attr` values (`slog.String`, `slog.Int`, `slog.Duration`). Typed attrs avoid allocations and mismatched pairs; `go vet` checks the alternating form for odd counts.
- The four levels are `Debug`, `Info`, `Warn` and `Error`. Records below the handler's level are dropped cheaply.

The example helper removes the `time` attribute only to make the output stable for testing. Real logs keep it.

## Handlers

A `slog.Logger` formats nothing itself; it passes records to a `slog.Handler`. The standard library includes:

- `slog.NewTextHandler(w, opts)`: `key=value` pairs, good for local development.
- `slog.NewJSONHandler(w, opts)`: one JSON object per line, good for production log pipelines.
- `slog.DiscardHandler` (Go 1.24+): drops everything, useful in tests and libraries.

`slog.HandlerOptions` sets the minimum `Level`, `AddSource` (file and line), and `ReplaceAttr`, a hook to rename, reformat or remove attributes.

Set a default once in `main` with `slog.SetDefault(logger)`, and the package-level functions (`slog.Info(...)`) and the old `log` package both write through it.

## `With` and groups



```gopath-example
example-231
```



`logger.With(attrs...)` returns a child logger that adds those attributes to every record. Create one per request with the request ID, route and user, and pass it down (or put it in the context). Handlers pre-format `With` attributes once, so this is cheap.

`slog.Group` nests attributes under a key: `user.id` in text, `"user":{"id":7}` in JSON.

## Dynamic levels



```gopath-example
example-232
```



A `slog.LevelVar` can be changed while the program runs, for example from an admin endpoint or a config reload, to turn on debug logging during an incident without a restart.

## Redacting secrets



```gopath-example
example-233
```



A type that implements `slog.LogValuer` decides how it appears in logs, **everywhere** it is logged. Give secret-bearing types (tokens, passwords, API keys, full card numbers) a `LogValue` that returns a redacted value, and nobody can leak them into logs by accident. `ReplaceAttr` is a second line of defense for keys like `password`.

## Context and custom handlers



```gopath-example
example-234
```



Handlers compose like `io.Writer` wrappers. `ContextHandler` embeds another handler and adds the request ID from the context to every record. Calling `log.InfoContext(ctx, ...)` instead of `log.Info(...)` gives handlers access to the context, which is also how tracing libraries attach trace and span IDs (lesson 12.5).

## Several destinations (Go 1.26+)



```gopath-example
example-235
```



`slog.NewMultiHandler` sends each record to every handler, for example human-readable text to the console and JSON to a file.

## What to log

- **Log events, not every function call.** Requests, state changes, errors with context, startup configuration (without secrets).
- **Log errors once**, at the edge where they are handled (lesson 5.6), with the attributes that identify the operation.
- **Keep keys consistent** across the codebase: `user_id` everywhere, not `userID` in one place and `uid` in another. A short list of shared key constants helps.
- **Do not log personal data** you do not need.

## Common mistakes

### Formatting values into the message

`slog.Info(fmt.Sprintf("user %d logged in", id))` throws away the structure. Use `slog.Info("user logged in", "user_id", id)`.

### Odd numbers of key-value arguments

`slog.Info("msg", "user_id")` produces a `!BADKEY` attribute. Run `go vet`, or use typed attrs.

### Expensive arguments at disabled levels

`log.Debug("state", "dump", expensiveDump())` computes the dump even when debug is off. Check `log.Enabled(ctx, slog.LevelDebug)` first, or make the value a `LogValuer` so it is only computed when logged.

### Logging secrets

Tokens in request headers, passwords in config structs. Use `LogValuer` and `ReplaceAttr`.

## Key takeaways

- Structured logs record key-value attributes that machines can query.
- `slog` loggers send records to handlers; use text locally and JSON in production.
- Add shared attributes with `With`, nest them with `Group`, and change levels at run time with `LevelVar`.
- Redact secrets with `LogValuer`; enrich records from the context with a wrapping handler.
- Go 1.26 adds `NewMultiHandler` for several destinations.

## Further reading

- [Package log/slog](https://pkg.go.dev/log/slog)
- [Structured Logging with slog](https://go.dev/blog/slog) on the Go blog
- [A Guide to Writing slog Handlers](https://github.com/golang/example/tree/master/slog-handler-guide)

lessons.title: 8.5 os, filepath, io/fs and embed
lessons.description: Read and write files, write atomically, walk directory trees, program against the io/fs interface, embed files into binaries, and confine file access with os.Root.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Reading, writing and appending files with `os`
- Building paths portably with `path/filepath`
- Writing files **atomically** so readers never see half-written data
- Walking directory trees with `filepath.WalkDir`
- The `io/fs` interface, and testing file code with `fstest.MapFS`
- Embedding files into your binary with `//go:embed`
- Restricting file access to one directory with `os.Root` (Go 1.24+)

## Reading and writing



```gopath-example
example-236
```



- `os.ReadFile` and `os.WriteFile` handle open, read or write, and close in one call. They are the right choice for small files.
- `os.Open` (read only), `os.Create` (truncate or create) and `os.OpenFile` (any combination of flags) return an `*os.File`, which is an `io.Reader` and `io.Writer`, for streaming larger files. Close it with `defer f.Close()`, and check the error of `Close` for files you wrote (lesson 2.7).
- Permissions like `0o644` (owner read and write, others read) and `0o755` for directories are the usual values.
- Missing files return an error matching `fs.ErrNotExist`; check with `errors.Is`, never by message.

Use `filepath.Join`, `filepath.Dir`, `filepath.Base` and `filepath.Ext` for operating system paths, so the same code works with `\` on Windows. The plain `path` package is for slash-separated paths such as URLs and `io/fs` names.

## Atomic writes

`os.WriteFile` truncates the file, then writes. If the program crashes in between, or another process reads at the wrong moment, it sees an empty or partial file. For config files, state files and caches, write atomically:



```gopath-example
example-237
```





```gopath-example
example-238
```



The temp file must be in the **same directory** (rename is only atomic within one filesystem), and `Sync` ensures the data is on disk before the rename makes it visible.

## Walking directories



```gopath-example
example-239
```



`filepath.WalkDir` calls your function for every file and directory, in lexical order. Return `filepath.SkipDir` to skip a directory, or `filepath.SkipAll` to stop. Prefer it to the older `filepath.Walk`, which calls `os.Lstat` on every entry and is slower.

## `io/fs`: one interface for every filesystem

`fs.FS` is a read-only filesystem interface with a single method, `Open(name)`. Real directories (`os.DirFS`), embedded files, zip archives (`zip.Reader`) and test fixtures all implement it, and helpers like `fs.ReadFile`, `fs.Glob` and `fs.WalkDir` work on any of them:



```gopath-example
example-240
```



Write functions that read files against `fs.FS` instead of calling `os` directly. Tests can then pass an in-memory `fstest.MapFS`, with no temporary directories. Names in `io/fs` always use forward slashes and are relative (no leading `/`).

## Embedding files



```gopath-example
example-241
```





```gopath-example
example-242
```



A `//go:embed` comment above a package-level variable copies files into the binary at build time:

- into a `string` or `[]byte` for a single file;
- into an `embed.FS` (which implements `fs.FS`) for patterns and whole directories.

This is how Go programs ship HTML templates, static web assets, SQL migrations and default config inside a single binary. Patterns are relative to the package directory, cannot reach outside the module, and skip files starting with `.` or `_` unless you use the `all:` prefix.

## Confining access with `os.Root`

Joining a user-supplied name to a base directory (`filepath.Join(uploads, name)`) is a classic **path traversal** hole: a name like `../../etc/passwd` escapes the directory. `os.Root` (Go 1.24) makes escaping impossible:



```gopath-example
example-243
```



Every operation on a `Root` is resolved inside its directory, including through symlinks. Go 1.25 added more methods (`MkdirAll`, `ReadFile`, `WriteFile`, `RemoveAll`, `Rename` and others). Use it whenever file names come from users, archives or network requests. `os.OpenInRoot(dir, name)` is a one-call shortcut.

## Common mistakes

### Building paths with string concatenation

`dir + "/" + name` breaks on Windows and makes traversal bugs easy. Use `filepath.Join`, and `os.Root` for untrusted names.

### Non-atomic writes of important files

A crash during `os.WriteFile` leaves a truncated file. Write to a temp file and rename.

### Forgetting that `embed` happens at build time

Changing an embedded file has no effect until you rebuild. And embedded files cannot be modified at run time.

### Not closing files

Each open file holds a file descriptor. Thousands of leaked ones produce `too many open files`.

## Key takeaways

- Use `os.ReadFile` and `os.WriteFile` for small files, `*os.File` streams for large ones.
- Build paths with `filepath`; write important files atomically via temp file, `Sync` and `Rename`.
- Walk trees with `filepath.WalkDir`.
- Program against `fs.FS` and test with `fstest.MapFS`.
- Embed assets with `//go:embed`; confine untrusted paths with `os.Root`.

## Further reading

- [Package os](https://pkg.go.dev/os), [path/filepath](https://pkg.go.dev/path/filepath) and [io/fs](https://pkg.go.dev/io/fs)
- [Package embed](https://pkg.go.dev/embed)
- [Traversal-resistant file APIs](https://go.dev/blog/osroot) on the Go blog

lessons.title: 8.6 strings, bytes, strconv and fmt verbs
lessons.description: The fmt verbs you need, fast number and string conversion with strconv, the strings helpers that save you loops, aligned table output with text/tabwriter, and allocation-free formatting.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The `fmt` verbs, widths and flags you will use most
- `strconv` for conversion and quoting, including allocation-free `Append` functions
- `strings` helpers: `Cut`, `CutLast` (Go 1.27), `NewReplacer`, `EqualFold`, `Map`
- Aligned, column-based output with `text/tabwriter`
- `fmt.Appendf` for building output without extra allocations

## `fmt` verbs



```gopath-example
example-244
```



| Verb | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `%v`, `%+v`, `%#v` | default format; with field names; as Go syntax |
| `%T` | the type |
| `%d`, `%x`, `%o`, `%b` | integer in decimal, hex, octal, binary |
| `%f`, `%.2f`, `%e`, `%g` | float: decimal, 2 decimals, scientific, compact |
| `%s`, `%q` | string; quoted and escaped |
| `%c`, `%U` | rune as character; as `U+XXXX` |
| `%t` | boolean |
| `%w` | error wrapping, only in `fmt.Errorf` (lesson 5.2) |
| `%%` | a literal percent sign |

Flags and widths go between `%` and the verb: `%5d` pads to 5 columns, `%-5d` left-aligns, `%05d` pads with zeros, `%8.3f` is width 8 with 3 decimals, and `%*d` takes the width from an argument.

`go vet` checks every `Printf`-style call: wrong verb for the type, missing or extra arguments. Keep it in CI.

## `strconv`



```gopath-example
example-245
```



- `Atoi`, `ParseInt`, `ParseFloat`, `ParseBool` parse text and return errors you must check (lesson 2.2).
- `Itoa`, `FormatInt(n, base)`, `FormatFloat` convert to text, faster than `fmt.Sprint`.
- `Quote` and `Unquote` handle Go-style quoted strings.
- `AppendInt`, `AppendFloat`, `AppendQuote` write into an existing `[]byte`. In hot paths (encoders, log formatters) they avoid allocating a string for every number.

## `strings` helpers



```gopath-example
example-246
```



- `strings.Cut(s, sep)` splits around the **first** separator and reports whether it was found. It replaces most `Index` plus slicing code and many `SplitN(s, sep, 2)` calls.
- `strings.NewReplacer` performs many replacements in one pass, and is safe for concurrent use, so build it once.
- `strings.EqualFold` compares case-insensitively without allocating. It uses simple Unicode case folding, so `"Straße"` and `"STRASSE"` are not equal; full language-aware comparison needs `golang.org/x/text`.
- `strings.Map` transforms or drops each rune.

`strings.Title` is deprecated because it handles many languages incorrectly; use `golang.org/x/text/cases` instead.

### `strings.CutLast` (Go 1.27)



```gopath-example
example-247
```



`CutLast` splits around the **last** separator: file extensions, the port in `host:port` (including IPv6 hosts with colons), the last path element. `bytes.CutLast` does the same for byte slices.

## Aligned output with `tabwriter`



```gopath-example
example-248
```



`text/tabwriter` turns tab-separated cells into aligned columns, the way `kubectl get pods` prints its tables. Write rows with `\t` between cells, then call `Flush`.

## Formatting without extra allocations



```gopath-example
example-249
```



`fmt.Appendf`, `fmt.Append` and `fmt.Appendln` (Go 1.19) format into a byte slice you provide, instead of returning a new string. Reusing one buffer across many lines saves allocations. Like the `strconv.Append` functions, this matters only in hot paths; elsewhere, `Sprintf` is perfectly fine.

## Common mistakes

### `fmt.Sprintf("%d", n)` in hot loops

`strconv.Itoa(n)` is several times faster and allocates less. Measure before optimizing, but know the option exists.

### Building SQL or shell commands with `Sprintf`

String formatting is not escaping. Use query parameters (lesson 13.1) and `exec.Command` with separate arguments.

### Ignoring `go vet` format warnings

A mismatched verb prints garbage like `%!d(string=three)` in production logs.

## Key takeaways

- Learn `%v`, `%+v`, `%T`, `%q`, widths and precision; let `go vet` check format strings.
- Use `strconv` for fast conversions, and its `Append` functions in hot paths.
- `strings.Cut` and `CutLast` (Go 1.27) replace manual index arithmetic.
- `text/tabwriter` aligns columns; `fmt.Appendf` formats into reusable buffers.

## Further reading

- [Package fmt](https://pkg.go.dev/fmt), especially the printing verbs section
- [Package strconv](https://pkg.go.dev/strconv) and [strings](https://pkg.go.dev/strings)
- [Package text/tabwriter](https://pkg.go.dev/text/tabwriter)

strconv.itoa(n) is several times faster and allocates less. measure before optimizing, but know the option exists.

 building sql or shell commands with sprintf

string formatting is not escaping. use query parameters (lesson 13.1) and exec.command with separate arguments.

 ignoring go vet format warnings

a mismatched verb prints garbage like %!d(string=three) in production logs.

 key takeaways

- learn %v, %+v, %t, %q, widths and precision; let go vet check format strings.
- use strconv for fast conversions, and its append functions in hot paths.
- strings.cut and cutlast (go 1.27) replace manual index arithmetic.
- text/tabwriter aligns columns; fmt.appendf formats into reusable buffers.

 further reading

- [package fmt](https://pkg.go.dev/fmt), especially the printing verbs section
- [package strconv](https://pkg.go.dev/strconv) and [strings](https://pkg.go.dev/strings)
- [package text/tabwriter](https://pkg.go.dev/text/tabwriter)

lessons.title: 8.7 net/http client done right
lessons.description: Make HTTP requests that cannot hang, leak connections or silently ignore errors: timeouts, contexts, closing and limiting bodies, checking status codes, and tuning the Transport.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why the default HTTP client is a production risk
- The steps every correct request needs
- Timeouts: `Client.Timeout`, request contexts and `Transport` timeouts
- Why you must close response bodies, and why status codes are not errors
- Testing clients against `httptest.Server`
- The `Transport` settings worth knowing

## The idea

`net/http` makes requests look trivial: `resp, err := http.Get(url)`. That line has three production problems:

1. The default client has **no timeout**. A server that accepts the connection and never answers blocks your goroutine forever.
2. If you forget `resp.Body.Close()`, the connection cannot be reused, and you leak file descriptors and goroutines.
3. A `404` or `500` response returns `err == nil`. If you only check `err`, failures look like successes.

## A correct request, step by step



```gopath-example
example-250
```



1. **One shared `http.Client`** for the whole program. Clients are safe for concurrent use and keep a pool of connections. Creating a client per request throws that pool away.
2. **`http.NewRequestWithContext`** so the caller's cancellation and deadline apply (lesson 7.1).
3. **Set headers** such as `Accept`, authentication and a `User-Agent`.
4. **Check `err` from `Do`.** It covers network failures, timeouts and cancellation, never HTTP status codes.
5. **`defer resp.Body.Close()`** immediately after the error check.
6. **Check `resp.StatusCode`** and turn unexpected statuses into errors.
7. **Limit and decode the body.** `io.LimitReader` stops a misbehaving server from filling your memory.

For connection reuse, the body should be read to the end before closing; since Go 1.27, closing an HTTP/1 response body drains a limited amount of unread content automatically, but reading or discarding what you do not need (as the error path does with `io.Copy(io.Discard, ...)`) keeps the behavior explicit.

## Testing against a fake server



```gopath-example
example-251
```



`httptest.NewServer` starts a real HTTP server on a local port with any handler you give it. Tests run fast, need no network, and can simulate every failure: slow responses, bad JSON, 500s. Go 1.27 adds `httptest.NewTestServer`, which uses an in-memory network and works with `testing/synctest` for deterministic timing.

## Timeouts



```gopath-example
example-252
```



There are several layers, and they combine:

| Setting | Limits | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `Client.Timeout` | the entire request, including reading the body | a safety net on every client |
| Request context deadline | the entire request, per call | when each call needs its own budget |
| `Transport.DialContext` timeout | establishing the TCP connection | detecting unreachable hosts quickly |
| `Transport.TLSHandshakeTimeout` | the TLS handshake | slow or broken TLS endpoints |
| `Transport.ResponseHeaderTimeout` | waiting for response headers after sending the request | servers that accept but never answer |

A timeout error satisfies `net.Error` with `Timeout() == true`, and a context deadline also matches `context.DeadlineExceeded`. Both are worth retrying for idempotent requests, with backoff (lesson 5.6).

## Tuning the Transport



```gopath-example
example-253
```



Clone `http.DefaultTransport` and adjust it instead of building one from scratch, so you keep its sensible defaults (proxy from environment, HTTP/2, keep-alives). The setting people most often need is **`MaxIdleConnsPerHost`**: its default of 2 means a service making many concurrent calls to one backend keeps opening new connections. Raise it to roughly your expected concurrency to that host.

## Retries

Only retry requests that are **safe to repeat**: `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent by definition; `POST` usually is not, unless the API supports idempotency keys. Retry on network errors, timeouts, `429` and `5xx`, with exponential backoff and jitter, and respect a `Retry-After` header.

## Common mistakes

### Using `http.Get` or `http.DefaultClient` in services

No timeout. Use your own client with `Timeout` set.

### A new `http.Client` (or `Transport`) per request

Destroys connection reuse. Every request pays for a TCP and TLS handshake, and idle connections pile up.

### Not closing the body

Leaks connections. `defer resp.Body.Close()` right after checking `err`.

### Treating non-2xx as success

`err == nil` with a 503 response. Always check `StatusCode`.

### Reading unlimited bodies

`io.ReadAll(resp.Body)` from a server you do not control. Wrap it in `io.LimitReader`.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m08/apiclient
```



## Key takeaways

- Use one shared `http.Client` with a `Timeout`; never the default client in services.
- Every request: context, headers, check `err`, close the body, check the status, limit the body.
- Status codes are not errors; translate them yourself.
- Test against `httptest.Server`; tune `MaxIdleConnsPerHost` for busy backends.
- Retry only idempotent requests, with backoff.

## Further reading

- [Package net/http](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http), especially Client and Transport
- [Package net/http/httptest](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http/httptest)
- [The complete guide to Go net/http timeouts](https://blog.cloudflare.com/the-complete-guide-to-golang-net-http-timeouts/) on the Cloudflare blog

lessons.title: 8.8 Project: a mini Redis server
lessons.description: Build a Redis-compatible TCP server with only the standard library: the RESP protocol with bufio, a concurrent keyspace with expiry, append-only file persistence, and graceful shutdown. Works with redis-cli.
lessons.body:
## What you will build

A small server that speaks the real Redis protocol, so the real `redis-cli` can talk to it:

```bash
go run ./projects/miniredis/cmd/miniredis -addr 127.0.0.1:6380 -aof /tmp/mini.aof
```

```bash
$ redis-cli -p 6380 set greeting "hello gopher"
OK
$ redis-cli -p 6380 get greeting
"hello gopher"
$ redis-cli -p 6380 incr visits
(integer) 1
```

Stop it with Ctrl+C, start it again, and the data is still there.

It brings together Modules 6, 7 and 8: TCP networking, `bufio` parsing, a mutex-protected store, background goroutines, `context` cancellation, files and `slog`. The code is in [`projects/miniredis`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/projects/miniredis).

## Architecture

```text
              ┌───────────────── server ──────────────────┐
redis-cli ──▶ │ accept loop ──▶ one goroutine per client  │
redis-cli ──▶ │                   │  resp.Reader / Writer  │
              │                   ▼                        │
              │              execute(cmd) ──▶ store (RWMutex, TTLs)
              │                   │                        │
              │                   └──▶ aof.Log (append writes)
              │ janitor goroutine: removes expired keys    │
              └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Four packages, each with one job:

| Package | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `internal/resp` | Parse commands and write replies in RESP2 |
| `internal/store` | The keyspace: values, expiry, concurrency safety |
| `internal/aof` | Append write commands to a file; replay it on startup |
| `internal/server` | Accept connections, dispatch commands, shut down gracefully |

## The protocol: `internal/resp`

Redis clients send each command as an **array of bulk strings**, each prefixed with its length:

```text
*3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$8\r\ngreeting\r\n$12\r\nhello gopher\r\n
```

Length prefixes make the protocol **binary safe**: a value can contain spaces, newlines or zero bytes.



```gopath-example
example-254
```



Things to notice:

- `bufio.Reader.ReadSlice('\n')` reads a line without allocating, and `io.ReadFull` reads exactly `size+2` bytes for a bulk string.
- **Limits** on array length, bulk size and line length stop a malicious client from making the server allocate gigabytes.
- **Errors are classified**: `ErrProtocol` for bad input (the server replies with an error and closes), `io.EOF` for a clean disconnect between commands, and `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF` for a disconnect in the middle of one.
- The writer buffers replies, and the server calls `Flush` once per command.

The tests include a **fuzz test** (Module 9 explains fuzzing): `go test -fuzz=FuzzReadCommand` throws millions of random inputs at the parser to make sure it never panics or hangs.

## The keyspace: `internal/store`



```gopath-example
example-255
```



- **One `sync.RWMutex`** guards the map. `GET`, `EXISTS` and `TTL` take the read lock, so many clients can read in parallel.
- **`INCR` is one critical section.** Reading, parsing, adding and writing back under one lock is what makes 1000 concurrent increments add up to exactly 1000 (the server test checks this). Doing it as `GET` then `SET` would lose updates.
- **Lazy expiry plus a janitor.** Reads treat expired keys as missing without deleting them (they only hold the read lock). `RunJanitor` periodically removes expired keys so memory is reclaimed even for keys nobody reads again. Redis uses the same two-part approach.
- **Injected clock** for deterministic expiry tests.

## Persistence: `internal/aof`



```gopath-example
example-256
```



An **append-only file** records every write command in RESP format. On startup, replaying the file rebuilds the data. Design decisions:

- **Only successful writes are appended** (a `DEL` that deleted nothing is skipped).
- **fsync policy.** Calling `Sync` after every write is safest and slowest. The default here, like Redis' default, syncs once per second, so a crash can lose up to a second of writes.
- **Truncated tail tolerance.** If the process crashed in the middle of an append, the last command is incomplete. Replay stops cleanly at that point instead of refusing to start.

## The server: `internal/server`



```gopath-example
example-257
```



- **One goroutine per connection** is the idiomatic Go server design. Goroutines are cheap, and blocking reads are simple to write; the runtime multiplexes them over a few threads with an efficient network poller underneath.
- **Graceful shutdown.** `context.AfterFunc` closes the listener when the context is cancelled, which makes `Accept` return. The server then closes every tracked client connection (unblocking their reads) and waits for their goroutines with a `WaitGroup`. The test `TestShutdownClosesClients` checks that idle clients cannot block shutdown.
- **Panic isolation.** A deferred `recover` in each connection handler means a bug triggered by one client's command does not crash the server for everyone (lesson 5.5).
- **Errors as replies.** Wrong argument counts and unknown commands get Redis-style `-ERR` replies, so real clients show sensible messages.

## The main program



```gopath-example
example-258
```



On startup it replays the AOF into the store **through a server without an AOF attached**, so replayed commands are not appended to the file again. Then it starts the janitor and the once-per-second sync goroutine, and serves until SIGINT or SIGTERM.

## Testing

```bash
go test -race ./projects/miniredis/...
go test -fuzz=FuzzReadCommand -fuzztime=30s ./projects/miniredis/internal/resp
```

The server tests start a real server on a random local port and talk to it with a tiny RESP client, including 20 concurrent clients incrementing one counter, inline commands like you would type in `telnet`, and shutdown with idle connections. The `main` test simulates a restart by writing through one server and replaying into a fresh store.

## Stretch goals

1. **Absolute expiry in the AOF.** `SET k v EX 100` is replayed with a fresh 100 seconds. Rewrite it in the log as `SET k v` plus `PEXPIREAT k <unix-ms>` so restarts do not extend TTLs.
2. **AOF rewriting.** The log grows forever. Add a `BGREWRITEAOF` command that writes the current dataset to a new file and swaps it in atomically (lesson 8.5).
3. **More commands.** `MGET`, `MSET`, `KEYS pattern` (use `path.Match`), `APPEND`, `GETDEL`.
4. **Sharded locks.** Split the store into 16 maps, each with its own mutex, chosen by a hash of the key. Benchmark it against the single lock in Module 10.
5. **Pipelining.** Real clients often send many commands before reading replies. The server already handles it; measure the speedup with `redis-benchmark -p 6380 -P 16`.

## Module 8 recap

You can now:

- Build streaming programs from `io` and `bufio` pieces
- Encode and decode JSON correctly with `encoding/json`, and use `encoding/json/v2` on Go 1.27
- Handle time, durations and time zones without the classic bugs
- Log with structured `slog` records
- Work with files safely, embed assets and confine paths with `os.Root`
- Format and convert text efficiently
- Make HTTP requests that cannot hang or leak

Next is **Part 3: Quality, performance and internals**, starting with **[Module 9: Testing in depth](/learn/09-testing/)**.

lessons.title: 9.1 Table-driven tests and subtests
lessons.description: Write tests as tables of cases with t.Run subtests, write failure messages that explain themselves, run tests in parallel, select tests with -run, and check that your tests actually catch bugs.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The anatomy of a Go test, and `t.Error` versus `t.Fatal`
- The table-driven pattern with `t.Run` subtests
- How to write failure messages that need no debugger
- Running subtests in parallel
- Selecting tests with `-run` and subtest names
- How to tell whether your tests are good enough: **mutation testing**

## The basics

A test is a function `func TestXxx(t *testing.T)` in a file ending with `_test.go`. `go test` finds, compiles and runs them. A test passes unless it calls one of the failure methods:

| Method | Effect |
|---|---|
| `t.Error`, `t.Errorf` | Mark the test failed and **keep going** |
| `t.Fatal`, `t.Fatalf` | Mark it failed and **stop this test** now |
| `t.Log`, `t.Logf` | Print only if the test fails, or with `-v` |
| `t.Skip`, `t.Skipf` | Skip the test with a reason |

Use `Error` when later checks still make sense, so one run reports every problem. Use `Fatal` when continuing is pointless (setup failed, a value you need is nil). There are no assertion functions in the standard library; plain `if` statements with good messages are the Go style.

## Table-driven tests

Here is a function to test:



```gopath-example
example-259
```



And its test, in the form you will see in almost every Go codebase:



```gopath-example
example-260
```



1. A slice of anonymous structs, one per case (lesson 3.6).
2. A loop over the cases.
3. `t.Run(name, func)` runs each case as a **subtest** with its own name, result and output.

Adding a case is one line. Reading the table tells you what the function is supposed to do. And because each case is a subtest, the output names the failing case:

```text
--- FAIL: TestSlugify (0.00s)
    --- FAIL: TestSlugify/unicode_letters (0.00s)
        slug_test.go:30: Slugify("Café Olé") = "caf-ol", want "café-olé"
```

## Failure messages

A good failure message lets someone fix the bug without rerunning anything. The Go convention:

```text
FunctionName(inputs) = got, want expected
```

- Include the **inputs**, so the failure can be reproduced.
- Print **got before want**.
- Use `%q` for strings so empty strings and whitespace are visible.
- Say what was being checked when it is not obvious: `status = 500, want 200`.

## Parallel subtests



```gopath-example
example-261
```



`t.Parallel()` lets a subtest run at the same time as other parallel subtests. Use it for tests that are slow because they wait (network calls to a test server, sleeps). Since Go 1.22, the loop variable `tt` is per iteration, so capturing it in the closure is safe; older code had a `tt := tt` line for this.

Parallel tests must not share mutable state, and `t.Setenv` and `t.Chdir` cannot be used in them because they change process-wide state.

## Selecting tests

```bash
go test ./...                                     # everything
go test -run TestSlugify ./examples/m09/tables    # regexp on test names
go test -run 'TestSlugify/unicode' ./...          # one subtest: spaces in names become _
go test -run TestSlugify -count=1 ./...           # bypass the test cache
go test -v -failfast ./...                        # stop at the first failure
```

`-count=1` matters when a test depends on something outside the code (files, environment, time), because `go test` caches passing results.

## Are your tests any good?

Coverage (lesson 9.8) tells you which lines ran, not whether your tests would **notice a bug** in them. A direct way to check: plant bugs in the code and see if the tests fail. This is called **mutation testing**. Tools can do it automatically; the exercise below does it by hand.

## Exercise: test your tests



  
Exercise

  


This exercise is reversed: the code is given and correct, and **you write the tests**.

In [`exercises/m09/wordwrap`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/exercises/m09/wordwrap), `wrap.go` contains a correct `Wrap(text, width)` function. Next to it are four files, `bug_overflow.go`, `bug_longword.go`, `bug_empty.go` and `bug_lastline.go`, each a subtly broken version selected with a build tag. Read the doc comment on `Wrap`, then extend `wrap_test.go` into a table-driven test that:

1. **passes** against the correct code, and
2. **fails** against every buggy version.

```bash
cd exercises
go test ./m09/wordwrap                       # must PASS
for b in bug_overflow bug_longword bug_empty bug_lastline; do
    go test -tags $b ./m09/wordwrap > /dev/null && echo "$b NOT caught"
```

`t.Error("wrong result")` forces whoever sees the failure to rerun it under a debugger.

### `t.Fatal` inside a goroutine

### One giant test function

A 200-line test that checks everything in sequence stops at the first `Fatal` and hides other failures. Split it into subtests.

Tests that check private fields or the exact sequence of internal calls break on every refactor. Test behavior through the public API, as an external test package (`package foo_test`) forces you to (lesson 1.5).

- Failure messages show inputs, got, then want.
- `t.Parallel()` speeds up waiting tests; `-run` selects tests and subtests.
- Good tests catch bugs: try planting some and see.
