lessons.title: 9.2 Test helpers, t.Cleanup, t.Context and golden files
lessons.description: Write helpers with t.Helper, manage resources with t.Cleanup and t.TempDir, set environment safely with t.Setenv, use t.Context, keep fixtures in testdata, and compare large outputs with golden files.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Writing helpers that report failures at the caller's line, with `t.Helper()`
- `t.TempDir`, `t.Setenv` and `t.Chdir` for safe, self-cleaning setup
- `t.Cleanup`, and how it differs from `defer`
- `t.Context` (Go 1.24) for tests of context-aware code
- The `testdata` directory and **golden files** with an `-update` flag

## Helpers



```gopath-example
example-262
```



- `t.Helper()` marks a function as a helper. When a helper calls `t.Fatalf`, the failure is reported at the line in the **test** that called the helper, which is where you want to look.
- Helpers take `t` (or `testing.TB`, which works for tests and benchmarks) as their first argument and call `t.Fatal` themselves, so the test reads as a clean sequence of steps.
- `t.TempDir()` returns a fresh directory that is **deleted automatically** when the test ends. No cleanup code, no leftovers, and parallel tests never collide.

The `testing` package has more of these self-cleaning helpers:

| Helper | Effect, undone automatically at the end of the test |
|---|---|
| `t.TempDir()` | create a temporary directory |
| `t.Setenv(k, v)` | set an environment variable |
| `t.Chdir(dir)` (Go 1.24) | change the working directory |
| `t.Context()` (Go 1.24) | a context cancelled when the test ends |
| `t.ArtifactDir()` (Go 1.26) | a directory for files you want to keep after the test, written under `-outputdir` |

## `t.Cleanup`



```gopath-example
example-263
```



`t.Cleanup(f)` registers `f` to run when the test (and all its subtests) finish, in last-in, first-out order. Unlike `defer`, a **helper** can register cleanup on behalf of the test:

```go
func startServer(t *testing.T) *httptest.Server {
	t.Helper()
	srv := httptest.NewServer(newHandler())
	t.Cleanup(srv.Close) // the test does not need to remember to close it
	return srv
}
```

## `t.Context`



```gopath-example
example-264
```



Pass `t.Context()` to the code under test instead of `context.Background()`. It is cancelled just before cleanup runs, so goroutines started by the test get a signal to stop, and cleanup code can then wait for them.

## `testdata` and golden files

The `go` tool ignores any directory named **`testdata`**, so it is the conventional home for fixture files. Tests run with the package directory as the working directory, so `filepath.Join("testdata", "input.json")` works.

When output is large (rendered templates, generated code, CLI output, JSON reports), writing the expected value inline is unwieldy. A **golden file** stores the expected output in `testdata`, and an `-update` flag rewrites it:



```gopath-example
example-265
```



```bash
go test ./examples/m09/helpers                 # compare with the golden file
go test ./examples/m09/helpers -update         # accept the current output
git diff examples/m09/helpers/testdata         # review the change before committing
```

The `git diff` step is the point of golden files: changes to output show up in code review as readable diffs.

## Common mistakes

### Helpers without `t.Helper()`

Every failure points to a line inside the helper, and you have to work out which caller it was.

### `os.Setenv` in tests

It changes the environment for every test in the process and is never restored. Use `t.Setenv`.

### Writing fixtures to the package directory

Tests that create files next to the source pollute the repository and break when run in parallel. Use `t.TempDir()`.

### Running `-update` without reviewing

Accepting golden files blindly turns tests into recorders of whatever the code currently does, bugs included.

## Key takeaways

- Call `t.Helper()` in helpers; let helpers call `t.Fatal`.
- Use `t.TempDir`, `t.Setenv`, `t.Chdir` and `t.Context`: they clean up after themselves.
- `t.Cleanup` runs registered functions after the test, and helpers can use it.
- Keep fixtures in `testdata`; use golden files with an `-update` flag for large outputs, and review the diffs.

## Further reading

- [Package testing: T](https://pkg.go.dev/testing#T)
- [Go 1.24 release notes: testing](https://go.dev/doc/go1.24#testing)

lessons.title: 9.3 Testable examples
lessons.description: Write Example functions that are both documentation on pkg.go.dev and tests run by go test, with naming rules, Output and Unordered output.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How `Example` functions become documentation and tests at the same time
- The naming rules that attach examples to packages, types and methods
- `// Output:` and `// Unordered output:`
- When an example is better than a unit test, and when it is not

## The idea

You have been reading testable examples since lesson 1.3: every example in this course is one. An `Example` function in a `_test.go` file is:

1. **Compiled and run by `go test`**, with its standard output compared to the `// Output:` comment.
2. **Shown in the documentation**, by `go doc` and on [pkg.go.dev](https://pkg.go.dev), next to whatever it documents.

So examples are documentation that cannot go out of date.

## Naming



```gopath-example
example-266
```



| Function name | Documents |
|---|---|
| `Example` | the package |
| `ExampleF` | the function `F` |
| `ExampleT` | the type `T` |
| `ExampleT_M` | the method `M` on type `T` |
| any of the above plus `_suffix` | an additional example; the suffix starts with a lowercase letter |

Examples are usually written in the external test package (`package examplesdoc_test`), so they show the API exactly as users call it, with the package name in front.

## Output checks

- `// Output:` followed by the expected lines. Leading and trailing whitespace of the whole output is trimmed before comparing (which is why trailing spaces inside lines bit us in earlier modules).
- `// Unordered output:` compares lines in any order, for output from maps or goroutines:



```gopath-example
example-267
```



- An example **without** an output comment is compiled but not run. That is useful for examples that need a network or print something machine-dependent, though they then only prove the code compiles.

## Examples or unit tests?

Use examples for **showing how to use an API**: the common path, written the way you want users to write it. Use unit tests for **edge cases, error paths and exhaustive tables**. An example with twenty asserts is a bad example; a test without readable usage is a bad tutorial. Most good packages have both.

## Common mistakes

### Machine-dependent output

Printing times, map iteration, pointers or goroutine timing makes examples flaky. Sort, round or use `Unordered output`.

### Wrong names

`ExampleStack_pop` (lowercase method name) does not attach to the `Pop` method, and `go vet` warns about examples that refer to unknown identifiers.

### Examples that hide errors

`v, _ := parse(...)` teaches readers to ignore errors. Show proper handling, even in examples.

## Key takeaways

- `Example` functions are run by `go test` and shown in the documentation.
- Names attach them to the package, functions, types and methods; suffixes add more examples.
- `// Output:` checks output exactly; `// Unordered output:` ignores order.
- Use examples to teach the API and unit tests to cover the edge cases.

## Further reading

- [Testable Examples in Go](https://go.dev/blog/examples) on the Go blog
- [Package testing: Examples](https://pkg.go.dev/testing#hdr-Examples)

lessons.title: 9.4 Mocks, fakes and interfaces for testing
lessons.description: Isolate code from email, databases, clocks and networks with small interfaces and hand-written fakes, and know when a mocking library or a real dependency is the better choice.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The kinds of test doubles: stubs, fakes, spies and mocks
- Why Go code usually needs no mocking framework
- How to design code so dependencies are easy to replace
- When to test against the real thing instead

## The idea

Code that sends email, charges cards, reads the clock or calls other services is hard to test directly: the dependencies are slow, cost money, have side effects or change over time. The fix is to make the dependency an **interface** the code accepts (lesson 4.8), and give it a **test double** in tests.

Go's implicit interfaces make this cheap: a test double is just a small struct with the right methods, written in a few lines.

## An example

Code under test, depending on two small interfaces:



```gopath-example
example-268
```



Test doubles for those interfaces:



```gopath-example
example-269
```



And the test:



```gopath-example
example-270
```



The test controls time completely, checks exactly what would have been emailed, and simulates a failing mail server, all without a network.

## Kinds of test doubles

| Kind | What it does | Example above |
|---|---|---|
| **Stub** | Returns canned answers | `fixedClock` |
| **Fake** | A working but simplified implementation | an in-memory store instead of Postgres |
| **Spy** | Records how it was called, for the test to inspect | `fakeMailer.sent` |
| **Mock** | Pre-programmed with expectations, fails if calls differ | (generated by a library) |

In Go, **hand-written fakes and spies** are the norm. They are explicit, need no reflection, and survive refactoring better than mocks that assert the exact sequence of calls.

## Design for replaceability

- **Accept small interfaces** defined by the consumer (lesson 4.2). A two-method `Mailer` is trivial to fake; a 30-method `CloudClient` is not.
- **Inject dependencies** through struct fields or constructor parameters, not package-level globals.
- **Make time, randomness and IDs dependencies** too: a `Clock` interface or a `now func() time.Time` field (the shortener and rate limiter projects do this).
- **Keep fakes close to the interface**, so several test packages can share them. A common place is a `xxxtest` package, like the standard library's `httptest` and `fstest`.

## When to use a mocking library

Generators like `go.uber.org/mock` (`mockgen`) or `github.com/vektra/mockery` create mocks from interfaces. They help when an interface is large, when you need to check call order or counts precisely, or when many tests need the same doubles. Use them sparingly; tests full of `EXPECT()` calls tend to test the implementation rather than the behavior.

## When to use the real thing

Test doubles prove your code works **with your assumption** about the dependency. They cannot prove the assumption is right. So also test against real implementations where it is affordable:

- **Databases**: run tests against a real PostgreSQL in a container (lesson 13.x) for the storage layer.
- **HTTP APIs**: test your client against `httptest.Server` with realistic responses, and run a few tests against the real API in a separate, opt-in suite (lesson 9.8).
- **Filesystem**: `t.TempDir()` is fast and real; there is rarely a reason to fake `os`.

A healthy suite has many fast unit tests with fakes and fewer, slower integration tests with real dependencies.

## Common mistakes

### Interfaces that exist only for mocking

Do not add an interface to every type "so it can be mocked". Add it where a consumer needs a replaceable dependency.

### Mocks that mirror the implementation

A test that asserts "calls `Get`, then `Set`, then `Get`" breaks when the code is refactored, even though behavior is unchanged. Assert outcomes.

### Fakes that diverge from reality

A fake store that never returns errors hides your error handling paths from tests. Give fakes a way to fail.

## Key takeaways

- Replace slow or side-effecting dependencies with test doubles behind small interfaces.
- In Go, hand-written stubs, fakes and spies are usually enough.
- Inject dependencies, including time and randomness.
- Use mocking libraries sparingly; assert behavior, not call sequences.
- Complement fakes with integration tests against real dependencies.

## Further reading

- [Go Code Review Comments: Interfaces](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments#interfaces)
- [Package net/http/httptest](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http/httptest) and [testing/fstest](https://pkg.go.dev/testing/fstest), the standard library's own test helpers
headings: When to use a mocking library
When to use the real thing

lessons.title: 9.5 httptest
lessons.description: Test HTTP handlers directly with httptest.NewRecorder, test clients and full stacks with httptest.NewServer, and use the in-memory NewTestServer from Go 1.27.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Unit testing handlers with `httptest.NewRequest` and `httptest.NewRecorder`
- End-to-end tests with `httptest.NewServer`
- Which style to use when
- Testing clients against fake servers
- `httptest.NewTestServer` (Go 1.27) for in-memory, synctest-friendly servers

## Handlers under test



```gopath-example
example-271
```



## Unit tests with `ResponseRecorder`



```gopath-example
example-272
```



- `httptest.NewRequest(method, target, body)` builds an incoming server request. Unlike `http.NewRequest`, it panics on errors (fine in tests) and fills in fields a server would set.
- `httptest.NewRecorder()` is an `http.ResponseWriter` that records the status code (`rec.Code`), headers (`rec.Header()`) and body (`rec.Body`).
- You call the handler directly: no network, no goroutines, microseconds per case. This is the right default for handler logic.

## End-to-end tests with `NewServer`



```gopath-example
example-273
```



`httptest.NewServer(handler)` starts a real HTTP server on a random localhost port. Use it to test:

- **routing, middleware and the full handler stack** (`ServeMux`, authentication, logging);
- **your HTTP clients** against a fake API (lesson 8.7 and its exercise);
- behavior that depends on real connections: timeouts, streaming, redirects, TLS (`httptest.NewTLSServer`).

`srv.Client()` returns a client configured for the server (it trusts the test TLS certificate). Always `defer srv.Close()` or register it with `t.Cleanup`.

## Which one?

| Test | Use |
|---|---|
| A handler's own logic: validation, status codes, body | `NewRecorder` |
| Routing, middleware chain, path parameters | `NewServer` (or call the mux with a recorder) |
| An HTTP client | `NewServer` with a fake handler |
| Timeouts and cancellation | `NewServer`, or `NewTestServer` with `synctest` |

## `httptest.NewTestServer` (Go 1.27)

Go 1.27 added `httptest.NewTestServer(t, handler)`, which runs the server over an **in-memory network** instead of a real socket. Combined with `testing/synctest` (lesson 9.9), timeouts in clients and servers become deterministic and instant: a test of a 30-second timeout runs on the virtual clock and finishes immediately. It also registers its own cleanup with `t`.

## Common mistakes

### Forgetting to check the status code

A handler test that only checks the body passes even when the status is wrong. Check both.

### Comparing JSON as strings

Encoders may change spacing or key order between versions. Decode the body and compare values, or compare against a canonical form.

### Not closing the test server

Leaks a listener and goroutines per test. Use `t.Cleanup(srv.Close)`.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m09/fizzhttp
```



## Key takeaways

- Test handler logic directly with `NewRequest` and `NewRecorder`.
- Use `NewServer` for routing, middleware, real connections and client tests.
- Check status, headers and body; decode JSON instead of comparing strings.
- Go 1.27's `NewTestServer` uses an in-memory network that works with `synctest`.

## Further reading

- [Package net/http/httptest](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http/httptest)
- [Go 1.27 release notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)

lessons.title: 9.6 Fuzzing
lessons.description: Use Go's built-in fuzzer to find inputs that break your code: writing fuzz targets, choosing properties to check, seed corpora, saved failures and running fuzzing in CI.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What fuzzing is and what kinds of bugs it finds
- How to write a fuzz target with `testing.F`
- **Properties** worth checking: round trips, no panics, agreement with a reference
- The seed corpus and the `testdata/fuzz` directory
- How to run the fuzzer and use what it finds

## The idea

Unit tests check the cases **you** thought of. A fuzzer generates **millions** of inputs automatically, guided by code coverage: when an input reaches new code, the fuzzer mutates it further. It is very good at finding the cases nobody thought of: empty input, huge input, invalid UTF-8, a dangling backslash, a length prefix that lies.

Since Go 1.18, fuzzing is built into `go test`.

## A fuzz target

Code to fuzz:



```gopath-example
example-274
```



Fuzz targets:



```gopath-example
example-275
```



- A fuzz target is `func FuzzXxx(f *testing.F)` in a test file.
- `f.Add(...)` adds **seed** inputs. They should be representative valid inputs.
- `f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, args...))` is called with each generated input. Argument types can be `[]byte`, `string`, integers, floats, `bool` and `rune`.

## What to check

The hard part of fuzzing is not generating inputs but deciding what is **wrong** for an arbitrary input. Useful properties:

| Property | Example |
|---|---|
| **No panics, no hangs** on any input | parsers, decoders, protocol readers |
| **Round trip** | `Unquote(Quote(s)) == s`, `Decode(Encode(x)) == x` |
| **Agreement with a reference** | a fast implementation matches a slow, obviously correct one |
| **Invariants** | output is always valid UTF-8, sorted, within bounds |
| **Idempotence** | `Normalize(Normalize(s)) == Normalize(s)` |

The mini Redis RESP parser (lesson 8.8) has a "no panics" fuzz target, and the exercise below uses round trips.

## Running the fuzzer

```bash
go test ./examples/m09/fuzzing                              # seeds only: fast, runs in CI
go test -run xxx -fuzz=FuzzRoundTrip ./examples/m09/fuzzing  # fuzz until a failure or Ctrl+C
go test -run xxx -fuzz=FuzzRoundTrip -fuzztime=30s ./...     # fuzz for a fixed time
```

- Without `-fuzz`, fuzz targets run like normal tests over the seed corpus, so they cost almost nothing in CI.
- With `-fuzz`, one target runs for as long as you allow, on all CPU cores. `-run xxx` skips the regular tests.
- Inputs that found new code paths are cached in your Go build cache, so later fuzzing sessions start where you left off.

## When the fuzzer finds a bug

The failing input is written to `testdata/fuzz/FuzzXxx/<hash>` in the package directory, and from then on **plain `go test` runs it** as a regression test. The workflow:

1. Fuzz, get a failure.
2. Commit the new `testdata/fuzz` file.
3. Fix the code; `go test` now passes and keeps passing.

## Fuzzing in CI

Run seed corpora in every CI build (they are just tests). Run actual fuzzing on a schedule, for example nightly for a few minutes per target, or continuously with a service like OSS-Fuzz, which supports native Go fuzzing.

## Common mistakes

### Fuzzing without a property

A target that only calls the function catches panics, which is useful, but most bugs produce wrong output rather than panics. Add a property.

### Non-deterministic targets

A target that depends on time, randomness or global state produces failures the fuzzer cannot reproduce.

### Slow targets

The fuzzer's power comes from speed. Avoid network calls and big allocations inside the target.

## Exercise



```gopath-exercise
m09/rle
```



## Key takeaways

- Fuzzing generates inputs automatically, guided by coverage, and finds the cases you did not think of.
- Write `FuzzXxx(f *testing.F)` with seeds from `f.Add` and a property in `f.Fuzz`.
- Good properties: no panics, round trips, agreement with a reference, invariants.
- Plain `go test` runs seeds and saved failures; `go test -fuzz` explores.
- Commit failing inputs from `testdata/fuzz` as regression tests.

## Further reading

- [Go Fuzzing](https://go.dev/doc/security/fuzz/) on go.dev
- [Tutorial: Getting started with fuzzing](https://go.dev/doc/tutorial/fuzz)

lessons.title: 9.7 Benchmarks with b.Loop
lessons.description: Write benchmarks with testing.B and the b.Loop method from Go 1.24, report allocations, structure sub-benchmarks, read the output, and turn allocation budgets into tests.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to write a benchmark, and why `b.Loop` (Go 1.24) is the modern form
- Reporting allocations with `-benchmem` and `b.ReportAllocs`
- Comparing implementations with sub-benchmarks
- Reading benchmark output
- Locking in allocation budgets with `testing.AllocsPerRun`

## Three implementations to compare



```gopath-example
example-276
```



Before benchmarking anything, make sure the variants are **correct and equivalent**:



```gopath-example
example-277
```



## Writing benchmarks



```gopath-example
example-278
```



`for b.Loop() { ... }` (Go 1.24) is the way to write the timed loop:

- The framework decides how many iterations are needed for a stable measurement.
- Code **before** the loop is setup and is excluded from the timing, so `b.ResetTimer()` is no longer needed.
- The compiler cannot optimize away calls inside the loop, so you do not need to assign results to a package-level "sink" variable.
- Since Go 1.26, `b.Loop` also no longer prevents inlining in the loop body.

Older code uses `for i := 0; i < b.N; i++`. It still works, but it is easy to get wrong (setup inside the loop, results optimized away). Prefer `b.Loop` in new code.

## Reading the output

Running the benchmark above on a 2-core cloud VM with Go 1.24 produced:

```text
BenchmarkJoin/plus/10-2           591.0 ns/op       296 B/op      18 allocs/op
BenchmarkJoin/builder/10-2         79.87 ns/op       64 B/op       1 allocs/op
BenchmarkJoin/append/10-2          95.57 ns/op       96 B/op       2 allocs/op
BenchmarkJoin/plus/1000-2      2002495 ns/op    5043136 B/op    2983 allocs/op
BenchmarkJoin/builder/1000-2     30777 ns/op       9984 B/op     986 allocs/op
BenchmarkJoin/append/1000-2      15133 ns/op      11008 B/op       2 allocs/op
```

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| name and `-2` | benchmark and subtest name; the suffix is `GOMAXPROCS` |
| `ns/op` | average time per iteration |
| `B/op` | bytes allocated per iteration (`-benchmem` or `b.ReportAllocs`) |
| `allocs/op` | heap allocations per iteration |

Your numbers will differ, but the shape is the lesson:

- Concatenation with `+=` is **quadratic**: for 1000 numbers it allocated about 5 MB and was over 100 times slower, because every `+=` copies the whole string so far.
- `strings.Builder` was fastest for 10 numbers, but at 1000 it made 986 allocations. They come from `strconv.Itoa`, which allocates a new string for each number above 99 (smaller ones come from a cache).
- Appending digits directly with `strconv.AppendInt` made exactly **2 allocations** at any size: the buffer and the final string.

**Allocations often matter more than raw instruction counts**, because each one costs time now and garbage collection work later.

## Benchmark hygiene

- **Run several times** and compare distributions, not single numbers: `go test -bench . -count=10 > old.txt`, then compare with `benchstat` (lesson 10.1).
- **Close other programs**; laptops on battery or thermal throttling give noisy results.
- **Benchmark realistic inputs.** Results for 10 items and 1000 items told different stories above.
- `-benchtime=3s` or `-benchtime=1000x` controls duration or iteration count; `-cpu=1,2,4` repeats with different `GOMAXPROCS`.
- `b.RunParallel` benchmarks code under concurrent load (the rate limiter project has an example).

## Allocation budgets as tests

Benchmarks are run by hand. A **test** can lock in an allocation budget so a regression fails CI:



```gopath-example
example-279
```



This test caught a real mistake while writing this lesson. The first version of `JoinAppend` sized its buffer at 4 bytes per number. With 4-digit numbers plus commas that was too small, the buffer grew once, and the test reported 3 allocations instead of 2. Allocation counts are exact, so these tests are not flaky the way timing assertions would be. (They can change between Go releases as the compiler improves, so keep budgets for code where it truly matters.)

## Common mistakes

### Benchmarking without checking correctness

A fast wrong answer is easy to produce. Test equivalence first.

### Setup inside the timed loop

Allocating the input on every iteration measures the setup, not the code. With `b.Loop`, put setup before the loop.

### Trusting one run

Variance of 5 to 10 percent between runs is normal. Use `-count` and `benchstat` before concluding anything.

### Asserting on timings in tests

`if elapsed > 10*time.Millisecond { t.Fail() }` is flaky on busy CI machines. Assert on allocations, or use benchmarks.

## Key takeaways

- Benchmarks are `BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B)` functions; write the timed loop as `for b.Loop()`.
- `-benchmem` reports bytes and allocations per operation; allocations are often the real cost.
- Compare variants with sub-benchmarks on realistic input sizes.
- Run multiple times and compare with `benchstat`.
- Lock in allocation budgets with `testing.AllocsPerRun` tests.

## Further reading

- [Package testing: Benchmarks](https://pkg.go.dev/testing#hdr-Benchmarks)
- [More predictable benchmarking with testing.B.Loop](https://go.dev/blog/testing-b-loop) on the Go blog

lessons.title: 9.8 Coverage and integration tests
lessons.description: Measure test coverage and read coverage reports, understand what coverage does not tell you, separate fast unit tests from integration tests, and use TestMain for shared setup.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Measuring coverage with `-cover` and viewing it as HTML
- Why 100% coverage does not mean the code is tested
- Coverage for integration tests of whole binaries
- Separating slow tests with `-short`, environment variables and build tags
- Shared setup with `TestMain`

## Measuring coverage



```gopath-example
example-280
```





```gopath-example
example-281
```



```bash
go test -cover ./examples/m09/coverage
```

```text
ok  	.../examples/m09/coverage	0.003s	coverage: 100.0% of statements
```

```bash
go test -coverprofile=cover.out ./...   # write a profile
go tool cover -func=cover.out           # per-function percentages
go tool cover -html=cover.out           # open an annotated view of the source in a browser
```

The HTML view colors each statement green (ran) or red (never ran), which is the fastest way to spot untested branches.

## What coverage does not tell you

The test above reaches **100%** of statements. Yet it never checks a member using the `WELCOME` coupon, where the inner `if d == 0` is false. Statement coverage records that the `if` line ran, not that both outcomes were tested. It also says nothing about whether the assertions are any good: a test that calls every function and checks nothing has full coverage.

Use coverage as a **flashlight** for finding untested code, not as a target. Lesson 9.1's mutation exercise is a much stronger check of test quality.

## Coverage for whole programs

Since Go 1.20 you can build a **binary** with coverage instrumentation and collect coverage from integration tests or manual runs:

```bash
go build -cover -o app ./cmd/app
GOCOVERDIR=/tmp/cov ./app --some-flags      # each run writes coverage data
go tool covdata percent -i=/tmp/cov
go tool covdata textfmt -i=/tmp/cov -o cover.out   # convert for `go tool cover`
```

This answers "which code did our end-to-end test suite actually exercise?".

## Separating slow tests



```gopath-example
example-282
```



Three common ways to keep the default `go test ./...` fast:

1. **`-short`**: slow tests call `t.Skip` when `testing.Short()` is true. Run `go test -short ./...` in the edit loop.
2. **Environment variables**: tests that need external systems skip unless their configuration is set (`PRICING_URL`, `DATABASE_URL`). CI sets them in a dedicated job.
3. **Build tags**: put integration tests in files starting with `//go:build integration` and run them with `go test -tags integration ./...`.

Pick one convention per project and document it in the README.

## `TestMain`



```gopath-example
example-283
```



`TestMain` runs once per test binary (once per package) and must call `m.Run()`. Use it for expensive shared setup: starting a database container, building a binary under test, loading large fixtures. Most packages do not need it; `t.Cleanup` and helpers are enough.

## Common mistakes

### Coverage targets

"Coverage must be 80%" leads to tests that execute code without checking it. Review what is tested, not just the number.

### Integration tests in the default run

Tests that need Docker or network access make `go test ./...` fail for new contributors. Gate them.

### Forgetting `os.Exit(m.Run())`

A `TestMain` that does not exit with `m.Run()`'s code makes failing tests look like passes.

## Key takeaways

- `go test -cover`, `-coverprofile` and `go tool cover -html` show what ran.
- Full statement coverage does not mean every branch or behavior is checked.
- `go build -cover` plus `GOCOVERDIR` measures coverage of whole-program runs.
- Keep slow tests out of the default run with `-short`, environment variables or build tags.
- `TestMain` is for rare, expensive shared setup.

## Further reading

- [The cover story](https://go.dev/blog/cover) on the Go blog
- [Coverage profiling support for integration tests](https://go.dev/doc/build-cover)
- [Package testing: Main](https://pkg.go.dev/testing#hdr-Main)
headings: What coverage does not tell you
lessons.searchText:
9.8 coverage and integration tests measure test coverage and read coverage reports, understand what coverage does not tell you, separate fast unit tests from integration tests, and use testmain for shared setup.  what you will learn

- measuring coverage with -cover and viewing it as html
- why 100% coverage does not mean the code is tested
- coverage for integration tests of whole binaries
- separating slow tests with -short, environment variables and build tags
- shared setup with testmain

 measuring coverage



















the html view colors each statement green (ran) or red (never ran), which is the fastest way to spot untested branches.

 what coverage does not tell you

the test above reaches 100% of statements. yet it never checks a member using the welcome coupon, where the inner if d == 0 is false. statement coverage records that the if line ran, not that both outcomes were tested. it also says nothing about whether the assertions are any good: a test that calls every function and checks nothing has full coverage.

use coverage as a flashlight for finding untested code, not as a target. lesson 9.1's mutation exercise is a much stronger check of test quality.

 coverage for whole programs

since go 1.20 you can build a binary with coverage instrumentation and collect coverage from integration tests or manual runs:



this answers "which code did our end-to-end test suite actually exercise?".

 separating slow tests







three common ways to keep the default go test ./... fast:

1. -short: slow tests call t.skip when testing.short() is true. run go test -short ./... in the edit loop.
2. environment variables: tests that need external systems skip unless their configuration is set (pricingurl, databaseurl). ci sets them in a dedicated job.
3. build tags: put integration tests in files starting with //go:build integration and run them with go test -tags integration ./....

pick one convention per project and document it in the readme.

 testmain







testmain runs once per test binary (once per package) and must call m.run(). use it for expensive shared setup: starting a database container, building a binary under test, loading large fixtures. most packages do not need it; t.cleanup and helpers are enough.

 common mistakes

 coverage targets

"coverage must be 80%" leads to tests that execute code without checking it. review what is tested, not just the number.

 integration tests in the default run

tests that need docker or network access make go test ./... fail for new contributors. gate them.

 forgetting os.exit(m.run())

a testmain that does not exit with m.run()'s code makes failing tests look like passes.

 key takeaways

- go test -cover, -coverprofile and go tool cover -html show what ran.
- full statement coverage does not mean every branch or behavior is checked.
- go build -cover plus gocoverdir measures coverage of whole-program runs.
- keep slow tests out of the default run with -short, environment variables or build tags.
- testmain is for rare, expensive shared setup.

 further reading

- [the cover story](https://go.dev/blog/cover) on the go blog
- [coverage profiling support for integration tests](https://go.dev/doc/build-cover)
- [package testing: main](https://pkg.go.dev/testinghdr-main)

lessons.title: 9.9 Testing concurrent code with testing/synctest
lessons.description: Test code with goroutines, timers and timeouts deterministically: synctest bubbles, virtual time, synctest.Wait and synctest.Sleep, and what can and cannot run inside a bubble.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why concurrent, time-based code is hard to test
- How `synctest.Test` runs a test in a **bubble** with a virtual clock
- What `synctest.Wait` guarantees, and `synctest.Sleep` (Go 1.27)
- The rules for what can run inside a bubble



```gopath-callout
callout-13
```



## The problem

Here is a cache whose entries expire, with a background goroutine that sweeps expired entries:



```gopath-example
example-284
```



Testing it the obvious way means real sleeps: wait 61 seconds for an entry to expire, then a bit more for the sweeper to run. Shrink the durations to milliseconds and the test becomes **flaky**: on a busy CI machine, the sweeper might not have run yet when you check.

## The solution: a bubble with fake time



```gopath-example
example-285
```



Inside `synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { ... })`:

- **Time is virtual.** It starts at a fixed instant and only advances when **every goroutine in the bubble is blocked**. Then it jumps straight to the next timer. So `time.Sleep(59 * time.Second)` returns immediately in real time, but `time.Now()` afterwards is exactly 59 seconds later.
- **Goroutines started inside belong to the bubble**, including the cache's sweeper and its ticker.
- **`synctest.Wait()`** blocks until every other goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked. After `Wait`, you know background work triggered by the last time step has finished. No polling, no sleeps.
- Go 1.27 adds **`synctest.Sleep(d)`**, which combines `time.Sleep(d)` and `synctest.Wait()`, the most common pairing.
- After the function returns, `Test` waits for every goroutine in the bubble to exit. If they are all blocked with no way to proceed, the test fails with a deadlock report, which catches leaked goroutines.

The whole test runs in microseconds and is fully deterministic: same result every time, on any machine.

## What "blocked" means

Time advances only when goroutines are **durably blocked**, meaning blocked on something only another goroutine in the bubble can unblock:

- channel operations on channels created in the bubble;
- `sync.WaitGroup.Wait`, `sync.Cond.Wait`, `select` with no ready case;
- `time.Sleep` and timers.

Blocking on **I/O** (a real network socket, a file) or on a `sync.Mutex` held by another goroutine does **not** count, because something outside the bubble could unblock it. That is why Go 1.27's `httptest.NewTestServer` uses an in-memory network: HTTP clients and servers then block on in-bubble operations, and timeouts become testable with virtual time.

## Rules and limits

- Channels, timers and tickers created inside a bubble must not be used from outside it, and vice versa.
- Do not call `t.Run`, `t.Parallel` or `t.Deadline` on the `*testing.T` passed into the bubble.
- Code that waits on real I/O will not advance virtual time; use fakes or the in-memory network.

## Common mistakes

### Mixing real and virtual time

Passing a timer or channel created outside the bubble into it panics or deadlocks. Create everything the test needs inside the function.

### Forgetting `Wait` before asserting

After `time.Sleep`, the goroutines woken by that time step may not have run yet. Call `synctest.Wait()` (or `synctest.Sleep`) before checking their effects.

### Leaving goroutines running

`Test` waits for every goroutine in the bubble to exit. Stop background workers (`defer c.Close()`) before the function returns, or the test reports a deadlock.

## Key takeaways

- `synctest.Test` runs a test in a bubble with a virtual clock that advances only when all bubble goroutines are blocked.
- Sleeps and timeouts become instant and deterministic.
- `synctest.Wait` waits for background goroutines to settle; Go 1.27's `synctest.Sleep` sleeps and waits.
- I/O does not count as blocked; use fakes or `httptest.NewTestServer` (Go 1.27) for network code.

## Further reading

- [Testing concurrent code with testing/synctest](https://go.dev/blog/synctest) on the Go blog
- [Package testing/synctest](https://pkg.go.dev/testing/synctest)

## Module 9 recap

You can now write table-driven tests with good failure messages, test your tests with planted bugs, use helpers and golden files, document APIs with examples, isolate dependencies with fakes, test HTTP code with `httptest`, fuzz parsers, benchmark with `b.Loop`, measure coverage honestly, and test concurrent code deterministically with `synctest`.

Next is **[Module 10: Profiling and performance](/learn/10-performance/)**.

lessons.title: 10.1 Measure first: benchmarks and benchstat
lessons.description: Set up a fair comparison between implementations, run benchmarks repeatedly, and use benchstat to tell real improvements from noise.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why intuition about performance is unreliable, and what to do instead
- How to structure a fair comparison: equivalence test first, then benchmarks
- How to use `benchstat` to compare runs with statistics
- How to read `±` and `p=` in benchstat output

## The idea

Performance work without measurement is guessing. Experienced engineers guess wrong all the time, because the cost of code depends on the compiler, the runtime, the CPU cache and the input data. The workflow for any optimization is:

1. **Write a test** proving the old and new code produce the same results.
2. **Write a benchmark** with realistic input.
3. **Run it several times** for each version.
4. **Compare statistically** with `benchstat`.
5. Only then **profile** to find the next thing to fix (lesson 10.2).

## The running example

A log analyzer that summarizes lines like `2026-10-16T09:30:00Z GET /api/users 200 12ms`. Here is the first version, written for clarity:



```gopath-example
example-286
```



Two later versions, which the next lessons motivate, are `AnalyzeBetter` and `AnalyzeFast`. First, an equivalence test so we can never "optimize" into a wrong answer:



```gopath-example
example-287
```



Note the extra malformed lines at the end. Optimized parsers are where edge cases break, so the test feeds them deliberately.

## One benchmark, several implementations



```gopath-example
example-288
```



Naming sub-benchmarks `impl=naive`, `impl=better` and `impl=fast` lets benchstat put them side by side as columns.

## benchstat

`benchstat` is the Go team's tool for comparing benchmark results. Install it once:

```bash
go install golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat@latest
```

Then run each benchmark several times (6 to 10 is typical) and compare:

```bash
go test -run xxx -bench BenchmarkAnalyze -benchmem -count=6 ./examples/m10/loganalyzer > bench.txt
benchstat -col /impl bench.txt
```

Actual output from the 2-core test VM, Go 1.24 (10,000 lines per operation):

```text
          │     naive      │                better                 │                fast                 │
          │     sec/op     │     sec/op      vs base               │    sec/op     vs base               │
Analyze-2   139186.4µ ± 9%   10538.1µ ± 16%  -92.43% (p=0.002 n=6)   997.4µ ± 15%  -99.28% (p=0.002 n=6)

          │      naive       │                better                 │                fast                 │
          │       B/op       │      B/op       vs base               │     B/op      vs base               │
Analyze-2   115223.15Ki ± 0%   1881.64Ki ± 0%  -98.37% (p=0.002 n=6)   29.15Ki ± 0%  -99.97% (p=0.002 n=6)

          │     naive      │               better                │                fast                │
          │   allocs/op    │  allocs/op    vs base               │  allocs/op   vs base               │
Analyze-2   1401.426k ± 0%   21.429k ± 0%  -98.47% (p=0.002 n=6)   1.638k ± 0%  -99.88% (p=0.002 n=6)
```

How to read it:

- Each cell is the **median** of the runs, and `±` is the confidence interval. `± 16%` says this VM is noisy; that is why one run is never enough.
- `vs base` is the change relative to the first column.
- `p=0.002` is the probability of seeing a difference this large if there were **no real difference**. benchstat reports `~` instead of a percentage when the difference is not statistically significant (by default p ≥ 0.05). When you see `~`, you have not proven anything.
- `n=6` is the number of runs used.

So: compiling the regular expression once (`better`) made the analysis about **13 times faster** and cut allocations by 98%. Replacing the regular expression with direct string scanning (`fast`) made it about **140 times faster** than the original. The next lesson shows how the profile pointed at exactly these changes.

### Comparing before and after a change

The more common workflow compares two versions of the **same** code:

```bash
go test -run xxx -bench . -count=10 ./pkg > old.txt
# ... make your change ...
go test -run xxx -bench . -count=10 ./pkg > new.txt
benchstat old.txt new.txt
```

## Making benchmarks trustworthy

- **Realistic input.** The analyzer benchmark generates 10,000 varied lines with a fixed random seed, including malformed ones. Benchmarking one repeated line would let caches and branch predictors flatter the code.
- **Stable machine.** Close other programs. On laptops, plug in power. In CI, results from shared runners are noisy; use them for big regressions only.
- **Enough runs.** If `±` is large, increase `-count`.
- **Look at allocations too.** `-benchmem` often explains a time difference.

## Common mistakes

### Concluding from one run

Run-to-run noise of 10% or more is normal on shared machines. Use `-count` and benchstat.

### Benchmarking the wrong thing

Tiny inputs that fit in cache, or setup code inside the loop. Check what the loop actually measures.

### Optimizing without a reason

Only optimize code that a profile or a production metric shows matters. A 99% speedup of something that takes 0.1% of total time saves nothing.

## Key takeaways

- Test equivalence first, then benchmark realistic inputs.
- Run benchmarks repeatedly and compare with `benchstat`; trust only significant results (no `~`).
- Name sub-benchmarks `key=value` to compare implementations as columns with `-col`.
- Look at `B/op` and `allocs/op` alongside time.

## Further reading

- [benchstat documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat)
- [Package testing: Benchmarks](https://pkg.go.dev/testing#hdr-Benchmarks)

lessons.title: 10.2 CPU and memory profiling with pprof
lessons.description: Collect CPU and memory profiles from benchmarks and running services, read top, list and flame graph views, and turn what the profile shows into a targeted fix.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How sampling profilers work, and what CPU and heap profiles contain
- Collecting profiles from benchmarks with `-cpuprofile` and `-memprofile`
- Reading `top`, `top -cum` and `list` output
- The flame graph view in the web UI
- Profiling running services with `net/http/pprof`

## The idea

A **profiler** shows where a program spends its time or memory. Go's CPU profiler is a **sampling** profiler: about 100 times per second it records the stack of whatever is running. Functions that appear in many samples are where the time goes. The heap profiler similarly samples allocations, recording where memory was allocated.

Profiles answer "**where** should I optimize?". Benchmarks (lesson 10.1) answer "**did** it help?". You need both.

## Profiling a benchmark

```bash
go test -run xxx -bench 'BenchmarkNaive$' -benchtime=20x \
  -cpuprofile cpu.out -memprofile mem.out ./examples/m10/loganalyzer
go tool pprof -top cpu.out
```

`go test` keeps the compiled test binary (`loganalyzer.test`) next to the profiles so `pprof` can show function names and source lines.

## Reading `top`

Real output for the naive analyzer (trimmed):

```text
Type: cpu
Duration: 3.42s, Total samples = 3950ms (115.42%)
      flat  flat%   sum%        cum   cum%
     170ms  4.30%  4.30%      170ms  4.30%  runtime.nextFreeFast (inline)
     160ms  4.05%  8.35%      160ms  4.05%  runtime.futex
     160ms  4.05% 12.41%      160ms  4.05%  runtime.memclrNoHeapPointers
     140ms  3.54% 15.95%      300ms  7.59%  regexp.onePassCopy
     130ms  3.29% 19.24%      360ms  9.11%  regexp/syntax.(*compiler).inst
     120ms  3.04% 22.28%      570ms 14.43%  regexp.makeOnePass.func1
     120ms  3.04% 25.32%      710ms 17.97%  runtime.growslice
```

- **flat**: time spent in the function itself.
- **cum** (cumulative): time in the function **and everything it calls**.
- Total samples above 100% means more than one CPU was busy (the garbage collector runs in parallel).

The flat view is confusing here: the top entries are memory allocator and regexp internals, each a few percent. The **cumulative** view tells the real story:

```bash
go tool pprof -top -cum cpu.out
```

```text
      flat  flat%   sum%        cum   cum%
     0.01s  0.25%  0.25%      2.96s 74.94%  .../loganalyzer.AnalyzeNaive
         0     0%  0.25%      2.52s 63.80%  regexp.MustCompile
         0     0%  0.25%      2.52s 63.80%  regexp.compile
     0.06s  1.52%  1.77%      1.19s 30.13%  runtime.mallocgc
     0.04s  1.01%  2.78%      1.01s 25.57%  regexp.compileOnePass
```

**64% of all CPU time is `regexp.MustCompile`**, called from our function. And 30% is spent allocating memory.

## Reading `list`

`list` shows time per source line of a function:

```bash
go tool pprof -list AnalyzeNaive cpu.out
```

```text
      10ms      2.96s (flat, cum) 74.94% of Total
         .      2.52s     18:		re := regexp.MustCompile(`^(\S+) (\S+) (\S+) (\d{3}) (\d+)ms$`)
         .      330ms     19:		m := re.FindStringSubmatch(line)
         .       70ms     28:		key := fmt.Sprintf("%s", strings.ToLower(m[3]))
```

Line 18 is the culprit: the pattern is compiled again for **every line**. Matching (line 19) is cheap by comparison. The fix is to compile once, in a package-level variable, which is exactly `AnalyzeBetter`:



```gopath-example
example-289
```



Lesson 10.1's benchstat output confirms it: 92% faster.

## Memory profiles

```bash
go tool pprof -top -sample_index=alloc_space mem.out
```

```text
Type: alloc_space
      flat  flat%   sum%        cum   cum%
  499.47MB 22.26% 22.26%   499.47MB 22.26%  regexp/syntax.(*compiler).inst
  492.05MB 21.93% 44.20%   492.05MB 21.93%  regexp/syntax.(*parser).newRegexp
  400.77MB 17.86% 62.06%   400.77MB 17.86%  regexp.onePassCopy
```

The heap profile has four views, selected with `-sample_index`:

| Index | Shows |
|---|---|
| `alloc_space` | total bytes allocated over time (find **allocation churn**) |
| `alloc_objects` | number of allocations over time |
| `inuse_space` | bytes still live when the profile was taken (find **memory leaks** and bloat) |
| `inuse_objects` | live object count |

For speed, `alloc_space` and `alloc_objects` matter most: every allocation costs time now and garbage collection work later. For "why is memory growing", look at `inuse_space`.

## The second round

After fixing the regexp compile, profile `AnalyzeBetter` the same way and the remaining time is mostly regular expression matching and the allocations it makes for submatches. That led to `AnalyzeFast`, which scans with `strings.Cut` and avoids allocating keys that are already lowercase:



```gopath-example
example-290
```



This is the normal rhythm: **profile, fix the biggest thing, measure, repeat**. Stop when the code is fast enough for its purpose.

## The web UI and flame graphs

```bash
go tool pprof -http=:8080 cpu.out
```

This opens an interactive UI. Since Go 1.26 it opens on the **flame graph** view, where each bar is a function, its width is its share of samples, and bars stack on top of the functions that called them. Wide bars near the top of the stack are your hot spots. The UI also has graph, top, source and disassembly views.

## Profiling running services

Import `net/http/pprof` and serve it on an **internal** port:

```go
import _ "net/http/pprof" // registers /debug/pprof/ handlers on http.DefaultServeMux

go func() { log.Println(http.ListenAndServe("localhost:6060", nil)) }()
```

```bash
go tool pprof -http=:8080 http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30  # CPU
go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap                              # memory
curl http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=1                          # goroutines
```

Never expose these endpoints publicly: they reveal internals and can be used to slow the service down. Profiling in production is cheap enough to do routinely; continuous profiling services collect these profiles from every instance, which is also how you get profiles for PGO (lesson 10.5).

## Common mistakes

### Optimizing by flat time only

Runtime functions (`mallocgc`, `memclr`) often top the flat list. Use `-cum` and `list` to find **your** code that causes them.

### Profiling a too-short run

A profile with a few dozen samples is noise. Run long enough to get thousands (use `-benchtime`).

### Forgetting the binary

Without the binary, `pprof` cannot always resolve symbols for older profiles. Keep the test binary or build with the same source.

## Key takeaways

- CPU profiles sample stacks; heap profiles sample allocations.
- Collect from benchmarks with `-cpuprofile` and `-memprofile`, or from services with `net/http/pprof`.
- `top -cum` and `list` lead you from runtime noise to your own code.

lessons.searchText:
10.2 cpu and memory profiling with pprof collect cpu and memory profiles from benchmarks and running services, read top, list and flame graph views, and turn what the profile shows into a targeted fix.  what you will learn

- how sampling profilers work, and what cpu and heap profiles contain
- collecting profiles from benchmarks with -cpuprofile and -memprofile
- reading top, top -cum and list output
- the flame graph view in the web ui
- profiling running services with net/http/pprof

 the idea

a profiler shows where a program spends its time or memory. go's cpu profiler is a sampling profiler: about 100 times per second it records the stack of whatever is running. functions that appear in many samples are where the time goes. the heap profiler similarly samples allocations, recording where memory was allocated.

profiles answer "where should i optimize?". benchmarks (lesson 10.1) answer "did it help?". you need both.

 profiling a benchmark



go test keeps the compiled test binary (loganalyzer.test) next to the profiles so pprof can show function names and source lines.

 reading top

real output for the naive analyzer (trimmed):



- flat: time spent in the function itself.
- cum (cumulative): time in the function and everything it calls.
- total samples above 100% means more than one cpu was busy (the garbage collector runs in parallel).

the flat view is confusing here: the top entries are memory allocator and regexp internals, each a few percent. the cumulative view tells the real story:





64% of all cpu time is regexp.mustcompile, called from our function. and 30% is spent allocating memory.

 reading list

list shows time per source line of a function:





line 18 is the culprit: the pattern is compiled again for every line. matching (line 19) is cheap by comparison. the fix is to compile once, in a package-level variable, which is exactly analyzebetter:







lesson 10.1's benchstat output confirms it: 92% faster.

 memory profiles





the heap profile has four views, selected with -sampleindex:

| index | shows |
|---|---|
| allocspace | total bytes allocated over time (find allocation churn) |
| allocobjects | number of allocations over time |
| inusespace | bytes still live when the profile was taken (find memory leaks and bloat) |
| inuseobjects | live object count |

for speed, allocspace and allocobjects matter most: every allocation costs time now and garbage collection work later. for "why is memory growing", look at inusespace.

 the second round

after fixing the regexp compile, profile analyzebetter the same way and the remaining time is mostly regular expression matching and the allocations it makes for submatches. that led to analyzefast, which scans with strings.cut and avoids allocating keys that are already lowercase:







this is the normal rhythm: profile, fix the biggest thing, measure, repeat. stop when the code is fast enough for its purpose.

 the web ui and flame graphs



this opens an interactive ui. since go 1.26 it opens on the flame graph view, where each bar is a function, its width is its share of samples, and bars stack on top of the functions that called them. wide bars near the top of the stack are your hot spots. the ui also has graph, top, source and disassembly views.

 profiling running services

import net/http/pprof and serve it on an internal port:





never expose these endpoints publicly: they reveal internals and can be used to slow the service down. profiling in production is cheap enough to do routinely; continuous profiling services collect these profiles from every instance, which is also how you get profiles for pgo (lesson 10.5).

 common mistakes

 optimizing by flat time only

runtime functions (mallocgc, memclr) often top the flat list. use -cum and list to find your code that causes them.

 profiling a too-short run

a profile with a few dozen samples is noise. run long enough to get thousands (use -benchtime).

 forgetting the binary

without the binary, pprof cannot always resolve symbols for older profiles. keep the test binary or build with the same source.

 key takeaways

- cpu profiles sample stacks; heap profiles sample allocations.
- collect from benchmarks with -cpuprofile and -memprofile, or from services with net/http/pprof.
- top -cum and list lead you from runtime noise to your own code.
- use allocspace for churn, inusespace for leaks.
- profile, fix the biggest problem, measure with benchstat, repeat.

 further reading

- [profiling go programs](https://go.dev/blog/pprof) on the go blog
- [diagnostics](https://go.dev/doc/diagnostics) on go.dev
- [package net/http/pprof](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http/pprof)

lessons.title: 10.3 The execution tracer and flight recorder
lessons.description: Use the execution tracer to see goroutine scheduling, blocking, GC pauses and latency, annotate traces with tasks and regions, and capture traces of rare events with the flight recorder.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What the execution tracer shows that profiles cannot
- Collecting traces from tests and programs, and opening them with `go tool trace`
- Annotating traces with tasks, regions and logs
- Capturing the moments before a rare problem with the **flight recorder** (Go 1.25)

## Profiles vs traces

A CPU profile tells you **where** CPU time goes, summed over the whole run. It cannot tell you why a particular request took 2 seconds while using only 5 milliseconds of CPU. That request was **waiting**: for a lock, a channel, the network, the garbage collector or a free processor.

The **execution tracer** records events with timestamps: goroutines starting, blocking and unblocking, system calls, GC phases, processor (P) activity. It answers questions about **latency and concurrency**:

- Why is this request slow when CPU usage is low?
- Are my workers actually running in parallel, or waiting on one lock?
- How long do GC pauses and assists take, and when?

## Collecting a trace

```bash
# From tests or benchmarks:
go test -run TestSomething -trace trace.out ./pkg
go tool trace trace.out
```

In a program:

```go
f, _ := os.Create("trace.out")
trace.Start(f)
defer trace.Stop()
```

Or from a running service with `net/http/pprof`: `curl -o trace.out http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/trace?seconds=5`.

`go tool trace` opens a browser UI with a timeline per processor and per goroutine, views of goroutine analysis, network and synchronization blocking, and scheduler latency. Tracing has a modest overhead (a few percent with the current implementation), so it is usable in production for short periods.

## Annotating traces

```go
ctx, task := trace.NewTask(ctx, "handleOrder")   // a logical operation, possibly across goroutines
defer task.End()

trace.WithRegion(ctx, "validate", func() { validate(order) })  // a timed region in one goroutine
trace.Log(ctx, "orderID", order.ID)                            // a message attached to the task
```

Tasks and regions appear in the trace UI, with per-task latency histograms. This turns "the trace of everything" into "the trace of slow `handleOrder` calls".

## The flight recorder (Go 1.25)

The hardest performance problems are rare: one request in ten thousand takes 5 seconds. You cannot trace everything all the time, and by the time you notice, the moment has passed.

The **flight recorder**, added in Go 1.25, keeps the last few seconds of trace data in a ring buffer in memory. When your code notices something interesting, it writes a snapshot of what led up to it:



```gopath-example
example-291
```



Use it with a latency threshold in a request middleware, or on errors that are hard to reproduce. Write the snapshot to a file (or upload it), then open it with `go tool trace` like any other trace. The `MinAge` and `MaxBytes` settings bound how much history is kept.

## Common mistakes

### Using CPU profiles for latency problems

If CPU is low but latency is high, the program is waiting. Trace it.

### Tracing for too long

Traces are large. A few seconds is usually enough; use the flight recorder for rare events.

### Unannotated traces of busy services

Thousands of goroutines are hard to read. Add tasks and regions around the operations you care about.

## Key takeaways

- The tracer records timestamped scheduling, blocking, syscall and GC events; use it for latency and concurrency questions.
- Collect with `go test -trace`, `trace.Start`, or `/debug/pprof/trace`, and view with `go tool trace`.
- Annotate with `trace.NewTask`, `trace.WithRegion` and `trace.Log`.
- The flight recorder (Go 1.25+) keeps recent trace data in memory and snapshots it when something goes wrong.

## Further reading

- [Package runtime/trace](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/trace)
- [More powerful Go execution traces](https://go.dev/blog/execution-traces-2024) on the Go blog
- [Flight Recorder in Go 1.25](https://go.dev/blog/flight-recorder) on the Go blog

lessons.title: 10.4 Allocation reduction and escape analysis
lessons.description: Understand stack versus heap, read the compiler's escape analysis with -gcflags=-m, see exactly when values and interfaces allocate, and apply the standard techniques to reduce allocations.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why heap allocations cost more than stack allocations
- How the compiler decides with **escape analysis**, and how to see its decisions
- Exactly when returning pointers and storing values in interfaces allocate
- Practical techniques to reduce allocations
- When to stop

## The idea

Go decides automatically whether each value lives on the **stack** (freed for free when the function returns) or the **heap** (managed by the garbage collector). Heap allocations are not slow individually, but each one costs allocator work, adds GC pressure, and hurts cache locality. In hot loops, the number of allocations often decides performance, as the benchmarks in this module have shown.

You do not choose stack or heap explicitly. The compiler's **escape analysis** proves when a value cannot outlive its function and keeps it on the stack. Your job is to write code where that proof is easy.

## Seeing escape analysis

```bash
go build -gcflags=-m ./examples/m10/escape
```

```text
examples/m10/escape/escape.go:16:45: &Point{...} escapes to heap
examples/m10/escape/escape.go:22:15: leaking param: v
examples/m10/escape/escape.go:25:12: v does not escape
```

`-gcflags=-m` prints the compiler's decisions: what escapes and why, and what was inlined. Use `-gcflags='-m -m'` for more detail on why.

## When values allocate



```gopath-example
example-292
```





```gopath-example
example-293
```



What the test shows, on both Go 1.24 and 1.27:

- **Returning a struct by value** does not allocate. Returning a **pointer** to a local makes it escape (lesson 2.8). For small structs, values are often faster.
- **Interfaces** need their contents somewhere. Storing a non-constant `int` in an interface that **escapes** (here, saved in a global) allocates. Three cases do not:
  - small integers 0 to 255, which the runtime keeps in a static table;
  - constants, which the compiler stores in read-only data;
  - interfaces that do **not** escape, whose contents can live on the stack.
- **Fixed-size arrays** live on the stack. Recent releases (Go 1.25 and 1.26) also put more variable-sized slice backing arrays on the stack when they are small, which is one reason allocation counts can drop when you upgrade Go.

The `//go:noinline` directives make the examples show each function on its own. Inlining often removes allocations entirely: once a function is inlined into its caller, a pointer it returns may not escape the caller. Do not add `//go:noinline` to real code.

## Techniques that reduce allocations

Roughly in order of how often they help:

1. **Do not repeat expensive setup**: compile regular expressions, templates and encoders once (lesson 10.2).
2. **Preallocate** slices and maps when you know the size: `make([]T, 0, n)`, `make(map[K]V, n)`.
3. **Build strings with `strings.Builder` or `append`**, not `+=` in loops (lesson 9.7).
4. **Use `strconv.Append*` and `fmt.Appendf`** in hot formatting paths (lesson 8.6).
5. **Avoid converting between `string` and `[]byte`** repeatedly; pick one representation for the hot path.
6. **Return small structs by value**; pass pointers only when you need sharing or the struct is large.
7. **Avoid `any` in hot paths**; generic functions or concrete types avoid boxing.
8. **Reuse buffers** across iterations (`buf = buf[:0]`), or across goroutines with `sync.Pool` (lesson 10.6).
9. **Do not allocate when the common case needs nothing**: `AnalyzeFast` only calls `strings.ToLower` when a path actually contains uppercase letters.

Lock in the result with an allocation test (`testing.AllocsPerRun`, lesson 9.7), so a later change cannot quietly undo it.

## When to stop

Allocation reduction makes code harder to read. Do it in code that profiles show is hot, stop when the code meets its performance goals, and leave a comment explaining any non-obvious trick (such as the size estimate in `JoinAppend`).

## Common mistakes

### Pointers everywhere "for speed"

Passing and returning pointers to small structs often adds heap allocations. Measure before assuming.

### Trusting `-m` output from a different build

Escape decisions depend on inlining, which depends on build flags and the Go version. Check with the same toolchain and flags you ship.

### Micro-optimizing cold code

A function called once per request rarely matters. Find the loops first.

## Key takeaways

- Escape analysis keeps values on the stack when it can prove they do not outlive the function.
- `go build -gcflags=-m` shows what escapes and what was inlined.
- Returning pointers, and storing non-constant values in escaping interfaces, allocate; inlining often removes allocations.
- Preallocate, reuse buffers, avoid repeated setup and avoid unnecessary conversions in hot paths.
- Measure, lock in gains with allocation tests, and stop when it is fast enough.

## Further reading

- [Go FAQ: stack or heap?](https://go.dev/doc/faq#stack_or_heap)
- [A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector](https://go.dev/doc/gc-guide), which explains the cost model

lessons.title: 10.5 Profile-guided optimization (PGO)
lessons.description: Feed a CPU profile from production into the compiler so it inlines and devirtualizes the hot paths, with a real measurement on the log analyzer.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What profile-guided optimization is and what the compiler does with a profile
- The `default.pgo` workflow for real services
- A measured result on this module's log analyzer
- What PGO does not do

## The idea

The compiler normally optimizes without knowing which code runs most. With **profile-guided optimization** (stable since Go 1.21), you give it a CPU profile from a representative run, and it spends its optimization budget where the profile says time is spent. Mainly it:

- **inlines** hot functions more aggressively, even ones over the normal size limit;
- **devirtualizes** hot interface method calls: if the profile shows a call through an interface almost always reaches one concrete type, the compiler adds a fast direct call for that type (lesson 11.5 explains why that helps).

You change no code. The Go team reports typical improvements of a few percent up to around 14% for representative programs.

## The workflow for a service

1. **Collect a CPU profile from production**, or from a load test that resembles it. With `net/http/pprof`: `curl -o cpu.pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30`. Merging profiles from several instances (`go tool pprof -proto a.pprof b.pprof > merged.pprof`) gives a more representative result.
2. **Save it as `default.pgo`** in the directory of your `main` package, and commit it.
3. **Build normally.** `go build` uses `default.pgo` automatically (the default is `-pgo=auto`). Use `-pgo=off` to disable it, or `-pgo=path/to/file` to choose a profile.
4. **Refresh the profile** from time to time, for example every release. A slightly stale profile still helps; Go's PGO is designed to tolerate code changes.

## A measurement

For the log analyzer, a profile was collected by running the `better` and `fast` benchmarks, and the benchmarks were then run 8 times without and with that profile (`go test -pgo=cpu.pprof`). Result from the 2-core test VM with Go 1.24:

```text
                      │  without PGO  │            with PGO                 │
                      │    sec/op     │    sec/op     vs base               │
Analyze/impl=better-2    10.88m ±  7%   10.06m ± 10%   -7.56% (p=0.021 n=8)
Analyze/impl=fast-2      1026.0µ ± 5%   935.0µ ±  6%   -8.88% (p=0.000 n=8)
geomean                   3.342m         3.067m        -8.22%
```

About **8% faster for free**, statistically significant even on a noisy VM. Your results will vary with the code: programs with many small hot functions and interface calls benefit most.

To reproduce:

```bash
cd examples/m10/loganalyzer
go test -run xxx -bench 'Analyze/impl=(better|fast)' -benchtime=2s -cpuprofile cpu.pprof .
go test -run xxx -bench 'Analyze/impl=(better|fast)' -count=8 . > nopgo.txt
go test -pgo=cpu.pprof -run xxx -bench 'Analyze/impl=(better|fast)' -count=8 . > pgo.txt
benchstat nopgo.txt pgo.txt
```

## What PGO does not do

- It does not fix algorithmic problems. Compiling a regexp per line is still slow with PGO.
- It does not reduce allocations directly (though inlining sometimes lets escape analysis keep values on the stack).
- Builds take somewhat longer, and a profile from an unrepresentative workload can optimize the wrong paths.

Do the big, obvious fixes first (lessons 10.2 and 10.4), then add PGO as a final, low-effort gain.

## Key takeaways

- PGO feeds a CPU profile to the compiler, which inlines and devirtualizes hot code.
- Put a production-representative profile in `default.pgo` next to your `main` package; `go build` uses it automatically.
- Expect a few percent to around 14%; this module's example measured about 8%.
- PGO complements, and never replaces, profiling and fixing your code.

## Further reading

- [Profile-guided optimization](https://go.dev/doc/pgo) on go.dev
- [Profile-guided optimization in Go 1.21](https://go.dev/blog/pgo) on the Go blog

lessons.title: 10.6 sync.Pool and when it helps
lessons.description: Reuse temporary objects across goroutines with sync.Pool, avoid its pitfalls (stale data, retained huge buffers, values instead of pointers), and measure whether it helps.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What `sync.Pool` is for, and how it interacts with the garbage collector
- The correct get, reset, use, copy out, put pattern
- The pitfalls: stale data, huge buffers, storing values instead of pointers
- A measured comparison, and when a pool is not worth it

## The idea

Some code allocates the same kind of **temporary** object over and over: a buffer to format a log line, a scratch slice to parse a request, an encoder state. `sync.Pool` keeps such objects around so they can be **reused** instead of allocated again.

Important properties:

- A pool is safe for concurrent use and scales well: each processor has its own local cache.
- The garbage collector may **empty pools at any time** (over two GC cycles). A pool is a cache of temporary objects, never storage for anything you need to keep.
- `Get` returns an arbitrary pooled object, or calls `New` if the pool is empty.

## The pattern

Without a pool:



```gopath-example
example-294
```



With a pool:



```gopath-example
example-295
```



The steps, each of which matters:

1. **Get and type-assert.** Store **pointers** in the pool (`*bytes.Buffer`). Putting a non-pointer value into a `sync.Pool` allocates when it is converted to `any`, which defeats the purpose (`go vet` and staticcheck can flag this).
2. **Reset.** A pooled object still contains whatever the previous user left in it.
3. **Use it.**
4. **Copy out results** before putting the object back. `buf.String()` copies; returning `buf.Bytes()` would hand the caller memory that another goroutine is about to overwrite.
5. **Put it back, unless it grew huge.** One request that needed a 10 MB buffer should not leave 10 MB buffers in the pool forever.

## Measured

`BenchmarkRender` runs both versions in parallel on all cores. Results from the 2-core test VM, Go 1.24, 6 runs:

```text
         │    nopool    │                pool                 │
         │    sec/op    │    sec/op     vs base               │
Render-2   79.83n ± 16%   56.85n ± 28%  -28.79% (p=0.004 n=6)

         │   nopool    │               pool                │
         │    B/op     │    B/op     vs base               │
Render-2   112.00 ± 0%   48.00 ± 0%  -57.14% (p=0.002 n=6)

         │   nopool   │               pool                │
         │ allocs/op  │ allocs/op   vs base               │
Render-2   2.000 ± 0%   1.000 ± 0%  -50.00% (p=0.002 n=6)
```

The pool removed the buffer allocation; the one remaining allocation is the result string, which must be a new value. The time saving is real but modest, and the `±` values show how noisy such small measurements are.

## When a pool is worth it

Use `sync.Pool` when **all** of these hold:

- the objects are temporary and expensive enough to matter (buffers, encoders, large scratch structures);
- a profile shows their allocation is significant;
- they are allocated very frequently, from many goroutines.

The standard library uses pools exactly this way, for example in `fmt` for its print state and in `encoding/json` for encode buffers.

Do **not** use a pool for small objects (a few bytes: the bookkeeping costs more than the allocation), for objects with expensive or error-prone reset logic, or as a connection pool (connections need lifecycle management; use `database/sql` or the HTTP transport's own pooling).

## Common mistakes

### Forgetting `Reset`

Output from one request leaks into the next, which is both a bug and potentially a security issue.

### Using an object after `Put`

Another goroutine may already be writing into it. Copy out first; never keep references.

### Pooling values instead of pointers

Every `Put` allocates. Pool `*T`.

### Retaining huge objects

Cap the size of objects you put back.

## Key takeaways

- `sync.Pool` reuses temporary objects across goroutines; the GC may drop them at any time.
- Pattern: Get, Reset, use, copy results out, Put (unless oversized). Pool pointers.
- Use it for frequent, expensive temporaries that a profile shows matter; measure the result.

## Further reading

- [Package sync: Pool](https://pkg.go.dev/sync#Pool)

## The task

This exercise is the module in miniature. The starter code is **correct**, and its correctness tests already pass. But it allocates wildly, and a test enforces an allocation budget it misses by a factor of about 50.



```gopath-exercise
m10/hashtags
```



## Suggested workflow

```bash
cd exercises

# 1. Where do we stand?
go test ./m10/hashtags                                  # TestAllocationBudget fails
go test -run xxx -bench . -benchmem ./m10/hashtags      # note ns/op, B/op, allocs/op

# 2. Where do the allocations come from?
go test -run xxx -bench . -memprofile mem.out ./m10/hashtags
go tool pprof -top -sample_index=alloc_objects mem.out
go tool pprof -list TopTags -sample_index=alloc_objects mem.out

# 3. Fix the biggest source, then repeat steps 1 and 2.
```

On the test VM, the starter measured about **19,840 allocations** and 760 µs per call; the reference solution measured **255 allocations** and about 95 µs.

## Hints

Try to find these yourself in the profile before reading them.



```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-0
```





```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-1
```





```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-2
```



The reference solution is in `exercises/m10/hashtags/solution.go`.

## Part 3, first half: recap

You can now measure performance honestly with benchmarks and benchstat, find hot spots with CPU and memory profiles, investigate latency with the tracer and flight recorder, reason about allocations with escape analysis, apply PGO, and reuse objects with `sync.Pool`, always checking the result with data.

Next is **[Module 11: Runtime internals](/learn/11-runtime-internals/)**, which explains the machinery behind what you have been measuring.
