lessons.title: 11.1 How the scheduler works: G, M and P
lessons.description: How the Go runtime runs many goroutines on few OS threads: Gs, Ms and Ps, run queues and work stealing, blocking system calls, preemption, and how GOMAXPROCS is chosen inside containers.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The three scheduler objects, **G**, **M** and **P**, and how they fit together
- Run queues, work stealing, and what happens when a goroutine blocks
- How preemption keeps a busy goroutine from starving others
- What `GOMAXPROCS` controls, and how Go 1.25 picks it inside containers
- How to observe the scheduler with `runtime/metrics` and `go test -cpu`

## The idea

You can start a million goroutines, but the machine has only a few CPU cores and the operating system only so many threads. The Go **scheduler**, part of the runtime linked into every Go binary, multiplexes goroutines onto threads. It uses three kinds of objects:

| Object | What it is |
|---|---|
| **G** (goroutine) | A goroutine: its stack, its saved registers, its status (running, runnable, waiting). Cheap: a few KiB. |
| **M** (machine) | An operating system thread. Ms execute code. |
| **P** (processor) | A scheduling context: the right to run Go code, plus a local queue of runnable Gs. There are exactly `GOMAXPROCS` Ps. |

An M must hold a P to run Go code. So `GOMAXPROCS` limits how many goroutines **execute Go code at the same moment**. It does not limit how many goroutines exist, and it does not limit threads: threads blocked in system calls do not hold a P.

```text
        P0                    P1                  global run queue
   ┌──────────┐          ┌──────────┐            ┌──────────────┐
   │ runq:    │          │ runq:    │            │ G G G ...    │
   │ G G G G  │          │ G        │            └──────────────┘
   └────┬─────┘          └────┬─────┘
        │ held by             │ held by
        M0 ── running G7      M1 ── running G2        M2: blocked in a syscall, no P
```

## Run queues and work stealing

Each P has a **local run queue** of up to 256 runnable goroutines, and there is one **global run queue** shared by all. When a goroutine is created with `go`, it usually goes onto the current P's local queue (in a special "run next" slot, so a newly created goroutine runs soon, which is good for producer and consumer pairs).

When a P runs out of work, it looks, roughly in this order: its own queue, the global queue, the network poller (goroutines whose I/O is ready), and then it **steals half** of another P's queue. Work stealing keeps all cores busy without a central lock.

## When goroutines block

- **Channels, mutexes, `time.Sleep`, `select`**: the goroutine is parked (status "waiting") and the M simply picks another G from the P. No thread is blocked. This is why blocking a goroutine is cheap.
- **Network I/O**: also parked. The runtime's **network poller** (epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD and macOS, IOCP on Windows) watches the sockets and makes goroutines runnable when data arrives. That is how one Go process serves tens of thousands of connections with a handful of threads, while your code reads like simple blocking code.
- **Blocking system calls** (file I/O on most systems, cgo calls): the thread really blocks. The runtime detaches the P from that M so another M can use it to run goroutines, starting a new thread if needed. When the system call returns, the goroutine needs a P again.

A background thread called **sysmon** watches for long system calls and long-running goroutines, and handles both.

## Preemption

What if a goroutine never blocks? This example pins the program to one P and starts a goroutine with a tight loop that makes no function calls:



```gopath-example
example-296
```



On Go 1.27 it prints something like `main goroutine ran again after 11.860807ms`. The main goroutine woke up from its 10 ms sleep, but the only P was busy spinning. sysmon noticed that the spinner had run for longer than its time slice (10 ms) and **preempted** it, so main could run and stop it.

Before Go 1.14 this program hung forever: goroutines could only be preempted at function calls, and this loop has none. Since Go 1.14, the runtime also uses **asynchronous preemption**: it sends the thread a signal (`SIGURG` on Unix) and stops the goroutine wherever it is. You can see the old behavior by turning that off:

```bash
go test -c -o sched.test ./examples/m11/sched
GODEBUG=asyncpreemptoff=1 timeout 10 ./sched.test -test.run Preemption   # hangs until timeout
```

You will never need `asyncpreemptoff` in real code; it exists for debugging.

## GOMAXPROCS

`GOMAXPROCS` is the number of Ps. You can set it with the `GOMAXPROCS` environment variable or `runtime.GOMAXPROCS(n)`, which returns the previous value (`runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0)` just reads it).

The default used to be simply the number of CPU cores the machine has (`runtime.NumCPU`). In a container that is often wrong: a Kubernetes pod with a CPU limit of 2 on a 64-core node got 64 Ps, so the Go program ran up to 64 threads at once, used up its CPU quota early in each scheduling period and was **throttled** by the kernel, causing latency spikes. For years, the fix was the `go.uber.org/automaxprocs` package.

Since **Go 1.25** the runtime handles this itself:

- On Linux, the default `GOMAXPROCS` respects the **cgroup CPU bandwidth limit**, which in Kubernetes is the pod's **CPU limit**. CPU **requests** are not considered. A limit of 2.5 CPUs gives `GOMAXPROCS=3` (rounded up, and at least 2 if the machine has 2 or more CPUs).
- On all systems, the runtime **re-checks periodically** and updates `GOMAXPROCS` if the limit or the number of available CPUs changes.
- Both behaviors are off if you set `GOMAXPROCS` yourself, and can be disabled with the `GODEBUG` settings `containermaxprocs=0` and `updatemaxprocs=0`. `runtime.SetDefaultGOMAXPROCS()` returns to the default.

These behaviors depend on the `go` line in your `go.mod` (GODEBUG defaults follow it), so a module that still says `go 1.24` keeps the old default even when built with a newer toolchain. Module 15 comes back to this when we deploy to Kubernetes.

## Seeing parallelism

`GOMAXPROCS` decides how much of your concurrency becomes parallelism. This function hashes 64 blocks of 64 KiB with 8 goroutines:



```gopath-example
example-297
```





```gopath-example
example-298
```



The `-cpu 1,2` flag runs the benchmark once per `GOMAXPROCS` value. On the 2-core test VM (`benchstat` output, 6 runs each):

```text
          │   sec/op     │
HashAll      2.903m ± 47%     (GOMAXPROCS=1)
HashAll-2    1.554m ±  2%     (GOMAXPROCS=2)
```

Same code, same 8 goroutines: twice the Ps, about twice the throughput. Asking for `-cpu 4` on a 2-core machine would not help further: there are only 2 cores to run on. The `-2` suffix that appears on every benchmark name in this course is exactly this value.

## Observing the scheduler

`runtime/metrics` exposes scheduler data without any profiling:



```gopath-example
example-299
```



Useful metrics include `/sched/gomaxprocs:threads`, `/sched/goroutines:goroutines`, and `/sched/latencies:seconds`, a histogram of how long runnable goroutines waited for a P. High scheduling latency means more work is runnable than there are Ps to run it. Go 1.26 added counts of goroutines by state under `/sched/goroutines`, `/sched/threads:threads`, and `/sched/goroutines-created:goroutines`. Run `go doc runtime/metrics` for the full list your version supports. For a timeline of scheduling decisions, use the execution tracer (lesson 10.3).

## Common mistakes

### Setting GOMAXPROCS higher "for more concurrency"

Concurrency comes from goroutines. More Ps than cores only adds contention.

### Assuming goroutines run in creation order

The scheduler gives no ordering guarantees. Synchronize explicitly (Modules 6 and 7).

### Ignoring CPU limits on older Go versions

On Go 1.24 and earlier, or with a `go.mod` that says so, a containerized service may run far more Ps than its CPU limit. Upgrade, or set `GOMAXPROCS` explicitly.

## Key takeaways

- Gs are goroutines, Ms are threads, Ps are the right to run Go code; there are `GOMAXPROCS` Ps.
- Each P has a local run queue; idle Ps steal work. Blocking on channels, locks and network I/O parks only the goroutine, not a thread.
- Since Go 1.14, long-running goroutines are preempted asynchronously, even in tight loops.
- Since Go 1.25, the default `GOMAXPROCS` respects the container's CPU limit and updates when it changes.
- Measure scaling with `go test -cpu`, and watch the scheduler with `runtime/metrics` and the tracer.

## Further reading

- [Go 1.25 release notes: container-aware GOMAXPROCS](https://go.dev/doc/go1.25#container-aware-gomaxprocs)
- [Package runtime/metrics](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/metrics)
- [Scalable Go Scheduler design document](https://golang.org/s/go11sched) by Dmitry Vyukov, the original design of Ps

lessons.title: 11.2 Stacks and goroutine growth
lessons.description: Why goroutines are cheap: small initial stacks that grow by copying, what that means for pointers and unsafe code, how deep recursion behaves, and what a stack overflow looks like.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How big a goroutine's stack starts, and how it grows and shrinks
- Why stacks **move**, and what that means for addresses
- How deep recursion behaves in Go, and what the limit is
- How much memory a blocked goroutine really costs

## The idea

An operating system thread typically gets a fixed stack of 1 to 8 MiB, reserved up front. That is why programs cannot have a million threads. A goroutine starts with a tiny stack, **2 KiB** at minimum, and the runtime grows it only when needed. That is the main reason goroutines are cheap enough to create one per request, per connection or per task.

## Measuring the cost

This function starts `n` goroutines that block on a channel, and measures how much stack memory they added:



```gopath-example
example-300
```



On both Go 1.24 and Go 1.27 it reports `about 2048 bytes of stack per blocked goroutine`. Ten thousand idle goroutines cost about 20 MiB of stack, plus a few hundred bytes each for the runtime's goroutine record. A thread per connection would need gigabytes of reserved address space for the same.

Since Go 1.19, the runtime adapts the starting size: if goroutines in your program typically need more than 2 KiB, new ones start with the average observed size, which avoids repeated growth. Goroutines like the ones above, which use very little, still start at the minimum.

## How stacks grow

Every Go function starts with a short **prologue** that compares the stack pointer with the end of the current stack. If the function's frame does not fit, it calls into the runtime, which:

1. allocates a new stack **twice as large**,
2. **copies** the old stack into it,
3. **adjusts every pointer** that points into the old stack, using the compiler's precise information about where pointers live in each frame,
4. frees the old stack and resumes the function.

Go used "segmented" stacks, linked chunks, before Go 1.3, but a function call in a loop right at a segment boundary kept allocating and freeing segments (the "hot split" problem). Contiguous, copied stacks avoid it: growth is amortized, like `append`.

Stacks also **shrink**: during garbage collection, a goroutine using less than a quarter of its stack gets it copied into one half the size.

## Stacks move

Because growth copies the stack, the **address** of a variable on the stack can change while the program runs:



```gopath-example
example-301
```



On the test VM with Go 1.27:

```text
stacks_test.go:20: before 0x369b47048f88, after 0x369b474bff88
```

Same variable `x`, different address after the recursion grew the stack. Ordinary Go code never notices, because the runtime updates every real pointer. But a `uintptr` is just a number, and the runtime does not update numbers. That is why the `unsafe` rules (lesson 11.4) forbid keeping an address in a `uintptr` and converting it back to a pointer later: by then it may point to freed memory.

Heap objects, by contrast, never move in Go's current garbage collector.

## Deep recursion

Go has no tail-call optimization, so every recursive call uses a new frame. With growable stacks that is usually fine:



```gopath-example
example-302
```



`Sum(1_000_000)` recurses a million levels and needs tens of MiB of stack; the test runs it in a fresh goroutine and it completes in about 40 ms. Deep recursion that would crash a C program with a fixed 8 MiB stack works in Go.

There is a limit: by default **1 GB** on 64-bit systems (250 MB on 32-bit). Infinite recursion hits it and the program dies:

```text
runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit
fatal error: stack overflow
```

This is a **fatal error**, not a panic: `recover` cannot catch it and the whole process exits, printing the repeating stack trace that shows where the recursion is. `debug.SetMaxStack` changes the limit, which is occasionally useful to make runaway recursion fail sooner in tests.

## Common mistakes

### Unbounded recursion on user input

Parsing deeply nested JSON or expressions recursively can be driven to the 1 GB limit by a malicious input, crashing the process. Limit the depth (the standard library's decoders do), or use an explicit stack.

### Keeping addresses in uintptr

The address may be stale after the next stack growth. Keep real pointers.

### Fearing goroutines for their memory

An idle goroutine costs about 2 KiB of stack plus a small record. The real costs of goroutines are what they hold on to and the work they do, and leaking them (lesson 7.6).

## Key takeaways

- Goroutine stacks start at 2 KiB (or the program's observed average) and grow by doubling and copying.
- Stack growth moves variables; the runtime fixes real pointers, never `uintptr` values.
- Stacks shrink during GC when mostly unused.
- Deep recursion works, up to a 1 GB default limit; exceeding it is a fatal, unrecoverable error.

## Further reading

- [Contiguous stacks design document](https://golang.org/s/contigstacks)
- [Package runtime/debug: SetMaxStack](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/debug#SetMaxStack)

lessons.title: 11.3 The garbage collector, GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT
lessons.description: How Go's concurrent mark-and-sweep collector works, how GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT trade memory for CPU (with measurements), how to read gctrace, what Green Tea changed in Go 1.26, and weak pointers and cleanups.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How Go's garbage collector works, at the level that affects your decisions
- How `GOGC` trades memory for CPU, measured
- How `GOMEMLIMIT` caps memory, and when to set it
- How to read `GODEBUG=gctrace=1` output
- What the Green Tea collector (default since Go 1.26) changed
- Weak pointers and cleanups (Go 1.24)

## How the collector works

Go's garbage collector is a **concurrent, tri-color, mark-and-sweep** collector. In plain words:

1. **Mark.** Starting from the **roots** (global variables and every goroutine's stack), the GC follows pointers and marks every object it can reach. This runs **concurrently** with your program, on about 25% of the CPU, plus "assists": goroutines that allocate quickly during marking are asked to help, so allocation cannot outrun the collector.
2. **Sweep.** Memory of unmarked objects is reclaimed, lazily, as new allocations need space.

While marking runs, a **write barrier** (a little extra work on pointer writes) tells the GC about pointers your program moves around, so nothing reachable is missed. There are two short **stop-the-world** pauses per cycle, typically well under a millisecond.

Two design choices to know:

- **Non-generational.** Every cycle marks the whole live heap. The cost of a cycle is proportional to the **live** heap (and the number of pointers in it), not to the garbage.
- **Non-moving.** Heap objects never move. (Stacks do, lesson 11.2.)

So the GC's total cost is roughly: **(cost per cycle, driven by live heap) × (number of cycles, driven by allocation rate and GOGC)**. You reduce it by allocating less (lesson 10.4), by keeping fewer pointers in the live heap, or by running fewer cycles.

## GOGC: trading memory for CPU

`GOGC` sets how much the heap may grow before the next cycle. With the default `GOGC=100`, the next cycle starts when the heap has grown by 100% of the live heap (plus GC roots such as stacks and globals):

```text
heap goal = live heap + (live heap + GC roots) × GOGC / 100
```

Higher `GOGC` means fewer cycles but a bigger heap. This experiment keeps 16 MiB live and allocates 512 MiB of short-lived garbage:



```gopath-example
example-303
```



GOGC is read once at start-up, so the test runs each setting in a **fresh process**, re-running its own test binary as a helper (a common Go testing pattern):



```gopath-example
example-304
```



Results on the 2-core test VM with Go 1.27:

```text
GOGC=50   cycles=58  heap goal about  26 MiB
GOGC=100  cycles=31  heap goal about  35 MiB
GOGC=200  cycles=15  heap goal about  52 MiB
GOGC=400  cycles=7   heap goal about  93 MiB
GOGC=off GOMEMLIMIT=64MiB: cycles=13  heap goal about  55 MiB
```

Each doubling of `GOGC` roughly halves the number of GC cycles and roughly doubles the extra memory above the live heap. Numbers vary between runs, and a lot on a busy machine, so the test only asserts the broad trend. There is no free lunch, only a dial: memory or CPU.

You can also set it in code with `debug.SetGCPercent`, and `GOGC=off` disables the collector entirely (dangerous on its own: memory grows without bound).

## GOMEMLIMIT: a ceiling

`GOMEMLIMIT` (Go 1.19) sets a **soft limit** on the total memory the Go runtime uses: heap, stacks and runtime structures. Values look like `GOMEMLIMIT=512MiB`, or plain bytes. As memory approaches the limit, the GC runs more often, whatever `GOGC` says.

The last line of the experiment combines `GOGC=off` with a 64 MiB limit: no cycles until the heap approaches the limit, then just enough to stay under it. That configuration makes the GC run as rarely as possible within a known memory budget, ideal for batch jobs with a fixed amount of memory.

For services in **containers**, the most useful setting is a limit a little **below the container's memory limit**, leaving 5 to 10% of headroom for memory the runtime does not control (cgo, the binary itself). With a pod memory limit of 1 GiB, `GOMEMLIMIT=900MiB` lets the GC work harder as memory gets tight, instead of the kernel killing the pod with OOMKilled. Keep `GOGC` at its default alongside it. Module 15 sets this in a Kubernetes manifest.

The limit is soft for a reason: if the live heap itself exceeds the limit, collecting constantly would freeze the program (a "death spiral"). The runtime caps GC CPU use at about 50% in that situation, so the program stays responsive and may go over the limit. A real leak still needs fixing.

## Reading gctrace

`GODEBUG=gctrace=1` prints one line per cycle to standard error:

```bash
GODEBUG=gctrace=1 go run ./examples/m11/gc/gcdemo
```

```text
gc 6 @0.015s 5%: 0.031+0.53+0.003 ms clock, 0.063+0.33/0.019/0+0.006 ms cpu, 28->31->18 MB, 33 MB goal, 0 MB stacks, 0 MB globals, 2 P
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `gc 6 @0.015s` | the 6th cycle, 15 ms after start |
| `5%` | share of CPU used by the GC since the program started |
| `0.031+0.53+0.003 ms clock` | first stop-the-world pause + concurrent mark + second pause. The pauses are microseconds. |
| `28->31->18 MB` | heap at cycle start → heap at mark end → **live heap** after marking |
| `33 MB goal` | the heap goal for this cycle |
| `2 P` | GOMAXPROCS |

If you see cycles many times per second with a small live heap, the program is allocating heavily: reduce allocations, or raise `GOGC`. If the live heap keeps growing, look for a leak with a heap profile (`inuse_space`, lesson 10.2).

## Green Tea (Go 1.26)

Go 1.25 shipped a new marking algorithm, **Green Tea**, as an experiment, and Go 1.26 made it the default. Instead of following pointers object by object around the heap, it scans memory **page by page**, batching the small objects that live together, which gives much better CPU cache locality and scales better to many cores. The Go team expects **10 to 40% less GC overhead** for programs that use the GC heavily, and about 10% more on recent amd64 CPUs that can use vector instructions for scanning.

Nothing changes in your code; you get it by upgrading. For now an opt-out exists, `GOEXPERIMENT=nogreenteagc` at build time, but it is planned for removal, so if you need it, report why.

## Weak pointers and cleanups (Go 1.24)

Sometimes you want to refer to an object **without** keeping it alive, for example in a cache keyed by large values. The `weak` package provides **weak pointers**:



```gopath-example
example-305
```



`w.Value()` returns the object while something else keeps it alive, and `nil` once it has been collected. Note the `alive` helper: `Value` returns an ordinary pointer, and while that pointer is in use, the object stays alive. This is easy to get wrong: an earlier version of this example checked `w.Value() != nil` directly inside `WeakDemo`, and in the test the Blob survived the `runtime.GC()` call: the temporary pointer from `Value` was most likely still considered live. Moving the check into its own small function fixed it.

`runtime.AddCleanup` runs a function after an object becomes unreachable, for example to release a non-memory resource it wraps:



```gopath-example
example-306
```



Cleanups replace the older `runtime.SetFinalizer`, which had sharp edges (finalizers could resurrect objects and prevented collecting cycles). Two rules: the cleanup function must not refer to the object itself (pass what it needs as the argument), and cleanups may run late or not at all before the program exits. Close files and connections explicitly with `defer`; use cleanups only as a safety net.

## Common mistakes

### Tuning GOGC before reducing allocations

Allocation reduction lowers both CPU and memory. GOGC only moves cost from one to the other.

### No GOMEMLIMIT in a memory-limited container

Without it, the GC does not know about the container limit. Heap growth between cycles can push the process over the limit, and the kernel kills it.

### Setting GOMEMLIMIT equal to the container limit

Leave headroom for non-heap memory, or the kernel may still kill the process first.

### Relying on cleanups or finalizers for correctness

They are not guaranteed to run promptly or at all. Release resources explicitly.

## Key takeaways

- Go's GC is concurrent mark-and-sweep, non-generational and non-moving; pauses are short, cost scales with the live heap and the number of cycles.
- `GOGC` trades memory for CPU: doubling it roughly halves cycles and doubles heap overhead.
- `GOMEMLIMIT` is a soft memory ceiling; in containers, set it 5 to 10% below the memory limit.
- `GODEBUG=gctrace=1` shows every cycle: pauses, heap sizes and goal.
- Green Tea is the default collector since Go 1.26.
- `weak.Pointer` refers to objects without keeping them alive; `runtime.AddCleanup` replaces `SetFinalizer`.

## Further reading

- [A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector](https://go.dev/doc/gc-guide), the definitive reference, with interactive graphs
- [Go 1.26 release notes: Green Tea](https://go.dev/doc/go1.26)
- [Package weak](https://pkg.go.dev/weak) and [runtime.AddCleanup](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime#AddCleanup)

lessons.title: 11.4 Memory layout, alignment and unsafe
lessons.description: How Go lays out values in memory: sizes, alignment and padding, the headers behind strings, slices and interfaces, false sharing between CPU cores, and how to use the unsafe package without breaking your program.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The size and alignment of Go's types, and where struct padding comes from
- How to shrink a struct by reordering its fields
- What strings, slices, interfaces and maps look like in memory
- **False sharing**, and a measured 5x slowdown it causes
- What the `unsafe` package can do, and the rules for using it safely

## Sizes and alignment

Every type has a **size** and an **alignment**. A value's address must be a multiple of its alignment, because CPUs read aligned data most efficiently (and some cannot read misaligned data at all). On 64-bit platforms:

| Type | Size | Alignment |
|---|---|---|
| `bool`, `int8`, `uint8` | 1 | 1 |
| `int16` | 2 | 2 |
| `int32`, `float32`, `rune` | 4 | 4 |
| `int64`, `float64`, `int`, `uintptr`, pointers | 8 | 8 |
| `string` | 16 | 8 |
| slice | 24 | 8 |
| interface | 16 | 8 |
| `struct{}` | 0 | 1 |

A struct's fields are laid out **in the order you declare them**. The compiler inserts **padding** before a field to align it, and at the end so the struct's size is a multiple of its alignment (so arrays of it stay aligned). The `unsafe` package shows the result:



```gopath-example
example-307
```





```gopath-example
example-308
```



`Wasteful` and `Compact` hold the same five fields, but `Wasteful` is **twice as big**: 32 bytes, of which 17 are padding. Ordering fields from largest alignment to smallest removes most padding. For one value, 16 bytes do not matter. For ten million values in a slice or cache, that is 160 MB.

The `fieldalignment` analyzer finds such structs for you:

```bash
go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/fieldalignment/cmd/fieldalignment@latest ./...
```

Do not reorder blindly, though. Field order is also documentation (related fields together), and a struct used once per request is not worth making less readable. Reorder the types you hold many of.

## What the headers tell you

The second example shows the sizes of Go's built-in "header" types:

- A **string** is a pointer to bytes plus a length (16 bytes). Assigning or passing a string copies only those 16 bytes, never the text.
- A **slice** is a pointer, a length and a capacity (24 bytes, lesson 3.2).
- An **interface** is two words: type information and a pointer to the value (16 bytes, lesson 11.5).
- A **map**, **channel** or **function** value is a single pointer (8 bytes) to a runtime structure. This is why passing a map to a function lets the function modify the caller's map.
- `struct{}` takes **zero** bytes, which makes `map[string]struct{}` the idiomatic set and `chan struct{}` the idiomatic signal.

## False sharing

CPUs move memory between main memory and their caches in **cache lines**, usually 64 bytes. When two cores write to different variables that happen to share a cache line, each write invalidates the line in the other core's cache, and the line bounces between cores. This is **false sharing**: no data is actually shared, but the hardware behaves as if it were.



```gopath-example
example-309
```



Two goroutines each increment their **own** counter a million times:



```gopath-example
example-310
```



On the 2-core test VM with Go 1.27:

```text
           │   adjacent   │               padded                │
           │    sec/op    │    sec/op     vs base               │
Counters-2   49.021m ± 8%   9.110m ± 11%  -81.42% (p=0.002 n=6)
```

The only difference is 120 bytes of padding: the padded version is about **5 times faster**. False sharing matters for per-core or per-worker counters, statistics and queue indices updated in hot loops. The standard library and runtime pad such structures; the `golang.org/x/sys/cpu` package provides a `CacheLinePad` type sized for the platform.

## The unsafe package

`unsafe` lets you step outside Go's type system. It is used inside the standard library and the runtime, and in a few performance-critical libraries. Ordinary application code should almost never import it. Its parts:

- `unsafe.Sizeof`, `Alignof` and `Offsetof`: compile-time constants about layout. These are safe.
- `unsafe.Pointer`: a pointer that can be converted to and from any pointer type, and to `uintptr`.
- `unsafe.String`, `unsafe.StringData`, `unsafe.Slice`, `unsafe.SliceData` (Go 1.17 and 1.20): build strings and slices from raw pointers without copying.

The danger is real. This converts a byte slice to a string without copying:



```gopath-example
example-311
```



The output is `jello`: a Go string **changed**, which the language promises can never happen. Code elsewhere that used `s` as a map key, or assumed it was immutable, is now silently broken. Zero-copy conversion is only correct if the bytes are **never modified again**, and nothing in the language checks that for you.

The rules for `unsafe.Pointer`, from the package documentation, allow a small set of patterns, for example converting `*T1` to `*T2` when the memory layouts are compatible, or doing pointer arithmetic with `uintptr` **within a single expression**. Anything else is invalid even if it seems to work. Two consequences you saw in this module:

- Never store a `uintptr` and convert it back later: the object may have moved (stacks, lesson 11.2) or been freed.
- Invalid `unsafe` code can break when the compiler improves. Go 1.25's release notes warn that allocating more slices on the stack can expose incorrect `unsafe.Pointer` use that previously appeared to work.

`go vet` checks some misuses (its `unsafeptr` check), and `-gcflags=all=-d=checkptr` (enabled automatically by `-race`) checks others at run time.

## Common mistakes

### Padding-heavy structs held by the million

Order large-alignment fields first in types you store in bulk.

### Per-goroutine counters packed into one array

`counts [8]int64` written by 8 goroutines puts them all in one or two cache lines. Pad each element, or let each goroutine accumulate locally and combine at the end (usually best).

### unsafe for convenience

If you reach for `unsafe` to avoid a copy, first measure that the copy matters. It usually does not.

- Fields are laid out in declaration order with padding for alignment; largest-alignment-first ordering minimizes size.
- Strings are 16 bytes, slices 24, interfaces 16; maps, channels and functions are pointers; `struct{}` is free.

- [fieldalignment analyzer](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/fieldalignment)

every type has a size and an alignment. a value's address must be a multiple of its alignment, because cpus read aligned data most efficiently (and some cannot read misaligned data at all). on 64-bit platforms:

| type | size | alignment |
|---|---|---|
| bool, int8, uint8 | 1 | 1 |
| int16 | 2 | 2 |
| int32, float32, rune | 4 | 4 |
| int64, float64, int, uintptr, pointers | 8 | 8 |
| string | 16 | 8 |
| slice | 24 | 8 |
| interface | 16 | 8 |
| struct{} | 0 | 1 |

a struct's fields are laid out in the order you declare them. the compiler inserts padding before a field to align it, and at the end so the struct's size is a multiple of its alignment (so arrays of it stay aligned). the unsafe package shows the result:

the fieldalignment analyzer finds such structs for you:

two goroutines each increment their own counter a million times:

lessons.title: 11.5 Interfaces and method dispatch under the hood
lessons.description: What an interface value is in memory, how itabs make method calls and type assertions work, why a typed nil is not nil, and what interface and generic calls cost compared with direct calls, measured.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The two-word layout of interface values, and what each word holds
- How **itabs** implement method calls and type assertions
- Why an interface holding a nil pointer is not nil, at the machine level
- The measured cost of interface calls and generic calls versus direct calls
- When that cost matters, and when it does not

## Two words

An interface value is two machine words, 16 bytes on 64-bit systems (lesson 11.4):

```text
any (empty interface)            Shape (interface with methods)
┌──────────────┐                 ┌──────────────┐
│ type  ───────┼──► type info    │ itab ────────┼──► itab: interface type, concrete type,
├──────────────┤                 ├──────────────┤          method table [Area → Square.Area]
│ data  ───────┼──► the value    │ data ────────┼──► the value
└──────────────┘                 └──────────────┘
```

- An **empty interface** (`any`) holds a pointer to the dynamic type's runtime type information, and a data pointer.
- A **non-empty interface** holds a pointer to an **itab** ("interface table") instead. The itab pairs one interface type with one concrete type, and contains the concrete type's method addresses in the order the interface lists them.

The **data word** points to the value. If the value is itself a pointer (or pointer-shaped, such as a map or channel), the pointer is stored directly. Other values are stored somewhere else and the data word points to them; that "somewhere" is a heap allocation unless the compiler can avoid it (the cases you measured in lesson 10.4: small integers, constants, zero-sized values and non-escaping interfaces).

You can peek at the two words with `unsafe`. This is for learning only: the layout is an internal detail.



```gopath-example
example-312
```





```gopath-example
example-313
```



Two `*int` values in interfaces share the same type word, a string has a different one, and for a pointer the data word is the pointer itself.

## How method calls work



```gopath-example
example-314
```



When you call `s.Area()` on a `Shape`, the compiled code:

1. loads the itab pointer from the interface's first word,
2. loads the address of `Area` from the itab's method table,
3. makes an **indirect call** to that address, passing the data word as the receiver.

Itabs are computed the first time a given (interface, concrete type) pair is needed, and cached in a global table. For conversions the compiler can see at compile time, such as `var s Shape = Square{}`, the itab is built statically and there is no lookup at all.

**Type assertions** use the same information:

- `v.(Square)`, asserting to a concrete type: compare the type or itab word with `Square`'s. One comparison: very cheap.
- `v.(Stringer)`, asserting to an interface: find or build the itab for `(Stringer, dynamic type)`, which needs a cache lookup. Still fast, but more work.
- A **type switch** is a sequence of these checks, optimized by the compiler.

## Why a typed nil is not nil

The `Example_typedNil` output above, `false true`, comes straight from the layout. An interface is nil only when **both** words are nil. Storing a nil `*Square` sets the type (or itab) word to `*Square` and the data word to nil, so the interface is not nil, even though calling a method on it may then dereference a nil pointer. This is the mechanism behind the nil interface trap from lesson 4.4, and the "nil error that is not nil" bug from Module 5: a function returning a nil `*MyError` as an `error`.

## What dispatch costs

Three ways to sum the areas of 1024 shapes:



```gopath-example
example-315
```





```gopath-example
example-316
```



Results on the 2-core test VM with Go 1.27 (`benchstat -col /call`, 6 runs):

```text
           │   direct    │     generic      │    interface     │  generic-iface   │
           │   sec/op    │ sec/op  vs base  │ sec/op  vs base  │ sec/op  vs base  │
Dispatch-2   627.7n ± 4%   2688.0n  +328%     2683.5n  +328%     3400.5n  +442%
```

Per element, that is about **0.6 ns** for the direct call against about **2.6 ns** through the interface. The difference is not only the indirect call: the direct call is **inlined**, so the loop becomes a few multiply and add instructions the CPU can pipeline, while an indirect call can never be inlined.

The generic version is as slow as the interface version, which surprises many people. Go compiles generic functions by **GC shape stenciling**: one compiled copy per "shape" of type argument, plus a **dictionary** that describes the actual type. Calling a method on a type parameter goes through the dictionary, an indirect call much like an interface call. Instantiated with an interface type (`generic-iface`), it pays for the dictionary and then the itab.

How to read these numbers:

- **2 ns per call does not matter** for code that does real work per call: an HTTP handler, a database query, a log line. Use interfaces freely for design: testing seams, plug-in points, the standard library's `io.Reader` and `io.Writer`.
- In **tight inner loops over many small items**, prefer concrete types, or check the profile. Generics are a tool for writing code once, not a performance optimization.
- **PGO** (lesson 10.5) helps exactly here: when the profile shows one concrete type dominates a call site, the compiler adds a direct, inlinable call for it (devirtualization).

## Common mistakes

### Returning a typed nil as an interface

Return a literal `nil` for "no error", not a nil pointer of a concrete type.

### Choosing generics for speed

They are about as fast as interfaces for method calls. Measure if it matters.

### Avoiding interfaces everywhere "for performance"

Nanoseconds per call are irrelevant outside hot loops, and interfaces make code testable.

## Key takeaways

- Interfaces are two words: type (or itab) and data. Non-pointer values are stored indirectly, sometimes with an allocation.
- An itab holds the method table for one (interface, concrete type) pair; method calls are indirect calls through it and cannot be inlined.
- An interface is nil only if both words are nil.
- Measured: about 0.6 ns per direct, inlined call against about 2.6 ns per interface or generic method call.
- Use interfaces for design; optimize only hot loops, with concrete types or PGO.

## Further reading

- [Go Data Structures: Interfaces](https://research.swtch.com/interfaces) by Russ Cox (from 2009; the itab idea is unchanged)
- [Generics implementation: GC shape stenciling](https://github.com/golang/proposal/blob/master/design/generics-implementation-gcshape.md)

lessons.title: 11.6 Slices and maps under the hood
lessons.description: How append grows slices (and why the exact steps change between Go versions), how Go 1.24's Swiss table maps work, and why maps never give memory back, with measurements.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How `append` chooses a new capacity, and why you should not rely on the exact numbers
- How the compiler can keep small slices on the stack (Go 1.25 and 1.26)
- How Go's maps work since Go 1.24: **Swiss tables**
- Why deleting from a map does not free memory, and what to do about it

## How slices grow

A slice is a pointer, a length and a capacity (lessons 3.2 and 11.4). When `append` needs more room than the capacity, the runtime allocates a bigger backing array, copies the elements, and returns a slice pointing to the new array. The rule for the new capacity, from the runtime's `nextslicecap` function:

- If you append many elements at once and need more than double, you get what you need.
- Below 256 elements, the capacity **doubles**.
- From 256 up, it grows by `(cap + 768) / 4` each step: a smooth transition from 2x toward **1.25x** for large slices.
- The result is then **rounded up** to one of the memory allocator's size classes, so no allocated memory is wasted.

Growing geometrically makes `append` **amortized O(1)**: each element is copied only a constant number of times on average.

This code records every capacity a slice passes through:



```gopath-example
example-317
```





```gopath-example
example-318
```



Here is the interesting part. The same test on the same machine with two Go versions:

```text
Go 1.24   heap slice:  [1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 256 512]
          local slice: [1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 256 512]

Go 1.27   heap slice:  [1 2 3 4 8 16 32 64 128 256 512]
          local slice: [4 8 16 32 64 128 256 512]
```

and for large slices (both versions): `512 848 1280 1792 2560 3408 5120 7168 9216 ...`, where you can see the growth factor fall from 2 toward 1.25, and the rounding to size classes.

Two things changed between versions:

- In the **local** slice, which never leaves its function, Go 1.27 starts with capacity 4. Go 1.25 and 1.26 taught the compiler to give such slices a small backing store **on the stack** (here 32 bytes, 4 ints) for their first appends, so short slices never touch the heap.
- Even the heap slice gets a different small-capacity sequence, a result of allocator and runtime changes.

The lesson: **the growth sequence is an implementation detail.** Code must never depend on `cap` after `append`. If you know the final size, preallocate with `make([]T, 0, n)`, which is faster than any growth policy and does not change between versions.

## How maps work: Swiss tables

Go 1.24 replaced the map implementation with one based on **Swiss tables**, a design created at Google for C++ (in the Abseil library). It was one of the changes the Go 1.24 release notes credit for a 2 to 3% average reduction in CPU overhead across representative benchmarks, and its higher load factor lowers memory use. Map behavior did not change; only speed and memory did.

The core ideas:

- Slots are organized in **groups of 8**. Each group has an 8-byte **control word**, one byte per slot. A control byte says the slot is empty, deleted, or in use; for slots in use, it holds **7 bits of the key's hash** (called H2).
- A lookup hashes the key. The other 57 bits (H1) choose the group where the search starts. Then it compares H2 with **all 8 control bytes at once** (with SIMD instructions on amd64, or a bit trick elsewhere). Only slots whose 7 bits match need a full key comparison, and a false match happens in about 1 slot in 128.
- If the group has no match but has an empty slot, the key is not in the map. Otherwise the search moves to the next group in a probe sequence.
- A table is filled to at most **7/8** before it grows, which keeps lookups short while wasting little memory.

Go adds one twist to the original design. Growing a hash table means rehashing everything, which would make a single insert into a huge map pause for a long time. So a Go map is split into **tables of at most 1024 slots**, selected by the top bits of the hash through a directory ("extendible hashing"). When a table fills, only that table grows or splits in two, so no single insert does more than a bounded amount of work.

The old design (before Go 1.24) used buckets of 8 entries with overflow buckets chained on, and moved entries to a doubled bucket array incrementally. The Swiss table opt-out (`GOEXPERIMENT=noswissmap`) existed in Go 1.24 and has since been removed; Go 1.27 rejects it.

## Maps never shrink



```gopath-example
example-319
```



On Go 1.24 and Go 1.27 alike:

```text
full: 20 MiB, deleted every key: 20 MiB, after clear: 20 MiB, replaced the map: 0 MiB
```

Deleting every key, or calling `clear(m)`, empties the map but keeps all its tables, ready to be reused. That is usually what you want: a map that was big once will likely be big again. But a long-lived map that grew during a traffic spike, a cache, a registry of connections, keeps its peak size forever.

The fix is to **replace** the map: make a new map sized for the current contents (`make(map[K]V, len(old))`), copy the live entries into it with a loop, and drop the old one, for example when its length falls far below its peak. The old tables become garbage and the GC frees them.

The same applies to slices: `s = s[:0]` keeps the backing array. To release a big backing array, set the slice to `nil` or copy the elements you need into a new, smaller slice (`slices.Clip` only trims the capacity in the slice header; it does not free memory).

## Common mistakes

### Depending on capacity after append

The sequence changes between Go versions, as measured above. Preallocate when you know the size.

### Expecting delete or clear to free memory

They do not. Replace long-lived maps that shrank a lot.

### Assuming map iteration order

It is deliberately randomized and was never specified. Sort the keys (lesson 3.4) when order matters.

## Key takeaways

- `append` doubles small slices and grows large ones toward 1.25x, rounded to allocator size classes; the exact steps are not part of the language and do change.
- Since Go 1.25 and 1.26, small slices that do not escape can start on the stack.
- Go 1.24 maps are Swiss tables: groups of 8 slots with a control word of 7-bit hash fragments, a 7/8 load limit, and tables of at most 1024 slots that grow independently.
- Maps and slices never give memory back on their own; replace them to release it.

## Further reading

- [Faster Go maps with Swiss Tables](https://go.dev/blog/swisstable) by Michael Pratt, on the Go blog
- [Go Slices: usage and internals](https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro)
- [Arrays, slices (and strings): The mechanics of 'append'](https://go.dev/blog/slices)

the old design (before go 1.24) used buckets of 8 entries with overflow buckets chained on, and moved entries to a doubled bucket array incrementally. the swiss table opt-out (goexperiment=noswissmap) existed in go 1.24 and has since been removed; go 1.27 rejects it.

 maps never shrink







on go 1.24 and go 1.27 alike:



deleting every key, or calling clear(m), empties the map but keeps all its tables, ready to be reused. that is usually what you want: a map that was big once will likely be big again. but a long-lived map that grew during a traffic spike, a cache, a registry of connections, keeps its peak size forever.

the fix is to replace the map: make a new map sized for the current contents (make(map[k]v, len(old))), copy the live entries into it with a loop, and drop the old one, for example when its length falls far below its peak. the old tables become garbage and the gc frees them.

the same applies to slices: s = s[:0] keeps the backing array. to release a big backing array, set the slice to nil or copy the elements you need into a new, smaller slice (slices.clip only trims the capacity in the slice header; it does not free memory).

 common mistakes

 depending on capacity after append

the sequence changes between go versions, as measured above. preallocate when you know the size.

 expecting delete or clear to free memory

they do not. replace long-lived maps that shrank a lot.

 assuming map iteration order

it is deliberately randomized and was never specified. sort the keys (lesson 3.4) when order matters.

 key takeaways

- append doubles small slices and grows large ones toward 1.25x, rounded to allocator size classes; the exact steps are not part of the language and do change.
- since go 1.25 and 1.26, small slices that do not escape can start on the stack.
- go 1.24 maps are swiss tables: groups of 8 slots with a control word of 7-bit hash fragments, a 7/8 load limit, and tables of at most 1024 slots that grow independently.
- maps and slices never give memory back on their own; replace them to release it.

 further reading

- [faster go maps with swiss tables](https://go.dev/blog/swisstable) by michael pratt, on the go blog
- [go slices: usage and internals](https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro)
- [arrays, slices (and strings): the mechanics of 'append'](https://go.dev/blog/slices)

lessons.title: 11.7 Exercise: shrink a struct
lessons.description: Apply what you learned about alignment and padding: reorder a struct's fields to save 25% of its memory, checked by unsafe.Sizeof.
lessons.body:
## The task



```gopath-exercise
m11/layout
```



```bash
cd exercises
go test ./m11/layout     # TestSize fails: 64 bytes
```

## Work it out on paper first

Before moving any field, write down each field's size and alignment (the table in lesson 11.4), then answer:

1. How many bytes of data does `Event` hold, ignoring padding?
2. What is the struct's alignment? (The largest alignment of any field.)
3. The size must be a multiple of the alignment. What is the smallest possible size?



```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-3
```





```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-4
```



The reference solution, with offsets in comments, is in `exercises/m11/layout/solution.go`.

## Going further

- Run the `fieldalignment` analyzer from lesson 11.4 on the starter and compare its suggestion with yours.
- Write a benchmark that allocates a `[]Event` of one million elements with each layout, and compare `B/op`.

## Part 3, second half: recap

You now know what happens underneath your code: how goroutines are scheduled onto threads and why `GOMAXPROCS` matters in containers, how stacks grow and move, how the garbage collector works and how `GOGC` and `GOMEMLIMIT` steer it, how values are laid out in memory, what interface and generic calls cost, and how slices and maps grow and hold on to memory.

Next is **Part 4: Production Go**, starting with **[Module 12: Building HTTP services](/learn/12-http-services/)**, where all of this comes together in real services.

lessons.title: 12.1 net/http and ServeMux routing
lessons.description: How a Go HTTP server is put together (Handler, ServeMux, Server), and the routing patterns of Go 1.22's ServeMux: methods, wildcards, exact matches, precedence and conflicts.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The three building blocks of a Go HTTP server: `Handler`, `ServeMux` and `Server`
- Routing patterns: methods, `{wildcards}`, `{rest...}`, `{$}` and subtrees
- How ServeMux chooses between overlapping patterns, and when it refuses
- Automatic `405 Method Not Allowed` and `HEAD` handling
- How to test handlers without opening a port

## The building blocks

Everything in `net/http` server code is built on one interface:

```go
type Handler interface {
	ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, *Request)
}
```

A handler receives the request and writes the response. `http.HandlerFunc` turns an ordinary function with that signature into a `Handler`, which is why most code just writes functions.

A **`ServeMux`** is a handler that dispatches to other handlers based on the request's method, host and path: a router. An **`http.Server`** listens on a port, parses HTTP, and calls one handler (usually a ServeMux) for each request, **each in its own goroutine**. That last point matters: handlers run concurrently, so any state they share needs synchronization (Module 6).

```go
mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.HandleFunc("GET /hello", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	fmt.Fprintln(w, "hello")
})
srv := &http.Server{Addr: ":8080", Handler: mux} // timeouts: lesson 12.6
log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServe())
```

You will see `http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux)` in tutorials. It creates a `Server` with **no timeouts**, which is fine for experiments but not for anything exposed to a network (lesson 12.6).

## Routing patterns (Go 1.22)

Before Go 1.22, ServeMux matched only path prefixes, and every project reached for a third party router to get methods and path parameters. Go 1.22 added both. A pattern has the form:

```text
[METHOD ][HOST]/[PATH]
```

This mux uses every kind of pattern:



```gopath-example
example-320
```



And this is what it does with a set of requests:



```gopath-example
example-321
```



Reading the results line by line:

- **`GET /{$}`** matches only `/`. A pattern ending in a slash matches a whole subtree, so a plain `"/"` would match every path. That surprises everyone once; `{$}` means "end of path".
- **`/nope`** matches nothing: 404, with ServeMux's default body.
- **`{id}`** matches one path segment. `r.PathValue("id")` returns it, already unescaped.
- **`/items/new`** goes to its own handler even though `/items/{id}` also matches. See precedence below.
- **`DELETE /items`**: the path exists, but only for `POST`. ServeMux answers `405 Method Not Allowed` with an `Allow` header listing the methods that would work. You get this for free by putting methods in your patterns.
- **`{path...}`** at the end matches all remaining segments, slashes included: `docs/a/b.txt`.
- **`/static/`**, with no method, matches any method and everything under `/static/`.

Two more details: a `GET` pattern also matches `HEAD` requests (the server then discards the body), and a pattern can start with a host, `"api.example.com/"`, to route by the `Host` header.

## Precedence and conflicts

When several patterns match a request, the **most specific** one wins. A pattern is more specific than another if it matches a strict subset of its requests. `/items/new` matches only one path, `/items/{id}` matches many, so `/items/new` wins. Registration order never matters.

But two patterns can overlap without either being more specific:



```gopath-example
example-322
```



`/posts/{id}` and `/{resource}/latest` both match `/posts/latest`, and neither is a subset of the other. Rather than guess, ServeMux **panics at registration** with a clear explanation:

```text
panic: pattern "GET /{resource}/latest" (registered at .../main.go:8) conflicts with pattern "GET /posts/{id}" (registered at .../main.go:7):
	GET /{resource}/latest and GET /posts/{id} both match some paths, like "/posts/latest".
	But neither is more specific than the other.
```

Panicking at start-up is a feature: an ambiguous route table fails the first test run, not a request in production.

## Testing handlers

`net/http/httptest` lets you call a handler directly, with no network:

```go
rec := httptest.NewRecorder()                                      // a ResponseWriter that records
mux.ServeHTTP(rec, httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/items/42", nil))   // a ready-made *Request
fmt.Println(rec.Code, rec.Body.String())                           // 200 item 42
```

Every example in this module is tested this way. For tests that need a real network connection (timeouts, TLS, a client under test), `httptest.NewServer` starts a server on a free local port; lesson 12.6 uses one.

## Do you need a framework?

For most JSON APIs, no. ServeMux now covers methods, path parameters and precedence; middleware is a plain function (lesson 12.2); JSON is `encoding/json` (lesson 12.3). Routers such as chi build on the same `http.Handler` interface, so moving between them is cheap. Frameworks that use their own handler and context types (Gin, Echo, Fiber) offer conveniences, but tie your code to their APIs. Start with the standard library and add a dependency when you can name what it gives you.

## Common mistakes

### Registering "/" for the home page

It matches every unknown path, which then returns your home page with 200 instead of 404. Use `"GET /{$}"`.

### Using http.ListenAndServe in production

It has no timeouts. Build an `http.Server` (lesson 12.6).

### Sharing state between handlers without locking

Each request runs in its own goroutine. Run your tests with `-race`.

### Using the DefaultServeMux

`http.HandleFunc` without a mux registers on a global ServeMux that any imported package can also register on (`net/http/pprof` does). Create your own with `http.NewServeMux()`.

## Key takeaways

- A `Handler` serves one request; a `ServeMux` routes to handlers; an `http.Server` runs each request in its own goroutine.
- Patterns: `"METHOD /path/{name}"`, `{rest...}` for the remaining path, `{$}` for an exact end, a trailing `/` for a subtree; read wildcards with `r.PathValue`.
- The most specific pattern wins regardless of order; ambiguous patterns panic at registration.
- Methods in patterns give you `405` with an `Allow` header automatically.
- Test handlers with `httptest.NewRecorder` and `httptest.NewRequest`.

## Further reading

- [Routing Enhancements for Go 1.22](https://go.dev/blog/routing-enhancements) on the Go blog
- [Package net/http: ServeMux](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#ServeMux), with the full pattern syntax and precedence rules

lessons.title: 12.2 Middleware
lessons.description: Write HTTP middleware as plain functions: chaining and ordering, capturing the status code safely, request IDs through the context, structured access logs, and panic recovery.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What middleware is in Go: a function from `http.Handler` to `http.Handler`
- How to chain middleware, and why the order matters
- How to capture the response status without breaking `Flush` and friends
- Request IDs carried through `context.Context`
- Access logs with `log/slog`, and turning panics into 500 responses

## The idea

Some behavior applies to every request: logging, metrics, authentication, request IDs, panic recovery. Instead of repeating it in each handler, you **wrap** the handler. In Go, middleware is just this:



```gopath-example
example-323
```



A middleware takes the next handler and returns a new handler that does something before and/or after calling it. No framework, no registration: plain functions.

## Order matters



```gopath-example
example-324
```



Middleware nests like function calls: `Chain(h, A, B)` is `A(B(h))`. The request passes through A, then B, then the handler; the response passes back through B, then A. Decide the order by asking what each middleware needs to see:

- **Request ID** goes outermost, so everything inside can log the ID.
- **Logging** must see the final status code, including the 500 produced when a handler panics, so it goes **outside** panic recovery.
- **Recovery** goes close to the handlers, so it catches their panics and writes a response the outer layers can observe.
- **Authentication** and **rate limiting** go before the expensive work, often only on some routes.

## Capturing the status code

`http.ResponseWriter` does not tell you which status a handler wrote. To log it, wrap the writer:



```gopath-example
example-325
```



Three details make this wrapper correct:

- If a handler calls `Write` without `WriteHeader`, the status is **200**. The wrapper records that.
- Only the **first** `WriteHeader` counts, like in net/http (a second call is ignored, with a log message).
- **`Unwrap`**. Handlers sometimes need features of the underlying writer: flushing a streaming response, setting per-request deadlines, hijacking for WebSockets. The modern way is `http.NewResponseController(w)`, which calls `Unwrap` to find the original writer through any number of wrappers. Without `Unwrap`, your middleware would silently break streaming. The test `TestResponseControllerThroughRecorder` proves it works.

## Request IDs and the context

A request ID ties together every log line about one request, across services. The middleware reuses a sane incoming `X-Request-ID` (set by a load balancer or calling service) or creates one, and stores it in the request's **context** (lesson 7.1):



```gopath-example
example-326
```



Notes:

- The context key is an unexported type (`requestIDKey{}`), so no other package can collide with it or read it except through `RequestIDFrom`.
- `r.WithContext` returns a **new** request; the middleware passes that one on.
- Incoming IDs are **validated**: a client controls this header, and writing raw client input to logs invites log injection (fake log lines via newlines) and enormous values.
- Request-scoped values like this are what the context's values are for. Do not use the context to pass optional function parameters.

## Access logs with slog



```gopath-example
example-327
```



One structured line per request, written **after** the handler returns, so it has the status and duration. `r.Pattern` (Go 1.23) is the ServeMux pattern that matched, such as `GET /hello/{name}`: much better for grouping than the raw path, which contains IDs. It is set by the ServeMux on the request it receives, so the logging middleware sees it as long as it passes the same `*Request` down; middleware that calls `r.WithContext` creates a new request, and must sit outside logging, as `RequestID` does here. `LogAttrs` with typed attributes avoids allocations in this hot path (lesson 8.4).

## Recovering from panics

`net/http` already recovers panics in handlers: it logs the stack trace and **closes the connection**, so the client sees a network error rather than a response. A recovery middleware does better: it logs through your structured logger, with the request ID, and sends a proper 500.



```gopath-example
example-328
```



`http.ErrAbortHandler` is a special panic value that handlers use to abort a response deliberately; it is re-panicked so net/http handles it as intended.

Putting it all together, with time and duration removed so the output is stable:



```gopath-example
example-329
```



The panicking request produces an error log line with the panic value (and, in real use, the stack), then an access log line showing status 500. Both carry the request ID.

## Middleware for specific routes

Middleware does not have to wrap the whole mux. Wrap individual handlers when only some routes need it:

```go
mux.Handle("POST /api/links", rateLimit(http.HandlerFunc(createLink)))
mux.Handle("GET /healthz", http.HandlerFunc(healthz)) // never rate limited
```

The shortener (lesson 12.8) does exactly this.

## Common mistakes

### Wrapping the writer without Unwrap

Streaming, `Flush` and deadlines stop working through your middleware. Add `Unwrap() http.ResponseWriter`.

### Logging inside recovery instead of outside

The access log then misses every panicking request. Order: logging outside, recovery inside.

### Trusting client headers in logs

Validate or sanitize request IDs and anything else from the client before logging it.

### Doing work after writing the response in the handler

The client is already waiting for the connection to finish; heavy work after the response delays it and runs without a deadline. Hand it to a background worker (Module 13).

## Key takeaways

- Middleware is `func(http.Handler) http.Handler`; chain it with plain function calls, first is outermost.
- Order by need: request ID outermost, logging outside recovery, route-specific middleware on individual handlers.
- Wrap `ResponseWriter` to capture the status; record 200 for bare writes and implement `Unwrap`.
- Store request-scoped values like request IDs in the context, with an unexported key type.
- Log with `r.Pattern` for the route, and recover panics into logged 500 responses.

## Further reading

- [Package net/http: ResponseController](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#ResponseController)
- [Package log/slog](https://pkg.go.dev/log/slog)

lessons.title: 12.3 Request validation and JSON APIs
lessons.description: Decode request bodies strictly and safely, validate business rules separately, choose the right status codes, and return errors as RFC 9457 problem details, with every failure path tested.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How to decode JSON request bodies safely: size limits, unknown fields, trailing data
- Turning decoding errors into helpful client messages
- Separating **decoding** from **validation**
- Which status codes to use: 400, 413, 415, 422 and friends
- Returning errors in the standard **problem details** format (RFC 9457)

## The idea

A JSON endpoint does three distinct things with a request body, and each can fail differently:

1. **Read** it: is it JSON, is it too big? → `415`, `413`
2. **Decode** it into a Go struct: is it well-formed, are the types right, are there unknown fields? → `400`
3. **Validate** it against business rules: is the email an email, is the age plausible? → `422`

Keeping these separate keeps handlers short and error messages precise.

## Decoding safely

`json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&v)` is how most tutorials decode. It has four problems in a public API: no size limit (a client can send gigabytes), unknown fields are silently ignored (a typo like `"emial"` is accepted and dropped), anything after the first value is ignored, and its error messages are not meant for clients. This helper fixes all four:



```gopath-example
example-330
```



- `mime.ParseMediaType` accepts `application/json; charset=utf-8` as well as the plain form.
- `http.MaxBytesReader` fails the read after `maxBytes`, and tells the server to close the connection rather than read the rest.
- `DisallowUnknownFields` rejects fields the struct does not have.
- The second `Decode` must hit `io.EOF`: the body holds exactly one JSON value.
- `decodeError` maps errors to messages a client can act on. It checks error **types** (`*json.SyntaxError`, `*json.UnmarshalTypeError`, `*http.MaxBytesError`) with `errors.As`, never message text.

That last rule matters more than ever: since Go 1.27, `encoding/json` is implemented on top of `encoding/json/v2` (lesson 8.2), and the wording of some error messages differs between versions. The example's test for unknown fields checks only the status and that the field name appears, so it passes on Go 1.24 and Go 1.27 alike.

## Validation is separate



```gopath-example
example-331
```



`Validate` is a method on the request type, returning one message per field. Nothing in it knows about HTTP, so it is easy to unit test, and the handler stays a straight line: decode, validate, act, respond. Validation libraries using struct tags exist, but for most services plain Go is clearer and checked by the compiler.

The response type `User` is a **different type** from the request type `CreateUser`. Separate types for input and output let them evolve independently and make it impossible to accidentally accept fields clients should not set (like `id`). Note `omitzero` (Go 1.24) on `Age`, which omits the field when it is zero.

## Problem details

For errors, use the standard format from **RFC 9457**, "Problem Details for HTTP APIs": a JSON object served as `application/problem+json` with `title`, `status` and an optional `detail`, extensible with your own members:



```gopath-example
example-332
```



Clients and API gateways recognize the format, and every error from your API has the same shape.

## Every path, tested



```gopath-example
example-333
```



Each line is one request and its exact response. Note:

- A successful create returns **201 Created** with a `Location` header pointing at the new resource.
- The missing `age` in the second request is valid and omitted from the response.
- Validation reports **all** field errors at once, so a client can fix everything in one round trip. (Map keys are sorted in JSON output, so the output is stable.)
- A string where a number belongs is a **decoding** error (400), not a validation error.
- Two JSON objects in one body are rejected.
- The wrong `Content-Type` gets **415 Unsupported Media Type**.

## Choosing status codes

| Code | Use it when |
|---|---|
| 200 OK | a successful read or update that returns a body |
| 201 Created | a resource was created; set `Location` |
| 204 No Content | success with no body, typically DELETE |
| 400 Bad Request | the request is malformed: not JSON, wrong types, unknown fields |
| 401 Unauthorized | no or invalid credentials |
| 403 Forbidden | valid credentials, but not allowed |
| 404 Not Found | the resource does not exist |
| 405 Method Not Allowed | ServeMux sends it for you |
| 409 Conflict | the request conflicts with current state, such as a duplicate key |
| 413 Content Too Large | the body is over your limit |
| 415 Unsupported Media Type | wrong `Content-Type` |
| 422 Unprocessable Content | well-formed, but fails validation |
| 429 Too Many Requests | rate limited; set `Retry-After` |
| 500 Internal Server Error | a bug or a failed dependency; never show internal details |
| 503 Service Unavailable | temporarily unable, for example during shutdown |

Some teams use 400 for validation errors too. Either is defensible; be consistent and document it.

## Common mistakes

### Decoding without a size limit

One request can exhaust memory. Always use `http.MaxBytesReader` (or `http.MaxBytesHandler` for the whole server, lesson 12.6).

### Matching error strings

They change between Go versions. Use `errors.As` with the error types.

### Showing internal errors to clients

`"pq: connection refused to 10.0.3.7"` helps attackers and confuses users. Log the details; return a generic message and a request ID (lesson 12.8 does this).

### Writing headers after the body

Headers and the status must be set before the first `Write`. `WriteJSON` sets `Content-Type`, then `WriteHeader`, then writes.

## Key takeaways

- Decode strictly: check `Content-Type`, limit size, disallow unknown fields, require a single value.
- Classify decode errors by type with `errors.As`, never by message.
- Validate separately with plain Go methods that return per-field errors.
- Use distinct request and response types.
- Return errors as `application/problem+json` (RFC 9457) with accurate status codes.

## Further reading

- [RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457)
- [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110), the definitions of every status code
- [Package encoding/json](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json)

lessons.title: 12.4 Configuration and the twelve-factor app
lessons.description: Load configuration from the environment into one typed struct, validate it at start-up with every error reported at once, read secrets from files, and keep secrets out of logs.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The twelve-factor rule for configuration, and why it fits containers
- Loading config into a typed struct with defaults and validation
- Testing configuration without touching the real environment
- Reading secrets from files, as Kubernetes provides them
- Logging configuration without leaking secrets

## The idea

The **twelve-factor app** methodology (written at Heroku in 2011, and still the norm for cloud services) says: store configuration in the **environment**. The same build artifact, one container image, then runs in development, staging and production, with only environment variables differing. Kubernetes, Docker and every platform support this directly.

Configuration is anything that varies between deployments: addresses, URLs of other services, credentials, limits, log levels. It is **not** things like your route table, which belong in code.

## One struct, loaded once



```gopath-example
example-334
```



The pattern:

- **One `Config` struct** with typed fields (`time.Duration`, `*url.URL`, `slog.Level`), not strings to be parsed later all over the code.
- **Defaults** for everything that has a sensible one; only truly deployment-specific values are required.
- **Validate at start-up** and report **every** problem at once with `errors.Join`. A service with bad configuration should refuse to start with a clear message, not fail on the first request an hour later.
- **`getenv` is a parameter.** `main` passes `os.Getenv`; tests pass a map. No test ever has to modify the process environment, and tests can run in parallel.
- **Load once, pass down.** No package reads environment variables on its own; they receive what they need as constructor arguments. That keeps dependencies visible and code testable.



```gopath-example
example-335
```



## Flags or environment variables?

Both are fine and many services accept both. Command-line flags (the `flag` package, Module 14) are self-documenting (`-help`) and natural for CLIs. Environment variables are natural for services in containers, where the platform sets them from manifests. A common approach: environment variables for services, flags for tools, and if you support both, flags win.

Avoid configuration **files** for the basics. They have to be built into the image or mounted, and they invite a second, hidden source of truth. Mount a file when the configuration is genuinely structured and large.

## Secrets

Passwords, API keys and database URLs with credentials are configuration too, with extra rules:

- Never commit them, never bake them into images.
- Prefer reading them from **files**. Kubernetes Secrets and Docker secrets are usually mounted as files, and file contents do not show up in `env` output, process listings, or crash reports that dump the environment.

A widely used convention is a `_FILE` suffix: `DATABASE_URL_FILE=/run/secrets/db-url` means "read the value from this file":



```gopath-example
example-336
```



## Logging the configuration safely

Logging the effective configuration at start-up is very useful when debugging deployments. Implementing `slog.LogValuer` controls exactly what is printed:



```gopath-example
example-337
```



`TestSecretFromFile` logs the whole config and checks that the password does not appear. The log shows only `config.database_url_set=true`. Writing that test is cheap insurance: a careless `slog.Any("config", cfg)` in the future still cannot leak the secret.

## Common mistakes

### Reading os.Getenv deep inside packages

Configuration becomes invisible and untestable. Read once in `main`, pass values down.

### Failing on the first error

Operators then fix one variable per deploy. Collect all errors with `errors.Join`.

### Secrets in environment variables printed at start-up

Redact with `LogValuer`, and prefer files.

### Silent defaults for required settings

A default `BASE_URL` of `localhost` in production produces wrong links quietly. Make settings that differ in every environment required, or at least log them at start-up.

## Key takeaways

- Store configuration in the environment; one image runs everywhere.
- Load into one typed struct with defaults; validate at start-up and report all errors at once.
- Inject `getenv` so tests use a map.
- Read secrets from files where possible (`NAME_FILE`), and redact them in logs with `slog.LogValuer`.

## Further reading

- [The Twelve-Factor App: Config](https://12factor.net/config)
- [Kubernetes: Secrets](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/)
