lessons.title: 12.5 Observability: logs, metrics and traces
lessons.description: The three signals of observability for a Go service: structured logs with slog, RED metrics with the Prometheus client, and distributed traces with OpenTelemetry, plus health checks and runtime metrics.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The three signals, **logs**, **metrics** and **traces**, and what each is for
- Structured logs that machines can query
- RED metrics with the Prometheus client, and the cardinality trap
- Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry: spans, context propagation, `traceparent`
- Liveness and readiness endpoints, and runtime metrics

## The three signals

When a service misbehaves in production, you cannot attach a debugger. You can only look at what it emits:

| Signal | Answers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Metrics** | Is something wrong? How much, since when? | 2% of `POST /api/links` returned 500 in the last 5 minutes; p99 latency doubled at 14:02 |
| **Logs** | What exactly happened in this case? | `request failed error="connection refused" request_id=a1b2...` |
| **Traces** | Where did the time go across services? | the request spent 1.8 s of its 2 s waiting on the database |

Metrics are cheap aggregates you alert on. Logs are detailed records of events. Traces follow one request through several services. A request ID, or better a **trace ID** present in all three, connects them.

## Logs: structured, one event per line

Lesson 8.4 introduced `log/slog`, and lesson 12.2 built the access log. For production:

- Use the **JSON handler**. Log platforms (Loki, Elasticsearch, CloudWatch) index the fields, so you can query `status >= 500 AND route = "POST /api/links"`.
- Write to **standard output**. In containers, the platform collects stdout; the twelve-factor app never manages log files.
- Log **events**, not narratives: one line per request, one per failure, with fields rather than formatted sentences.
- Choose levels deliberately: `ERROR` for failures someone should look at, `INFO` for normal events like requests and start-up, `DEBUG` for details you turn on temporarily with `LOG_LEVEL=debug`.

## Metrics with Prometheus

**Prometheus** is the standard metrics system in the Kubernetes world. Your service exposes current metric values as text at `/metrics`; Prometheus **scrapes** that endpoint every few seconds and stores the time series.

For a request-driven service, start with the **RED** metrics: **R**ate (requests per second), **E**rrors (failed requests per second), **D**uration (latency distribution). Three metrics cover all of it:



```gopath-example
example-338
```



This example uses the official client library `github.com/prometheus/client_golang`, so it lives in the `examples/thirdparty` module (the main course module has no dependencies). Run `go mod tidy` in `examples/thirdparty` once to download the dependencies. The metric types:

- **Counter**: only goes up (`http_requests_total`). Prometheus computes rates from it: `rate(http_requests_total[5m])`.
- **Gauge**: goes up and down (`http_requests_in_flight`).
- **Histogram**: counts observations in buckets (`http_request_duration_seconds`), from which Prometheus estimates percentiles: `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)`.

The test scrapes the registry like Prometheus would:



```gopath-example
example-339
```



```text
# TYPE http_requests_total counter
http_requests_total{code="200",route="GET /items/{id}"} 3
http_requests_total{code="404",route="unmatched"} 1
```

### The cardinality trap

Every distinct combination of label values is a separate time series that Prometheus stores. Labelling by the **route pattern** gives a handful of series. Labelling by the **raw path** (`/items/1`, `/items/2`, ...) creates a new series for every ID ever requested, and eventually takes down your monitoring. Never put unbounded values (IDs, user names, raw paths, error messages) in labels. Here `r.Pattern` gives the route for free, and unmatched paths share one label value.

## Traces with OpenTelemetry

A **trace** is the tree of operations performed for one request, possibly across many services. Each operation is a **span**: a name, start and end time, attributes, and a parent. **OpenTelemetry** (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for producing traces (and metrics and logs), supported by Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Honeycomb, Datadog and the cloud providers.

For a trace to cross service boundaries, the caller sends its trace context in the W3C **`traceparent`** header: `00-<trace id>-<parent span id>-<flags>`. The receiving service **extracts** it and creates its spans as children:



```gopath-example
example-340
```



The test sends a request with a `traceparent`, as an upstream service would, and inspects the recorded spans:



```gopath-example
example-341
```



```text
server span "GET /items/{id}" trace=4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736 parent=00f067aa0ba902b7 attrs=[{"http.route":"GET /items/{id}"} {"http.request.method":"GET"} {"http.response.status_code":200}]
child span "load item" parent=c251016ee117c350
```

The server span joined the caller's trace (same trace ID, the caller's span as parent), and the span the handler started from `r.Context()` became its child. That is the whole mechanism: **pass the context**, and spans nest correctly.

In real services:

- The **OTel SDK** is configured once in `main` with an **exporter** that sends spans to a collector (usually OTLP over gRPC or HTTP), and a **sampler** so you do not record every request at high traffic.
- You rarely write the HTTP middleware yourself. The contrib package `go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/instrumentation/net/http/otelhttp` provides server middleware and a client transport that injects `traceparent` into outgoing requests. Most database drivers and RPC libraries have OTel instrumentation too. The middleware in this lesson exists to show what those packages do.
- Use the attribute names from the OTel **semantic conventions** (`http.route`, `http.response.status_code`, as above), available as constants in `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv`, so dashboards work across services.
- Put the trace ID into your log lines, and logs and traces link up.

## Health checks

Orchestrators need to ask two questions, which deserve separate endpoints:

- **Liveness** (`/healthz`): is the process alive, or stuck and in need of a restart? Keep it trivial. Do **not** check dependencies here: if the database is down, restarting every instance of your service makes things worse.
- **Readiness** (`/readyz`): should this instance receive traffic right now? Report not ready during start-up and **during shutdown** (lesson 12.8), and optionally when a critical dependency is unreachable.

Module 15 wires these into Kubernetes probes.

## Runtime metrics

The Prometheus client's Go collector exports the runtime's own metrics (from `runtime/metrics`, lesson 11.1): goroutine count, GC cycles and pause times, heap size, GOMAXPROCS. Register it and you can graph exactly the things Module 11 explained:

```go
reg := prometheus.NewRegistry()
reg.MustRegister(collectors.NewGoCollector(), collectors.NewProcessCollector(collectors.ProcessCollectorOpts{}))
```

A steadily growing `go_goroutines` is a goroutine leak (lesson 7.6); a growing heap after GC is a memory leak; frequent GC cycles point to allocation churn (lesson 10.4).

## Where to expose it

Metrics, pprof (lesson 10.2) and similar endpoints reveal internals. Serve them on a **separate port** (an "admin" port) that is reachable by Prometheus inside the cluster but never routed publicly. The shortener listens on `:8080` for the API and `:9090` for admin.

## Common mistakes

### Unbounded label values

One label with user IDs can create millions of series. Use route patterns and status codes.

### Logging instead of counting

Counting errors by grepping logs is slow and expensive. Emit a metric and alert on it; use logs for the details.

### Liveness checks that test dependencies

A database outage then becomes a restart storm.

### Breaking the context chain

A handler that starts work with `context.Background()` instead of `r.Context()` starts a new, disconnected trace, and loses cancellation too.

## Key takeaways

- Metrics tell you something is wrong, logs tell you what happened, traces tell you where time went.
- Log structured JSON to stdout, one event per line, with a request or trace ID.
- Expose RED metrics with the Prometheus client, labelled by route pattern and status, never by raw path.
- OpenTelemetry traces cross services via the `traceparent` header; pass `r.Context()` and spans nest.
- Separate liveness from readiness, and serve metrics and pprof on an internal admin port.

## Further reading

- [Prometheus: instrumenting a Go application](https://prometheus.io/docs/guides/go-application/)
- [OpenTelemetry Go documentation](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/go/)
- [W3C Trace Context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/)

prometheus is the standard metrics system in the kubernetes world. your service exposes current metric values as text at /metrics; prometheus scrapes that endpoint every few seconds and stores the time series.

for a request-driven service, start with the red metrics: rate (requests per second), errors (failed requests per second), duration (latency distribution). three metrics cover all of it:







this example uses the official client library github.com/prometheus/clientgolang, so it lives in the examples/thirdparty module (the main course module has no dependencies). run go mod tidy in examples/thirdparty once to download the dependencies. the metric types:

- counter: only goes up (httprequeststotal). prometheus computes rates from it: rate(httprequeststotal[5m]).
- gauge: goes up and down (httprequestsinflight).
- histogram: counts observations in buckets (httprequestdurationseconds), from which prometheus estimates percentiles: histogramquantile(0.99, ...).

the test scrapes the registry like prometheus would:









 the cardinality trap

every distinct combination of label values is a separate time series that prometheus stores. labelling by the route pattern gives a handful of series. labelling by the raw path (/items/1, /items/2, ...) creates a new series for every id ever requested, and eventually takes down your monitoring. never put unbounded values (ids, user names, raw paths, error messages) in labels. here r.pattern gives the route for free, and unmatched paths share one label value.

 traces with opentelemetry

a trace is the tree of operations performed for one request, possibly across many services. each operation is a span: a name, start and end time, attributes, and a parent. opentelemetry (otel) is the vendor-neutral standard for producing traces (and metrics and logs), supported by jaeger, grafana tempo, honeycomb, datadog and the cloud providers.

for a trace to cross service boundaries, the caller sends its trace context in the w3c traceparent header: 00-<trace id>-<parent span id>-<flags>. the receiving service extracts it and creates its spans as children:







the test sends a request with a traceparent, as an upstream service would, and inspects the recorded spans:









the server span joined the caller's trace (same trace id, the caller's span as parent), and the span the handler started from r.context() became its child. that is the whole mechanism: pass the context, and spans nest correctly.

in real services:

- the otel sdk is configured once in main with an exporter that sends spans to a collector (usually otlp over grpc or http), and a sampler so you do not record every request at high traffic.
- you rarely write the http middleware yourself. the contrib package go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/instrumentation/net/http/otelhttp provides server middleware and a client transport that injects traceparent into outgoing requests. most database drivers and rpc libraries have otel instrumentation too. the middleware in this lesson exists to show what those packages do.
- use the attribute names from the otel semantic conventions (http.route, http.response.statuscode, as above), available as constants in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv, so dashboards work across services.
- put the trace id into your log lines, and logs and traces link up.

 health checks

orchestrators need to ask two questions, which deserve separate endpoints:

- liveness (/healthz): is the process alive, or stuck and in need of a restart? keep it trivial. do not check dependencies here: if the database is down, restarting every instance of your service makes things worse.
- readiness (/readyz): should this instance receive traffic right now? report not ready during start-up and during shutdown (lesson 12.8), and optionally when a critical dependency is unreachable.

module 15 wires these into kubernetes probes.

 runtime metrics

the prometheus client's go collector exports the runtime's own metrics (from runtime/metrics, lesson 11.1): goroutine count, gc cycles and pause times, heap size, gomaxprocs. register it and you can graph exactly the things module 11 explained:



a steadily growing gogoroutines is a goroutine leak (lesson 7.6); a growing heap after gc is a memory leak; frequent gc cycles point to allocation churn (lesson 10.4).

 where to expose it

metrics, pprof (lesson 10.2) and similar endpoints reveal internals. serve them on a separate port (an "admin" port) that is reachable by prometheus inside the cluster but never routed publicly. the shortener listens on :8080 for the api and :9090 for admin.

 common mistakes

 unbounded label values

one label with user ids can create millions of series. use route patterns and status codes.

 logging instead of counting

counting errors by grepping logs is slow and expensive. emit a metric and alert on it; use logs for the details.

 liveness checks that test dependencies

a database outage then becomes a restart storm.

 breaking the context chain

a handler that starts work with context.background() instead of r.context() starts a new, disconnected trace, and loses cancellation too.

 key takeaways

- metrics tell you something is wrong, logs tell you what happened, traces tell you where time went.
- log structured json to stdout, one event per line, with a request or trace id.
- expose red metrics with the prometheus client, labelled by route pattern and status, never by raw path.
- opentelemetry traces cross services via the traceparent header; pass r.context() and spans nest.
- separate liveness from readiness, and serve metrics and pprof on an internal admin port.

 further reading

- [prometheus: instrumenting a go application](https://prometheus.io/docs/guides/go-application/)
- [opentelemetry go documentation](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/go/)
- [w3c trace context](https://www.w3.org/tr/trace-context/)

lessons.title: 12.6 Security basics: timeouts, limits, TLS and CSRF
lessons.description: The settings every Go HTTP server exposed to a network needs: server timeouts (with a slowloris test), header and body limits, TLS configuration, security headers, Go 1.25's CrossOriginProtection against CSRF, and handling secrets.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why `http.Server`'s zero values are unsafe on the internet, and which timeouts to set
- How a slowloris attack works, and a test that shows the defense
- Limiting header and body sizes
- TLS in Go, and when to terminate it elsewhere
- Security headers, and CSRF protection with `http.CrossOriginProtection` (Go 1.25)

## Timeouts

`http.Server` with no timeouts waits **forever** for a client. One client can open thousands of connections and send nothing, or send a byte every few seconds, and the server keeps a goroutine and a socket for each until it runs out of file descriptors or memory. Set all four timeouts:



```gopath-example
example-342
```



| Field | Limits |
|---|---|
| `ReadHeaderTimeout` | reading the request line and headers. The most important one. |
| `ReadTimeout` | reading the entire request, body included. |
| `WriteTimeout` | from the end of reading the headers to the end of writing the response. It caps how long a handler can take, so streaming endpoints need a different value (set per request with `http.ResponseController.SetWriteDeadline`). |
| `IdleTimeout` | how long a keep-alive connection may wait for its next request. |

### Slowloris, tested

A **slowloris** client sends headers slowly and never finishes, to tie up the server. This test does exactly that against a real server:



```gopath-example
example-343
```



```text
security_test.go:37: server gave up after 200ms (err=EOF)
```

With `ReadHeaderTimeout` set, the server closes the connection when the time runs out. Remove that line and the test fails after 5 seconds: the server would have waited forever.

Timeouts are also needed in the other direction. Every outgoing `http.Client` needs a `Timeout` and every outgoing request a context with a deadline (lesson 8.7), or one slow dependency can make all your handlers hang.

## Size limits

- **Headers**: `MaxHeaderBytes` defaults to 1 MiB. 64 KiB is plenty for most APIs.
- **Bodies** have no default limit. Limit them per handler with `http.MaxBytesReader` (lesson 12.3) or for a whole server with `http.MaxBytesHandler`:



```gopath-example
example-344
```



Also bound everything a client controls in size or count: list page sizes, batch sizes, upload sizes, query complexity.

## TLS

Go's `crypto/tls` is a complete, well-maintained TLS implementation with secure defaults: TLS 1.2 as the minimum for servers, modern cipher suites only, TLS 1.3 preferred, and post-quantum key exchange enabled by default in recent releases. To serve HTTPS directly:

```go
srv := NewServer(":8443", handler)
log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServeTLS("cert.pem", "key.pem"))
```

You rarely need to change the `tls.Config`; setting `MinVersion` explicitly, as above, documents the intent. For automatic certificates from Let's Encrypt, the `golang.org/x/crypto/acme/autocert` package handles issuance and renewal.

In **Kubernetes**, TLS is usually terminated at the **ingress controller** or a service mesh, and the Go service speaks plain HTTP inside the cluster (Module 15). That is a reasonable default; teams that need encryption inside the cluster add mesh mTLS rather than certificates in every service.

## Security headers

APIs consumed by browsers should send a few headers that make browsers stricter:



```gopath-example
example-345
```



`nosniff` stops browsers from interpreting a JSON response as HTML or script; the CSP tells them this response may load nothing and may not be framed; HSTS tells them to use HTTPS for this host from now on, and is only sent over TLS.

## CSRF protection (Go 1.25)

**Cross-site request forgery**: a malicious page makes the victim's browser send a request to your site, and the browser attaches the victim's cookies. If your site uses cookie sessions, the request is authenticated. The traditional defense was CSRF tokens in every form.

Go 1.25 added `http.CrossOriginProtection`, which uses headers that all browsers since 2023 send: **`Sec-Fetch-Site`**, falling back to comparing **`Origin`** with `Host`. It rejects state-changing requests (anything except GET, HEAD and OPTIONS) that come from another origin:



```gopath-example
example-346
```





```gopath-example
example-347
```



Same-origin POSTs pass, cross-site POSTs get 403, safe methods always pass, trusted origins pass, and requests without browser headers (curl, other servers) pass because they cannot carry a victim's cookies. Two consequences:

- Your GET handlers must **never change state**, because they are always allowed.
- APIs authenticated with an `Authorization` header instead of cookies are not exposed to CSRF in the first place, since browsers do not attach that header automatically.

These files carry `//go:build go1.25`, because the course's main module still supports Go 1.24.

## Secrets

- Read secrets from files or the environment at start-up (lesson 12.4); never log them, never put them in URLs (URLs end up in logs and browser history).
- Compare secrets such as API keys with `crypto/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare`, so the comparison time does not leak how many characters matched.
- Generate tokens and IDs with `crypto/rand` (`rand.Text()` since Go 1.24 returns a secure random string), never `math/rand`.

## Common mistakes

### No timeouts

`http.ListenAndServe` and a bare `&http.Server{}` have none. Always set them.

### Unlimited bodies

`io.ReadAll(r.Body)` on a public endpoint reads whatever a client sends.

### State changes on GET

Browsers, crawlers and link previewers follow GET links freely, and CSRF protection lets them through.

### Comparing secrets with ==

Use `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare`.

## Key takeaways

- Set `ReadHeaderTimeout`, `ReadTimeout`, `WriteTimeout` and `IdleTimeout` on every server; the zero values mean "wait forever".
- Limit header size with `MaxHeaderBytes` and body size with `MaxBytesReader` or `MaxBytesHandler`.
- Go's TLS defaults are good; in Kubernetes, TLS usually terminates at the ingress.
- Send `nosniff`, a restrictive CSP and, over TLS, HSTS.
- Wrap cookie-authenticated, state-changing endpoints with `http.CrossOriginProtection` (Go 1.25), and keep GET handlers free of side effects.

## Further reading

- [The complete guide to Go net/http timeouts](https://blog.cloudflare.com/the-complete-guide-to-golang-net-http-timeouts/) on the Cloudflare blog
- [Package net/http: CrossOriginProtection](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#CrossOriginProtection)
- [OWASP Cheat Sheet Series](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/)

lessons.title: 12.7 Exercise: a notes JSON API
lessons.description: Build a small JSON CRUD API from a written specification with ServeMux patterns, correct status codes and headers, checked by table-driven tests.
lessons.body:
## The task

The store is written for you: a concurrency-safe, in-memory collection of notes. Your job is the HTTP layer, written to this specification:

| Request | Success | Errors |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /notes` | 200, JSON array of all notes (`[]` when empty) | |
| `POST /notes` with `{"title": "...", "body": "..."}` | 201, the created note, `Location: /notes/{id}` | 400 if the body is not a JSON object, 422 if `title` is empty |
| `GET /notes/{id}` | 200, the note | 400 if `id` is not a number, 404 if it does not exist |
| `DELETE /notes/{id}` | 204, no body | 400, 404 |
| anything else on these paths | | 405 |



```gopath-exercise
m12/notes
```



```bash
cd exercises
go test ./m12/notes
```

## Hints



```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-5
```





```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-6
```





```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-7
```



The reference solution is in `exercises/m12/notes/solution.go`.

## Going further

- Use the strict `DecodeJSON` from lesson 12.3, and return problem details for errors.
- Add `PUT /notes/{id}` to replace a note, returning 200 or 404.
- Wrap the handler with the request ID and logging middleware from lesson 12.2.

lessons.title: 12.8 Project milestone: the shortener's HTTP API
lessons.description: Milestone 2 of the URL shortener: a production-shaped HTTP service with a JSON API, redirects, error mapping, request IDs, access logs, Prometheus metrics, per-client rate limiting, health checks and graceful shutdown, tested end to end.
lessons.body:
## The milestone

In milestone 1 (lesson 5.7) you built the shortener's core: the `link` package, with no knowledge of HTTP. Milestone 2 puts a service in front of it, using everything from this module. The core does not change at all; that is the payoff of keeping it independent.

| Milestone | After module | Adds | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Core | 5. Errors | Domain types, errors, validation, `Service`, in-memory store | done |
| **2. HTTP API** (this lesson) | 12. HTTP services | JSON API, redirects, middleware, metrics, shutdown | done |
| 3. Postgres | 13. Working with data | A database-backed `Store`, migrations | next |
| 4. Deploy | 15. Cloud native | Container image and Kubernetes manifests | |

The code is in [`projects/shortener`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/projects/shortener). The shortener is now **its own Go module**, because it uses two third party packages: the Prometheus client, and `golang.org/x/time/rate` for rate limiting (the production version of the token bucket you built in lesson 7.8).

```text
cmd/shortener/      main: wiring, the two servers, graceful shutdown
internal/link/      the domain from milestone 1, unchanged
internal/httpapi/   routes, JSON, error mapping, middleware, metrics, rate limiting
internal/config/    configuration from environment variables
```

Everything is under `internal/`, so no other module can import it: the only public interface of this program is HTTP.

## Try it

```bash
cd projects/shortener
go mod tidy                      # first time only
LOG_FORMAT=text go run ./cmd/shortener
```

```bash
$ curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/links -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"url": "https://go.dev/doc", "code": "godoc"}'
{"code":"godoc","url":"https://go.dev/doc","short_url":"http://localhost:8080/godoc","created_at":"..."}

$ curl -si localhost:8080/godoc | grep -E '^(HTTP|Location)'
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://go.dev/doc

$ curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/links -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"url": "https://go.dev", "code": "godoc"}'
{"title":"Conflict","status":409,"detail":"create \"godoc\": code already in use","request_id":"..."}

$ curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep 'shortener_http_requests_total{'
shortener_http_requests_total{code="201",route="POST /api/links"} 1
shortener_http_requests_total{code="302",route="GET /{code}"} 1
shortener_http_requests_total{code="409",route="POST /api/links"} 1
```

## The routes and the middleware stack



```gopath-example
example-348
```



Things to notice:

- **Rate limiting wraps individual routes** (lesson 12.2), so health checks are never limited. Because it runs inside the mux, rate limited requests still get their route label in metrics.
- **Recovery sits inside logging and metrics**, so a panicking request is logged and counted as a 500 like any other.
- **`GET /{code}` and `GET /healthz` do not conflict**: `/healthz` is more specific (lesson 12.1). It does mean `healthz`, `readyz` and `api` can never be short codes; a real service would reserve them in validation.

## The handlers



```gopath-example
example-349
```



Each handler is a straight line: decode, call the service, respond or hand the error to `writeError`. The redirect uses **302 Found**, not 301: browsers cache permanent redirects indefinitely, so a 301 could never be counted or changed again.

## Mapping errors to status codes

Milestone 1 promised that "the HTTP layer maps each sentinel error to a status code". Here it is, in one place:



```gopath-example
example-350
```



Because the service wraps errors with `%w`, `errors.Is` finds `link.ErrCodeTaken` inside `create "godoc": code already in use`. Client errors show their detail; server errors are **logged in full and hidden from the client**, who gets a generic message and the request ID to quote in a bug report. `TestServerErrorsAreNotLeaked` checks both halves with a store that fails like a broken database.

## Wiring it together

`main` is three lines: create a context that is cancelled on SIGINT or SIGTERM, call `run`, and exit non-zero if it fails. Everything else is in `run`:



```gopath-example
example-351
```



`run` takes `getenv` and `stdout` as parameters and stops when its context is cancelled. That makes the **whole program testable**: `TestRun` starts it on free ports (`ADDR=127.0.0.1:0`), finds the actual addresses in the JSON log, creates a link over real HTTP, follows the redirect, scrapes the admin port's metrics, then cancels the context, exactly what a SIGTERM does, and checks that `run` returns `nil`.

Two servers: the **API** on `:8080` and the **admin** server on `:9090` with `/metrics` and pprof, never exposed publicly (lesson 12.5). The pprof handlers are registered on the admin mux explicitly instead of importing `net/http/pprof` for its side effect on the default mux.

## Graceful shutdown, Kubernetes style



```gopath-example
example-352
```



Lesson 7.7 introduced `Server.Shutdown`. In Kubernetes there is one more subtlety: when a pod is terminated, removing it from the Service's endpoints and sending it SIGTERM happen **at the same time**. For a few seconds, other components may still route new requests to a pod that has started shutting down. So the shortener:

1. turns `/readyz` to 503 immediately,
2. keeps serving normally for `SHUTDOWN_DELAY` (default 0 locally; about 5 seconds in Kubernetes),
3. then calls `Shutdown`, which stops accepting connections and waits up to `SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT` for in-flight requests.

Module 15 sets these values in the Deployment manifest, along with probes on `/healthz` and `/readyz`.

## What the tests cover

```bash
go test ./...
```

| Test | Checks |
|---|---|
| `TestCreateResolveRedirect` | the happy path: 201 with `Location`, JSON fields, 302 redirect |
| `TestErrorMapping` | 409, 422, 400, 415, 404 and 405, table-driven |
| `TestServerErrorsAreNotLeaked` | internal errors are logged, not shown; problem includes the request ID |
| `TestRateLimit` | burst of 3 then 429; health checks never limited |
| `TestReadiness` | `/readyz` is 503 until ready |
| `TestMetricsAndLogs` | counters by route pattern and status; access log fields |
| `TestRun` | the real program over real HTTP, and a clean shutdown on cancel |
| `config` tests | defaults, and every invalid variable reported at once |

## Your turn

Ideas to extend the milestone, in rough order of difficulty:

1. Reserve `api`, `healthz` and `readyz` so they cannot be used as custom codes. Where does that rule belong: `link` or `httpapi`?
2. Design `DELETE /api/links/{code}`: which status codes, and which new `Store` method? Then compare with the version milestone 4 adds (lesson 15.4 needs it).
3. Count redirects per code. Should that be a Prometheus label? (Lesson 12.5 says no. Why?) Where should it be stored instead?
4. Add OpenTelemetry tracing with the middleware from lesson 12.5, or with `otelhttp`.

Next, Module 13 replaces the in-memory store with PostgreSQL, without changing a line of `httpapi`.

- get /{code} and get /healthz do not conflict: /healthz is more specific (lesson 12.1). it does mean healthz, readyz and api can never be short codes; a real service would reserve them in validation.

 the handlers







each handler is a straight line: decode, call the service, respond or hand the error to writeerror. the redirect uses 302 found, not 301: browsers cache permanent redirects indefinitely, so a 301 could never be counted or changed again.

 mapping errors to status codes

milestone 1 promised that "the http layer maps each sentinel error to a status code". here it is, in one place:







because the service wraps errors with %w, errors.is finds link.errcodetaken inside create "godoc": code already in use. client errors show their detail; server errors are logged in full and hidden from the client, who gets a generic message and the request id to quote in a bug report. testservererrorsarenotleaked checks both halves with a store that fails like a broken database.

 wiring it together

main is three lines: create a context that is cancelled on sigint or sigterm, call run, and exit non-zero if it fails. everything else is in run:







run takes getenv and stdout as parameters and stops when its context is cancelled. that makes the whole program testable: testrun starts it on free ports (addr=127.0.0.1:0), finds the actual addresses in the json log, creates a link over real http, follows the redirect, scrapes the admin port's metrics, then cancels the context, exactly what a sigterm does, and checks that run returns nil.

two servers: the api on :8080 and the admin server on :9090 with /metrics and pprof, never exposed publicly (lesson 12.5). the pprof handlers are registered on the admin mux explicitly instead of importing net/http/pprof for its side effect on the default mux.

 graceful shutdown, kubernetes style







lesson 7.7 introduced server.shutdown. in kubernetes there is one more subtlety: when a pod is terminated, removing it from the service's endpoints and sending it sigterm happen at the same time. for a few seconds, other components may still route new requests to a pod that has started shutting down. so the shortener:

1. turns /readyz to 503 immediately,
2. keeps serving normally for shutdowndelay (default 0 locally; about 5 seconds in kubernetes),
3. then calls shutdown, which stops accepting connections and waits up to shutdowntimeout for in-flight requests.

module 15 sets these values in the deployment manifest, along with probes on /healthz and /readyz.

 what the tests cover



| test | checks |
|---|---|
| testcreateresolveredirect | the happy path: 201 with location, json fields, 302 redirect |
| testerrormapping | 409, 422, 400, 415, 404 and 405, table-driven |
| testservererrorsarenotleaked | internal errors are logged, not shown; problem includes the request id |
| testratelimit | burst of 3 then 429; health checks never limited |
| testreadiness | /readyz is 503 until ready |
| testmetricsandlogs | counters by route pattern and status; access log fields |
| testrun | the real program over real http, and a clean shutdown on cancel |
| config tests | defaults, and every invalid variable reported at once |

 your turn

ideas to extend the milestone, in rough order of difficulty:

1. reserve api, healthz and readyz so they cannot be used as custom codes. where does that rule belong: link or httpapi?
2. design delete /api/links/{code}: which status codes, and which new store method? then compare with the version milestone 4 adds (lesson 15.4 needs it).
3. count redirects per code. should that be a prometheus label? (lesson 12.5 says no. why?) where should it be stored instead?
4. add opentelemetry tracing with the middleware from lesson 12.5, or with otelhttp.

next, module 13 replaces the in-memory store with postgresql, without changing a line of httpapi.

lessons.title: 13.1 database/sql and connection pooling
lessons.description: How database/sql works: drivers, the connection pool and its settings, queries and rows, NULL values, sql.ErrNoRows, and why parameters prevent SQL injection, with a measured pool limit.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How `database/sql` and drivers fit together
- What `*sql.DB` really is: a **pool**, and how to size it
- Querying one row, many rows, and executing statements, correctly
- NULLs, `sql.ErrNoRows`, and closing rows
- How parameters prevent SQL injection, demonstrated

## The idea

`database/sql` is the standard library's interface to SQL databases. It contains **no driver**: it defines the API your code uses, and a driver package implements it for a specific database. You import the driver for its side effect of registering itself:

```go
import _ "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib" // registers the driver name "pgx"
```

For PostgreSQL, **pgx** is the most widely used and most complete driver; its `stdlib` package provides the `database/sql` driver. (You will also meet the older `lib/pq` in existing code.) Lesson 13.2 shows pgx's own, richer API.

## sql.DB is a pool



```gopath-example
example-353
```



`sql.Open` does not connect; it only checks its arguments. The `*sql.DB` it returns is a **pool of connections**, safe for concurrent use. Create one at start-up, share it everywhere, and close it at shutdown. Opening a `sql.DB` per request is a classic, expensive mistake.

Each query borrows a connection from the pool and returns it when done. The settings:

| Setting | Default | What to set |
|---|---|---|
| `SetMaxOpenConns` | unlimited | Always set it. The database has a connection limit (PostgreSQL's default is 100) shared by every instance of every service. 10 replicas × 25 connections is already 250. |
| `SetMaxIdleConns` | 2 | Usually equal to MaxOpenConns, so bursts do not open and close connections constantly. |
| `SetConnMaxLifetime` | forever | Minutes to an hour, so connections are recycled (helps with load balancers and failovers). |
| `SetConnMaxIdleTime` | forever | A few minutes, so idle capacity is released. |

### What happens when the pool is full

When all connections are busy, the next query **waits** for one to be returned. This test allows 2 connections and runs 6 queries that each take 200 ms:



```gopath-example
example-354
```



```text
6 queries of 200ms with 2 connections took 610ms; waited 4 times for 1.22s in total
```

Three rounds of two queries: 600 ms. `db.Stats()` shows the waiting directly. Export these stats as metrics (lesson 12.5): a growing `WaitCount` means the pool is too small, or queries are too slow, and requests are queuing. The wait respects the query's context, so a request deadline also bounds the time spent waiting for a connection.

## Queries



```gopath-example
example-355
```



The three methods, always the `Context` variants so that cancellation and deadlines apply:

- **`QueryRowContext(...).Scan(...)`** for exactly one row. If there is none, `Scan` returns **`sql.ErrNoRows`**; translate it into your own "not found" error, so callers do not depend on `database/sql`.
- **`QueryContext`** for many rows. Three rules: `defer rows.Close()` immediately (an unclosed `Rows` keeps its connection out of the pool, a pool leak), check `rows.Scan`'s error, and check **`rows.Err()`** after the loop, because a network error mid-result just ends the loop.
- **`ExecContext`** for statements that return no rows. Its `Result` has `RowsAffected`.

**NULL** needs a type that can represent it. `string` cannot be NULL, so scanning a NULL into it fails. Use `sql.Null[string]` (Go 1.22), which has `V` and `Valid`, or a pointer (`*string`). Better still, avoid nullable columns that do not need to be.

PostgreSQL uses `$1, $2, ...` placeholders; MySQL and SQLite use `?`. `RETURNING id` gets the generated ID in the same round trip.

## SQL injection

Never build SQL by formatting values into the string:



```gopath-example
example-356
```





```gopath-example
example-357
```



```text
unsafe query matched 2 users, safe query matched 0
```

The input `nobody' OR '1'='1` closes the string literal and adds a condition that is always true, so the unsafe query matches every user. With a parameter, the value is sent **separately** from the SQL text, and the database never parses it as SQL: it simply looks for a user with that strange name. Parameters work for values only; if you must vary an identifier (a column to sort by), choose it from a fixed allowlist in code.

## Common mistakes

### A new sql.DB per request

Create one pool at start-up and share it.

### No MaxOpenConns

Under load, every instance opens connections until the database refuses them, failing every service that uses it.

### Forgetting rows.Close or rows.Err

The first leaks connections until the pool is exhausted; the second silently returns partial results.

### Formatting values into SQL

Use parameters, always.

## Key takeaways

- `database/sql` is an interface; import a driver such as `github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib`.
- `*sql.DB` is a concurrency-safe pool: one per database per program, with `SetMaxOpenConns` and friends set deliberately.
- When the pool is full, queries wait; `db.Stats()` shows it.
- Use the `Context` methods; map `sql.ErrNoRows` to your own error; always `rows.Close()` and check `rows.Err()`.
- Pass values as parameters (`$1`), never with string formatting.

## Further reading

- [Go database/sql tutorial](https://go.dev/doc/database/) on go.dev
- [Managing connections](https://go.dev/doc/database/manage-connections)
- [pgx documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jackc/pgx/v5)

lessons.title: 13.2 pgx and PostgreSQL
lessons.description: Use pgx's native API: pgxpool, scanning rows into structs, PostgreSQL arrays, handling constraint violations by error code, and bulk inserts with batches and COPY, measured.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- When to use pgx's native API instead of `database/sql`
- Connecting with `pgxpool`
- Scanning rows into structs with `pgx.CollectRows`, and PostgreSQL types like arrays
- Handling errors by **SQLSTATE code**, such as unique violations
- Bulk inserts: one by one, batched, and `COPY`, with measurements

## database/sql or native pgx?

pgx offers two APIs. Through `database/sql` (lesson 13.1), your code is portable between databases and works with tools built on that interface. Through its **native API**, you get PostgreSQL-specific features and better performance: native types (arrays, JSONB, ranges, UUIDs), batches, `COPY`, `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, and helpers that scan rows into structs.

If you know you are on PostgreSQL, and most Go services are, the native API is the better default. The shortener and job queue projects use it.

## Connecting



```gopath-example
example-358
```



`pgxpool.Pool` plays the same role as `*sql.DB`: a concurrency-safe pool, created once. Settings can also come from the connection URL (`?pool_max_conns=10`), which is convenient when the URL is the only configuration a platform passes.

## Rows into structs



```gopath-example
example-359
```



`pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[Product])` reads every row into a `Product`, matching columns to fields by `db` tag (or by field name), and closes the rows. There are variants for positional mapping (`RowToStructByPos`), single values (`RowTo[string]`), and exactly one row (`CollectOneRow`, which returns `pgx.ErrNoRows` if there is none).

`Tags []string` maps to a PostgreSQL `text[]` column in both directions, and `$1 = ANY(tags)` searches it. One trap the test hit while this lesson was written: a **nil** Go slice is sent as SQL `NULL`, not as an empty array, and the `NOT NULL` column rejected it. `Insert` therefore sends `[]string{}` for a nil slice.

## Errors by code

PostgreSQL reports every error with a five-character **SQLSTATE** code. pgx exposes it as `*pgconn.PgError`:



```gopath-example
example-360
```



```text
duplicate: insert "GO-MUG": duplicate SKU
check violation: insert "NEG": ERROR: new row for relation "products" violates check constraint "products_price_cents_check" (SQLSTATE 23514)
```

Codes worth knowing:

| Code | Name | Typical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `23505` | unique_violation | duplicate key: map it to "already exists" (409) |
| `23503` | foreign_key_violation | referenced row missing |
| `23514` | check_violation | a `CHECK` constraint failed |
| `40001` | serialization_failure | retry the transaction (lesson 13.4) |
| `40P01` | deadlock_detected | retry, and fix the lock order (lesson 13.4) |
| `57014` | query_canceled | the context was cancelled or timed out |

Let the **database enforce** invariants (unique keys, foreign keys, checks) and translate its errors, rather than checking first in Go: "check, then insert" is a race between two requests, while a unique constraint is atomic.

## Bulk inserts

Inserting 5000 rows three ways, against PostgreSQL 16 on the same machine:



```gopath-example
example-361
```





```gopath-example
example-362
```



```text
one by one 5000 rows in 2.379s
batch      5000 rows in 80ms
copy       5000 rows in 23ms
```

One by one is **30 times** slower than a batch, and **100 times** slower than `COPY`, even with the database on the same machine. Two costs add up:

- **Round trips.** Each `Exec` waits for its answer before the next is sent. Over a real network, with a millisecond or so per round trip, this grows much worse than here.
- **Commits.** Outside a transaction, each statement is its own transaction, and each commit waits for the write-ahead log to reach disk.

A **batch** queues all statements and sends them together, and pgx runs them in a single implicit transaction. **`COPY`** is PostgreSQL's bulk-loading protocol: it streams rows in a compact format, without parsing an `INSERT` per row. Use batches for many statements of any kind, and `CopyFrom` for loading many rows into one table.

## Common mistakes

### Checking for duplicates before inserting

Two requests can both pass the check. Use a unique constraint and handle `23505`.

### Nil slices for NOT NULL array columns

They become NULL. Send an empty slice.

### Inserting rows in a loop

Use `SendBatch` or `CopyFrom` for anything more than a handful.

### Matching error message text

Use `pgErr.Code` (and `pgErr.ConstraintName` when a table has several constraints).

## Key takeaways

- On PostgreSQL, prefer pgx's native API and `pgxpool`.
- `pgx.CollectRows` with `RowToStructByName` scans rows into structs; arrays and other PostgreSQL types map to Go types.
- Classify errors with `errors.As` into `*pgconn.PgError` and its SQLSTATE `Code`; let constraints enforce invariants.
- For bulk work, batches were 30x and `COPY` 100x faster than one statement at a time, here.

## Further reading

- [pgx documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jackc/pgx/v5)
- [PostgreSQL error codes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/errcodes-appendix.html)
- [PostgreSQL: COPY](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-copy.html)

lessons.title: 13.3 Migrations
lessons.description: Version your database schema with migrations: embed SQL files in the binary, apply them in a transaction under an advisory lock so replicas can start together, and change schemas without downtime using expand and contract.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What migrations are and why schema changes must be versioned
- A complete, small migrator: embedded SQL files, a version table, a transaction and an advisory lock
- Testing that migrations are idempotent and safe to run concurrently
- Changing a schema without downtime: **expand and contract**
- When to run migrations, and which tools to use

## The idea

Your code expects a particular database schema: these tables, these columns. As the code changes, so must the schema, in every environment, in the same order. A **migration** is one numbered schema change, kept in version control next to the code. The database records which migrations it has applied, and a migrator applies the missing ones in order.

## A small migrator

The shortener (lesson 13.7) has its own migrator, short enough to read in full. The migrations are plain SQL files:



```gopath-example
example-363
```



And the code that applies them:



```gopath-example
example-364
```



Every part has a job:

- **`//go:embed migrations/*.sql`** compiles the SQL into the binary (lesson 8.5). A deployment is one file, and version 2.3 of the program always carries exactly the migrations of version 2.3.
- **`schema_migrations`** records the applied versions. Files are applied in name order, which is why they start with a zero-padded number.
- **One transaction.** PostgreSQL can roll back schema changes (DDL), so either all pending migrations apply or none do. A half-applied migration is the worst state to debug at 3 a.m.
- **`pg_advisory_xact_lock`** takes a lock identified by a number, held until the transaction ends. When three replicas of a service start at the same moment, the first takes the lock and migrates; the others wait, then find nothing left to do.

The tests check exactly those properties, against a real database:

```text
store_test.go:33: applied [0001_create_links.sql], then nothing
```

`TestMigrateIsIdempotent` runs it twice; `TestMigrateConcurrently` runs it from five goroutines at once and checks every migration was applied exactly once.

A rule that keeps migrations sane: **never edit a migration that has been applied anywhere** outside your laptop. Fix mistakes with a new migration. Applied migrations are history.

A limitation of running everything in one transaction: a few statements cannot run inside a transaction, notably `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, which builds an index without blocking writes. Migration tools let you mark such migrations as non-transactional.

## Changing schemas without downtime

During a rolling deployment, old and new versions of your service run **at the same time**, against the same database. Every migration must therefore work with both the code before it and the code after it. That rules out a single-step rename:

```sql
ALTER TABLE links RENAME COLUMN url TO target;  -- old replicas break immediately
```

Instead, **expand and contract**, over several deployments:

1. **Expand.** Add the new column (`target`). Deploy code that writes **both** columns and reads the old one.
2. **Migrate data.** Backfill `target` from `url` in batches.
3. **Switch.** Deploy code that reads `target` (still writing both).
4. **Contract.** Once no running code uses `url`, stop writing it, and in a later migration drop it.

It is slower, but no step ever breaks a running version. The same thinking applies to adding `NOT NULL` columns (add with a default, or nullable first), and to dropping anything.

Also watch for **locks**: some `ALTER TABLE` forms rewrite or lock the whole table, blocking all queries for the duration. Set a `lock_timeout` in migrations so a blocked migration fails fast instead of queueing every request behind it.

## When to run migrations

- **At start-up**, as the shortener does by default (`MIGRATE=true`). Simple, and the advisory lock makes it safe with many replicas. The cost: a slow migration delays start-up, and the service's database user needs permission to change the schema.
- **As a separate step** before rolling out the new version: a Kubernetes Job, an init container, or a CI/CD stage running the same binary with a `migrate` command. This gives you more control, and lets the service run with a user that cannot alter tables. Larger teams usually end up here.

## Tools

The migrator above is about 60 lines because PostgreSQL does the heavy lifting. Established tools add down migrations, non-transactional migrations, CLIs and multi-database support:

- **goose** (`github.com/pressly/goose`): SQL or Go migrations, embeddable, popular in Go services.
- **golang-migrate** (`github.com/golang-migrate/migrate`): many databases and sources, with a CLI.
- **Atlas** (`ariga.io/atlas`): declarative: you describe the desired schema and it plans the changes.

Whichever you use, the principles are the same: versioned files in the repository, applied in order, recorded in the database, never edited after release.

## Common mistakes

### Editing applied migrations

Environments diverge silently. Add a new migration instead.

### Breaking changes in one step

Renames and drops break the old version during a rolling deploy. Expand, then contract.

### Long-locking migrations at peak traffic

Know which `ALTER TABLE` forms lock or rewrite tables; set `lock_timeout`; build indexes concurrently.

## Key takeaways

- Migrations are numbered, versioned schema changes applied in order and recorded in the database.
- Embed them in the binary; apply them in one transaction under an advisory lock so concurrent replicas are safe.
- Never edit an applied migration.
- For zero downtime, every migration must work with both the old and new code: expand, migrate, switch, contract.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL: advisory locks](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html#ADVISORY-LOCKS)
- [goose](https://github.com/pressly/goose) and [golang-migrate](https://github.com/golang-migrate/migrate)

13.3 migrations version your database schema with migrations: embed sql files in the binary, apply them in a transaction under an advisory lock so replicas can start together, and change schemas without downtime using expand and contract.  what you will learn

- what migrations are and why schema changes must be versioned
- a complete, small migrator: embedded sql files, a version table, a transaction and an advisory lock
- testing that migrations are idempotent and safe to run concurrently
- changing a schema without downtime: expand and contract
- when to run migrations, and which tools to use

 the idea

your code expects a particular database schema: these tables, these columns. as the code changes, so must the schema, in every environment, in the same order. a migration is one numbered schema change, kept in version control next to the code. the database records which migrations it has applied, and a migrator applies the missing ones in order.

 a small migrator

the shortener (lesson 13.7) has its own migrator, short enough to read in full. the migrations are plain sql files:







and the code that applies them:







every part has a job:

- //go:embed migrations/.sql compiles the sql into the binary (lesson 8.5). a deployment is one file, and version 2.3 of the program always carries exactly the migrations of version 2.3.
- schemamigrations records the applied versions. files are applied in name order, which is why they start with a zero-padded number.
- one transaction. postgresql can roll back schema changes (ddl), so either all pending migrations apply or none do. a half-applied migration is the worst state to debug at 3 a.m.
- pgadvisoryxactlock takes a lock identified by a number, held until the transaction ends. when three replicas of a service start at the same moment, the first takes the lock and migrates; the others wait, then find nothing left to do.

the tests check exactly those properties, against a real database:



testmigrateisidempotent runs it twice; testmigrateconcurrently runs it from five goroutines at once and checks every migration was applied exactly once.

a rule that keeps migrations sane: never edit a migration that has been applied anywhere outside your laptop. fix mistakes with a new migration. applied migrations are history.

a limitation of running everything in one transaction: a few statements cannot run inside a transaction, notably create index concurrently, which builds an index without blocking writes. migration tools let you mark such migrations as non-transactional.

 changing schemas without downtime

during a rolling deployment, old and new versions of your service run at the same time, against the same database. every migration must therefore work with both the code before it and the code after it. that rules out a single-step rename:



instead, expand and contract, over several deployments:

1. expand. add the new column (target). deploy code that writes both columns and reads the old one.
2. migrate data. backfill target from url in batches.
3. switch. deploy code that reads target (still writing both).
4. contract. once no running code uses url, stop writing it, and in a later migration drop it.

it is slower, but no step ever breaks a running version. the same thinking applies to adding not null columns (add with a default, or nullable first), and to dropping anything.

also watch for locks: some alter table forms rewrite or lock the whole table, blocking all queries for the duration. set a locktimeout in migrations so a blocked migration fails fast instead of queueing every request behind it.

 when to run migrations

- at start-up, as the shortener does by default (migrate=true). simple, and the advisory lock makes it safe with many replicas. the cost: a slow migration delays start-up, and the service's database user needs permission to change the schema.
- as a separate step before rolling out the new version: a kubernetes job, an init container, or a ci/cd stage running the same binary with a migrate command. this gives you more control, and lets the service run with a user that cannot alter tables. larger teams usually end up here.

 tools

the migrator above is about 60 lines because postgresql does the heavy lifting. established tools add down migrations, non-transactional migrations, clis and multi-database support:

- goose (github.com/pressly/goose): sql or go migrations, embeddable, popular in go services.
- golang-migrate (github.com/golang-migrate/migrate): many databases and sources, with a cli.
- atlas (ariga.io/atlas): declarative: you describe the desired schema and it plans the changes.

whichever you use, the principles are the same: versioned files in the repository, applied in order, recorded in the database, never edited after release.

 common mistakes

 editing applied migrations

environments diverge silently. add a new migration instead.

 breaking changes in one step

renames and drops break the old version during a rolling deploy. expand, then contract.

 long-locking migrations at peak traffic

know which alter table forms lock or rewrite tables; set locktimeout; build indexes concurrently.

 key takeaways

- migrations are numbered, versioned schema changes applied in order and recorded in the database.
- embed them in the binary; apply them in one transaction under an advisory lock so concurrent replicas are safe.
- never edit an applied migration.
- for zero downtime, every migration must work with both the old and new code: expand, migrate, switch, contract.

 further reading

- [postgresql: advisory locks](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.htmladvisory-locks)
- [goose](https://github.com/pressly/goose) and [golang-migrate](https://github.com/golang-migrate/migrate)

lessons.title: 13.4 Transactions and context
lessons.description: Use transactions correctly from Go: a WithTx helper, the lost update problem and its fixes, row locks with FOR UPDATE, deadlocks and lock ordering, isolation levels and retries, and cancelling queries with context, all demonstrated against PostgreSQL.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- A safe pattern for transactions in Go: commit on success, roll back on everything else
- The **lost update** problem, reproduced, and two ways to fix it
- Row locks with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
- **Deadlocks**, reproduced, and the lock-ordering fix
- Isolation levels and retrying serialization failures
- How a context deadline cancels a running query

## The pattern

A transaction groups statements so they succeed or fail together. In Go, the shape is always the same:



```gopath-example
example-365
```



- **`defer tx.Rollback(...)`** runs on every exit path: an error, an early return, a panic. After a successful `Commit` it does nothing, so it is safe to defer unconditionally.
- **`context.WithoutCancel`** for the rollback: if the request was cancelled, we still want the rollback to reach the database.
- The callback gets a `pgx.Tx` and runs every statement through it. A statement accidentally run on the pool instead of `tx` executes **outside** the transaction, a subtle bug.

pgx ships the same idea as `pgx.BeginFunc`, which the migrator in lesson 13.3 uses. The test confirms the rollback:



```gopath-example
example-366
```



## The lost update

A transaction alone does not make read-then-write logic safe. This withdrawal reads the balance, computes, and writes the result:



```gopath-example
example-367
```



Two withdrawals of 10 from a balance of 100, at the same time:



```gopath-example
example-368
```



```text
racy:   two withdrawals of 10 from 100 left 90
locked: two withdrawals of 10 from 100 left 80
```

In the racy version, both transactions read 100 and both write 90: one withdrawal vanished. PostgreSQL's default isolation level, **READ COMMITTED**, does not prevent this, and neither does a transaction by itself. (The test widens the gap between read and write with a pause, so the race happens every time instead of occasionally in production.)

Two fixes:

1. **Lock the row** with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. The second transaction blocks at its `SELECT` until the first commits, then reads 90. That is `WithdrawLocked`, which leaves 80.
2. **Do the arithmetic in the database**: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2`. A single statement reads and writes atomically, with no window for a race. This is simpler and faster whenever the logic fits in SQL; the `Transfer` function below uses it, with `AND balance >= $1` to refuse overdrafts.

## Deadlocks

`TransferNaive` moves money with two atomic `UPDATE`s in one transaction. Now run transfers in **both** directions at once:



```gopath-example
example-369
```





```gopath-example
example-370
```



```text
naive transfers, errors by code: map[40P01:6 insufficient funds:4] (40P01 is deadlock_detected)
ordered locking, errors by code: map[]
```

A transfer from alice to bob locks alice's row, then bob's. A transfer from bob to alice locks bob's, then alice's. When they interleave, each holds the lock the other needs, forever. PostgreSQL detects the cycle (after `deadlock_timeout`, one second by default) and aborts one of the transactions with SQLSTATE **40P01**. The total money stays correct, because the aborted transaction rolls back, but requests fail.

The fix is the same as for code that takes several `sync.Mutex` locks (lesson 6.4): **acquire locks in a consistent order**. `Transfer` first locks both rows with `SELECT ... ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE`, so every transfer locks alice before bob regardless of direction, and no cycle can form. Zero deadlocks.

## Isolation levels and retries

PostgreSQL offers three isolation levels in practice:

| Level | Guarantees | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| READ COMMITTED (default) | each statement sees data committed before it started | lost updates possible, as shown |
| REPEATABLE READ | the whole transaction sees one snapshot; concurrent updates to the same row fail with **40001** | you must retry |
| SERIALIZABLE | the result equals some serial order of the transactions; conflicts fail with **40001** | you must retry, more often |

```go
tx, err := pool.BeginTx(ctx, pgx.TxOptions{IsoLevel: pgx.Serializable})
```

Higher levels replace "silently wrong" with "fails, please retry". Code using them needs a retry loop: run the whole transaction again, a few times with backoff, when the error code is `40001` (serialization_failure) or `40P01` (deadlock_detected). Never retry part of a transaction.

A practical approach: use READ COMMITTED with explicit locking (`FOR UPDATE`) or single-statement updates for the hot paths you understand, and SERIALIZABLE for complex invariants that are hard to protect by hand.

## Context cancels queries

Every pgx method takes a context. When the context ends, pgx asks the server to cancel the running query:



```gopath-example
example-371
```



```text
a 5 s query with a 100 ms deadline returned after 100ms: timeout: context deadline exceeded
```

This is why handlers pass `r.Context()` to every query: when a client disconnects or a deadline passes, the database stops working on a result nobody will read. The error wraps `context.DeadlineExceeded` (or `context.Canceled`), so `errors.Is` identifies it.

Keep transactions **short**. While a transaction is open it holds a connection and its locks; calling another service or waiting for user input inside one turns a slow dependency into blocked rows for everyone.

## Common mistakes

### Read, compute, write without a lock

Lost updates under concurrency. Use one `UPDATE ... SET x = x - $1`, or `FOR UPDATE`.

### Locking rows in different orders

Deadlocks. Lock in a consistent order, such as by primary key.

### Using the pool inside a transaction function

The statement runs outside the transaction. Use the `tx` you were given.

### Long transactions

Network calls inside a transaction hold locks and connections. Do them before or after.

### Retrying only the failed statement

After 40001 or 40P01 the whole transaction is aborted. Retry the whole function.

## Key takeaways

- Begin, `defer Rollback`, run everything on `tx`, `Commit`: or use a helper like `WithTx` or `pgx.BeginFunc`.
- READ COMMITTED allows lost updates: compute in a single `UPDATE`, or lock with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.
- Lock rows in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks (40P01).
- REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE turn anomalies into 40001 errors, which require retrying the whole transaction.
- Contexts cancel running queries; pass the request context everywhere, and keep transactions short.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL: transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
- [PostgreSQL: explicit locking](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html)

lessons.title: 13.5 Caching with Redis
lessons.description: Cache-aside with Redis and go-redis: TTLs, invalidation, request coalescing against cache stampedes (measured), and making the cache optional so a Redis outage never takes the service down.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- When a cache helps, and what it costs
- The **cache-aside** pattern with Redis and the go-redis client
- TTLs and invalidation: the two ways cached data stops being stale
- **Cache stampedes**, and coalescing concurrent misses with `singleflight`, measured
- Designing the cache so that a Redis outage degrades performance, not availability

## When to cache

A cache keeps copies of data somewhere faster than its source. It helps when the same data is read **much more often than it changes**, and reading it from the source is slow or expensive: a popular product page, a user's permissions, a rendered fragment, or a short link that will be followed thousands of times.

It costs you complexity and **staleness**: from the moment you cache a value, readers may see an old one. So the first questions are "how stale may this be?" and "is the database actually the bottleneck?" (measure it, Module 10). Databases are fast at reading rows by primary key; a cache in front of a 1 ms query rarely pays for itself.

**Redis** is an in-memory data store used as a shared cache by many instances of a service. `github.com/redis/go-redis/v9` is the official Go client; like `*sql.DB`, a `*redis.Client` is a concurrency-safe connection pool you create once.

## Cache-aside

The most common pattern, also called lazy loading: the application checks the cache, and on a miss loads from the source and fills the cache.



```gopath-example
example-372
```



- **A hit** returns immediately.
- **`redis.Nil`** is go-redis's "key does not exist" error. It is a miss, not a failure.
- **Every entry has a TTL** (`Set(ctx, key, value, ttl)`): Redis deletes it when it expires, so stale data has a maximum age, and unused keys do not fill memory forever.
- **Keys are namespaced** (`prefix`), such as `shortener:link:abc`, so several applications or data types can share one Redis safely.

The test shows the timing:

```text
call 1: 52ms, loads so far 1
call 2: 100µs, loads so far 1
call 3: 100µs, loads so far 1
```

The first call pays for the slow load; the next ones take about a tenth of a millisecond, a round trip to Redis on the same machine. After the TTL, or after `Invalidate`, the next call loads again.

## Invalidation

There are two ways to deal with data that changes:

- **Expiry only.** Accept up to one TTL of staleness. Simple, and often enough: a product description that is five minutes old is fine.
- **Invalidate on write.** When the source changes, delete the cached key (`Invalidate`). Delete rather than update: concurrent writers updating the cache can leave it with the older value. Even then, keep a TTL as a safety net.

The famous difficulty of cache invalidation comes from data that changes often and must never be stale. For that, reconsider caching at all. Data that **never changes**, like a short link, is the easy case: there is nothing to invalidate.

## Cache stampedes

A popular key expires. In the next millisecond, a hundred requests miss at once, and all hundred run the expensive load against the database, which was exactly what the cache was protecting. This is a **cache stampede** (or thundering herd):



```gopath-example
example-373
```



```text
coalesce=false 100 concurrent misses caused 100 loads
coalesce=true  100 concurrent misses caused 1 loads
```

`golang.org/x/sync/singleflight` fixes it within one process: concurrent calls to `group.Do(key, fn)` with the same key wait for a single execution of `fn` and share its result. Across many instances, each instance does at most one load per key, which is usually good enough. (Distributed locks in Redis can reduce it further, at a price in complexity.)

Note `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` inside `Do`: the shared load must not be cancelled because the **first** caller's request was cancelled, since other callers are waiting for it too. Exercise 13.6 builds this coalescing by hand.

## The cache is optional

A cache must make the service faster, never less available. If Redis goes down and every request fails, you have added a single point of failure. `Get` therefore treats Redis errors like misses: it logs a warning and loads from the source.



```gopath-example
example-374
```



Two details make this work in practice: **short timeouts** for Redis (a cache that takes two seconds to fail is worse than no cache), and making sure the source can survive the full load for a while, or protecting it with rate limits (lesson 7.5), because during an outage every request reaches it.

## Common mistakes

### Caching without a TTL

Memory fills up, and stale data lives forever.

### Updating the cache on write

Concurrent writers can leave the old value. Delete instead.

### Treating Redis errors as request failures

The cache becomes a dependency. Fall back to the source.

### Caching errors or "not found" by accident

A brief database error, cached for an hour, becomes an hour of failures. Cache successes; if you cache "not found" (negative caching), use a short TTL.

### Unbounded key space

Keys built from user input (search queries, full URLs) can create millions of entries. Bound them, and set a Redis `maxmemory` with an eviction policy.

## Key takeaways

- Cache data that is read far more often than it changes, after measuring that the source is the bottleneck.
- Cache-aside: check Redis, on `redis.Nil` load from the source and `Set` with a TTL.
- Invalidate by deleting keys; keep TTLs as a safety net.
- Coalesce concurrent misses with `singleflight` to prevent stampedes: measured, 100 loads became 1.
- Redis failures must fall back to the source, with short timeouts.

## Further reading

- [go-redis documentation](https://redis.uptrace.dev/)
- [Package golang.org/x/sync/singleflight](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/singleflight)
- [Redis: key eviction](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)

lessons.title: 13.6 Exercise: a read-through cache
lessons.description: Build an in-memory read-through cache with expiry, no caching of errors, and request coalescing, without holding a lock during loads; tested with a fake clock and the race detector.
lessons.body:
## The task

Lesson 13.5 used Redis for storage and `singleflight` for coalescing. Here you build both ideas yourself, in memory and with only the standard library, which is the best way to understand what those packages do.



```gopath-exercise
m13/readthrough
```



```bash

go test -race ./m13/readthrough
```

lessons.title: 13.7 Project milestone: the shortener on PostgreSQL
lessons.description: Milestone 3 of the URL shortener: a PostgreSQL store with embedded migrations, an optional Redis cache, and one conformance test suite that every store implementation must pass.
lessons.body:
## The milestone

| Milestone | After module | Adds | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Core | 5. Errors | Domain types, errors, validation, `Service`, in-memory store | done |
| 2. HTTP API | 12. HTTP services | JSON API, redirects, middleware, metrics, shutdown | done |
| **3. Postgres** (this lesson) | 13. Working with data | PostgreSQL store, migrations, Redis cache | done |
| 4. Deploy | 15. Cloud native | Container image and Kubernetes manifests | next |

Links now survive restarts and can be shared by many replicas. The interesting part is what did **not** change: the `link` package and the whole HTTP layer are untouched. The `Store` interface from milestone 1 was designed for this moment.

```text
internal/link/linktest/   a conformance suite every Store must pass      (new)
internal/postgres/        Store on pgx, migrations embedded in the binary (new)
internal/cache/           a caching Store wrapping another Store          (new)
internal/pgtest/          a fresh schema per test                         (new)
cmd/shortener/            chooses the store from the configuration        (changed)
```

## Run it with a database

```bash
docker run -d --name gopath-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pg -p 5432:5432 postgres:16
docker run -d --name gopath-redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7

cd projects/shortener
DATABASE_URL='postgres://postgres:pg@localhost:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable' \
REDIS_ADDR=localhost:6379 LOG_FORMAT=text go run ./cmd/shortener
```

On start-up it applies migrations and logs `migrations applied=[0001_create_links.sql]`; the second start logs `applied=[]`. Without `DATABASE_URL` it still runs in memory, with a warning.

## The Postgres store



```gopath-example
example-375
```



Two translations make it a correct `link.Store`:

- **Unique violation (23505) becomes `link.ErrCodeTaken`.** The primary key on `code` makes the database decide, atomically, which of two concurrent requests for the same custom code wins. The service's retry loop for random codes (milestone 1) keeps working unchanged, because it only looks for `ErrCodeTaken`.
- **`pgx.ErrNoRows` becomes `link.ErrNotFound`**, which the HTTP layer already maps to 404.

And one normalization: pgx returns `timestamptz` values in the local time zone, so `Get` converts to UTC, as the in-memory store returns them.

Migrations are the ones from lesson 13.3, embedded in the binary and applied under an advisory lock.

## One test suite for every store

How do you know the Postgres store behaves like the memory store that all the HTTP tests used? Write the expectations once, as a **conformance suite**, and run it against every implementation:



```gopath-example
example-376
```



Each implementation needs only a few lines:

```go
func TestStoreContract(t *testing.T) {
	linktest.Run(t, func(t *testing.T) link.Store {
		pool := pgtest.Pool(t)          // a fresh, empty schema
		if _, err := postgres.Migrate(context.Background(), pool); err != nil {
			t.Fatal(err)
		}
		return postgres.NewStore(pool)
	})
}
```

The suite runs for `MemoryStore`, the Postgres store, and the cached store. It pins down details that are easy to get subtly different, such as returning `CreatedAt` in UTC even though pgx returns local time, and keeping only microseconds as PostgreSQL does. `ConcurrentCreateSameCode` checks that 20 simultaneous creates of one code produce exactly one success and 19 `ErrCodeTaken`, in memory (a mutex) and in Postgres (the primary key) alike.

This pattern, an exported test suite in a `...test` package, is how the standard library tests interfaces too: `testing/fstest.TestFS` checks any `fs.FS` implementation, and `golang.org/x/net/nettest` does the same for `net.Conn`.

## The cache is just another Store



```gopath-example
example-377
```



`cache.Store` wraps any `link.Store` and is itself a `link.Store`: the decorator pattern, through a one-method-plus-one interface. Links never change after creation, so there is no invalidation, only a TTL to bound memory. Misses are not cached, so a link created a moment after a failed lookup is found immediately. Redis errors fall back to the database (lesson 13.5).

## Choosing the store



```gopath-example
example-378
```



`openStore` builds the chain from configuration: memory or Postgres, optionally wrapped in the cache, and returns one function that closes everything in reverse order (`slices.Backward`, Go 1.23). The database URL is a secret, so it can come from `DATABASE_URL_FILE` (lesson 12.4) and is never logged. Note the different attitude to failures: an unreachable **database** stops start-up (the service cannot work), an unreachable **Redis** only produces a warning (the service works, just slower).

## Tests

```bash
export TEST_DATABASE_URL='postgres://postgres:pg@localhost:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable'
export TEST_REDIS_ADDR=localhost:6379
go test -race ./...
```

Without those variables, the database tests are skipped and the rest still run, so the project stays easy to work on without Docker. CI runs everything, with PostgreSQL 16 and Redis 7 as service containers. `TestRunWithPostgresAndRedis` runs the whole program, as `TestRun` does in memory, against both real servers.

## Your turn

1. Milestone 4 adds `Delete` to the `Store` interface. Before reading it, try it yourself: add the case to the conformance suite **first**, then implement it in each store. What must the cache do on delete, and in which order?
2. Count visits per link. Increment a column with `UPDATE links SET visits = visits + 1` (atomic, lesson 13.4); add the column with a new migration. Does doing this on every redirect undo the benefit of the cache? Consider enqueueing increments in batches (lesson 13.8).
3. Make readiness check the database with a short timeout. Then argue whether it should: what happens to all replicas when the database has a five second hiccup?
headings: One test suite for every store
The cache is just another Store
