lessons.title: 13.8 Project: a PostgreSQL job queue
lessons.description: Build a background job queue on PostgreSQL: transactional enqueue, workers that claim jobs with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, retries with exponential backoff, crash recovery through lock expiry, and graceful shutdown, all tested against a real database.
lessons.body:
## The project

Sending an email, resizing an image, calling a slow partner API: work that should not happen while an HTTP client waits belongs in a **background job queue**. Producers record jobs; workers process them later, retrying failures.

You can use a dedicated broker (RabbitMQ, SQS, Kafka) for this, but many teams start with the PostgreSQL database they already run, and some never leave. This project builds such a queue in about 300 lines, comments included, using the patterns of this module and of Module 7. The code is in [`projects/jobqueue`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/projects/jobqueue).

What it provides:

- Enqueue with a JSON payload, delay and retry limit, **optionally inside your own transaction**.
- Many workers, in one process or many, each job claimed by exactly one of them.
- Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, then `failed` with the last error.
- **Crash recovery**: if a worker dies mid-job, another picks the job up when its lock expires.
- Graceful shutdown that lets running jobs finish.

## The table



```gopath-example
example-379
```



A job moves through `queued` → `running` → `done`, or back to `queued` for a retry, or to `failed`. The partial index covers only jobs that can still run, so it stays small however many finished jobs the table keeps.

## Enqueue, in your transaction



```gopath-example
example-380
```



`EnqueueWith` accepts anything with a `QueryRow` method: the pool, a connection, or a **transaction**. This is the main reason to keep a queue in your own database. Consider "create an order, then queue the confirmation email": with an external broker, the order can commit while the enqueue fails, or the email can be sent for an order that was then rolled back. With the job in the same transaction as the order, both happen or neither does:



```gopath-example
example-381
```



## Claiming a job: SKIP LOCKED



```gopath-example
example-382
```



The inner `SELECT` finds the oldest runnable job and locks it with `FOR UPDATE`. On its own, that would make concurrent workers **wait** for each other's locks, processing jobs one at a time. **`SKIP LOCKED`** tells PostgreSQL to skip rows that another transaction has locked and take the next one. Eight workers claiming at once get eight different jobs, without blocking.

The outer `UPDATE` marks the job `running`, counts the attempt, and sets `locked_until`: the job's **visibility timeout**. The same `WHERE` clause also accepts `running` jobs whose lock has expired. That single condition is the whole crash-recovery mechanism.



```gopath-example
example-383
```



```text
8 workers processed 200 jobs in 159ms
```

Every job processed, each exactly once.

## Finishing, retrying, giving up



```gopath-example
example-384
```



Both updates include `AND attempts = $2`. Suppose a job takes longer than its visibility timeout: its lock expires, another worker claims it (attempts goes from 1 to 2), and then the first worker finishes. Without the check, the first worker would mark a job done that the second is still running. With it, the stale update matches no row. This is **optimistic concurrency control**, with the attempt counter as the version number.

## The worker



```gopath-example
example-385
```



The structure is a worker pool from lesson 7.2, with three production details:

- **Jitter** on the poll interval, so idle workers spread out instead of hitting the database in lockstep.
- **Panics become failures** (`safeCall`), so one bad payload cannot crash the process.
- **Two contexts.** The `Run` context means "stop taking new work". Each job gets its own context with the visibility timeout as its deadline: shutting down does not interrupt a running job, and a job cannot run past its lock without its handler being told.

## Crash recovery, tested



```gopath-example
example-386
```



```text
job 1 reclaimed after 220ms, on attempt 2
```

The test claims a job and abandons it, like a worker killed by the OOM killer. A real worker picks it up once the 200 ms lock expires.

This is also the honest limit of the design: delivery is **at least once**. A worker that sends the email and then dies before marking the job done will cause a second email. Every queue that survives crashes has this property; the remedy is **idempotent handlers**, for example recording "email for order 42 sent" in the same database and checking it first.

## Graceful shutdown



```gopath-example
example-387
```



```text
Run returned 300ms after cancel
```

`Run` returns only after the running job completes. In Kubernetes, set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` longer than your longest job, or a job will be killed mid-way and retried after its lock expires, which is safe, but slower.

## Try the demo

```bash
cd projects/jobqueue
DATABASE_URL='postgres://postgres:pg@localhost:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable' go run ./cmd/demo
```

It enqueues 20 fake emails for 4 workers; every fifth job fails once and is retried with backoff.

## When to use a dedicated broker instead

A PostgreSQL queue is a good fit for up to hundreds of jobs per second, when you value transactional enqueue and one less system to operate. Consider a broker when you need much higher throughput, fan-out of one message to many consumers, or long retention of event streams. Mature Go libraries built on the same Postgres ideas exist too, such as River (`github.com/riverqueue/river`).

## Your turn

1. Replace polling with **`LISTEN/NOTIFY`**: `Enqueue` runs `NOTIFY jobs`, and idle workers wait on `conn.WaitForNotification` with the poll interval as a fallback.
2. Add a **dead-letter** view: an admin endpoint listing `failed` jobs with their last error, and a way to re-queue one.
3. Export metrics (lesson 12.5): jobs processed and failed by queue, processing duration, and the queue depth from `Counts`.
4. Add **unique jobs**: a nullable `unique_key` column with a partial unique index on queued and running jobs, so "send welcome email to user 42" cannot be enqueued twice.

lessons.title: 14.1 flag vs Cobra
lessons.description: Build command-line tools with subcommands using the standard flag package, handle files and standard input, use exit codes properly, make the whole program testable, and see what Cobra adds.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The conventions users expect from a command-line tool
- Subcommands with the standard `flag` package, one `FlagSet` per command
- Reading files or standard input, writing to stdout and stderr
- Exit codes, and how Ctrl+C should behave
- Testing a CLI completely, in-process
- What **Cobra** gives you, and when it is worth the dependency

## Conventions worth following

Unix tools agree on a few rules, and tools that follow them compose with everything else:

- **Results go to stdout, messages to stderr.** Then `tool | jq` works, and errors still reach the terminal.
- **Read the files named as arguments, or standard input if there are none.** Then `tool file.json` and `cat file.json | tool` both work.
- **Exit code 0 means success.** 1 is a general error; 2 is a usage error (the `flag` package exits with 2). Scripts check exit codes, not messages.
- **`-h` prints help**, and is not an error.
- **Ctrl+C stops promptly** and cleanly.

## The example: jsonq

`jsonq` is a small tool with three subcommands, built with only the standard library:

```bash
$ echo '{"name":"Ada","emails":["ada@example.com","countess@example.org"]}' | jsonq get -raw emails.1
countess@example.org
$ jsonq get -h
usage: jsonq get [flags] PATH [FILE...]
  -raw
    	print strings without quotes
```

### main is three lines



```gopath-example
example-388
```



`main` connects the program to the real process: a context cancelled by Ctrl+C, the real arguments and streams, and the exit code. Everything else is in `run`, which takes all of these as parameters. This is the same pattern as the greet CLI (lesson 1.8) and the shortener's `run` (lesson 12.8), and it is what makes the program testable.

### Subcommands



```gopath-example
example-389
```



The `flag` package has no notion of subcommands, but you do not need one: look at `args[0]`, and give each command its own **`flag.FlagSet`**. A table of commands keeps dispatch and the usage message in one place.

Errors are classified once, at the top: wrapping `errUsage` marks errors that are the caller's fault (exit 2), anything else is a runtime error (exit 1), and `flag.ErrHelp` (the user asked for `-h`) is success.



```gopath-example
example-390
```



`flag.ContinueOnError` makes `Parse` **return** errors instead of calling `os.Exit(2)` itself, which is what a testable program needs. `SetOutput` sends the flag package's messages to the command's stderr, and a custom `Usage` adds the positional arguments to the help text.

Note a limitation of `flag`: it stops parsing at the first non-flag argument. `jsonq get emails.1 -raw` treats `-raw` as a file name; flags must come first. Cobra (below) relaxes this.

### Files or standard input



```gopath-example
example-391
```



Reading through an `io.Reader` makes files and stdin the same thing (lesson 8.1). A `json.Decoder` reads value after value, so files with several JSON documents (JSON Lines) work for free. Checking `ctx.Err()` between documents makes Ctrl+C stop the tool cleanly in the middle of a large input.

## Testing the whole CLI



```gopath-example
example-392
```



Because `run` takes its arguments, input and outputs as parameters, a test can execute the whole program in-process, many times per millisecond, and check exactly what a user would see: stdout, stderr and the exit code. No subprocess, no build step. The other tests cover help, unknown commands, missing files and cancellation.

## Cobra

`github.com/spf13/cobra` is the library behind `kubectl`, `docker`, `gh`, `hugo` and many more. Here are two of jsonq's commands in Cobra:



```gopath-example
example-393
```



What you get, compared with `flag`:

- **A command tree**, with nested subcommands (`kubectl config set-context ...`).
- **POSIX-style flags** through `pflag`: `--long` and `-s` short forms, and flags allowed after positional arguments.
- **Persistent flags** inherited by subcommands (`--compact` here, `--namespace` in kubectl).
- **Argument validation** (`cobra.ExactArgs(1)`), and generated help and usage:

```text
Answer simple questions about JSON

Usage:
  jsonq [command]

Available Commands:
  completion  Generate the autocompletion script for the specified shell
  get         Print the value of a top-level key
  help        Help about any command
  keys        Print the top-level keys of an object read from stdin

Flags:
      --compact   print JSON without indentation
  -h, --help      help for jsonq
```

- **Shell completion** for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell, generated: `jsonq completion bash`.

Two habits keep Cobra code testable. Build the tree in a **function** (`NewRootCmd`) instead of package-level variables wired up in `init`, so each test gets a fresh tree. And use `cmd.InOrStdin()`, `cmd.OutOrStdout()` and `RunE` (returning errors) rather than the global `os.Stdin`, `fmt.Println` and `os.Exit`:



```gopath-example
example-394
```



## Which to use

Use **`flag`** for tools with a handful of flags and up to a few subcommands: no dependencies, and everything is visible in a page of code. Most internal tools and many open source ones never need more. Use **Cobra** when the tool grows a real command hierarchy, when users expect GNU-style flags and completion, or when you are building a `kubectl` plugin or another tool in that ecosystem. (`urfave/cli` and `kong` are popular alternatives with different styles.)

## Common mistakes

### Calling os.Exit or log.Fatal deep in the code

Deferred functions do not run, and the code becomes untestable. Return errors to `run`; exit only in `main`.

### Printing errors to stdout

They end up in the next program of a pipeline. Errors go to stderr.

### Exit code 0 on failure

Scripts and CI then believe it worked. Return non-zero on any failure.

### Global state in Cobra commands

Package-level flag variables leak between tests. Build commands in functions.

## Key takeaways

- Results to stdout, messages to stderr; files as arguments or stdin; exit 0, 1 or 2.
- Keep `main` tiny; put the program in `run(ctx, args, stdin, stdout, stderr) int` and test it in-process.
- With `flag`, use one `FlagSet` per subcommand with `ContinueOnError`; classify errors once at the top.
- Cobra adds command trees, POSIX flags, persistent flags, generated help and shell completion; build its commands in functions and use `RunE` and the command's streams.

## Further reading

- [Package flag](https://pkg.go.dev/flag)
- [Cobra user guide](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/main/site/content/user_guide.md)
- [Command Line Interface Guidelines](https://clig.dev/)

unix tools agree on a few rules, and tools that follow them compose with everything else:

- results go to stdout, messages to stderr. then tool | jq works, and errors still reach the terminal.
- read the files named as arguments, or standard input if there are none. then tool file.json and cat file.json | tool both work.
- exit code 0 means success. 1 is a general error; 2 is a usage error (the flag package exits with 2). scripts check exit codes, not messages.
- -h prints help, and is not an error.
- ctrl+c stops promptly and cleanly.

 the example: jsonq

jsonq is a small tool with three subcommands, built with only the standard library:



 main is three lines







main connects the program to the real process: a context cancelled by ctrl+c, the real arguments and streams, and the exit code. everything else is in run, which takes all of these as parameters. this is the same pattern as the greet cli (lesson 1.8) and the shortener's run (lesson 12.8), and it is what makes the program testable.

 subcommands







the flag package has no notion of subcommands, but you do not need one: look at args[0], and give each command its own flag.flagset. a table of commands keeps dispatch and the usage message in one place.

errors are classified once, at the top: wrapping errusage marks errors that are the caller's fault (exit 2), anything else is a runtime error (exit 1), and flag.errhelp (the user asked for -h) is success.







flag.continueonerror makes parse return errors instead of calling os.exit(2) itself, which is what a testable program needs. setoutput sends the flag package's messages to the command's stderr, and a custom usage adds the positional arguments to the help text.

note a limitation of flag: it stops parsing at the first non-flag argument. jsonq get emails.1 -raw treats -raw as a file name; flags must come first. cobra (below) relaxes this.

 files or standard input







reading through an io.reader makes files and stdin the same thing (lesson 8.1). a json.decoder reads value after value, so files with several json documents (json lines) work for free. checking ctx.err() between documents makes ctrl+c stop the tool cleanly in the middle of a large input.

 testing the whole cli







because run takes its arguments, input and outputs as parameters, a test can execute the whole program in-process, many times per millisecond, and check exactly what a user would see: stdout, stderr and the exit code. no subprocess, no build step. the other tests cover help, unknown commands, missing files and cancellation.

 cobra

github.com/spf13/cobra is the library behind kubectl, docker, gh, hugo and many more. here are two of jsonq's commands in cobra:







what you get, compared with flag:

- a command tree, with nested subcommands (kubectl config set-context ...).
- posix-style flags through pflag: --long and -s short forms, and flags allowed after positional arguments.
- persistent flags inherited by subcommands (--compact here, --namespace in kubectl).
- argument validation (cobra.exactargs(1)), and generated help and usage:



- shell completion for bash, zsh, fish and powershell, generated: jsonq completion bash.

two habits keep cobra code testable. build the tree in a function (newrootcmd) instead of package-level variables wired up in init, so each test gets a fresh tree. and use cmd.inorstdin(), cmd.outorstdout() and rune (returning errors) rather than the global os.stdin, fmt.println and os.exit:







 which to use

use flag for tools with a handful of flags and up to a few subcommands: no dependencies, and everything is visible in a page of code. most internal tools and many open source ones never need more. use cobra when the tool grows a real command hierarchy, when users expect gnu-style flags and completion, or when you are building a kubectl plugin or another tool in that ecosystem. (urfave/cli and kong are popular alternatives with different styles.)

 common mistakes

 calling os.exit or log.fatal deep in the code

deferred functions do not run, and the code becomes untestable. return errors to run; exit only in main.

 printing errors to stdout

they end up in the next program of a pipeline. errors go to stderr.

 exit code 0 on failure

scripts and ci then believe it worked. return non-zero on any failure.

 global state in cobra commands

package-level flag variables leak between tests. build commands in functions.

 key takeaways

- results to stdout, messages to stderr; files as arguments or stdin; exit 0, 1 or 2.
- keep main tiny; put the program in run(ctx, args, stdin, stdout, stderr) int and test it in-process.
- with flag, use one flagset per subcommand with continueonerror; classify errors once at the top.
- cobra adds command trees, posix flags, persistent flags, generated help and shell completion; build its commands in functions and use rune and the command's streams.

 further reading

- [package flag](https://pkg.go.dev/flag)
- [cobra user guide](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/main/site/content/userguide.md)
- [command line interface guidelines](https://clig.dev/)

lessons.title: 14.2 Configuration for CLIs: files, environment and flags
lessons.description: Give a CLI layered configuration with a predictable order of precedence: defaults, a config file in the user's config directory, environment variables and flags, using flag.Visit to know which flags were actually set.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The standard order of precedence for CLI configuration
- Where config files belong: `os.UserConfigDir`
- Telling "flag not given" apart from "flag given with its default value" with `flag.Visit`
- Strict config files that reject typos
- Showing users where each setting came from

## The idea

A service gets its configuration from the environment (lesson 12.4). A CLI is used by people, interactively and in scripts, so it usually accepts several sources, each overriding the previous one:

```text
defaults  <  config file  <  environment variables  <  command-line flags
```

The logic: the config file holds a user's long-term preferences, environment variables adjust them for a shell session or a CI job, and a flag is the most specific, deliberate choice for one run. `git`, `kubectl`, `aws` and most well-behaved tools follow this order.

## The loader



```gopath-example
example-395
```



The interesting line is **`fs.Visit`**. A flag's default value cannot be told apart from a value the user typed by looking at the variable: if `-timeout` defaults to `0` and the environment says `5s`, did the user type `-timeout 0`? `fs.Visit` calls its function only for flags that were **set on the command line**, while `fs.VisitAll` visits all of them. Applying flags inside `Visit` means an unset flag never overrides the file or the environment.

That is also why the flags are declared with empty defaults, and the real defaults live in the `Config` literal: the help text explains them in words instead.

## The config file



```gopath-example
example-396
```



- **Location.** `os.UserConfigDir()` returns the platform's convention: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` or `~/.config` on Linux, `~/Library/Application Support` on macOS, `%AppData%` on Windows. Put files in a subdirectory named after the tool.
- **Optional, unless asked for.** A missing default file is normal. A missing file the user named explicitly (with `-config` or `SHORTCTL_CONFIG`) is an error.
- **Pointers for "not set".** `*string` fields distinguish a key that is absent from a key set to `""`.
- **Strict.** `DisallowUnknownFields` turns `"sever": "..."` into an error instead of a silently ignored setting.

JSON keeps this dependency-free. Many tools prefer YAML or TOML for config files people edit by hand, which need a third party package; the layering logic is the same.

## Precedence, demonstrated



```gopath-example
example-397
```



The file sets the server and a 3s timeout, the environment overrides the timeout to 5s, and a flag sets the output format. Recording the **source** of each value costs a few lines and saves a lot of confused debugging: a `shortctl config` command that prints this table is a feature users love ("why is it talking to staging?").

## Common mistakes

### Flag defaults overriding the environment

Applying every flag value, set or not, silently discards the file and environment. Use `fs.Visit`.

### Config files in the home directory root

`~/.mytoolrc` clutters home directories. Use `os.UserConfigDir()`.

### Ignoring unknown keys

Typos then do nothing, silently. Reject them.

### Secrets in flags

Command lines are visible to other users of the machine (`ps`) and saved in shell history. Read tokens from environment variables, files, or the OS keychain.

## Key takeaways

- Order sources as defaults < config file < environment < flags.
- Use `flag.Visit` to apply only the flags the user actually set.
- Keep config files in `os.UserConfigDir()`, optional by default, strict about unknown keys.
- Track where each setting came from, and say so in error messages.

## Further reading

- [Package flag: Visit](https://pkg.go.dev/flag#FlagSet.Visit)
- [os.UserConfigDir](https://pkg.go.dev/os#UserConfigDir)
- [XDG Base Directory Specification](https://specifications.freedesktop.org/basedir-spec/latest/)

lessons.title: 14.3 Code generation with go generate
lessons.description: Generate Go code instead of writing it by hand: go:generate directives, running tools pinned with the go.mod tool directive (Go 1.24), writing your own generator with go/types and text/template, and keeping generated code honest in CI.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What `go generate` does, and what it deliberately does not do
- Running a pinned generator with `go tool` and the **`tool` directive** (Go 1.24)
- Writing your own generator with `go/parser`, `go/types` and `text/template`
- The conventions for generated files
- Making sure generated code never goes stale

## The idea

Some code is mechanical: `String` methods for enum constants, mocks for interfaces, Go types from a protobuf or OpenAPI schema, database access code from SQL queries. Writing it by hand is tedious and error-prone; generating it means changing one source and re-running a tool.

`go generate` is the standard way to run such tools. It scans Go files for comments like:

```go
//go:generate go tool stringer -type=Level -trimprefix=Level
```

and runs each command in the directory of the file that contains it. That is all it does. It is **not** part of `go build`: you run it yourself when the inputs change, and you **commit the generated files**. This keeps builds simple and fast, and means people using your package never need your generators installed.

```bash
go generate ./...     # run every directive in the module
```

## Pinned tools: the tool directive (Go 1.24)

Generators are programs, and everyone on a team should run the same version. Since Go 1.24, a module can declare tools in `go.mod`:

```bash
go get -tool golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer
```

adds a line to `go.mod`, and the version to the `require` block:

```text
tool golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer
```

Now `go tool stringer` builds and runs exactly that version, with no separate installation and no `tools.go` file with blank imports (the old workaround). The `examples/thirdparty` module does this:



```gopath-example
example-398
```



Running `go generate` there writes `level_string.go`:



```gopath-example
example-399
```



Two details of `stringer`'s output are worth noticing. The strange `func _()` block is a **compile-time check**: if someone renumbers the constants without regenerating, an array index goes out of range and the build fails. And all names are packed into one string with an index table, avoiding a `switch` and allocations.

## Writing your own generator

When no existing tool fits, writing one is easier than it sounds, because the standard library ships the Go parser and type checker. This generator produces `String`, `Parse`, `Values` and text marshaling methods for an enum type:



```gopath-example
example-400
```



The generator is a normal Go program in the same module, run with `go run`:



```gopath-example
example-401
```



The steps every generator follows:

1. **Parse** the package's files with `go/parser` (skipping tests and its own output).
2. **Type-check** them with `go/types`. This is what makes the generator reliable: the type checker evaluates `iota` and constant expressions, so `ColorRed Color = iota + 1` is known to be 1 without the generator interpreting anything itself.
3. **Collect** the facts it needs: here, every constant whose type is `Color`.
4. **Render** code with `text/template`:



```gopath-example
example-402
```



5. **Format** with `go/format`, so the output is always `gofmt`-clean.

The result is used like hand-written code:



```gopath-example
example-403
```



Because the generated type implements `encoding.TextMarshaler`, JSON encodes it as `"red"` rather than `1`; the same methods also make it work with `flag.TextVar` and in `slog` output.

## Conventions for generated files

- Start the file with a comment matching `^// Code generated .* DO NOT EDIT\.$` (the convention is documented in `go help generate`). Tools recognize it: linters such as golangci-lint skip such files by default, coverage and review tools can leave them out, and GitHub collapses them in pull request diffs. Both generators above follow it.
- Name the file after its source and generator: `level_string.go`, `color_enum.go`.
- Put the `//go:generate` line next to the declaration it is about.
- Never edit generated files by hand. Change the input or the generator, and regenerate.

## Keeping generated code honest

The risk with committed generated code is that someone changes the input and forgets to regenerate. Two defenses, both used in this course:



```gopath-example
example-404
```



A **test** that runs the generator in memory and compares with the committed file. And a **CI step** that regenerates everything and fails if anything changed:

```yaml
- name: Generated code is up to date
  run: |
    go generate ./...
    git diff --exit-code
```

## Generators you will meet

| Tool | Generates |
|---|---|
| `stringer` (golang.org/x/tools) | `String` methods for constants |
| `protoc-gen-go`, `buf` | Go types and gRPC code from protobuf |
| `oapi-codegen`, `ogen` | servers and clients from OpenAPI |
| `sqlc` | type-safe database code from SQL queries |
| `mockgen`, `moq` | mocks from interfaces |
| `controller-gen` | Kubernetes CRDs and deep-copy methods (Module 15) |

## When not to generate

Generics (Module 4) removed the most common reason for generators before Go 1.18: writing the same container or algorithm for several types. Prefer a generic function to generated copies. And `//go:embed` (lesson 8.5) is the right tool for including static files; do not generate Go source from them.

## Common mistakes

### Expecting go build to run generators

It never does. Run `go generate` and commit the output.

### Unpinned generator versions

Different developers produce different output, and diffs churn. Use the `tool` directive.

### Editing generated files

The next `go generate` erases the change.

### Generated code that is not gofmt-clean

Run the output through `go/format.Source`.

## Key takeaways

- `go generate` runs `//go:generate` commands; it is a developer tool, not part of the build. Commit generated files.
- Pin generators with `go get -tool` and run them with `go tool name` (Go 1.24).
- Write generators with `go/parser` + `go/types` (to understand the code) and `text/template` + `go/format` (to write it).
- Mark files with `// Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.`, and check freshness with a test or `git diff --exit-code` in CI.

## Further reading

- [Generating code](https://go.dev/blog/generate) on the Go blog
- [go.mod reference: tool directive](https://go.dev/ref/mod#go-mod-file-tool)
- [Package go/types](https://pkg.go.dev/go/types), and Alan Donovan's [go/types tutorial](https://github.com/golang/example/tree/master/gotypes)

lessons.title: 14.4 Releasing binaries
lessons.description: Ship Go binaries people can trust: the version and VCS information the toolchain embeds (Go 1.24 stamps the module version from git tags), cross-compilation, reproducible builds verified by checksum, GoReleaser, and checking for known vulnerabilities.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What the Go toolchain records in every binary, and how to read it with `go version -m`
- How Go 1.24 stamps the main module's version from your git tag
- When you still need `-ldflags -X`
- Cross-compiling for every platform from one machine
- Reproducible builds, checked by comparing checksums
- Releasing with GoReleaser, and scanning for vulnerabilities with `govulncheck`

## What a binary knows about itself

Every Go binary carries its build information: the Go version, the module path and version, every dependency with its version and checksum, the build settings, and version control details. `go version -m` prints it. Here is the greet CLI (lesson 1.8), built from a git checkout tagged `v1.4.0`:

```text
$ go version -m dist/greet_linux_amd64_v1/greet
dist/greet_linux_amd64_v1/greet: go1.27.2
	path	github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/projects/greet/cmd/greet
	mod	github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy	v1.4.0
	build	-buildmode=exe
	build	-compiler=gc
	build	-trimpath=true
	build	DefaultGODEBUG=containermaxprocs=0,...,updatemaxprocs=0,...
	build	CGO_ENABLED=0
	build	GOARCH=amd64
	build	GOOS=linux
	build	GOAMD64=v1
	build	vcs=git
	build	vcs.revision=0c493c488ab4c76d293de9b7580151f174c04a6b
	build	vcs.time=2026-10-16T12:19:20Z
	build	vcs.modified=false
```

A program reads the same data with `runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo()` (lesson 1.8 showed it). Three lines deserve attention:

- **`mod ... v1.4.0`.** Since **Go 1.24**, `go build` sets the main module's version from the VCS tag on the current commit, or a pseudo-version for untagged commits, with `+dirty` added when the working tree has uncommitted changes. Before Go 1.24, local builds always said `(devel)`. A test build of the same tree with an untracked `dist/` folder in it said `v1.4.0+dirty`, which is why build output directories belong in `.gitignore`.
- **`vcs.revision`, `vcs.time`, `vcs.modified`** are recorded automatically too (since Go 1.18), unless you build with `-buildvcs=false`.
- **`DefaultGODEBUG`** lists the compatibility settings this binary uses. The course's main module says `go 1.24` in `go.mod`, so even though Go 1.27 built it, the binary keeps Go 1.24's behavior, including `containermaxprocs=0` and `updatemaxprocs=0`: the container-aware `GOMAXPROCS` of lesson 11.1 is **off**. Raising the `go` line in `go.mod` turns it on. This line is how you check.

So for many tools, `debug.ReadBuildInfo()` already gives a correct version, with nothing to configure. The shortctl client (lesson 14.6) does exactly that.

## When to use -ldflags -X

`-ldflags "-X importpath.name=value"` sets a package-level string variable at link time. It is still useful when:

- you want a version string formatted your own way, or a build date (build info records the commit time, not the build time);
- the build happens outside a git checkout, for example from a source tarball, where there is no VCS information;
- you build with a release tool that knows the version better than the checkout does.

The greet project uses both: `-X` for a human-friendly version line, and build info is there anyway.

## Cross-compiling

The Go toolchain compiles for any supported platform from any other, with two environment variables:

```bash
GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build -o greet.exe ./cmd/greet
GOOS=darwin  GOARCH=arm64 go build -o greet-mac ./cmd/greet
go tool dist list    # every supported GOOS/GOARCH pair
```

The one thing that breaks this is **cgo**: C code needs a C cross-compiler for the target. With `CGO_ENABLED=0`, Go uses pure Go implementations (for example of DNS resolution) and produces a **static binary** with no dependency on the system's C library, which also runs in the smallest container images (lesson 15.1). Prefer pure Go dependencies for tools you distribute; SQLite drivers, for instance, exist in both forms.

## Reproducible builds

Go builds are reproducible: the same source, Go version and settings produce byte-identical binaries on any machine (and since Go 1.21, so are the Go toolchain downloads themselves). Two things you add:

- **`-trimpath`** removes your local file paths from the binary (they otherwise appear in stack traces and break reproducibility between machines).
- **Fixed timestamps** in archives. GoReleaser's `mod_timestamp: "{{ .CommitTimestamp }}"` sets file times to the commit time instead of "now".

The proof is cheap. Building all six greet archives twice, with the build cache wiped in between, gave identical checksums:

```text
$ diff first/checksums.txt dist/checksums.txt && echo identical
identical
```

Reproducibility lets anyone verify that a published binary was built from the source it claims, which is increasingly expected for anything security sensitive.

## GoReleaser

Building six platforms, archiving, writing checksums, generating a changelog and publishing a GitHub release by hand is tedious. **GoReleaser** does all of it from one config file:



```gopath-example
example-405
```



Try it without publishing anything:

```bash
cd projects/greet
goreleaser check                     # validate the config
goreleaser release --snapshot --clean
```

```text
  • building binaries
    • building    paths=cmd/greet binaries=greet target=linux_amd64_v1
    ...
  • archives
    • archiving   name=dist/greet_1.4.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz
    ...
  • calculating checksums
  • release succeeded
```

In a repository of its own, the release flow is: push a tag (`git tag v1.4.0 && git push --tags`), and a CI job runs `goreleaser release`, which builds everything and creates the GitHub release with the archives and `checksums.txt` attached. This course's repository holds many projects, so its workflow (`.github/workflows/greet-release.yml`) runs in snapshot mode and uploads the archives as a build artifact instead; the comments in the file show the two lines to change for real releases. GoReleaser can also publish Homebrew formulas, Linux packages, container images and signed checksums.

## Known vulnerabilities

Before releasing, check your dependencies and the standard library for known vulnerabilities:

```bash
go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest
govulncheck ./...
```

`govulncheck` uses the Go vulnerability database and, unlike most scanners, analyzes **which functions you actually call**: a vulnerable package you import but whose vulnerable function you never reach is reported separately, as informational. That keeps the signal high. The course's CI runs it on every module.

Keep the Go toolchain itself up to date too: security fixes for the standard library ship in minor releases (1.27.1, 1.27.2, ...), and a rebuilt binary is the only way to get them.

## Common mistakes

### Version "dev" in released binaries

Release from a clean, tagged checkout, or stamp the version explicitly.

### Build directories inside the repository, not ignored

They make every build `+dirty`. Add them to `.gitignore`.

### cgo enabled by accident

A dependency that needs cgo silently breaks cross-compilation and static binaries. Build releases with `CGO_ENABLED=0` and notice when that fails.

### No checksums

Users cannot verify downloads. Always publish `checksums.txt`.

## Key takeaways

- `go version -m` (and `debug.ReadBuildInfo`) show a binary's Go version, dependencies, build settings and VCS revision.
- Since Go 1.24, the module version comes from your git tag automatically, with `+dirty` for uncommitted changes.
- `DefaultGODEBUG` reveals which compatibility behaviors your `go.mod` line selected.
- Cross-compile with `GOOS`/`GOARCH`; `CGO_ENABLED=0` gives static, portable binaries.
- `-trimpath` plus fixed timestamps give reproducible builds; verify by comparing checksums.
- GoReleaser turns a tag into a full release; `govulncheck` checks what you actually call.

## Further reading

- [Go 1.24 release notes: go build version stamping](https://go.dev/doc/go1.24#go-command)
- [Perfectly Reproducible, Verified Go Toolchains](https://go.dev/blog/rebuild) on the Go blog
- [GoReleaser documentation](https://goreleaser.com/)
- [govulncheck tutorial](https://go.dev/doc/tutorial/govulncheck)

lessons.title: 14.5 Exercise: a to-do CLI
lessons.description: Build a small command-line tool from a specification: global flags, subcommands with their own flags, configuration from flag or environment, file storage, and correct exit codes.
lessons.body:
## The task



```gopath-exercise
m14/todo
```



```bash
cd exercises
go test ./m14/todo
```

A session with the finished tool looks like this:

```text
$ todo add buy milk
added 1. buy milk
$ todo add write tests
added 2. write tests
$ todo done 2
$ todo list -all
1. buy milk
2. [x] write tests
$ todo done 7; echo "exit $?"
todo: no item 7 (the list has 2)
exit 1
$ todo remove 1; echo "exit $?"
todo: usage: unknown command "remove"
exit 2
```

## Hints



```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-12
```





```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-13
```





```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-14
```



The reference solution is in `exercises/m14/todo/solution.go`. Notice how `save` in `store.go` writes a temporary file and renames it: a crash in the middle of saving can never leave a half-written list, because a rename within one directory is atomic.

- Wire it to a real `main` package and try `go install` and `go version -m` on the result (lesson 14.4).

lessons.title: 14.6 Project: shortctl, a CLI for the shortener
lessons.description: Build a command-line client for the shortener API: layered configuration, text or JSON output, problem details turned into clear errors, proper exit codes, and tests that run the real API in-process.
lessons.body:
## The project

Services get command-line clients: `kubectl` for Kubernetes, `gh` for GitHub, `stripe` for Stripe. **shortctl** is the shortener's, and it uses every lesson of this module. It lives next to the server, in [`projects/shortener/cmd/shortctl`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/projects/shortener/cmd/shortctl), so the two can share tests.

```text
$ shortctl create -code godoc https://go.dev/doc
http://localhost:8080/godoc

$ shortctl get godoc
http://localhost:8080/godoc -> https://go.dev/doc (created 2026-10-16 12:25 UTC)

$ shortctl -output json get godoc
{
  "code": "godoc",
  "url": "https://go.dev/doc",
  "short_url": "http://localhost:8080/godoc",
  "created_at": "2026-10-16T12:25:10.316877532Z"
}

$ shortctl create -code godoc https://go.dev; echo "exit $?"
shortctl: create "godoc": code already in use (HTTP 409)
exit 1

$ shortctl get; echo "exit $?"
shortctl: usage: get needs exactly one CODE
exit 2
```

That output is from a real run against the shortener service from Module 12.

## Try it

```bash
cd projects/shortener
go run ./cmd/shortener &                     # the API, in memory
go run ./cmd/shortctl create https://go.dev  # prints a short URL
go run ./cmd/shortctl -h
```

Point it at another server with `-server`, `SHORTCTL_SERVER`, or a config file at `<user config dir>/shortctl/config.json`:

```json
{"server": "https://sho.rt", "timeout": "5s"}
```

## The structure

`main` is three lines (lesson 14.1). `run` loads configuration, picks the command, and turns errors into exit codes in one place:



```gopath-example
example-406
```



Configuration (`config.go`) is the layered loader of lesson 14.2: defaults, then the config file, then `SHORTCTL_*` variables, then only the flags actually given, found with `fs.Visit`.

Output has two modes. **Text** is a single line for people; **JSON** (`-output json`) is for scripts, so `shortctl -output json get godoc | jq -r .url` works. Offering both is cheap with a small `printer` type, and it saves users from parsing text with `awk`.

## The API client



```gopath-example
example-407
```



Things to notice:

- **A timeout on the `http.Client`** (lesson 8.7), configurable, and the request carries the command's context, so Ctrl+C cancels a slow request.
- **Error responses are decoded.** The server answers errors with problem details (lesson 12.3), so the client shows the server's `detail`, `create "godoc": code already in use`, plus the status. If the body is not JSON (a proxy's HTML error page, say), it falls back to the status text.
- **The response body is limited** with `io.LimitReader`, so a misbehaving server cannot make the client read gigabytes.
- **Network errors say what was unreachable**: `cannot reach http://localhost:8080: ... connection refused`.
- **`url.PathEscape`** for the code in the path, even though the server validates codes: never build URLs from unescaped input.

## Testing against the real API



```gopath-example
example-408
```



The tests start the **real** HTTP handler from `internal/httpapi` with an in-memory store on an `httptest.Server`, and run shortctl's `run` against it. This tests the client and the server's contract together: if the API changes a field name or a status code, these tests fail. It is only possible because both live in one module; for a client in another repository, the same idea becomes a contract test against a recorded or shared specification.

## Version

`shortctl version` prints `debug.ReadBuildInfo().Main.Version`. Built with `go install github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/projects/shortener/cmd/shortctl@v1.0.0`, it prints `v1.0.0`; built from a tagged git checkout with Go 1.24 or later, it prints the tag (lesson 14.4). No `-ldflags` needed.

## Your turn

1. Add `shortctl open CODE`, which opens the target URL in the browser (`xdg-open`, `open` or `rundll32` depending on `runtime.GOOS`).
2. Add `shortctl config`, printing the effective configuration and where each value came from (lesson 14.2's `Source` map).
3. Add a `-quiet` flag that prints only the short URL, for use in scripts: `url=$(shortctl -quiet create https://go.dev)`.
4. Add `shortctl` to the greet project's release setup (lesson 14.4): a second build in `.goreleaser.yaml`.

## Module 14 recap

You can now build command-line tools that behave the way users and scripts expect, with the standard `flag` package or Cobra; configure them from files, environment and flags in a predictable order; generate code with pinned tools or your own generator; and ship reproducible, versioned binaries for every platform with GoReleaser.

Next is **[Module 15: Go for cloud native](/learn/15-cloud-native/)**, where the shortener goes into a container and onto Kubernetes, and you write Go that talks to Kubernetes itself.

lessons.title: 15.1 Containerizing Go
lessons.description: Build small, secure container images for Go services: multi-stage Dockerfiles with build caches, static binaries, distroless versus scratch versus alpine, numeric non-root users, and multi-platform builds.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- Why Go is unusually easy to containerize
- A production multi-stage Dockerfile, line by line
- Layer caching and BuildKit cache mounts: a 62 second build becomes 1.6 seconds
- Choosing a base image: distroless, scratch, alpine
- Why `USER 65532` and not `USER nonroot`
- Multi-platform images, and `ko`

## Why Go is easy to containerize

A container image needs everything the program needs at run time. For an interpreted language that means the interpreter, libraries and packages. A Go program built with `CGO_ENABLED=0` is a **single static binary** (lesson 14.4): no runtime, no shared libraries. The image can contain that file and almost nothing else.

That makes images small (fast to pull, fast to start a new pod) and secure (nothing to exploit: no shell, no package manager, no extra libraries with their own vulnerabilities).

## The Dockerfile

This is the shortener's (milestone 4):



```gopath-example
example-409
```



Two **stages**. The `build` stage has the full Go toolchain, about 400 MB, and produces the binary. The final stage starts again from a tiny base and copies in only the binary. Nothing from the build stage, not the toolchain and not the source code, ends up in the final image.

Notes on each part:

- **`COPY go.mod go.sum` and `go mod download` come first.** Docker caches each step and reruns a step only if its inputs changed. Dependencies change rarely and code changes constantly, so downloading them in their own step means a code change does not re-download them. (`go.sum` must exist: run `go mod tidy` once and commit it.)
- **`--mount=type=cache`** (BuildKit) keeps the module cache and the **Go build cache** between builds, outside the image. Without it, every build compiles every dependency from scratch.
- **`CGO_ENABLED=0`, `-trimpath`, `-ldflags="-s -w"`**: a static binary, no local paths, no debug symbols (lesson 14.4).
- **`TARGETOS` and `TARGETARCH`**: see multi-platform builds below.
- **`.dockerignore`** keeps `.git`, tests and manifests out of the build context, so they cannot invalidate the cache or leak into the image.

The effect of the cache mounts, measured while writing this lesson:

```text
first build:                         62 s   (compiling pgx, Prometheus client, go-redis, ...)
rebuild after changing one .go file:  1.6 s
```

The image itself:

```text
$ docker history shortener:dev
SIZE      CREATED BY
0B        ENTRYPOINT ["/shortener"]
0B        EXPOSE [8080/tcp 9090/tcp]
0B        USER 65532:65532
16MB      COPY /out/shortener /shortener # buildkit
...                                         (the distroless base)
```

The whole image is about 24 MB, of which 16 MB is the binary. It starts in milliseconds and contains no shell:

```text
$ docker exec sh1 sh
OCI runtime exec failed: exec failed: unable to start container process: exec: "sh": executable file not found in $PATH
```

## Choosing a base image

| Base | Size | Contains | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `scratch` | 0 | nothing at all | You add CA certificates and time zone data yourself (or embed them with `import _ "time/tzdata"`). |
| `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12` | about 2 MB | CA certificates, time zone data, `/etc/passwd` with a `nonroot` user | The default for static Go binaries. |
| `alpine` | about 8 MB | a shell, `apk` | You need to debug inside the container, or the program shells out to tools. |
| `debian`/`ubuntu` slim | 30+ MB | glibc and a shell | The binary needs cgo and glibc. |

Distroless is the usual choice: everything a Go program needs (CA certificates for outgoing HTTPS, time zone data for `time.LoadLocation`) and nothing else. The "no shell" property surprises people when they first try `kubectl exec`; use `kubectl debug` with an ephemeral debug container instead, which attaches a container that has tools to the running pod.

## Run as a numeric non-root user

Containers run as root by default. If an attacker breaks out of your process, root inside the container is one step closer to root on the node. Every image should run as an unprivileged user, and Kubernetes can enforce it with `runAsNonRoot: true` (lesson 15.2).

Here is a trap this course fell into while testing the operator in lesson 15.4. The Dockerfile said `USER nonroot:nonroot`, and Kubernetes refused to start the pod:

```text
Error: container has runAsNonRoot and image has non-numeric user (nonroot), cannot verify user is non-root
```

Kubernetes cannot look inside the image's `/etc/passwd` to find out whether `nonroot` is UID 0. With a **numeric** user (`USER 65532:65532`, which is distroless's `nonroot`), it can verify. All Dockerfiles in this course now use the number.

## Multi-platform images

Your laptop may be arm64 (Apple silicon) while the cluster runs amd64, or the reverse; many clusters now run both. `docker buildx` builds one image for several platforms:

```bash
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t ghcr.io/you/shortener:v1.0.0 --push .
```

For each platform, BuildKit sets `TARGETOS` and `TARGETARCH`. Because the build stage passes them to `go build`, Go **cross-compiles** each binary natively on the build machine, which takes seconds, instead of building under slow CPU emulation. This is one of Go's quiet advantages: in many other languages, a multi-platform image means emulating the other architecture for the whole build.

## ko: no Dockerfile at all

For Go services there is an even simpler option: **ko** (`github.com/ko-build/ko`) builds a Go main package straight into an image on a distroless base, without a Dockerfile and without Docker:

```bash
KO_DOCKER_REPO=ghcr.io/you ko build ./cmd/shortener
```

It uses the Go build cache, produces multi-platform and reproducible images, and is used by projects such as Knative and Tekton. The trade-off is less control over what goes into the image.

## Common mistakes

### Copying everything before downloading modules

Every code change then re-downloads every dependency. Copy `go.mod` and `go.sum` first.

### Shipping the toolchain

A single-stage build produces a 1 GB image with your source code in it. Use two stages.

### Running as root, or as a named user

Use `USER 65532:65532`, and `runAsNonRoot` in the pod.

### Forgetting CA certificates with scratch

Every outgoing HTTPS request then fails with `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority`. Use distroless, or copy the certificates.

## Key takeaways

- Go builds static binaries, so the runtime image can be almost empty: about 24 MB for the shortener, mostly the binary.
- Multi-stage Dockerfiles: build with the toolchain, copy only the binary into distroless.
- Order steps for caching and use BuildKit cache mounts; rebuilds went from 62 s to 1.6 s.
- Run as a numeric non-root user so Kubernetes can enforce `runAsNonRoot`.
- Multi-platform images build fast because Go cross-compiles; `ko` builds Go images without a Dockerfile.

## Further reading

- [Docker: multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)
- [Distroless images](https://github.com/GoogleContainerTools/distroless)
- [ko](https://ko.build/)

 why go is easy to containerize

a container image needs everything the program needs at run time. for an interpreted language that means the interpreter, libraries and packages. a go program built with cgoenabled=0 is a single static binary (lesson 14.4): no runtime, no shared libraries. the image can contain that file and almost nothing else.

that makes images small (fast to pull, fast to start a new pod) and secure (nothing to exploit: no shell, no package manager, no extra libraries with their own vulnerabilities).

 the dockerfile

this is the shortener's (milestone 4):







two stages. the build stage has the full go toolchain, about 400 mb, and produces the binary. the final stage starts again from a tiny base and copies in only the binary. nothing from the build stage, not the toolchain and not the source code, ends up in the final image.

notes on each part:

- copy go.mod go.sum and go mod download come first. docker caches each step and reruns a step only if its inputs changed. dependencies change rarely and code changes constantly, so downloading them in their own step means a code change does not re-download them. (go.sum must exist: run go mod tidy once and commit it.)
- --mount=type=cache (buildkit) keeps the module cache and the go build cache between builds, outside the image. without it, every build compiles every dependency from scratch.
- cgoenabled=0, -trimpath, -ldflags="-s -w": a static binary, no local paths, no debug symbols (lesson 14.4).
- targetos and targetarch: see multi-platform builds below.
- .dockerignore keeps .git, tests and manifests out of the build context, so they cannot invalidate the cache or leak into the image.

the effect of the cache mounts, measured while writing this lesson:



the image itself:



the whole image is about 24 mb, of which 16 mb is the binary. it starts in milliseconds and contains no shell:



 choosing a base image

| base | size | contains | use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| scratch | 0 | nothing at all | you add ca certificates and time zone data yourself (or embed them with import  "time/tzdata"). |
| gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12 | about 2 mb | ca certificates, time zone data, /etc/passwd with a nonroot user | the default for static go binaries. |
| alpine | about 8 mb | a shell, apk | you need to debug inside the container, or the program shells out to tools. |
| debian/ubuntu slim | 30+ mb | glibc and a shell | the binary needs cgo and glibc. |

distroless is the usual choice: everything a go program needs (ca certificates for outgoing https, time zone data for time.loadlocation) and nothing else. the "no shell" property surprises people when they first try kubectl exec; use kubectl debug with an ephemeral debug container instead, which attaches a container that has tools to the running pod.

 run as a numeric non-root user

containers run as root by default. if an attacker breaks out of your process, root inside the container is one step closer to root on the node. every image should run as an unprivileged user, and kubernetes can enforce it with runasnonroot: true (lesson 15.2).

here is a trap this course fell into while testing the operator in lesson 15.4. the dockerfile said user nonroot:nonroot, and kubernetes refused to start the pod:



kubernetes cannot look inside the image's /etc/passwd to find out whether nonroot is uid 0. with a numeric user (user 65532:65532, which is distroless's nonroot), it can verify. all dockerfiles in this course now use the number.

 multi-platform images

your laptop may be arm64 (apple silicon) while the cluster runs amd64, or the reverse; many clusters now run both. docker buildx builds one image for several platforms:



for each platform, buildkit sets targetos and targetarch. because the build stage passes them to go build, go cross-compiles each binary natively on the build machine, which takes seconds, instead of building under slow cpu emulation. this is one of go's quiet advantages: in many other languages, a multi-platform image means emulating the other architecture for the whole build.

 ko: no dockerfile at all

for go services there is an even simpler option: ko (github.com/ko-build/ko) builds a go main package straight into an image on a distroless base, without a dockerfile and without docker:



it uses the go build cache, produces multi-platform and reproducible images, and is used by projects such as knative and tekton. the trade-off is less control over what goes into the image.

 common mistakes

 copying everything before downloading modules

every code change then re-downloads every dependency. copy go.mod and go.sum first.

 shipping the toolchain

a single-stage build produces a 1 gb image with your source code in it. use two stages.

 running as root, or as a named user

use user 65532:65532, and runasnonroot in the pod.

 forgetting ca certificates with scratch

every outgoing https request then fails with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. use distroless, or copy the certificates.

 key takeaways

- go builds static binaries, so the runtime image can be almost empty: about 24 mb for the shortener, mostly the binary.
- multi-stage dockerfiles: build with the toolchain, copy only the binary into distroless.
- order steps for caching and use buildkit cache mounts; rebuilds went from 62 s to 1.6 s.
- run as a numeric non-root user so kubernetes can enforce runasnonroot.
- multi-platform images build fast because go cross-compiles; ko builds go images without a dockerfile.

 further reading

- [docker: multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)
- [distroless images](https://github.com/googlecontainertools/distroless)
- [ko](https://ko.build/)

lessons.title: 15.2 Go in Kubernetes: probes, signals and graceful shutdown
lessons.description: Run a Go service well on Kubernetes: what happens when a pod stops, why a shutdown delay prevents failed requests (59 failures versus 0, measured), liveness, readiness and startup probes, resources with GOMEMLIMIT and GOMAXPROCS, security contexts, and Kustomize.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What happens, step by step, when Kubernetes stops a pod
- Why a Go service should keep serving for a few seconds after SIGTERM, with measurements
- Liveness, readiness and startup probes, and what each should check
- Requests, limits, `GOMEMLIMIT`, and how Go 1.25+ sets `GOMAXPROCS` in a pod
- A locked-down security context
- Managing manifests with Kustomize

## The Deployment

This lesson walks through the shortener's Deployment from milestone 4 (lesson 15.7). Here it is in full; the sections below explain each part.



```gopath-example
example-410
```



## How a pod stops

During a rolling update, a scale-down or a node drain, Kubernetes terminates pods. Two things then happen **at the same time**, driven by different components:

1. The kubelet sends the container **SIGTERM**, and starts the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` countdown (30 s here). If the process is still running at the end, it gets **SIGKILL**.
2. The endpoints controller removes the pod from the Service's endpoints, and every kube-proxy, ingress controller and load balancer then has to notice and update its own routing.

Step 2 takes time, typically a second or more. If your program exits as soon as it receives SIGTERM (which is what a Go program does by default), new requests are still being sent to it for that time, and they fail.

The shortener handles SIGTERM like this (lesson 12.8): mark itself not ready, **keep serving for `SHUTDOWN_DELAY`**, then call `http.Server.Shutdown`, which stops accepting connections and waits up to `SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT` for in-flight requests.

### Measured

To see the difference, `examples/m15/rollcheck` sends a steady stream of requests through the ingress (4 clients, a new connection per request) while the Deployment is restarted:



```gopath-example
example-411
```



```bash
rollcheck -url http://127.0.0.1/healthz -host shortener.localtest.me -duration 50s &
kubectl -n shortener rollout restart deployment/shortener
```

Results on a k3s cluster with Traefik as the ingress controller, same image, only `SHUTDOWN_DELAY` changed:

```text
SHUTDOWN_DELAY=5s:   15364 requests, 0 failed
                       HTTP 200: 15364

SHUTDOWN_DELAY=0s:   13889 requests, 59 failed
                       HTTP 200: 13830
                       HTTP 502: 55
                       error "...context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)": 4
```

Without the delay, the ingress kept routing to pods that had already stopped listening: 55 requests got `502 Bad Gateway` and 4 hung until the client gave up. With a 5 second delay, nothing failed. The same test on this website's own Deployment (`deploy/k8s`, with `-shutdown-delay 5s`) gave 12,454 requests and 0 failures.

Rules that follow:

- Handle **SIGTERM** (`signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)`); `os.Interrupt` alone only covers Ctrl+C.
- Keep serving for a few seconds after SIGTERM before calling `Shutdown`. (Some teams use a `preStop` hook with `sleep` instead; that needs a `sleep` binary in the image, which distroless does not have. Kubernetes 1.30+ also offers a built-in `sleep` action for `preStop`.)
- Set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` longer than delay plus shutdown timeout (here 30 > 5 + 20), or the kubelet kills the process mid-shutdown.
- Do not exit with an error code for a normal SIGTERM: the shortener's `run` returns `nil`.

## Probes

| Probe | Question | On failure | The shortener |
|---|---|---|---|
| **startupProbe** | Has it finished starting? | Keep waiting (up to `failureThreshold × periodSeconds`), then restart | `/healthz`, up to 60 s |
| **readinessProbe** | Should it get traffic now? | Removed from Service endpoints; **not** restarted | `/readyz` |
| **livenessProbe** | Is it alive, or stuck? | **Restarted** | `/healthz` |

The startup probe holds the other two back until the program is up, so a slow start (migrations, cache warm-up) is not mistaken for a hang. Liveness checks must be **trivial**: if `/healthz` checked the database, a database outage would restart every replica at once, which helps nobody (lesson 12.5). Readiness is where "not now" belongs: during start-up, during shutdown, and optionally when a dependency the pod cannot work without is unavailable.

## Resources, GOMEMLIMIT and GOMAXPROCS

```yaml
resources:
  requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi}   # what the scheduler reserves
  limits:   {cpu: "1",  memory: 128Mi}  # what the kernel enforces
env:
  - {name: GOMEMLIMIT, value: 115MiB}   # about 90% of the memory limit
```

- **Memory limit.** Exceeding it gets the container killed (`OOMKilled`). The Go GC does not know about the limit unless you tell it: `GOMEMLIMIT` at about 90% of the limit makes the GC work harder as memory approaches it, instead of the kernel killing the pod (lesson 11.3). The admin port confirms it: `go_gc_gomemlimit_bytes 1.2058624e+08`, which is 115 MiB.
- **CPU limit and GOMAXPROCS.** Since Go 1.25, when the module's `go` line is 1.25 or later, the runtime reads the cgroup CPU limit and sets `GOMAXPROCS` to match (lesson 11.1), rounding up, with a **minimum of 2**. On the 2-CPU test node, the shortener with a limit of 1 CPU reported `go_sched_gomaxprocs_threads 2`, exactly as that rule says. On a large node, the same limit prevents a pod from running 64 threads against a 1 CPU quota and being throttled. Older Go versions, or modules whose `go.mod` says `go 1.24` (check with `go version -m`, lesson 14.4), keep the old default; use `go.uber.org/automaxprocs` there.
- Whether to set CPU limits at all is debated: limits cause throttling, while requests alone share spare CPU. Either way, set **requests** for every container, so the scheduler can place pods sensibly.

## Security context

```yaml
securityContext:              # pod level
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 65532
  seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
containers:
  - securityContext:          # container level
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}
```

A Go service on distroless needs none of the things these settings take away: no root, no writable filesystem (the shortener writes nothing to disk), no Linux capabilities. These settings satisfy the **restricted** Pod Security Standard, which a namespace can enforce with a label (the read-only root filesystem goes further than it requires). As lesson 15.1 showed, `runAsNonRoot` needs a numeric user in the image or in `runAsUser`.

## Kustomize

The manifests are split into a **base** that holds what every environment shares, and **overlays** that change it per environment:

```text
projects/shortener/k8s/
  base/                 Deployment, Service, Ingress, PodDisruptionBudget
  overlays/local/       namespace, PostgreSQL and Redis in the cluster, secrets, image settings
```



```gopath-example
example-412
```



`kubectl apply -k projects/shortener/k8s/overlays/local` renders and applies it; `kubectl kustomize ...` only renders, which is useful in reviews. `secretGenerator` adds a hash of the content to the Secret's name and rewrites every reference, so changing a secret automatically rolls the Deployment. Kustomize is built into `kubectl`; Helm is the main alternative, with templates and packaging for distributing software to others.

## Common mistakes

### Exiting immediately on SIGTERM

Requests in the routing window fail, as measured above. Keep serving for a few seconds.

### Liveness probes that check dependencies

One database hiccup restarts every replica. Keep liveness trivial.

### No GOMEMLIMIT in a memory-limited pod

The GC lets the heap grow past the limit and the kernel kills the pod.

### A grace period shorter than your shutdown

The kubelet sends SIGKILL in the middle of draining.

## Key takeaways

- SIGTERM and endpoint removal happen concurrently; keep serving, unready, for a few seconds after SIGTERM. Measured: 59 failed requests without a delay, 0 with one.
- Startup probes protect slow starts, readiness controls traffic, liveness restarts: keep liveness trivial.
- Set `GOMEMLIMIT` to about 90% of the memory limit; Go 1.25+ derives `GOMAXPROCS` from the CPU limit (minimum 2).
- Run as non-root with a read-only root filesystem and no capabilities.
- Kustomize keeps a shared base and per-environment overlays, built into `kubectl`.

## Further reading

- [Kubernetes: Pod lifecycle and termination](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination)
- [Kubernetes: Configure liveness, readiness and startup probes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/)
- [Pod Security Standards](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/)
- [Kustomize](https://kubectl.docs.kubernetes.io/references/kustomize/)

lessons.title: 15.3 client-go basics
lessons.description: Talk to Kubernetes from Go with client-go: connecting in and out of the cluster, typed clientsets, label selectors, optimistic concurrency and RetryOnConflict, informers and their local cache, and testing with a fake clientset.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- How a Go program connects to Kubernetes, inside a pod or from your laptop
- Listing and reading objects with the typed clientset
- Updates, `resourceVersion`, and retrying conflicts
- Informers: LIST plus WATCH plus a local cache, the foundation of every controller
- Testing without a cluster, using the fake clientset

## The idea

Everything in Kubernetes goes through one HTTP API. `kubectl`, controllers, the scheduler and your own programs all read and write objects through it. **client-go** is the official Go library for that API; `kubectl` itself is built on it.

The examples live in `examples/thirdparty/k8s`. The module needs `go mod tidy` once; the tests need no cluster.

## Connecting



```gopath-example
example-413
```



Inside a pod, `rest.InClusterConfig` uses the service account token and CA certificate that Kubernetes mounts into every pod, and the API server address from environment variables. Outside, the same loading rules as `kubectl` read `$KUBECONFIG` or `~/.kube/config`, so the program uses whatever cluster and context `kubectl` uses. Setting a **user agent** makes your program identifiable in API server audit logs.

The program can then only do what its identity is allowed to do: in a pod, what **RBAC** grants the pod's service account (lesson 15.4 generates those rules).

## Reading objects



```gopath-example
example-414
```



`cs.CoreV1().Pods(namespace).List(...)` mirrors the API path `/api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/pods`. Every built-in kind has the same shape: `AppsV1().Deployments(ns)`, `NetworkingV1().Ingresses(ns)`, and so on, with `Get`, `List`, `Create`, `Update`, `Patch`, `Delete` and `Watch`. A **label selector** filters on the server, which matters in big clusters.

Run against the cluster from lesson 15.2, the `podlist` command prints:

```text
$ go run ./k8s/podlist -n shortener
NAME                        READY  STATUS   RESTARTS  AGE
postgres-0                  1/1    Running  0         13m58s
redis-84f65c4d6f-hwpz7      1/1    Running  0         13m58s
shortener-6b7df6c565-d7vfr  1/1    Running  0         7m45s
shortener-6b7df6c565-d9g7b  1/1    Running  0         7m48s

$ go run ./k8s/podlist -n shortener -l app.kubernetes.io/name=shortener
NAME                        READY  STATUS   RESTARTS  AGE
shortener-6b7df6c565-d7vfr  1/1    Running  0         7m46s
shortener-6b7df6c565-d9g7b  1/1    Running  0         7m49s
```

## Updates and conflicts

Every object has a **`resourceVersion`**, which changes on every write. An `Update` sends back the object you read, including that version; if someone else wrote the object in the meantime, the API server rejects your update with **409 Conflict** instead of silently overwriting their change. This is optimistic concurrency, the same idea as the job queue's attempts check in lesson 13.8.

The standard response is to read again, reapply your change, and retry:



```gopath-example
example-415
```



`retry.RetryOnConflict` retries only on conflicts, with a short backoff. The function must **re-read** the object each time; retrying the same stale object would conflict forever. For changes that touch only a few fields, a **patch** (`Patch` with a JSON merge patch, or server-side apply) avoids the read entirely, and with it most conflicts.

## Informers

A program that reacts to changes could poll with `List` every few seconds. With many programs and many objects that would overload the API server, and it would still react late. Instead, client-go programs use **informers**:



```gopath-example
example-416
```



An informer does one **LIST** to fill a local cache, then opens a **WATCH**: a long-lived stream of changes. It keeps the cache up to date, calls your handlers for each change, and if the watch breaks (it will, eventually) it re-lists and resumes. Reads from the cache cost nothing on the API server. A **shared** informer factory lets every part of a program share one cache per kind.

Two details in the code are easy to miss. `WaitForCacheSync` blocks until the initial LIST has been processed: acting before that means acting on an incomplete picture. And a delete handler can receive a `DeletedFinalStateUnknown` instead of the object, when the watch missed the delete and the informer only found out on re-list.

Watching the shortener's namespace during `kubectl rollout restart`:

```text
$ go run ./k8s/podlist -n shortener -watch
added    shortener-6d454586f7-jln2b    Running     <- initial LIST
added    shortener-6d454586f7-hvfwg    Running
added    shortener-656cf6c78-g56kq     Pending     <- the rollout creates a new pod
updated  shortener-656cf6c78-g56kq     Pending
updated  shortener-656cf6c78-g56kq     Running
updated  shortener-6d454586f7-jln2b    Running     <- an old pod is told to terminate
added    shortener-656cf6c78-v2kvc     Pending
...
```

The old pods' `deleted` events follow a few seconds later, after their `SHUTDOWN_DELAY` and graceful shutdown (lesson 15.2).

Informers, a work queue, and a reconcile function together make a **controller**. Writing that machinery by hand is how the core Kubernetes controllers are built; for your own, controller-runtime (lesson 15.4) provides it.

## Testing without a cluster

`k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes/fake` provides a clientset backed by an in-memory object tracker. It implements the same `kubernetes.Interface`, so code written against the interface works with either:



```gopath-example
example-417
```



**Reactors** inject behavior, such as a conflict on the first update, to test the retry path:



```gopath-example
example-418
```



The fake does not implement everything the real API server does (validation, defaulting, admission, server-side apply), so add tests against a real API server for those: `envtest` from controller-runtime runs a local `etcd` and `kube-apiserver`, and a throwaway kind or k3s cluster covers the rest.

## Common mistakes

### Polling with List

Use informers: one LIST, then a WATCH, and cheap cached reads.

### Updating a stale object in a retry loop

Re-read inside the retry function, or use a patch.

### Acting before the cache has synced

Your program then believes objects do not exist. Wait for `HasSynced`.

### Accepting kubernetes.Clientset instead of kubernetes.Interface

Then the fake cannot be substituted. Accept the interface (lesson 4.8).

## Key takeaways

- `rest.InClusterConfig` inside pods, kubeconfig loading rules outside; RBAC decides what the program may do.
- The typed clientset mirrors the API: `CoreV1().Pods(ns).List(ctx, opts)`.
- Updates carry `resourceVersion`; on 409 Conflict, re-read and retry with `retry.RetryOnConflict`, or patch.
- Informers LIST once, then WATCH, keeping a local cache; wait for it to sync.
- Test with the fake clientset and reactors; use envtest or a real cluster for API server behavior.

## Further reading

- [client-go](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go) and its [examples](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/tree/master/examples)
- [Kubernetes API concepts: resource versions, watches](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/)
- [Sample controller](https://github.com/kubernetes/sample-controller), a controller written with client-go only
