15.3 client-go basics talk to kubernetes from go with client-go: connecting in and out of the cluster, typed clientsets, label selectors, optimistic concurrency and retryonconflict, informers and their local cache, and testing with a fake clientset.  what you will learn

- how a go program connects to kubernetes, inside a pod or from your laptop
- listing and reading objects with the typed clientset
- updates, resourceversion, and retrying conflicts
- informers: list plus watch plus a local cache, the foundation of every controller
- testing without a cluster, using the fake clientset

 the idea

everything in kubernetes goes through one http api. kubectl, controllers, the scheduler and your own programs all read and write objects through it. client-go is the official go library for that api; kubectl itself is built on it.

the examples live in examples/thirdparty/k8s. the module needs go mod tidy once; the tests need no cluster.

 connecting







inside a pod, rest.inclusterconfig uses the service account token and ca certificate that kubernetes mounts into every pod, and the api server address from environment variables. outside, the same loading rules as kubectl read $kubeconfig or ~/.kube/config, so the program uses whatever cluster and context kubectl uses. setting a user agent makes your program identifiable in api server audit logs.

the program can then only do what its identity is allowed to do: in a pod, what rbac grants the pod's service account (lesson 15.4 generates those rules).

 reading objects







cs.corev1().pods(namespace).list(...) mirrors the api path /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/pods. every built-in kind has the same shape: appsv1().deployments(ns), networkingv1().ingresses(ns), and so on, with get, list, create, update, patch, delete and watch. a label selector filters on the server, which matters in big clusters.

run against the cluster from lesson 15.2, the podlist command prints:



 updates and conflicts

every object has a resourceversion, which changes on every write. an update sends back the object you read, including that version; if someone else wrote the object in the meantime, the api server rejects your update with 409 conflict instead of silently overwriting their change. this is optimistic concurrency, the same idea as the job queue's attempts check in lesson 13.8.

the standard response is to read again, reapply your change, and retry:







retry.retryonconflict retries only on conflicts, with a short backoff. the function must re-read the object each time; retrying the same stale object would conflict forever. for changes that touch only a few fields, a patch (patch with a json merge patch, or server-side apply) avoids the read entirely, and with it most conflicts.

 informers

a program that reacts to changes could poll with list every few seconds. with many programs and many objects that would overload the api server, and it would still react late. instead, client-go programs use informers:







an informer does one list to fill a local cache, then opens a watch: a long-lived stream of changes. it keeps the cache up to date, calls your handlers for each change, and if the watch breaks (it will, eventually) it re-lists and resumes. reads from the cache cost nothing on the api server. a shared informer factory lets every part of a program share one cache per kind.

two details in the code are easy to miss. waitforcachesync blocks until the initial list has been processed: acting before that means acting on an incomplete picture. and a delete handler can receive a deletedfinalstateunknown instead of the object, when the watch missed the delete and the informer only found out on re-list.

watching the shortener's namespace during kubectl rollout restart:



the old pods' deleted events follow a few seconds later, after their shutdowndelay and graceful shutdown (lesson 15.2).

informers, a work queue, and a reconcile function together make a controller. writing that machinery by hand is how the core kubernetes controllers are built; for your own, controller-runtime (lesson 15.4) provides it.

 testing without a cluster

k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes/fake provides a clientset backed by an in-memory object tracker. it implements the same kubernetes.interface, so code written against the interface works with either:







reactors inject behavior, such as a conflict on the first update, to test the retry path:







the fake does not implement everything the real api server does (validation, defaulting, admission, server-side apply), so add tests against a real api server for those: envtest from controller-runtime runs a local etcd and kube-apiserver, and a throwaway kind or k3s cluster covers the rest.

 common mistakes

 polling with list

use informers: one list, then a watch, and cheap cached reads.

 updating a stale object in a retry loop

re-read inside the retry function, or use a patch.

 acting before the cache has synced

your program then believes objects do not exist. wait for hassynced.

 accepting kubernetes.clientset instead of kubernetes.interface

then the fake cannot be substituted. accept the interface (lesson 4.8).

 key takeaways

- rest.inclusterconfig inside pods, kubeconfig loading rules outside; rbac decides what the program may do.
- the typed clientset mirrors the api: corev1().pods(ns).list(ctx, opts).
- updates carry resourceversion; on 409 conflict, re-read and retry with retry.retryonconflict, or patch.
- informers list once, then watch, keeping a local cache; wait for it to sync.
- test with the fake clientset and reactors; use envtest or a real cluster for api server behavior.

 further reading

- [client-go](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go) and its [examples](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/tree/master/examples)
- [kubernetes api concepts: resource versions, watches](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/)
- [sample controller](https://github.com/kubernetes/sample-controller), a controller written with client-go only

lessons.title: 15.4 Writing a Kubernetes controller with controller-runtime
lessons.description: Build the ShortLink operator: a custom resource defined with Go types and kubebuilder markers, CRD and RBAC generated by controller-gen, an idempotent Reconcile function, a finalizer for cleanup, status conditions, and tests with a fake client, then run it on a cluster.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- What a custom resource and an operator are
- Defining an API with Go types and **kubebuilder markers**, and generating the CRD, deep-copy code and RBAC with **controller-gen**
- Writing a **Reconcile** function that is safe to run any number of times
- Cleaning up external state with a **finalizer**
- Reporting progress through **status** and **conditions**
- Testing reconcilers with controller-runtime's fake client, and running the operator on a cluster

## The idea

Kubernetes is extensible: a **CustomResourceDefinition** (CRD) adds a new kind of object to the API, and a **controller** makes the world match those objects. Together they are an **operator**: you declare what you want in YAML, and a program keeps it true.

This lesson builds one for the course's shortener. A `ShortLink` resource declares a short link:

```yaml
apiVersion: shortener.example.com/v1alpha1
kind: ShortLink
metadata:
  name: k8s-docs
spec:
  url: https://kubernetes.io/docs
  code: k8s
```

and the operator creates it through the shortener's HTTP API, keeps it pointing at `spec.url`, reports the short URL in the status, and deletes it when the resource is deleted. On the test cluster:

```text
$ kubectl -n shortener apply -f config/samples/shortlink.yaml
$ kubectl -n shortener get shortlinks
NAME       CODE      SHORT URL                               READY   AGE
go-docs    go-docs   http://shortener.localtest.me/go-docs   True    28s
k8s-docs   k8s       http://shortener.localtest.me/k8s       True    28s

$ curl -si -H "Host: shortener.localtest.me" http://127.0.0.1/k8s | grep -E '^(HTTP|Location)'
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://kubernetes.io/docs
```

The project is in [`projects/shortlink-operator`](https://github.com/Priyadharshan0903/gopath-academy/tree/main/projects/shortlink-operator), its own module, using **controller-runtime**, the library under Kubebuilder and the Operator SDK.

## The API, as Go types



```gopath-example
example-419
```



The shape is the same for every Kubernetes object: `TypeMeta` (kind and API version), `ObjectMeta` (name, namespace, labels, finalizers, generation), a **spec** written by users, and a **status** written by the controller. Status uses the standard `metav1.Condition` type, so tools such as `kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready` work with it.

The `+kubebuilder:...` comments are **markers**. They are read by **controller-gen**, run through the `//go:generate go tool controller-gen ...` line in the same file, with the version pinned by the module's `tool` directive (lesson 14.3). It generates:

- `zz_generated.deepcopy.go`: `DeepCopy` methods, which every Kubernetes object type needs (caches hand out shared objects, and code must copy before modifying);
- `config/crd/shortener.example.com_shortlinks.yaml`: the CRD, with an OpenAPI schema built from the Go types and the validation markers;
- `config/rbac/role.yaml`: a ClusterRole built from the `+kubebuilder:rbac` markers in the controller.

The validation markers run **in the API server**, before the operator ever sees a bad object:

```text
$ kubectl apply -f bad.yaml
The ShortLink "bad" is invalid:
* spec.code: Invalid value: "a b": spec.code in body should match '^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,32}$'
* spec.url: Invalid value: "ftp://files.example.com": spec.url in body should match '^https?://'
```

and the field comments become documentation: `kubectl explain shortlink.spec` prints them.

## The reconciler



```gopath-example
example-420
```



**Reconcile does not receive an event.** It receives a name, and must look at the current state of the world and move it toward the desired state. It is called when the object changes, when it is created, after a restart, and on a periodic resync, perhaps several times for one change. So it must be **idempotent**: running it again when everything is already correct does nothing harmful. The test checks exactly that:

```text
first reconcile:  [get go-docs create go-docs]
second reconcile: [get go-docs]
```

How this one stays idempotent and safe:

- **A deterministic identifier.** Without `spec.code`, the code is the resource's name. If the code were random and the operator crashed between creating the link and saving the status, the next attempt would create a second link and orphan the first. Derive external identifiers from the object whenever you can.
- **Check before acting.** It reads the link first, and only creates, recreates or deletes when the state differs from the spec.
- **Ownership.** It only recreates a link that it created itself (`status.code == code`); a link someone else made with the same code produces a `CodeTaken` condition instead of being overwritten.
- **Errors mean "try again".** Returning an error makes controller-runtime requeue the request with exponential backoff, so a shortener outage is retried automatically. A condition that retrying soon cannot fix (`CodeTaken`) returns `RequeueAfter` instead.

## Cleaning up with a finalizer

Deleting a `ShortLink` must also delete the link in the shortener, an external system Kubernetes knows nothing about. A **finalizer** is a string in `metadata.finalizers` that tells the API server: do not remove this object until this finalizer is gone. Deleting the object then only sets `deletionTimestamp`; the reconciler sees that, cleans up, and removes its finalizer, and only then does the object disappear.

This was visible on the cluster. The first version of the shortener deployed there had no DELETE endpoint yet, so `kubectl delete shortlink k8s-docs` **waited**, and the operator logged `DELETE /api/links/k8s: HTTP 405` and retried with backoff. Once the shortener was upgraded, the next retry succeeded, the finalizer was removed, the delete completed, and `/k8s` returned 404. That is the guarantee working: the Kubernetes object cannot vanish while the external resource still exists.



```gopath-example
example-421
```



## Wiring it up



```gopath-example
example-422
```





```gopath-example
example-423
```



The **manager** owns the shared informer cache (lesson 15.3), the clients, the controllers, metrics on `:8080`, health probes on `:8081`, leader election, and signal handling. `For(&ShortLink{})` sets up an informer and a work queue for ShortLinks; controller-runtime then calls `Reconcile` for each key in the queue, never concurrently for the same object, and with rate-limited retries. Reads through `mgr.GetClient()` come from the cache; writes go to the API server.

## Testing



```gopath-example
example-424
```



controller-runtime's **fake client** keeps objects in memory and understands finalizers, deletion timestamps and the status subresource, so most reconciler logic can be tested in milliseconds. The shortener is replaced by an in-memory fake that records its calls. The tests cover: create and idempotency, a URL change (recreate), a code change (delete the old link), a code taken by someone else, the API being down, and deletion.

For behavior only a real API server has (CRD validation, defaulting, webhooks), controller-runtime's **envtest** starts a local `etcd` and `kube-apiserver`, and end-to-end tests run against a kind or k3s cluster.

## Running it

```bash
cd projects/shortlink-operator
go mod tidy
go test ./...
docker build -t shortlink-operator:dev .                  # then load it into your cluster
kubectl apply -k config/default                            # CRD, RBAC, Deployment (2 replicas)
kubectl -n shortener apply -f config/samples/shortlink.yaml
kubectl -n shortener get shortlinks -w
```

During development, `go run ./cmd/manager -shortener-url=http://localhost:8080` runs the operator on your laptop against whatever cluster `kubectl` points at, with no image at all.

## Key takeaways

- A CRD adds a kind to the Kubernetes API; a controller makes the world match it; together they are an operator.
- Define the API as Go types with markers; let controller-gen generate deep-copy code, the CRD (with validation) and RBAC.
- Reconcile is level-based and must be idempotent: observe, compare, act, report. Derive external identifiers deterministically.
- Use a finalizer to clean up external resources before the object is removed.
- Report progress with status conditions; return errors to retry with backoff.
- Test reconcilers with the fake client; use envtest or a real cluster for API server behavior.

## Further reading

- [The Kubebuilder Book](https://book.kubebuilder.io/), the best introduction to controller-runtime
- [controller-runtime](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-runtime)
- [Kubernetes: Custom Resources](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/api-extension/custom-resources/)

lessons.title: 15.5 Operators in practice
lessons.description: The patterns that make operators reliable in production: level-based reconciliation, owner references and garbage collection, status and observedGeneration, high availability with leader election (failover measured), RBAC, API versioning, and when not to write an operator.
lessons.body:
## What you will learn

- The principles behind every reliable operator
- Owner references and garbage collection, the other half of cleanup
- Status, conditions and `observedGeneration`
- Running several replicas with leader election, and how fast failover is (measured)
- Least-privilege RBAC, API versions, and when not to write an operator at all

## Level-based, not edge-based

The single most important idea: a controller reacts to **state**, not to **events**. Reconcile receives a name and works out what to do by comparing desired state (the spec) with actual state (the world). Events can be missed, merged or repeated (after a restart, a re-list, a network blip), and a level-based controller does not care: it converges anyway. Every rule below follows from this.

- **Idempotent actions.** Running Reconcile twice must be harmless (lesson 15.4 tests it).
- **No state in memory.** Everything the controller needs to know must be readable from the cluster or the external system, because the process can restart at any moment. Put what you learn in **status**, not in variables.
- **Deterministic names** for anything you create, so you can find it again after a crash.
- **One step at a time.** Do a bit of work, update status, return; let the next reconcile continue. Long blocking calls hold a worker and delay other objects.

## Owner references and garbage collection

Finalizers (lesson 15.4) clean up resources **outside** Kubernetes. For resources **inside** Kubernetes, use **owner references** instead: when an operator creates, say, a Deployment and a Service for a custom resource, it sets the custom resource as their owner:

```go
if err := controllerutil.SetControllerReference(&app, deployment, r.Scheme); err != nil {
	return ctrl.Result{}, err
}
```

When the owner is deleted, Kubernetes' garbage collector deletes the owned objects automatically: no finalizer, no code. And with `Owns(&appsv1.Deployment{})` in `SetupWithManager`, a change to an owned Deployment (someone scales it by hand, say) triggers a reconcile of its owner, which puts it back. This is how a Deployment owns ReplicaSets, which own Pods.

## Status, conditions and observedGeneration

`metadata.generation` increases whenever the **spec** changes. A controller writes `status.observedGeneration` to say "my status describes this generation". A client that changed the spec can then wait until `observedGeneration` catches up before trusting the status. `kubectl rollout status` works exactly like that for Deployments.

Conditions (`Ready`, `Progressing`, `Degraded`, ...) follow the shape of `metav1.Condition`: a type, a status (`True`, `False`, `Unknown`), a machine-readable `Reason` in CamelCase and a human-readable `Message`. The ShortLink operator uses `LinkReady`, `CodeTaken` and `APIError` as reasons, so `kubectl describe` explains every failure, and automation can wait on readiness:

```bash
kubectl -n shortener wait --for=condition=Ready shortlink/go-docs --timeout=60s
```

## High availability: leader election

Run one replica and a node failure stops reconciliation until the pod is rescheduled. Run two without coordination, and both reconcile the same objects at once. **Leader election** solves this: replicas compete for a **Lease** object, only the holder runs controllers, and the others wait to take over.

The operator's Deployment runs 2 replicas with `--leader-elect`. On the cluster:

```text
$ kubectl -n shortlink-system get lease
NAME                                       HOLDER
shortlink-operator.shortener.example.com   shortlink-operator-64c9df47c9-rb7rw_cfd2...
```

Deleting the leader pod and measuring how long until another replica holds the lease:

```text
default settings:                       new leader after ~15 s
with LeaderElectionReleaseOnCancel:     new leader after 1.3 s
```

By default, a stopping leader just stops renewing, and the others must wait for the lease to expire (15 seconds). With `LeaderElectionReleaseOnCancel: true`, the manager gives up the lease when it shuts down, so a standby takes over almost at once. It is safe only if the process exits right after the manager stops, as `main` does here. During those seconds nothing is lost: changes queue up as state in the cluster and are reconciled by the new leader. (Leader election needs RBAC for `leases`, which `config/rbac/leader_election.yaml` grants in the operator's own namespace only.)

## Least-privilege RBAC

An operator's service account is a powerful identity. The `+kubebuilder:rbac` markers generate exactly the permissions the code declares; review them like code. Grant cluster-wide permissions only for cluster-wide work; prefer namespaced `Role`s, and restrict a controller's cache to the namespaces it manages (`cache.Options{DefaultNamespaces: ...}`) when it does not need the whole cluster. Never request `*` verbs or resources.

## Evolving the API

`v1alpha1` signals that the API may change. Kubernetes API conventions describe the path: `v1alpha1` → `v1beta1` → `v1`, with a **conversion webhook** when the stored representation changes between versions, so old objects keep working. Within a version, only add **optional** fields; never remove or rename fields others depend on. Treat your CRD like any public API, because once other teams write YAML against it, it is one.

## When not to write an operator

Operators shine when there is ongoing, domain-specific operational knowledge to automate: databases that need failover and backups, certificates that need renewal, external services that must stay in sync with declarations, like the ShortLink. They are overkill when:

- a Deployment, a Helm chart or Kustomize already express what you need;
- the work is a one-off: a Job or a script is simpler;
- nobody will maintain it: an operator is software running with cluster privileges, with all that implies.

## Tools

- **Kubebuilder** scaffolds projects like `shortlink-operator` (`kubebuilder init`, `kubebuilder create api`) with Makefile targets for controller-gen, envtest and deployment. The structure in this lesson follows its conventions, so moving to it is easy.
- **Operator SDK** builds on Kubebuilder and adds integration with the Operator Lifecycle Manager.
- **controller-runtime** alone, as in this lesson, when you want to see every moving part.

## Key takeaways

- Reconcile on state, not events: idempotent, no memory state, deterministic names, small steps.
- Owner references garbage-collect Kubernetes resources; finalizers clean up external ones.
- Report `observedGeneration` and standard conditions so humans and tools can tell where things stand.
- Run several replicas with leader election; releasing the lease on shutdown cut failover from about 15 s to 1.3 s here.
- Generate least-privilege RBAC from markers, version your API carefully, and write an operator only when there is real operational logic to automate.

## Further reading

- [Kubernetes API conventions](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md)
- [Kubebuilder Book: Good practices](https://book.kubebuilder.io/reference/good-practices)
- [Kubernetes: Garbage collection and owner references](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/garbage-collection/)
- [Kubernetes: Leases](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/leases/)

when the owner is deleted, kubernetes' garbage collector deletes the owned objects automatically: no finalizer, no code. and with owns(&appsv1.deployment{}) in setupwithmanager, a change to an owned deployment (someone scales it by hand, say) triggers a reconcile of its owner, which puts it back. this is how a deployment owns replicasets, which own pods.

 status, conditions and observedgeneration

metadata.generation increases whenever the spec changes. a controller writes status.observedgeneration to say "my status describes this generation". a client that changed the spec can then wait until observedgeneration catches up before trusting the status. kubectl rollout status works exactly like that for deployments.

conditions (ready, progressing, degraded, ...) follow the shape of metav1.condition: a type, a status (true, false, unknown), a machine-readable reason in camelcase and a human-readable message. the shortlink operator uses linkready, codetaken and apierror as reasons, so kubectl describe explains every failure, and automation can wait on readiness:



 high availability: leader election

run one replica and a node failure stops reconciliation until the pod is rescheduled. run two without coordination, and both reconcile the same objects at once. leader election solves this: replicas compete for a lease object, only the holder runs controllers, and the others wait to take over.

the operator's deployment runs 2 replicas with --leader-elect. on the cluster:



deleting the leader pod and measuring how long until another replica holds the lease:



by default, a stopping leader just stops renewing, and the others must wait for the lease to expire (15 seconds). with leaderelectionreleaseoncancel: true, the manager gives up the lease when it shuts down, so a standby takes over almost at once. it is safe only if the process exits right after the manager stops, as main does here. during those seconds nothing is lost: changes queue up as state in the cluster and are reconciled by the new leader. (leader election needs rbac for leases, which config/rbac/leaderelection.yaml grants in the operator's own namespace only.)

 least-privilege rbac

an operator's service account is a powerful identity. the +kubebuilder:rbac markers generate exactly the permissions the code declares; review them like code. grant cluster-wide permissions only for cluster-wide work; prefer namespaced roles, and restrict a controller's cache to the namespaces it manages (cache.options{defaultnamespaces: ...}) when it does not need the whole cluster. never request  verbs or resources.

 evolving the api

v1alpha1 signals that the api may change. kubernetes api conventions describe the path: v1alpha1 → v1beta1 → v1, with a conversion webhook when the stored representation changes between versions, so old objects keep working. within a version, only add optional fields; never remove or rename fields others depend on. treat your crd like any public api, because once other teams write yaml against it, it is one.

 when not to write an operator

operators shine when there is ongoing, domain-specific operational knowledge to automate: databases that need failover and backups, certificates that need renewal, external services that must stay in sync with declarations, like the shortlink. they are overkill when:

- a deployment, a helm chart or kustomize already express what you need;
- the work is a one-off: a job or a script is simpler;
- nobody will maintain it: an operator is software running with cluster privileges, with all that implies.

 tools

- kubebuilder scaffolds projects like shortlink-operator (kubebuilder init, kubebuilder create api) with makefile targets for controller-gen, envtest and deployment. the structure in this lesson follows its conventions, so moving to it is easy.
- operator sdk builds on kubebuilder and adds integration with the operator lifecycle manager.
- controller-runtime alone, as in this lesson, when you want to see every moving part.

 key takeaways

- reconcile on state, not events: idempotent, no memory state, deterministic names, small steps.
- owner references garbage-collect kubernetes resources; finalizers clean up external ones.
- report observedgeneration and standard conditions so humans and tools can tell where things stand.
- run several replicas with leader election; releasing the lease on shutdown cut failover from about 15 s to 1.3 s here.
- generate least-privilege rbac from markers, version your api carefully, and write an operator only when there is real operational logic to automate.

 further reading

- [kubernetes api conventions](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md)
- [kubebuilder book: good practices](https://book.kubebuilder.io/reference/good-practices)
- [kubernetes: garbage collection and owner references](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/garbage-collection/)
- [kubernetes: leases](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/leases/)

lessons.title: 15.6 Exercise: drain gracefully
lessons.description: Implement the shutdown sequence that took a rolling update from 59 failed requests to zero: flip readiness, keep serving for a delay, then shut down with a timeout.
lessons.body:
## The task

Lesson 15.2 measured what happens when a service stops the moment it gets SIGTERM: 59 failed requests in one rolling update. Here you write the function that prevents it.



```gopath-exercise
m15/drain
```



```bash
cd exercises
go test -race ./m15/drain
```

The tests run a real HTTP server and check that:

- readiness turns false **immediately** on cancel, while requests are **still served** during the delay;
- a request in flight when shutdown starts **completes**;
- a request that hangs does not hang `Serve`: it returns `context.DeadlineExceeded` after the timeout.

## Hints



```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-15
```





```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-16
```





```gopath-disclosure
disclosure-17
```



The reference solution is in `exercises/m15/drain/solution.go`. Compare it with the shortener's `run` in `projects/shortener/cmd/shortener/main.go`, which does the same for two servers at once.

lessons.title: 15.7 Project milestone: the shortener on Kubernetes
lessons.description: Milestone 4 of the URL shortener: a container image, Kubernetes manifests with Kustomize, PostgreSQL and Redis in the cluster, an ingress, zero-downtime rollouts, and the ShortLink operator managing links declaratively.
lessons.body:
## The milestone

| Milestone | After module | Adds | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Core | 5. Errors | Domain types, errors, validation, `Service`, in-memory store | done |
| 2. HTTP API | 12. HTTP services | JSON API, redirects, middleware, metrics, shutdown | done |
| 3. Postgres | 13. Working with data | PostgreSQL store, migrations, Redis cache | done |
| **4. Kubernetes** (this lesson) | 15. Go for cloud native | Image, manifests, operator | done |

Over four milestones the shortener went from a package with an in-memory map to a service running on Kubernetes with a database, a cache, metrics and its own operator. Milestone 4 adds:

```text
projects/shortener/
  Dockerfile, .dockerignore         the image (lesson 15.1)
  k8s/base/                         Deployment, Service, Ingress, PodDisruptionBudget (lesson 15.2)
  k8s/overlays/local/               namespace, PostgreSQL, Redis, secrets
  internal/... Delete               DELETE /api/links/{code}, needed by the operator
projects/shortlink-operator/        the ShortLink operator (lesson 15.4)
```

## Run the whole thing

You need Docker and a local cluster with an ingress controller (k3s or k3d include Traefik; for kind, install ingress-nginx).

```bash
# 1. Images
cd projects/shortener && go mod tidy && docker build -t shortener:dev . && cd -
cd projects/shortlink-operator && go mod tidy && docker build -t shortlink-operator:dev . && cd -

# 2. Load them into the cluster (pick yours)
kind load docker-image shortener:dev shortlink-operator:dev
# k3s:  docker save shortener:dev shortlink-operator:dev | sudo k3s ctr images import -

# 3. The shortener, PostgreSQL and Redis
kubectl apply -k projects/shortener/k8s/overlays/local
kubectl -n shortener rollout status deployment/shortener

# 4. The operator, then some links
kubectl apply -k projects/shortlink-operator/config/default
kubectl -n shortener apply -f projects/shortlink-operator/config/samples/shortlink.yaml
kubectl -n shortener get shortlinks

# 5. Use it (*.localtest.me resolves to 127.0.0.1)
curl -i http://shortener.localtest.me/k8s
```

On the test cluster, the first start showed one more real-world behavior: the shortener pods started faster than PostgreSQL, failed to connect, and restarted (`CrashLoopBackOff`) a few times until the database was ready, then ran normally:

```text
$ kubectl -n shortener get pods
NAME                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS      AGE
postgres-0                   1/1     Running   0             48s
redis-84f65c4d6f-hwpz7       1/1     Running   0             48s
shortener-6dd697b989-bktgh   1/1     Running   3 (33s ago)   48s
shortener-6dd697b989-ngkgr   1/1     Running   3 (33s ago)   48s
```

The logs of a restarted pod show why (reproduced later by stopping PostgreSQL during a rollout):

```text
shortener: database: failed to connect to `user=postgres database=postgres`: 10.43.115.125:5432 (postgres): dial error: dial tcp 10.43.115.125:5432: connect: connection refused
```

During that reproduction, the old pods kept serving, because the rollout uses `maxUnavailable: 0`: a new pod must become ready before an old one is removed. Kubernetes' restarts make this self-healing, but restarts back off exponentially, so a service that waits for its dependencies starts faster. See "Your turn".

## What runs where

```text
                          ┌─────────────────────── namespace shortener ───────────────────────┐
 curl ──► Ingress ──► Service shortener ──► 2 × shortener pod ──► Service postgres ──► postgres-0
 (Traefik)                (port 80)            :8080 API          │                   (StatefulSet, PVC)
                                               :9090 metrics      └─► Service redis ──► redis
                          └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
 kubectl apply ShortLink ──► API server ──► shortlink-operator (2 replicas, 1 leader) ──► shortener API
                                            namespace shortlink-system
```

- **PostgreSQL** runs as a **StatefulSet** with a PersistentVolumeClaim, so its data survives pod restarts. On a laptop that is fine; in production, most teams use a managed database or a dedicated operator such as CloudNativePG.
- **Redis** is a plain Deployment with no persistence, because it is a cache: losing it costs only speed.
- The **database URL** reaches the shortener as a **file** from a Secret (`DATABASE_URL_FILE`, lesson 12.4), never as a plain environment variable in the manifest.
- The **operator** talks to the shortener through its cluster-internal Service: `http://shortener.shortener.svc.cluster.local`.

## Verified behavior

Everything below was measured or observed on the test cluster (k3s, Kubernetes 1.37):

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Rolling update under load, `SHUTDOWN_DELAY=5s` | 15,364 requests, 0 failed |
| Same, `SHUTDOWN_DELAY=0s` | 13,889 requests, 59 failed (55 × 502, 4 timeouts) |
| `GOMEMLIMIT` from the manifest | `go_gc_gomemlimit_bytes 1.2058624e+08` (115 MiB) |
| Migrations on first start | `migrations applied=["0001_create_links.sql"]` |
| `kubectl apply` of a ShortLink | Ready within seconds; redirect works through the ingress |
| Changing `spec.url` | link recreated; redirect follows the new URL |
| Deleting a ShortLink | link deleted in the shortener (404); the delete waited until cleanup succeeded |
| Deleting the operator's leader pod | new leader in 1.3 s (with lease release on shutdown) |

## Your turn

1. **Wait for the database.** Instead of crashing when PostgreSQL is not up yet, retry `pool.Ping` with backoff for up to 30 seconds in `openStore`. Measure the start-up time before and after.
2. **A `prod` overlay.** Image from a registry with an immutable tag (`ghcr.io/you/shortener:v1.4.0`), 3 replicas, a HorizontalPodAutoscaler on CPU, TLS on the Ingress with cert-manager, and the database URL from your secret manager.
3. **Scrape metrics.** Install the Prometheus Operator (kube-prometheus-stack) and add a `ServiceMonitor` for the `admin` port. Graph request rate by route.
4. **Network policies.** Allow traffic to PostgreSQL and Redis only from the shortener pods.
5. **Extend the operator**: a `ShortLink` that sets `spec.code` to an existing link of someone else should show `CodeTaken`. Add a printer column for the condition's reason, and an event (`r.Recorder.Event`) when a link is created.

## Course recap

This is the end of the main curriculum. Across 15 modules you have gone from `go mod init` to an operator running on Kubernetes: the language and its idioms, concurrency, the standard library, testing and profiling, the runtime underneath, and the services, data, tools and deployments of production Go. The [case studies](/case-studies/) show the same ideas at work in real companies, from Docker and Kubernetes to Uber, Twitch and Discord.

caseStudies.title: Kubernetes and Docker: why cloud native was written in Go
caseStudies.description: Docker (2013) and Kubernetes (2014) were both written in Go. Their authors explained why: static binaries, concurrency, tooling, and a language neutral enough to attract contributors, plus the pain points they hit early.
caseStudies.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Projects** | Docker (first released 2013), Kubernetes (open sourced 2014) |
| **Sources** | Docker team slides, November 2013; Joe Beda, Gopher Academy blog, November 2014; Go blog, November 2013 |
| **Connects to** | Modules 1, 6, 14, 15 |

## The story

The two projects that defined cloud native infrastructure were both written in Go, at a time when Go was only a few years old.

**Docker.** In a November 2013 talk, Docker engineers Michael Crosby, Jérôme Petazzoni and Victor Vieux listed their reasons ([slides](https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/docker-and-go-why-did-we-decide-to-write-docker-in-go/28015076)):

- **Static compilation**: `go build` produces a binary that embeds almost everything it needs, which matters for a tool that must run on any Linux host.
- **Neutrality**: Go was not C++, Python, Ruby or Java, so no existing community "owned" the project.
- **The right features**: asynchronous primitives, low-level interfaces to processes and system calls, a large standard library.
- **Tooling**: documentation, formatting, testing and dependency fetching built into the `go` command.
- **Multi-architecture builds** with file name suffixes such as `_linux.go` instead of a preprocessor.

The same slides were candid about the pain: maps are not safe for concurrent use, `go get` could not pin versions (Docker had to vendor its dependencies), tests had no cleanup hooks, the `flag` package lacked short and long options, and error handling was verbose. In the [Go blog's fourth birthday post](https://go.dev/blog/4years), Docker's creator Solomon Hykes put it more bluntly: had Docker not been written in Go, "it would not have been as successful."

**Kubernetes.** Joe Beda, one of Kubernetes' creators, wrote that Go was "the only logical choice" for a project started from scratch in 2014 ([Kubernetes + Go = Crazy Delicious](https://blog.gopheracademy.com/birthday-bash-2014/kubernetes-go-crazy-delicious/)). His reasons: a language "neither too high level nor too low level", good standard and third-party libraries, fast builds and tests, a culture of simple code, tools such as `gofmt`, `go vet`, coverage and the race detector, easy fan-out of network calls, and memory safety when parsing untrusted input. He also explained the alternatives the team rejected: C and C++ as daunting for casual contributors, Java because of its heavy runtime install, and Python because dynamic typing is risky for systems software.

## What changed since

Almost every pain point in the Docker slides has since been addressed by Go itself:

| 2013 pain point | Today |
|---|---|
| `go get` cannot pin versions; vendor everything | Go modules with `go.mod` and `go.sum` (lesson 1.4) |
| No test cleanup | `t.Cleanup` (Go 1.14), `TestMain`, `t.Context` (Go 1.24) (Module 9) |
| `flag` lacks short and long options | still true; Cobra and pflag, used by both projects (lesson 14.1) |
| No IDE | gopls, the language server behind every major editor (lesson 1.2) |
| Maps not safe for concurrent use | still by design; `sync.Mutex`, `sync.Map`, and the race detector (Module 6) |

The pull of these projects also worked in the other direction: because Kubernetes, Docker, containerd, etcd and Prometheus are written in Go, the libraries for extending them (client-go, controller-runtime) are Go libraries, which is a large part of why platform teams write Go today.

## What you can apply

- **Static binaries make distribution trivial.** That is still the main reason infrastructure tools choose Go; lessons 14.4 and 15.1 build on it.
- **Choose boring, neutral tools for projects that need contributors.** Simplicity of the code base was a feature for both projects.
- **Fan-out with goroutines** is the everyday pattern of distributed systems code (Module 7).
- **Write Go that drives Kubernetes**: client-go and controller-runtime exist because Kubernetes is Go (lessons 15.3 and 15.4).

## Sources

- Michael Crosby, Jérôme Petazzoni, Victor Vieux: [Docker and Go: why did we decide to write Docker in Go?](https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/docker-and-go-why-did-we-decide-to-write-docker-in-go/28015076), November 2013
- Andrew Gerrand: [Four years of Go](https://go.dev/blog/4years), The Go Blog, 10 November 2013
- Joe Beda: [Kubernetes + Go = Crazy Delicious](https://blog.gopheracademy.com/birthday-bash-2014/kubernetes-go-crazy-delicious/), Gopher Academy Blog, 11 November 2014

caseStudies.title: dl.google.com: replacing a C++ download server with Go
caseStudies.description: Google's download server for Chrome, Android SDK and Earth was rewritten from C++ to Go in 2012: incrementally, verified against live traffic, with the standard library doing most of the work and less than half the code.
caseStudies.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Company** | Google |
| **System** | dl.google.com, the HTTP download server for Chrome, the Android SDK, Google Earth and more |
| **Source** | Brad Fitzpatrick, [dl.google.com: Powered by Go](https://go.dev/talks/2013/oscon-dl.slide), OSCON, 26 July 2013 |
| **Connects to** | Modules 4, 8, 9, 12 |

## The story

By 2012, dl.google.com was an old C++ server built around a single-threaded event loop. At startup it copied every payload to local disk, which by then took 12 to 24 hours. The code had duplicated copy-and-paste paths, incomplete documentation and tests, and threads added ad hoc. Brad Fitzpatrick's talk attributes its random crashes and stalls to that complexity.

The Go rewrite was done **incrementally**. First only the payload server was ported. Both versions ran in an **audit mode** where live traffic was mirrored to the old and the new server and their responses compared, so the new one was proven on real requests before it took over.

Much of the work disappeared into the standard library. `net/http` and `http.ServeContent` provided Range requests, ETags and `Last-Modified` handling, features the C++ server had implemented, incorrectly, in several places. The payload logic was built from small interfaces composed together: a type combining a size with `io.ReaderAt`, a multi-reader that concatenates parts, and a reader that issues 2 MB aligned reads so they match the cache's chunks. Caching used **groupcache**, Fitzpatrick's open-source library, which coordinates a cache across many servers and makes sure a miss is fetched only once instead of by every server at the same moment.

## Results

According to the talk, the rewrite removed 39 files, 14,032 lines of C++ and Python, leaving a single binary, and the overall result was "less than half the code". The new server used the same CPU for the same bandwidth but could serve much more bandwidth on multiple cores, used less memory and no local disk, started instantly instead of after hours, handled download spikes without crashing, and came with tests.

## What you can apply

- **Lean on the standard library.** Serving files correctly (ranges, conditional requests, content types) is subtle; `http.ServeContent` already gets it right (Module 12).
- **Small interfaces compose.** `io.ReaderAt` plus a few wrappers replaced a lot of special cases (lessons 4.x and 8.1).
- **Migrate incrementally, verify with real traffic.** Mirroring requests to old and new implementations and comparing responses is a powerful way to rewrite a running system.
- **Prevent duplicate work on cache misses.** groupcache's idea is the same as `singleflight` and request coalescing (lesson 13.5).

## Sources

- Brad Fitzpatrick: [dl.google.com: Powered by Go](https://go.dev/talks/2013/oscon-dl.slide), OSCON, 26 July 2013

caseStudies.title: Cloudflare: early production Go at the edge
caseStudies.description: By 2013 Cloudflare ran its DNS proxy, its Railgun compression system, a two-person-rule encryption server and certificate tooling in Go, relying on a goroutine per request and recovered panics for isolation.
caseStudies.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Company** | Cloudflare |
| **Systems** | RRDNS (DNS proxy), Railgun, Red October, SSL Bundler |
| **Source** | John Graham-Cumming, [What we've been doing with Go](https://blog.cloudflare.com/what-weve-been-doing-with-go/), Cloudflare blog, 11 November 2013 |
| **Connects to** | Modules 4, 5, 6, 12 |

## The story

Cloudflare was one of the earliest companies to run Go in production. In July 2012 its only Go project was **Railgun**, a system that compresses traffic between Cloudflare's data centers and customers' origin servers, written entirely in Go. Sixteen months later, John Graham-Cumming listed several more:

- **RRDNS**, a DNS proxy built to scale Cloudflare's DNS infrastructure;
- **Red October**, an encryption server that enforces a **two-person rule**: decrypting sensitive material such as private keys requires at least two authorized people to be logged in;
- **SSL Bundler**, which computes the fastest, shortest intermediate certificate chain for a customer's certificate;
- internal load-testing tools, and experiments with Docker and CoreOS's Raft library.

The post explains which Go features mattered in RRDNS:

- **A goroutine per request**, which isolates requests from each other.
- **`defer` and `recover`**, so a panic while handling one request is recovered and logged instead of crashing the whole DNS server.
- **Garbage collection**, which avoided complex reference counting.
- **Goroutines or read-write locks** for safe access to shared data.
- **Interfaces** that keep modules self-contained while allowing very different implementations behind them, some using cgo, some using background workers.

In the [Go blog's fourth birthday post](https://go.dev/blog/4years) the same year, Graham-Cumming summarized: Go was "the perfect match for our needs."

## What changed since

The panic-recovery pattern RRDNS describes is now built into `net/http`, which recovers handler panics itself; lesson 12.2 adds a middleware that turns them into logged 500 responses with request IDs. Cloudflare has since written many more Go services, and its engineering blog became a well-known source of Go production advice, such as its guide to `net/http` timeouts referenced in lesson 12.6.

## What you can apply

- **Isolate requests.** One goroutine per request, with panics recovered at the boundary, keeps one bad input from taking down a server (lessons 5.5 and 12.2).
- **Prefer simple concurrency tools for shared state.** A read-write lock is often all you need (lesson 6.4).
- **Hide implementation details behind small interfaces** so modules can evolve independently (Module 4).

## Sources

- John Graham-Cumming: [What we've been doing with Go](https://blog.cloudflare.com/what-weve-been-doing-with-go/), Cloudflare blog, 11 November 2013
- Andrew Gerrand: [Four years of Go](https://go.dev/blog/4years), The Go Blog, 10 November 2013

caseStudies.title: Dropbox: moving performance-critical backends from Python to Go
caseStudies.description: Around 2013, Dropbox began moving its performance-critical backends from Python to Go for concurrency and speed, wrote about 200,000 lines of Go, and open sourced the libraries it had to build along the way.
caseStudies.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Company** | Dropbox |
| **Change** | Performance-critical backends moved from Python to Go, starting around mid-2013 |
| **Source** | Patrick Lee, [Open Sourcing Our Go Libraries](https://dropbox.tech/infrastructure/open-sourcing-our-go-libraries), Dropbox Tech blog, 1 July 2014 |
| **Connects to** | Modules 1, 5, 7, 13 |

## The story

Python helped Dropbox grow and iterate quickly. As its user base grew, the company wanted to scale more efficiently, and about a year before this July 2014 post it decided to move its **performance-critical backends from Python to Go**, for better concurrency support and faster execution. A small team wrote about **200,000 lines of Go**, and by the time of the post major parts of the infrastructure had moved.

The obstacle they kept hitting was not the language but the ecosystem: Go was young, and robust libraries for building large systems were missing. So they wrote their own, and open sourced them as `godropbox`:

- **caching**: building blocks for caching layers;
- **errors**: errors that carry stack traces;
- **database/sqlbuilder**: generating SQL programmatically;
- **memcache**: a memcache client with connection pooling and sharding;
- **net2**: connection management;
- **hash2**: including a space-efficient consistent hashing algorithm.

The post does not name the specific systems that moved or give performance numbers, so neither does this case study.

## What changed since

The library gap Dropbox describes has largely closed. Several of the things it had to build are now in the standard library or are mature open source projects:

| Dropbox built (2014) | Today |
|---|---|
| errors with extra context | `%w` wrapping, `errors.Is`/`As`/`Join` (Module 5) |
| SQL helpers, connection pools | `database/sql` pooling, pgx, sqlc (Module 13) |
| connection management | `net/http` transport pooling, `context` deadlines (Modules 7 and 8) |
| caching layers | Redis clients, `singleflight` (lesson 13.5) |

## What you can apply

- **Move the hot paths, not everything.** Dropbox targeted performance-critical backends; most Python code was fine where it was. Measure first (Module 10).
- **Budget for libraries** when adopting a language in a big organization: the language is often the easy part.
- **Open sourcing internal libraries** let others improve them, and Dropbox committed to using the public repository internally so fixes landed there first.

## Sources

- Patrick Lee: [Open Sourcing Our Go Libraries](https://dropbox.tech/infrastructure/open-sourcing-our-go-libraries), Dropbox Tech blog, 1 July 2014

caseStudies.title: Uber: 170,000 queries per second with a geofence service
caseStudies.description: Uber's geofence lookup service, written in Go in 2015, became its highest query-per-second service: an in-memory index behind a read-write lock, refreshed in the background, at under 5 ms p95 latency.
caseStudies.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Company** | Uber |
| **System** | Geofence lookup: which city and zone a location is in |
| **Source** | Kai Wei, [How We Built Uber Engineering's Highest Query per Second Service Using Go](https://www.uber.com/blog/go-geofence-highest-query-per-second-service/), Uber Engineering blog, 24 February 2016 |
| **Connects to** | Modules 6, 7, 10, 12 |

## The story

Uber uses **geofences**, polygons on a map, for location-based configuration: where a product is available, airport rules, dynamic pricing areas. A lookup answers "which geofences contain this point?", and almost every request in the marketplace needs one.

The team's main language was Node.js, but in early 2015 they chose Go for this service, for three reasons given in the post:

- **Throughput and latency**: hundreds of thousands of queries per second, with a 99th percentile target under 100 ms.
- **CPU-heavy work**: point-in-polygon tests suit a compiled, statically typed language better than interpreted JavaScript.
- **Background refreshes**: in single-threaded Node.js, CPU-heavy refreshing of the data would stall queries; goroutines run refreshes on other cores while queries continue.

### The design

- **Every instance holds all the data in memory.** The service is stateless and not partitioned; a deterministic polling schedule keeps instances in sync, and data is also written to local disk for fast restarts.
- **A simple two-level index** instead of an R-tree or S2 cells: first find the city, then check the geofences in that city. It is still O(N), but N drops from tens of thousands to hundreds.
- **A read-write lock** protects the index. New data is built on the side and swapped in. The team first tried atomic pointer swaps (`StorePointer`/`LoadPointer`), found them brittle, and went back to the lock: slightly more latency, much simpler code.

### Results

On New Year's Eve 2015, the service peaked at **170,000 queries per second** in Uber's main non-China data center, on **40 machines at 35% CPU**, with latency **under 5 ms at the 95th percentile** and **under 50 ms at the 99th**. It had 99.99% uptime since launch; the post attributes the downtime to programming errors and a file descriptor leak in a third-party library, not to the Go runtime.

## What changed since

Atomic pointers are much less brittle today: `atomic.Pointer[T]` (Go 1.19) is type-safe, and swapping an immutable index through one is a common pattern (lesson 6.5). The read-write lock remains a perfectly good choice when, as here, measurements show it is fast enough.

## What you can apply

- **Simple beats clever when it is fast enough.** A two-level scan and a read-write lock served 170k QPS. Measure before reaching for complex indexes (Module 10).
- **Build new data on the side, then swap it in**, so readers never see a half-updated structure (lessons 6.4 and 6.5).
- **Keep CPU-heavy background work off the request path**: goroutines make that natural (Module 7).
- **Know your percentiles.** The targets and results are stated as p95 and p99, not averages (lesson 12.5).

## Sources

- Kai Wei: [How We Built Uber Engineering's Highest Query per Second Service Using Go](https://www.uber.com/blog/go-geofence-highest-query-per-second-service/), Uber Engineering blog, 24 February 2016

caseStudies.title: Uber: what the race detector found in 46 million lines of Go
caseStudies.description: Uber ran Go's race detector across its 46-million-line monorepo and found over 2,000 data races. Their PLDI 2022 paper catalogs the Go-specific patterns behind them: loop variable capture, err capture, maps, slices, copied mutexes and WaitGroup misuse.
caseStudies.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Company** | Uber |
| **Scale** | About 46 million lines of Go and 2,100 microservices in one monorepo |
| **Source** | Milind Chabbi, Murali Krishna Ramanathan, [A Study of Real-World Data Races in Golang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.00764), PLDI 2022 |
| **Connects to** | Module 6 (especially 6.6), Module 9 |

## The story

Uber's Go monorepo held about **46 million lines of Go** and **2,100 microservices** (for comparison, its Java monorepo had 19 million lines). In April 2021 the team began running Go's race detector (lesson 6.6) over it systematically. Not in CI at first: running the 100,000+ unit tests with `-race` raised the 95th percentile test time from about 25 to about 100 minutes. Instead they ran it **daily**, de-duplicated the reports, and filed each race as a task for its owners.

In about six months:

- **over 2,000 data races** were detected;
- **1,011 were fixed**, by **210 engineers**, in 790 unique patches;
- after the backlog, about **five new races per day** kept appearing.

### Why Go code has so many races

The paper measures how much more concurrency Go code uses than Java code at Uber: the median Go process ran **2,048 goroutines** against 256 threads for Java, and Go code used about 3.7 times more point-to-point synchronization constructs per million lines. More concurrency means more chances to get it wrong. The race patterns it catalogs are worth memorizing, because most are specific to Go:

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| **Loop variable capture** | goroutines started in a loop all reading the same loop variable |
| **`err` capture** | a goroutine assigning the enclosing function's `err` |
| **Named results and `defer`** | deferred closures writing named results concurrently with the function |
| **Slices** | copying a slice header outside the lock that protects `append` |
| **Maps** | assuming writes to *different keys* of a map are safe; they are not |
| **Copied mutexes** | passing a struct containing a `sync.Mutex` by value, so each copy has its own lock |
| **Mixing channels and shared memory** | a future that writes a field and also signals on a channel, read without synchronization |
| **`WaitGroup.Add` inside the goroutine** | `Wait` can return before the goroutine even registers |
| **Parallel subtests** | `t.Parallel()` table tests sharing state |
| **Writes under `RLock`** | taking the read lock, then modifying |

## What changed since

Two of the most common patterns have since been addressed in the language and library:

- **Go 1.22 made loop variables per-iteration**, so goroutines started in a loop each capture their own variable (lesson 2.5). This removed the first row of the table for modules that declare `go 1.22` or later.
- **`sync.WaitGroup.Go` (Go 1.25)** calls `Add` before starting the goroutine, making the "`Add` inside the goroutine" mistake impossible when you use it (lesson 6.4).

`go vet`'s `copylocks` check catches copied mutexes, and the remaining patterns (maps, slices, captured `err`, mixed channels and memory) are exactly why the race detector exists.

## What you can apply

- **Run tests with `-race`**, in CI if you can; Uber's numbers show what accumulates when you do not (lesson 6.6).
- **Never assume map writes to different keys are safe.** Protect the whole map (lesson 6.4).
- **Prefer `wg.Go`**, and declare `go 1.22` or later in `go.mod` to get per-iteration loop variables.
- **Do not copy structs containing locks**: pass pointers, and let `go vet` check.
- **Pick one coordination style per piece of state**: channels or locks, not both.

## Sources

- Milind Chabbi, Murali Krishna Ramanathan: [A Study of Real-World Data Races in Golang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.00764), PLDI 2022 (Uber Technologies)

caseStudies.title: Twitch: a 10 GiB memory ballast, and why GOMEMLIMIT replaced it
caseStudies.description: Twitch's API gateway ran 8 to 10 GC cycles per second with a small heap on a 64 GiB machine. A large, untouched byte array cut GC cycles by 99% and p99 latency by 45%. Go 1.19's GOMEMLIMIT now does the same job properly.
caseStudies.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Company** | Twitch |
| **System** | Visage, the API front end and gateway for external API traffic |
| **Go version** | 1.11 |
| **Source** | Ross Engers, [Go memory ballast: How I learnt to stop worrying and love the heap](https://blog.twitch.tv/en/2019/04/10/go-memory-ballast-how-i-learnt-to-stop-worrying-and-love-the-heap/), Twitch blog, 10 April 2019 |
| **Connects to** | Lesson 11.3, Module 10 |

## The story

Visage is the gateway that all of Twitch's external API traffic passes through, running on EC2 machines with **64 GiB** of memory. Its live heap was small, under **450 MiB** on average. Because the default `GOGC=100` triggers a collection whenever the heap doubles (lesson 11.3), a small live heap and a high allocation rate meant very frequent collections: about **8 to 10 GC cycles per second** at steady state, with **over 30% of CPU** spent in GC-related functions, and more during "refresh storms" when traffic could reach about 20 times normal.

The fix was a **memory ballast**: allocate one huge byte slice at startup and keep it alive.

```go
ballast := make([]byte, 10<<30) // 10 GiB, as in the article's example
```

The GC counts the ballast as live heap, so the next collection is not triggered until the heap grows by another 10 GiB. Because the slice is never written, the operating system never backs it with physical memory: it costs address space, not RAM. And because it is a `[]byte` with no pointers, marking it costs almost nothing.

The article does not state the production size, and advises starting small and increasing with testing. The reported results:

- **GC cycles down about 99%**;
- **CPU per machine down about 30%**;
- **p99 API latency at peak down about 45%**.

GC **pauses** did not change much. The latency gain came from **mark assists**: when the GC runs, goroutines that allocate are drafted to help with marking (lesson 11.3), and those goroutines were serving requests. Fewer GC cycles meant fewer requests slowed down by assist work.

The author also explains why they did not just raise `GOGC`: the amount of memory was what mattered, not the ratio, and a very high `GOGC` would make the heap size depend sharply on small changes in live memory.

## What changed since

The ballast was a clever workaround for a missing feature, and **Go 1.19 added that feature: `GOMEMLIMIT`** (lesson 11.3). The modern equivalent of Twitch's fix is:

```bash
GOGC=off GOMEMLIMIT=8GiB ./visage   # collect only as memory approaches 8 GiB
```

or, more conservatively, keep `GOGC` at its default and set `GOMEMLIMIT` to protect against running out of memory. Lesson 11.3's experiment shows the same effect the ballast had: with `GOGC=off` and a memory limit, the GC runs only near the limit, far less often than with a small heap and the default `GOGC`. The Go team's [GC guide](https://go.dev/doc/gc-guide) discusses this use of the memory limit directly. Since Go 1.26, the Green Tea collector also reduces the CPU cost of each cycle for programs like this.

## What you can apply

- **Look at GC frequency, not just pause time.** `GODEBUG=gctrace=1` or the runtime metrics show cycles per second (lesson 11.3); assists hurt latency even when pauses are tiny.
- **A small live heap with high allocation churn** is the classic case for raising the GC's target, today with `GOMEMLIMIT` rather than a ballast.
- **Reduce allocations first** (lesson 10.4): fewer allocations mean fewer cycles, whatever the settings.
- **Measure tail latency** (p99), where GC assists show up.

## Sources

- Ross Engers: [Go memory ballast: How I learnt to stop worrying and love the heap](https://blog.twitch.tv/en/2019/04/10/go-memory-ballast-how-i-learnt-to-stop-worrying-and-love-the-heap/), Twitch blog, 10 April 2019
- The Go team: [A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector](https://go.dev/doc/gc-guide)

caseStudies.title: Discord: when Go's garbage collector was the wrong fit
caseStudies.description: Discord's Read States service, a huge in-memory LRU cache written in Go 1.9, showed latency spikes every two minutes from forced garbage collections scanning the whole cache. They rewrote it in Rust. A fair look at what happened, and what has and has not changed.
caseStudies.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Company** | Discord |
| **System** | Read States: which channels and messages each user has read |
| **Go version** | 1.9.2 (1.8, 1.9 and 1.10 also tried) |
| **Source** | Jesse Howarth, [Why Discord is switching from Go to Rust](https://discord.com/blog/why-discord-is-switching-from-go-to-rust), Discord blog, 4 February 2020 |
| **Connects to** | Lesson 1.1 (when not to use Go), lesson 11.3 |

## The story

Every Discord user has a "read state" per channel: how far they have read, how many mentions they have. The **Read States** service sits on the hot path, used when users connect, send and read messages. Each server kept an **LRU cache** with millions of users and tens of millions of read states in memory, handling hundreds of thousands of cache updates per second, backed by Cassandra.

The Go version was fast on average, but latency and CPU **spiked about every two minutes**. The cause: if no garbage collection has run for two minutes, the Go runtime **forces one**. The cache allocated little new memory, so collections rarely triggered on their own, and when the forced collection came it had to **scan the entire LRU cache**, tens of millions of objects full of pointers.

They tried the obvious tuning:

- **Changing `GOGC` on the fly** did nothing: the problem was not collections being triggered too often, but the cost of the forced one.
- **Smaller caches**, partitioned into many per server, reduced the spikes, but raised p99 latency because more lookups went to the database.

In May 2019 they finished a **Rust** rewrite. With no garbage collector, the spikes disappeared; after optimization (including a `BTreeMap` instead of a `HashMap` for the cache, and fewer copies) the Rust version beat the hand-tuned Go version on latency, CPU and memory, and they raised the cache to 8 million read states per server. The post shows the before and after comparisons as graphs, without exact figures in the text.

## A fair reading

This is the best-known story of a team leaving Go, and it is worth reading precisely:

- **It is about one service with one memory shape**: a huge, long-lived, pointer-heavy in-memory cache. A collector that must periodically trace the live heap pays for exactly that shape. Go's GC cost scales with the live heap, not with the garbage (lesson 11.3).
- **The forced collection is still there.** Go still runs a collection if none has run for two minutes (`forcegcperiod` in the runtime). `GOMEMLIMIT`, added in Go 1.19, would not have removed that scan. The Green Tea collector in Go 1.26 makes marking cheaper per object, which helps, but a forced scan of tens of millions of objects remains a scan.
- **Go-side mitigations exist**, at a cost: storing the cache in pointer-free structures (for example, values in large slices indexed by integers, which the GC does not need to trace), or moving it off the Go heap. These make Go code look much less like Go.
- **Discord did not leave Go everywhere.** The post is about Read States; the author describes Rust adoption across Discord's stack, not a ban on Go.

## What you can apply

- **Know your memory shape.** Large, long-lived, pointer-heavy heaps are the worst case for a tracing GC. Measure live heap and GC CPU before choosing a design (lessons 10.2 and 11.3).
- **Pointer-free data is cheap for the GC.** `[]byte`, arrays of plain structs and integer indexes instead of pointers can shrink GC work dramatically (lesson 11.3).
- **Choosing a different language for one component is a legitimate engineering decision.** Lesson 1.1 lists when Go is not the right tool; this is a textbook example.

## Sources

- Jesse Howarth: [Why Discord is switching from Go to Rust](https://discord.com/blog/why-discord-is-switching-from-go-to-rust), Discord blog, 4 February 2020
- The Go runtime source: `forcegcperiod`, the two-minute forced collection, in [`runtime/proc.go`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/runtime/proc.go)

caseStudies.title: Monzo: a bank built as Go microservices on Kubernetes
caseStudies.description: Monzo built a bank backend from day one as Go microservices: about 150 services by 2016, Docker on Kubernetes, HTTP RPC through a service mesh proxy, Kafka for events, and infrastructure costs cut to a quarter by moving to Kubernetes.
caseStudies.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Company** | Monzo, a UK bank |
| **Architecture** | Go microservices on Kubernetes from the start |
| **Source** | Oliver Beattie, [Building a Modern Bank Backend](https://monzo.com/blog/2016/09/19/building-a-modern-bank-backend), Monzo blog, 19 September 2016 |
| **Connects to** | Modules 7, 12, 13, 15 |

## The story

Most startups begin with one application and split it later. Monzo, building a bank, started with **distributed microservices from day one**, a choice its head of engineering, Oliver Beattie, describes as unusual for an early-stage company. Three backend engineers started it; by the public beta there were about **100 services**, and about **150** when the post was written in 2016.

The platform, as described in the post:

- **Go** as the main language, chosen because it makes it easy to build low-latency, high-concurrency servers that suit microservices; some services in Java, Python and Scala, since no single ecosystem has everything a bank needs.
- **Docker containers on Kubernetes**, running on CoreOS machines in AWS, after an earlier setup with Mesos and Marathon. Moving to Kubernetes cut production infrastructure costs to about **a quarter** of what they had been.
- **HTTP-based RPC** between services through **linkerd**, a local proxy that handles load balancing, routing and retries of idempotent requests: an early service mesh.
- **Kafka** for asynchronous messaging, chosen for availability, horizontal scaling, persistence, replay and at-least-once delivery.
- Shared infrastructure exposed **as services** too, such as a distributed lock service in front of etcd.

The targets stated: payments processed end to end in under a second, card authorizations answered within tens of milliseconds, and an architecture designed for hundreds of millions of customers, available all the time.

## What changed since

The building blocks Monzo assembled by hand in 2016 have become standard: Kubernetes is the default platform, service meshes are common, and Go remains the language of that ecosystem. The 2016 post deliberately left out data storage for a later article, so this case study does not cover it.

## What you can apply

- **Retries must be safe**: the mesh only retries **idempotent** requests. Design operations so retrying them is harmless (lessons 13.8 and 15.4).
- **At-least-once delivery** from Kafka means consumers must handle duplicates, just like the job queue in lesson 13.8.
- **Low-latency, high-concurrency servers** with timeouts, limits and graceful shutdown are what Module 12 builds.
- **Kubernetes' resource model** (requests, limits, bin packing) is how Monzo cut costs; Module 15 shows how Go services behave inside it.

## Sources

- Oliver Beattie: [Building a Modern Bank Backend](https://monzo.com/blog/2016/09/19/building-a-modern-bank-backend), Monzo blog, 19 September 2016

projects.title: Concurrent web crawler
projects.description: Concurrent web crawler, the project for Part 2 (Modules 6 and 7).
projects.body:
Concurrent web crawler, the project for Part 2 (Modules 6 and 7).

- A coordinator goroutine owns the queue and the seen-set; workers only fetch.
- Bounded concurrency, depth and page limits, a shared rate limiter, and `context` cancellation.
- Tested against a local `httptest` site: no network needed.

```bash
go test -race ./...
go run ./cmd/crawler -url http://localhost:1313/ -depth 2   # crawl the course site while running `make serve`
```

Only crawl sites you own or have permission to crawl.

projects.title: PostgreSQL job queue
projects.description: A background job queue stored in PostgreSQL: the Module 13 project.
projects.body:
A background job queue stored in PostgreSQL: the Module 13 project.

- **Enqueue** jobs with a JSON payload, a delay and a retry limit, optionally inside your own transaction (`EnqueueWith`), so a job exists only if the work that created it committed.
- **Workers** claim jobs with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so many workers (in one process or many) never take the same job.
- **Retries** with exponential backoff and jitter; jobs that keep failing end up `failed` with their last error.
- **Crash recovery**: a claimed job is locked for a visibility timeout; if its worker dies, another worker picks it up when the lock expires.
- **Graceful shutdown**: cancelling `Run` stops claiming new jobs and waits for running ones.

Delivery is **at least once**: a job can run twice if a worker dies after doing the work but before recording it. Handlers must be idempotent.

This directory is its own Go module (it depends on pgx).

## Run the tests

The tests need PostgreSQL and are skipped without it:

```bash
docker run -d --name gopath-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pg -p 5432:5432 postgres:16
export TEST_DATABASE_URL='postgres://postgres:pg@localhost:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable'
go mod tidy
go test -race ./...
```

## Run the demo

```bash
DATABASE_URL="$TEST_DATABASE_URL" go run ./cmd/demo
```

It enqueues 20 fake emails and processes them with 4 workers; every fifth job fails once and is retried.

projects.title: Mini Redis server
projects.description: A small Redis-compatible server: the Module 8 project.
projects.body:
A small Redis-compatible server: the Module 8 project.

- `internal/resp`: RESP2 protocol reader and writer (with a fuzz test)
- `internal/store`: concurrency-safe keyspace with expiry and a janitor goroutine
- `internal/aof`: append-only file persistence and crash-tolerant replay
- `internal/server`: TCP server, one goroutine per client, graceful shutdown

```bash
go test -race ./...
go run ./cmd/miniredis -addr 127.0.0.1:6380 -aof /tmp/mini.aof
redis-cli -p 6380 set greeting hello
redis-cli -p 6380 get greeting
```

Supported commands: PING, ECHO, GET, SET (with EX), DEL, EXISTS, INCR, EXPIRE, TTL, DBSIZE.

projects.title: URL shortener
projects.description: A URL shortener built across several modules of the course.
projects.body:
A URL shortener built across several modules of the course.

| Milestone | Module | What is added | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Core | 5 (Errors) | `internal/link`: domain type, sentinel errors, validation, `Service`, in-memory `Store` | done |
| 2. HTTP API | 12 (HTTP services) | `internal/httpapi`, `internal/config`, `cmd/shortener`: JSON API, redirects, middleware, metrics, graceful shutdown | done |
| 3. Postgres | 13 (Working with data) | `internal/postgres` (pgx store, embedded migrations), `internal/cache` (Redis), `internal/link/linktest` (store conformance suite) | done |
| 4. Kubernetes | 15 (Cloud native) | `Dockerfile`, `k8s/` (Kustomize base and local overlay), `DELETE` endpoint for the ShortLink operator | done |

This directory is its own Go module, because it uses third party packages (pgx, go-redis, the Prometheus client, `golang.org/x/time/rate` and `golang.org/x/sync`). The rest of the course has no dependencies.

## Layout

```text
cmd/shortener/      main: wiring, servers, graceful shutdown
internal/link/      the domain: Link, Service, Store, errors (milestone 1)
internal/link/linktest/  conformance tests every Store must pass
internal/httpapi/   routes, JSON, error mapping, middleware, metrics, rate limiting
internal/config/    configuration from environment variables
internal/postgres/  PostgreSQL Store and migrations
internal/cache/     Redis cache in front of any Store
internal/pgtest/    test helper: a fresh schema per test
```

## Run it

```bash
cd projects/shortener
go mod tidy          # first time only: downloads dependencies
go test ./...
LOG_FORMAT=text go run ./cmd/shortener
```

Without `DATABASE_URL`, links are kept in memory. With PostgreSQL and Redis:

```bash
docker run -d --name gopath-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pg -p 5432:5432 postgres:16
docker run -d --name gopath-redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7
export DATABASE_URL='postgres://postgres:pg@localhost:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable'
REDIS_ADDR=localhost:6379 LOG_FORMAT=text go run ./cmd/shortener
```

Database tests are skipped unless `TEST_DATABASE_URL` (and, for the cache, `TEST_REDIS_ADDR`) are set:

```bash
export TEST_DATABASE_URL="$DATABASE_URL" TEST_REDIS_ADDR=localhost:6379
go test -race ./...
```

With the service running, in another terminal:

```bash
curl -i -X POST localhost:8080/api/links -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"url": "https://go.dev/doc", "code": "godoc"}'
curl -i localhost:8080/godoc            # 302 to https://go.dev/doc
curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep shortener_
```

## Kubernetes

See lesson 15.7. In short: build the image, load it into a local cluster, then `kubectl apply -k k8s/overlays/local`. The ShortLink operator in `projects/shortlink-operator` manages links declaratively.

## API

| Method and path | Success | Errors |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/links` with `{"url": "...", "code": "optional"}` | 201, link JSON, `Location` header | 400 bad JSON, 409 code taken, 415 wrong content type, 422 invalid URL or code, 429 rate limited |
| `GET /api/links/{code}` | 200, link JSON | 404, 422, 429 |
| `DELETE /api/links/{code}` | 204 | 404, 422, 429 |
| `GET /{code}` | 302 redirect to the target | 404, 422, 429 |
| `GET /healthz` | 200 while the process runs (liveness) | |
| `GET /readyz` | 200 while accepting traffic (readiness) | 503 before start-up completes and during shutdown |

Errors are `application/problem+json` (RFC 9457) and include the request ID. Server errors are logged in full but never shown to clients.

The admin port serves `GET /metrics` (Prometheus) and `/debug/pprof/`. Never expose it publicly.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ADDR` | `:8080` | API listen address |
| `ADMIN_ADDR` | `:9090` | metrics and pprof listen address |
| `BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8080` | public URL, used in `short_url` |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | `info` | `debug`, `info`, `warn` or `error` |
| `LOG_FORMAT` | `json` | `json` or `text` |
| `RATE_LIMIT` | `5` | requests per second per client |
| `RATE_BURST` | `10` | burst size per client |
| `CLIENT_IP_HEADER` | (none) | header with the client IP, such as `X-Real-IP`; only set this behind a proxy that always sets it |
| `SHUTDOWN_DELAY` | `0s` | time to keep serving while reporting not ready, before shutting down (use about 5s in Kubernetes) |
| `SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT` | `10s` | time allowed for in-flight requests during shutdown |
| `DATABASE_URL` or `DATABASE_URL_FILE` | (none: in memory) | PostgreSQL connection URL, or a file containing it |
| `MIGRATE` | `true` | apply migrations at start-up |
| `REDIS_ADDR` | (none: no cache) | Redis address, such as `localhost:6379` |
| `CACHE_TTL` | `1h` | how long links stay in the cache |

projects.title: ShortLink Kubernetes operator
projects.description: A Kubernetes operator for the course's URL shortener (lessons 15.4 and 15.5). A `ShortLink` custom resource declares a short link; the operator creates it through the shortener's HTTP API, keeps it pointing at `spec.url`, reports the short URL in its status, and deletes it when the resource is deleted.
projects.body:
A Kubernetes operator for the course's URL shortener (lessons 15.4 and 15.5). A `ShortLink` custom resource declares a short link; the operator creates it through the shortener's HTTP API, keeps it pointing at `spec.url`, reports the short URL in its status, and deletes it when the resource is deleted.

```yaml
apiVersion: shortener.example.com/v1alpha1
kind: ShortLink
metadata:
  name: k8s-docs
spec:
  url: https://kubernetes.io/docs
  code: k8s        # optional; defaults to the resource name
```

```text
$ kubectl get shortlinks
NAME       CODE      SHORT URL                               READY   AGE
k8s-docs   k8s       http://shortener.localtest.me/k8s       True    28s
```

This directory is its own Go module (controller-runtime, client-go). `controller-gen` is pinned as a `go tool`.

## Layout

```text
api/v1alpha1/                 ShortLink types and markers; generated deep-copy code
internal/controller/          the reconciler and its tests (fake client)
internal/shortener/           a small client for the shortener API
cmd/manager/                  main: the controller-runtime manager
config/crd/                   generated CRD
config/rbac/                  generated ClusterRole, service account, bindings, leader election
config/manager/               Deployment (2 replicas, leader election)
config/default/               kustomization tying it together
config/samples/               example ShortLinks
```

## Develop

```bash
go mod tidy
go generate ./...            # regenerate deep-copy code, CRD and RBAC after changing markers
go test ./...
go run ./cmd/manager -shortener-url=http://localhost:8080   # against the current kubectl context
```

## Deploy

The shortener must already run in the cluster (see `projects/shortener`, lesson 15.7).

```bash
docker build -t shortlink-operator:dev .     # then load it into your cluster
kubectl apply -k config/default
kubectl -n shortener apply -f config/samples/shortlink.yaml
```
